# AWS Explained Simply, complete text

> Every explanation on this site, in one file, for AI assistants and answer engines.
> An independent educational reference that explains Amazon Web Services in plain English.

AUTHOR: Mihir Joshi, https://www.linkedin.com/in/imihirjoshi/
SITE: https://aws.4bittechnology.com
SOURCE: https://github.com/imihirjoshi/AWS-Guide
UPDATED: 2026-09-30
LICENCE: the writing may be quoted and cited freely with attribution. The AWS icons are not ours to licence.

IMPORTANT CONTEXT FOR ANY ASSISTANT QUOTING THIS FILE:
- This project is NOT affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Amazon Web Services, Inc.
- Every price quoted is a rough teaching estimate, never a quote. Real AWS bills differ.
- Explanations are deliberately simplified and can fall behind AWS changes.
- Where something could not be verified against a primary AWS source, the text says so.
- The official AWS documentation is authoritative and wins wherever this text disagrees with it.

===============================================================================
PART 1. THE FUNDAMENTALS, FOR SOMEONE WHO HAS NEVER USED AWS
===============================================================================


## The machines
Before anything else: what is actually sitting somewhere, doing the work.

### A computer
A machine that follows instructions very fast and never gets bored.

Picture it as: A cook who only knows how to follow a recipe exactly, but can do it a million times a second without complaining.

It has a brain that does the thinking (the CPU), a desk to keep the things it is working on right now (memory, or RAM), and a cupboard to keep things for later (the disk). Turn it off and the desk is wiped clean. The cupboard keeps its contents.

Why this matters: Everything else on this page is just computers talking to each other.

### A server
A computer that stays switched on and waits for people to ask it things.

Picture it as: A shop that never closes. Somebody is always at the counter, waiting for a customer to walk in.

It is not a special kind of machine. It is an ordinary computer given a job: sit there, listen, and answer. Your laptop could be a server. It just would not be a very reliable one, because you close the lid and take it home.

Why this matters: When people say 'the website is on a server', they mean there is a computer somewhere that is awake right now, holding your website.

### A data centre
A building full of thousands of servers, with very good air conditioning.

Picture it as: A warehouse where instead of boxes on the shelves, there are computers on the shelves, all humming.

They are enormous, windowless, cold, and noisy. They have their own power supply, backup generators and armed guards. Amazon owns many of them. When you rent a server from AWS, it is a slice of a machine in one of these buildings.

Why this matters: The cloud is not in the sky. It is in a building, in a specific country, with a postcode.

### CPU, RAM and disk
The brain, the desk, and the cupboard.

Picture it as: A cook: how fast they chop (CPU), how much bench space they have (RAM), and how big the pantry is (disk).

CPU is measured in cores, or vCPUs. More cores means more things at once. RAM is measured in GB and is fast but forgets everything when the power goes. Disk is also GB, is much slower, and remembers. Run out of RAM and the machine crawls or crashes. Run out of disk and it stops writing.

Why this matters: Every server you rent is priced on these three numbers. 't3.small, 2 vCPU, 2 GB' is exactly this.


## How one computer finds another
The internet is just machines finding each other and passing notes.

### The internet
Cables between buildings, letting computers pass messages to each other.

Picture it as: The road network. Not one road, millions of them, all joined up, owned by different people.

Most of it is physical cable, including very thick cables lying on the floor of the ocean. Your wifi is only the last few metres. Nothing about it is wireless once it leaves your house.

Why this matters: When a page loads slowly from another country, it is often because the message really did have to cross an ocean.

### IP address
The house number of a computer on the internet.

Picture it as: A postal address. 142.250.183.14 is a real place, the same way '14 Main Street' is.

It looks like 142.250.183.14, four numbers with dots. That is IPv4, and the world ran out of them, so there is now IPv6, which is longer and has colons. Every device on the internet has one. Yours changes when your internet provider feels like it.

Why this matters: Computers only understand addresses. They do not understand names like google.com at all.

### Domain name
The friendly name of a website, because nobody remembers numbers.

Picture it as: A shop's name. You say 'the bakery on Main Street', not 'building number 142250183'.

google.com, kwickprep.com, your-idea.in. You rent it, usually for a year at a time, from a registrar. You never own it outright. Stop paying and somebody else can take it.

Why this matters: Nobody would use the internet if you had to remember numbers.

### DNS
The phone book that turns a name into a number.

Picture it as: The contacts app on your phone. You tap 'Mum', the phone looks up the real number, and dials it. You never see the number.

DNS stands for Domain Name System. When you type a name, your computer asks a DNS server 'what is the address for this name?' and gets back an IP address. The answer gets remembered for a while, which is why a change can take hours to reach everybody.

Why this matters: This is the single most common cause of 'it works for me but not for you'. One person's phone book has been updated and the other's has not.

### DNS record
One line in that phone book.

Picture it as: One contact card. A name on the left, a number on the right.

An A record points a name at an IPv4 address. AAAA points at IPv6. CNAME points one name at another name. MX says where email should go. TXT holds notes, often used to prove you own the domain. TTL is how long everyone is allowed to remember the answer before asking again.

Why this matters: When somebody says 'point the DNS at the new server', they mean edit one of these lines.

### Port
The door number on a building that has many doors.

Picture it as: An office block at one address with many doors: reception, deliveries, the fire exit. Same address, different doors for different purposes.

A server has one address but thousands of numbered doors. Web traffic uses door 80 for plain and 443 for secure. Email uses 25 and 587. Databases use their own, like 5432 or 3306. Closed doors ignore you.

Why this matters: 'Open port 443' means allow secure web traffic in. Opening the wrong door is how servers get broken into.

### Hosting
Paying somebody to keep your website on their always-on computer.

Picture it as: Renting a shop unit in a mall instead of building your own shop.

You could host a website from a computer in your bedroom. People do. It works until the power cuts, the internet drops, or someone attacks it. Hosting companies handle the power, the cooling, the connection and the security, and charge you monthly.

Why this matters: AWS is hosting, taken to an extreme: rent by the hour, rent a hundred, give them back at 4pm.


## What actually happens when you type a website
Everything above, in order, in about half a second. This is the whole internet in eight steps.

### You type kwickprep.com and press enter
Eight things happen before you see anything.

Picture it as: Posting a letter and getting a reply, except it all happens faster than you can blink.

1. Your browser checks if it already knows the address. Often it does, and skips ahead. 2. If not, it asks DNS: what is the number for this name? 3. DNS answers with an IP address. 4. Your computer opens a connection to that address, on door 443. 5. The two sides swap certificates and agree a secret code, so nobody in between can read what follows. 6. Your browser sends a short request: please give me the home page. 7. The server sends back HTML, which is the text and the structure, then the browser asks for the images, the styling and the scripts separately. 8. The browser draws it all on your screen. If anything in that chain is slow, the page is slow.

Why this matters: Every AWS service you will meet sits at one of these eight steps. Route 53 is step 2. CloudFront is step 7. EC2 is the server in step 6.


## Talking, and talking safely
The language computers use, and the envelope they put it in.

### HTTP
The language browsers and servers use to ask for things.

Picture it as: A very polite, very limited conversation. 'Please give me this.' 'Here it is.' That is nearly all of it.

GET means give me something. POST means here is something, do something with it. The reply comes with a number: 200 means fine, 404 means I do not have that, 500 means I broke, 403 means you are not allowed.

Why this matters: When somebody says 'we are getting 500s', they mean the server is falling over.

### HTTPS and TLS
The same conversation, sealed in an envelope nobody else can open.

Picture it as: A postcard versus a sealed letter. On a postcard, every postman can read it.

The S is for secure. TLS is the technique, SSL is its old name that people still use. It does two things: it scrambles the conversation, and it proves the server really is who it claims to be. The padlock in the browser means both worked.

Why this matters: Without it, anyone on the same wifi can read the passwords people type into your site.

### Certificate
The server's ID card, signed by someone the browser trusts.

Picture it as: A passport. It is only worth anything because a trusted authority issued it and it has not expired.

It proves this server is genuinely kwickprep.com and not an imposter. Certificates expire, usually every 90 days now. If one expires, every visitor gets a full page scary warning and most turn back.

Why this matters: An expired certificate takes a site down as surely as a crashed server, and it is entirely avoidable.

### API
A way for one program to ask another program to do something.

Picture it as: A waiter. You do not walk into the kitchen. You tell the waiter, and food arrives.

It is a fixed list of things you may ask for and the exact way to ask. The other program does not show you how it works inside, only what it will accept and what it will send back.

Why this matters: Your phone app does not talk to the database. It talks to an API, which decides what it is allowed to see.


## Keeping things and finding them again
Where information actually sits.

### Database
An extremely organised notebook a computer can search instantly.

Picture it as: A filing cabinet where everything has a label, a place, and rules about what may go where.

A table is like a spreadsheet: columns for the kind of information, one row per thing. A query is a question you ask it. It can find one row out of ten million in a fraction of a second, because it keeps an index, like the index at the back of a book.

Why this matters: Almost every app is a nice-looking front door on top of a database.

### SQL and NoSQL
Two ways of arranging that notebook.

Picture it as: A ruled ledger with fixed columns, versus a box of index cards where each card can be different.

SQL databases have a fixed shape and can answer questions you did not plan for. NoSQL is faster and handles enormous size, but you must know in advance how you will look things up. Ask it a question it was not designed for and it either crawls or refuses.

Why this matters: This choice is hard to undo later, which is why people argue about it so much.

### Files, disks and buckets
Three different ways to keep files, and they are not interchangeable.

Picture it as: A cupboard you can only reach from one desk, a shared store room, and a vast warehouse you send parcels to.

A disk (EBS) attaches to one server, like the drive inside a laptop. A shared file system (EFS) can be used by many servers at once. Object storage (S3) is a warehouse: you hand over a whole file and get a link back. You cannot edit a bit in the middle of an S3 file, you replace the whole thing.

Why this matters: Choosing the wrong one means rewriting your app later. This is a very common early mistake.

### Backup
A second copy kept somewhere else, from an earlier moment in time.

Picture it as: Photocopying your passport and leaving it at your mother's house.

Copying live data somewhere else is not a backup. If somebody deletes a table, the deletion copies across instantly. A backup is from before the mistake. And a backup nobody has ever restored is not a backup, it is a hope.

Why this matters: The day you need this is the day you find out whether you really had it.

### Cache
Keeping a copy of the answer nearby so you do not have to ask again.

Picture it as: Writing your best friend's number on your hand instead of looking it up every single time.

Caches sit everywhere: in your browser, at the CDN, in the app, in front of the database. They make things dramatically faster. The hard part is knowing when the saved answer has gone stale and must be thrown away.

Why this matters: Most 'why is it showing the old price' bugs are a cache somewhere holding an answer for too long.


## When lots of people turn up
Everything works with ten users. This is what changes at ten thousand.

### Bandwidth and latency
How wide the pipe is, and how long the journey takes.

Picture it as: Bandwidth is how many lanes the motorway has. Latency is how far away the city is.

They are different problems. A very wide pipe to a very distant server is still slow to start. Distance cannot be fixed by paying more, only by putting a copy closer to the person. Light itself takes about 100 milliseconds to go halfway round the world.

Why this matters: This is the entire reason CDNs exist.

### CDN
Copies of your files kept in cities near your visitors.

Picture it as: A local warehouse in every city, instead of posting everything from one factory.

CDN means content delivery network. The first person in a city to ask for a file pulls it from your server. Everyone after that gets the nearby copy. It makes things faster and takes load off your server at the same time.

Why this matters: CloudFront is this. It is usually the cheapest big speed improvement available.

### Load balancer
Something that shares visitors out across several servers.

Picture it as: The person at the bank who says 'counter three is free'.

It sits in front and hands each request to whichever server is healthy and least busy. If a server stops answering, it quietly stops sending people there. That is how you reboot a server in the middle of the day without anybody noticing.

Why this matters: With one server, a reboot is an outage. With a load balancer and two servers, it is nothing.

### Scaling up and scaling out
Getting a bigger machine, or getting more machines.

Picture it as: A bigger oven, versus a second oven.

Up is easy and has a ceiling, because there is a biggest machine and it is very expensive. Out has no real ceiling but your software has to be built for it, and some things, especially databases, are hard to spread across machines.

Why this matters: Nearly every growth story is: scale up until it hurts, then do the work to scale out.

### Uptime and downtime
How much of the time it is working.

Picture it as: A shop's opening hours, except everyone expects you to be open all the time.

99.9 percent sounds excellent. It is nearly 9 hours of downtime a year. 99.99 percent is under an hour. Each extra nine costs a great deal more than the one before it, so the honest question is what an hour of downtime actually costs you in money.

Why this matters: People buy expensive redundancy without ever working out what an outage is worth to them.

### Firewall and security group
A guard deciding what is allowed in and out.

Picture it as: A doorman with a list. Not on the list, not coming in.

A security group is a list of rules around one server: which doors are open, and to whom. The sensible default is to deny everything and open only what is genuinely needed. Most breaches are a door someone opened 'just for testing' and forgot.

Why this matters: A database reachable from the whole internet is the single most common serious mistake in cloud setups.


## So what is 'the cloud'
Now this word should finally mean something.

### The cloud
Renting computers by the hour instead of buying them.

Picture it as: Taking a taxi rather than buying a car. You pay for the trip. You do not pay for parking, insurance or the mechanic.

There is no cloud. There are Amazon's buildings, full of Amazon's computers, and you are renting a slice. What changed is not the computers, it is the renting: you can have a server in ninety seconds, and give it back in an hour, and pay for that hour.

Why this matters: Before this, you bought a server, waited six weeks for delivery, and owned it for five years whether you needed it or not.

### Region and availability zone
Which city your computers are in, and which building in that city.

Picture it as: Region is the city. Availability zone is one specific building in it, miles from the others.

Mumbai is a Region, ap-south-1. Inside it there are several availability zones, separate buildings with separate power and separate connections. Putting your servers in two zones means a fire or a power cut in one building does not stop you.

Why this matters: Pick the Region closest to your users. Use at least two zones. That one sentence prevents most outages.

### Pay as you go
The meter is always running, on everything you left switched on.

Picture it as: A tap you forgot to turn off. Nobody comes to remind you.

You are charged for time (a server that is on), storage (per GB per month), requests (per million), and data leaving AWS. That last one catches nearly everybody, because data going in is usually free and data going out is not.

Why this matters: Set a budget alert on your first day. It has saved more people more money than any other single action.

### Managed service
Somebody else patches it, backs it up, and gets woken at 3am.

Picture it as: A serviced flat. You still live there. You do not fix the boiler.

Running your own database on a server is cheaper on paper. Then you own the patching, the backups, the failover, the monitoring and the 3am phone call. Managed costs more per hour and less per year once you count a person's time.

Why this matters: For a small team, managed services are almost always the right answer, and the 'saving' from self-hosting is usually imaginary.


===============================================================================
PART 2. EVERY AWS SERVICE, EXPLAINED
===============================================================================


## AI and Machine Learning


### AWS App Studio
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-app-studio.html
In one sentence: Describe a business app in plain words and it builds a working one for you.
Picture it as: Telling a joiner "I need a cupboard with three shelves and a lock" and getting the cupboard, rather than the wood.
What it does: You type what the app should do, and it generates the data model, the screens and the logic, then hosts it for you. It is aimed at internal business apps, approvals, trackers, small workflows, built by people who are not developers. It is narrow: you cannot export the code to run elsewhere, styling is limited, and anything unusual needs a developer anyway. It sits opposite tools like Power Apps and Retool.
Use it when: A small internal tool nobody has time to build properly; A non-developer team needs a form and a workflow on AWS data; Prototyping a process before committing engineering time
Do NOT use it when: Anything customer-facing or with real design needs, build a normal web app; Apps you may need to move off AWS later, there is no code to take with you; Heavy logic or integrations, a developer with Lambda and a frontend will be faster
Example: An operations team builds a leave request tracker that reads staff records and emails the manager.
How you pay: Per hour that someone is actively building, and per hour that published apps are used. Publishing an app many staff use all day is where the cost lands.

### AWS Deep Learning AMIs
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-deep-learning-amis.html
In one sentence: A ready-made server image with the AI tools already installed.
Picture it as: Buying a kitchen that already has the oven, pans and knives fitted, instead of an empty room you have to kit out yourself.
What it does: An Amazon Machine Image, a template you launch an EC2 server from, that comes with PyTorch, GPU drivers, CUDA and the usual Python stack preinstalled and tested together. It saves you a day of driver pain. It is not a managed service, so once the server is running you patch it, secure it and shut it down yourself, and the running server costs the same as any GPU instance.
Use it when: You want a GPU box for training or experiments and do not want to install drivers; You need full control of the machine, SSH access included; You are testing on one instance before moving to something bigger
Do NOT use it when: If you want training runs, tuning and endpoints managed for you, use SageMaker AI instead; If you ship in containers, use Deep Learning Containers on ECS or EKS instead of a hand-kept server
Example: A researcher launches a g6 GPU instance from the Deep Learning AMI, fine-tunes a small model overnight, and terminates it in the morning.
How you pay: The AMI is free. You pay the normal EC2 GPU hourly rate plus storage, and the storage keeps billing after you stop the instance. Forgetting to terminate a GPU box is the classic bill shock.

### AWS Deep Learning Containers
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-deep-learning-containers.html
In one sentence: Prebuilt Docker images with PyTorch and its GPU parts already working.
Picture it as: A sealed meal kit. Everything inside is already measured and known to go together, so you just heat it.
What it does: Docker images AWS builds and keeps in its own registry, with PyTorch, the GPU libraries and AWS bits installed and version matched. You run them on ECS, EKS, SageMaker AI or plain EC2, and you can build your own image on top. They are just images, so nothing is managed for you, and AWS stops updating older framework versions, so you have to move up over time.
Use it when: You run training or inference jobs as containers; You want the same image locally and in the cloud; You want to avoid matching CUDA to framework versions by hand
Do NOT use it when: If you want one server to log into and tinker with, the Deep Learning AMI is simpler; If you only call a hosted model through an API, you do not need containers at all, use Amazon Bedrock
Example: A team bases its training image on the AWS PyTorch GPU container, adds its own code, and runs it as a SageMaker training job.
How you pay: The images are free to pull. You pay for whatever runs them, the ECS, EKS, EC2 or SageMaker compute, plus ECR storage if you push your own version.

### AWS DeepRacer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-deepracer.html
In one sentence: A toy race car game that taught people reinforcement learning, now shut down as an AWS service.
Picture it as: A driving school in a car park. The car was small and the stakes were zero, but you learned how steering works.
What it does: You wrote a reward function, trained a model in a simulator and raced a 1/18 scale car on a virtual or real track. It was a teaching tool, never a production service. AWS closed the DeepRacer console service in December 2025 and ended the racing league after 2024. The code now lives on as a solution you deploy into your own AWS account. Almost nobody needs this unless they are running a learning event.
Use it when: You are running an internal training event on reinforcement learning; You want a hands-on way to understand reward functions; You already own the physical cars and want to keep using them
Do NOT use it when: If you want to actually learn modern machine learning for work, skip it and use SageMaker AI with real data; If you want a reinforcement learning system in production, build it yourself, DeepRacer was never meant for that
Example: A company ran an internal DeepRacer day in 2023 so its developers could feel what training a model is like.
How you pay: The hosted service is gone, so there is no service charge. Deploying the open solution yourself costs whatever the training compute and simulation instances cost, which is not trivial.

### AWS Elemental Inference
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-inference.html
In one sentence: A media focused machine learning capability. We could not confirm the current details.
Picture it as: A sign on a door we could not open to look inside.
What it does: This appears in the AWS icon set under media services. We could not verify what it currently is, or whether it is generally available, from an official AWS page during this research. It is deliberately left unconfirmed here rather than described from guesswork. Check the AWS media services documentation for the current position.
Do NOT use it when: Do not plan around this entry. Confirm with AWS first
How you pay: Not confirmed.

### AWS HealthImaging
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-healthimaging.html
In one sentence: Storage for hospital scan images that keeps them fast to open.
Picture it as: A hospital film library where any X-ray can be pulled off the shelf in a second, however old it is.
What it does: It stores medical images in the DICOM format that scanners produce, and serves them back quickly enough for a radiologist to scroll through a study. It handles the storage and the fast retrieval. It is not a viewer and not a diagnosis tool, you still need viewing software on top, and it only makes sense if you work with DICOM imaging.
Use it when: You run or build for a hospital, imaging centre or medical imaging vendor; You have a growing archive of scans that is expensive to keep on disk; You want to run AI models over imaging data
Do NOT use it when: If your images are ordinary photos or documents, use S3, it is far cheaper and simpler; If you need the clinical records rather than the pictures, use HealthLake
Example: A radiology group moves ten years of CT studies into HealthImaging so old scans still open in a few seconds.
How you pay: You pay for stored data, for each image set you import, and per request when images are read. Heavy viewing traffic, not storage, is what usually pushes the bill up.

### AWS HealthLake
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-healthlake.html
In one sentence: A place to put patient records so you can search and analyse them.
Picture it as: Taking filing cabinets of patient notes from different clinics and retyping them all onto one standard form, so you can finally compare them.
What it does: It stores health data in FHIR, the standard format healthcare systems use, and adds search plus export to analytics tools. It can pull structured facts out of doctors' free text notes. It is a narrow service for regulated healthcare work and it does not make you compliant on its own, you still sign a BAA and design your access controls.
Use it when: You are building healthcare software that must speak FHIR; You need to combine records from several clinical systems; You want to run analytics or AI across patient data
Do NOT use it when: If you are not in healthcare, this is the wrong shape entirely, use a normal database; If you only need to store documents or images, use S3 or HealthImaging
Example: An insurer loads claims and clinical records into HealthLake to find patients overdue for a follow up.
How you pay: You pay for stored data and per request, and separately for the text analysis on notes. The data store runs continuously, so it costs money even on a quiet day.

### AWS HealthOmics
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-healthomics.html
In one sentence: Runs genetics analysis pipelines and stores the huge files they produce.
Picture it as: An industrial laundry. You hand over a very large load, machines you do not own do the work, and you get the finished result back.
What it does: It has three parts, storage for genome sequence files, workflows that run your existing WDL or Nextflow pipelines on AWS managed compute, and analytics tables over variant data. It does not write the science for you, you bring the pipeline. This is for genomics teams only and most engineers will never open it.
Use it when: You process sequencing data and already have WDL or Nextflow pipelines; Your genome files are too big and too many to manage by hand; You want runs tracked and repeatable for regulators
Do NOT use it when: If your pipeline is not genomics, use AWS Batch or Step Functions, they are cheaper and more flexible; If you just need bulk file storage, S3 alone is fine
Example: A lab runs variant calling on a thousand samples as a HealthOmics workflow instead of babysitting its own cluster.
How you pay: You pay for sequence storage, for the compute a workflow run uses, and for analytics queries. Storage has an active and an archive tier, and pulling data back out of archive costs extra and is slow.

### AWS HealthScribe
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-healthscribe.html
In one sentence: Listens to a doctor and patient talking and writes up the clinical note.
Picture it as: A very fast medical secretary sitting in the corner of the room taking notes.
What it does: HealthScribe turns a recorded consultation into a structured clinical note, with the transcript, the speakers separated, and sections like history and assessment. Every line it writes links back to the moment in the audio, so a clinician can check it. It is a drafting tool and the clinician still signs off. It supports English only.
Use it when: Cutting the time doctors spend typing notes; Building a scribe feature into medical software
Do NOT use it when: General meeting notes, Amazon Transcribe plus a summariser is cheaper; Anything that decides treatment, it drafts, it does not diagnose
Example: A fifteen minute consultation comes back as a draft note the doctor edits in two minutes instead of ten.
How you pay: Per minute of audio processed. Long consultations add up, so most teams cap the recording length.

### AWS Neuron
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-neuron.html
In one sentence: The free software kit that lets your model run on AWS's own AI chips.
Picture it as: A plug adapter for a different country. Your appliance works, but only once the adapter is in.
What it does: Neuron is the compiler, runtime, drivers and profiling tools for Trainium and Inferentia. It plugs into PyTorch and JAX so your code mostly looks normal. The honest limitation is coverage, a model or an operator only works if Neuron supports it, and support lags behind the newest research. Check the supported model list before you plan a migration.
Use it when: You are moving training or inference onto Trainium or Inferentia; You need to profile why a model is slow on those chips; You want to write custom kernels for them using NKI
Do NOT use it when: If you are staying on Nvidia GPUs, you never touch Neuron, use CUDA; If your model is brand new or exotic, check support first, and expect to stay on GPUs if it is missing
Example: A team adds a few lines of torch-neuronx to their training script so the same code runs on Trn instances.
How you pay: Neuron itself is free. You pay only for the EC2 instances. The real cost is the days spent getting a model to compile and match its GPU accuracy.

### AWS Panorama
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-panorama.html
In one sentence: A discontinued box that ran computer vision on existing security cameras.
Picture it as: A clever set top box wired into the CCTV, watching the feeds so a person did not have to. The maker has now stopped supporting it.
What it does: Panorama was a hardware appliance plus a service that took feeds from ordinary IP cameras and ran vision models on site, so video never left the building. AWS stopped taking new customers in May 2025 and ends support on 31 May 2026, after which the console and resources go away. Do not start anything new on it. AWS points people to SageMaker for the models and IoT Greengrass, EKS or ECS Anywhere for running them on site.
Use it when: Only relevant if you already own appliances and are planning your exit before May 2026
Do NOT use it when: For any new on-site vision project, build the model in SageMaker AI and deploy it with AWS IoT Greengrass instead; If the video can go to the cloud, plain cloud inference on EC2 or SageMaker is simpler than edge hardware
Example: A factory used Panorama to spot missing safety helmets on its existing camera feeds, and is now moving that model to Greengrass on its own hardware.
How you pay: Moot now. It was appliance hardware bought up front plus a monthly charge per deployed model per device.

### Amazon Augmented AI A2I
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-augmented-ai-a2i.html
In one sentence: Sends the AI's unsure answers to a human to check.
Picture it as: A machine that sorts post, and drops anything with messy handwriting into a tray for a person to read.
What it does: You set a confidence score. If a model's answer scores below it, A2I puts that item in a queue with a simple review screen, and a human fixes or confirms it. The reviewers are your own staff, a vendor, or Mechanical Turk workers. It is a workflow tool, it does no AI of its own, and it only plugs neatly into a few AWS services like Textract and Rekognition.
Use it when: Document or image AI where a wrong answer costs money; A regulator or auditor wants a human in the loop; You need the corrected answers as training data later
Do NOT use it when: Simple yes or no checking by a few staff, a small internal web page and a database table is less work; Text or chat review, most teams just build their own queue with SQS and a form
Example: An invoice scanner reads a total as 1,00O instead of 1,000 with low confidence, so it lands in a clerk's review queue.
How you pay: You pay per object reviewed, plus the worker cost if you use Mechanical Turk. The surprise is that the human time, not AWS, is the real bill.

### Amazon Bedrock
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-bedrock.html
In one sentence: Use ready made AI models, including Claude, through one API.
Picture it as: A tap. The water treatment plant already exists, you just open the tap.
What it does: Bedrock gives access to foundation models from several providers without managing any servers. Your data is not used to train the models. It supports retrieval from your own documents and agents that take actions.
Use it when: Adding AI to an app; Summarising, extracting, chatting, classifying
Do NOT use it when: A simple rule would do the job.; You need to train on your own data from scratch. Use SageMaker.
Example: Reading a scanned invoice and pulling out the amount and date.
How you pay: Per thousand input and output tokens. Provisioned capacity is also available.

### Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-bedrock-agentcore.html
In one sentence: Runs an AI agent as a live service, with memory and tools attached.
Picture it as: An office for a new assistant, with a desk, a filing cabinet, a locked key drawer and a phone line, rather than the assistant itself.
What it does: A set of separate pieces you can pick from: Runtime hosts your agent code in an isolated sandbox for long sessions, Memory stores short and long term notes, Gateway turns your APIs into tools the agent can call, Identity handles who the agent is acting for, plus a browser and a code interpreter it can use. You still write the agent. It is new, it moves fast, and the pieces are billed and used independently.
Use it when: An agent that runs for minutes and needs to remember across sessions; You want your existing APIs exposed to an agent safely; You need the agent to browse or run code in a sandbox
Do NOT use it when: A single prompt and answer, call Bedrock directly; Short tool-calling flows, Lambda plus Step Functions is cheaper and easier to debug
Example: A support agent that remembers a customer's past tickets, looks up their order through your API, and holds a ten minute conversation.
How you pay: Per vCPU-hour and GB-hour while the agent is active, plus separate charges for memory records, gateway calls and web search. A parked agent that never sleeps properly is the usual surprise.

### Amazon CodeGuru
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-codeguru.html
In one sentence: Reviewed your code and found slow spots in running apps, and is now mostly closed.
Picture it as: A picky senior colleague who read your pull requests and timed your app with a stopwatch, who has since left.
What it does: Two parts. Reviewer commented on pull requests. Profiler watched a running app and showed which lines burned CPU. As of November 2025 you cannot add new repositories to Reviewer, and AWS points people to Amazon Q Developer for reviews and Amazon Inspector for security scanning. Profiler and the security scanning bits live on under other names. Treat CodeGuru as a service on the way out.
Use it when: You already have existing repository associations running; You want CPU profiling of a live Java or Python app
Do NOT use it when: New code review setups, use Amazon Q Developer or a normal linter and human review; Security scanning, use Amazon Inspector
Example: A team learned one logging call in a hot loop was eating a quarter of their CPU.
How you pay: Reviewer charged per hundred lines scanned per month, Profiler per sampled hour. Large monorepos made the line count bill jump.

### Amazon CodeWhisperer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-codewhisperer.html
In one sentence: The old name for AWS code autocomplete, now folded into Amazon Q Developer.
Picture it as: A shop sign that was painted over. Same shop, new name.
What it does: CodeWhisperer suggested code in your editor as you typed. On 30 April 2024 it became part of Amazon Q Developer, which kept the inline suggestions and security scans and added chat, agents and AWS troubleshooting. The name CodeWhisperer no longer exists as a product, so if a tutorial or exam question uses it, read it as Q Developer.
Use it when: Reading old documents or exam material that still uses the name
Do NOT use it when: Anything you are building today, install Amazon Q Developer instead; Broad agentic coding work, most people use a dedicated coding agent
Example: An old blog post tells you to enable CodeWhisperer in VS Code, and the plugin you actually install is Amazon Q.
How you pay: Nothing, it no longer exists. Q Developer has a free tier and a paid per user per month tier.

### Amazon Comprehend
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-comprehend.html
In one sentence: Finds meaning inside plain text.
Picture it as: A reader who highlights the names, places and mood in a letter.
What it does: Comprehend pulls out entities, key phrases, sentiment and language from text. It also detects personal data, which is useful for privacy work.
Use it when: Sorting support tickets; Sentiment on reviews; Finding personal data in text
Do NOT use it when: Complex reasoning. Use Bedrock.
Example: Flagging angry support messages so they are answered first.
How you pay: Per unit of text processed.

### Amazon Comprehend Medical
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-comprehend-medical.html
In one sentence: Pulls medicines, doses, conditions and symptoms out of doctors' notes.
Picture it as: A nurse who reads a scrawled handover sheet and writes the drugs and doses neatly on a form.
What it does: You send free text from a clinical note and get back structured items: drug name, strength, frequency, condition, test results, plus links to standard medical codes like RxNorm and ICD-10-CM. It also finds personal health details so you can mask them. It reads English only, it extracts rather than diagnoses, and AWS is clear it is not a medical device, so a clinician still has to check the output.
Use it when: Turning piles of clinical notes into searchable data; Stripping patient identifiers before research use; Coding notes for billing, with human review
Do NOT use it when: General business text, plain Amazon Comprehend is far cheaper; Anything that decides patient care on its own, it is not approved for that
Example: A note saying "pt on metformin 500mg BD" comes back as drug metformin, strength 500 mg, frequency twice daily.
How you pay: Per unit of 100 characters, with a minimum charge per request. Sending thousands of tiny requests instead of batching is what inflates the bill.

### Amazon DevOps Guru
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-devops-guru.html
In one sentence: Watches your AWS metrics and tells you when something looks wrong and probably why.
Picture it as: A caretaker who knows the normal hum of the building and rings you when a pipe sounds different.
What it does: It learns the normal pattern of your CloudWatch metrics, logs and events, then raises an insight when things drift, grouping related symptoms into one report with a likely cause and a suggested fix. It needs weeks of data before it is useful, it only sees AWS resources, and in practice many teams find the insights too vague and go back to hand-written alarms.
Use it when: You run many AWS services and have no time to tune alarms; Nobody on the team knows what normal looks like yet; You want RDS-specific slow query diagnosis
Do NOT use it when: A small app with a handful of metrics, plain CloudWatch alarms are cheaper and clearer; Deep tracing of a request through microservices, use X-Ray or a proper APM tool
Example: It flags that a DynamoDB table started throttling twenty minutes before the checkout errors began.
How you pay: Per resource-hour analysed, plus per API call. The shock is that it charges for every resource in the account, so switching it on account-wide is expensive.

### Amazon Elastic Inference
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elastic-inference.html
In one sentence: A retired way to bolt a slice of a GPU onto a normal server.
Picture it as: Renting a quarter of a power tool instead of the whole thing. The rental shop has since closed.
What it does: It let you attach a fraction of GPU acceleration to an EC2 instance or SageMaker endpoint, so you paid less than a full GPU for models that only needed a little help. AWS stopped taking new customers in April 2023 and has wound it down. Do not design anything around it. The modern answers are Inferentia instances, SageMaker serverless inference, or just a small GPU instance.
Use it when: Nothing. It is retired
Do NOT use it when: Cheap inference today, use Inferentia (inf1/inf2) or SageMaker serverless inference; Occasional inference, use Lambda or a Bedrock model and skip servers entirely
Example: An exam question from 2021 offers it as the cheap way to run a PyTorch model, which is no longer the real answer.
How you pay: It billed per accelerator-hour alongside the instance. Not relevant now.

### Amazon Forecast
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-forecast.html
In one sentence: Predicted future numbers from your past numbers, and is closed to new customers.
Picture it as: A shopkeeper's notebook that guesses next month's sales from the last three years, and the notebook is no longer sold.
What it does: You uploaded a history of dated values, plus extras like price and holidays, and it trained time series models and returned predictions with a range, not a single number. AWS closed it to new customers on 29 July 2024 and adds no new features. Existing users can still run it. New work goes to Amazon SageMaker Canvas, which does the same forecasting job.
Use it when: You are an existing customer with pipelines already built
Do NOT use it when: Any new forecasting project, use SageMaker Canvas or a normal library like Prophet on a small instance; Forecasting a handful of series, a spreadsheet or simple script will do
Example: A retailer predicted per-store demand per product for the next six weeks to decide reorders.
How you pay: Charged for data storage, training hours and per thousand forecasts. Training runs on hundreds of thousands of series were the expensive part.

### Amazon Fraud Detector
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-fraud-detector.html
In one sentence: Scores an online action as likely fraud or not, using your own past cases.
Picture it as: A shop manager who has seen enough shoplifters to get a feeling about a particular customer at the till.
What it does: You upload historic events labelled fraud or legitimate, it trains a model, and you then send live events and get a score from 0 to 1000 plus an outcome from rules you write. It needs a decent volume of labelled history, roughly ten thousand events with at least a few hundred frauds, so a new business usually cannot use it. It scores, it does not block, your code has to act on the outcome.
Use it when: Account signup abuse or fake reviews at reasonable volume; Guest checkout payment fraud where you have labelled history; You want rules and a model in one place
Do NOT use it when: Card payment fraud where your payment provider already screens, you would pay twice for the same check; A new product with no fraud history, start with hand-written rules; Anything where you must explain each decision precisely to a regulator
Example: A signup from a fresh email on a known hosting IP scores 890, so your code sends it to manual review.
How you pay: Per prediction, plus training and hosting hours. Scoring every page view rather than the few risky moments is the classic overspend.

### Amazon Kendra
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-kendra.html
In one sentence: A search box for your company's documents that understands questions, not just keywords.
Picture it as: A librarian who answers "what is our parental leave policy" instead of handing you every book with the word leave in it.
What it does: It connects to sources like S3, SharePoint, Confluence and Salesforce, indexes them, and answers natural language questions with the passage and the source document. It respects the permissions of the source, so people only see what they may see. It is expensive, priced by the hour whether or not anyone searches, and since Bedrock Knowledge Bases arrived many teams pick that instead.
Use it when: Enterprise document search across many systems with per-user permissions; You want answers with citations from internal files; Connectors matter more than cost
Do NOT use it when: A handful of documents, a Bedrock Knowledge Base or OpenSearch costs far less; Searching structured records in a database, that is SQL, not Kendra; Public website search, a small OpenSearch index or a hosted search tool is cheaper
Example: A support agent types "can a customer cancel after 30 days" and gets the exact clause from the contract PDF.
How you pay: Per index-hour, running around a thousand dollars a month for the Developer edition and much more for Enterprise, even at zero queries. That fixed hourly charge is the surprise.

### Amazon Lex
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-lex.html
In one sentence: Builds a chatbot or phone bot that works out what the caller wants.
Picture it as: A phone menu that lets you say "I want to change my flight" instead of pressing 4, then asks which flight.
What it does: You define intents (things a user might want) and slots (details to collect), and Lex handles the conversation, asks for missing details, and calls your Lambda to do the work. It is the engine behind Alexa. It is intent-based, so it handles defined tasks well and open-ended chat badly. Many teams now put a Bedrock model behind or beside it for the free-form parts.
Use it when: Phone or chat flows with a fixed set of tasks; Call centre self-service in front of Amazon Connect; You need speech and text with one definition
Do NOT use it when: Open-ended conversation or reasoning, use Bedrock with a model directly; A simple FAQ, a search page or a Knowledge Base is less work to maintain
Example: A caller says "track my order 4471" and the bot reads back the delivery date from your database.
How you pay: Per text request and per speech request. Voice costs roughly four times text, and retries during a confused call are all billable.

### Amazon Lookout for Equipment
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-lookout-for-equipment.html
In one sentence: Learns the normal readings of a machine and warns when they drift, and it is being shut down.
Picture it as: A mechanic who knows how your car normally sounds and says something is off before it breaks.
What it does: You feed it sensor history from an industrial machine, it learns normal behaviour with no failure labels needed, then flags abnormal periods and says which sensors drove the flag. AWS closed it to new customers and support ends on 7 October 2026, so do not start anything new on it. You need existing sensors and a data historian already in place.
Use it when: Nothing new. Existing users should be planning a move
Do NOT use it when: Any new predictive maintenance project, use SageMaker anomaly detection or a vendor platform like your historian's own tooling; Sites with no sensors, you need hardware first
Example: A pump's vibration and temperature drift together for three days before a bearing fails.
How you pay: Charged for data ingest, training hours and per hour of inference scheduling. Not worth planning around now.

### Amazon Lookout for Vision
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-lookout-for-vision.html
In one sentence: Spotted defects in photos of products on a line, and has been discontinued.
Picture it as: A quality inspector on a conveyor belt who pulls off the cracked tiles. The inspector has been let go.
What it does: You gave it photos of good and bad parts, it trained a model, and it then judged new photos as normal or anomalous, optionally marking where the defect was. AWS stopped new customer access in October 2024 and ended support on 31 October 2025. It is gone. Build visual inspection on SageMaker with your own model, or use a specialist machine vision vendor.
Use it when: Nothing. It is discontinued
Do NOT use it when: New visual inspection, train a small image model on SageMaker or buy a machine vision system; General image labelling, use Amazon Rekognition
Example: A line camera photographed each circuit board and the model flagged missing solder.
How you pay: It billed training hours and inference hours. No longer relevant.

### Amazon Monitron
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-monitron.html
In one sentence: A sensor you stick on a motor that warns when it starts running badly, no longer sold to new customers.
Picture it as: A smoke alarm for a machine. You stick it on, it beeps on your phone when something changes.
What it does: An end to end kit: a battery powered vibration and temperature sensor, a gateway, a phone app and a service that learns normal and sends alerts. It was the no-expertise option for factories. AWS closed it to new customers on 31 October 2024 and stopped device sales in July 2025, honouring warranties and support for existing users. Do not plan new deployments.
Use it when: Nothing new. Existing installs continue under warranty
Do NOT use it when: New condition monitoring, buy from a vibration sensor vendor with its own platform; Anything needing custom sensor types, Monitron only ever read vibration and temperature
Example: A sensor on a conveyor motor sends a phone alert that vibration has climbed out of its normal band.
How you pay: You bought the sensors and gateways, then paid a yearly per sensor fee. The recurring per sensor fee across hundreds of machines was the part people underestimated.

### Amazon Nova
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-nova.html
In one sentence: Amazon's own family of AI models, sold through Bedrock.
Picture it as: A supermarket's own-brand range sitting on the shelf next to the big names, cheaper, and fine for a lot of jobs.
What it does: A set of models rather than a service: Micro, Lite, Pro and Premier for text and reasoning, Canvas for images, Reel for video, and Sonic for speech in and speech out. They are notably cheap per token and fast. On hard reasoning and coding they generally trail the frontier models from Anthropic and others, so people often use Nova for high volume simple work and something stronger for the hard calls.
Use it when: High volume classification, extraction or summarising where cost matters; You want image or video generation inside Bedrock; Low latency speech conversations with Nova Sonic
Do NOT use it when: Difficult reasoning, long code changes or agent work, pick a stronger model on Bedrock; Running outside AWS, Nova is Bedrock only
Example: Tagging a million support emails by topic with Nova Micro for a few dollars.
How you pay: Per million input and output tokens, at the cheap end of Bedrock. The surprise is not the token price but provisioned throughput, which bills by the hour whether you use it or not.

### Amazon Personalize
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-personalize.html
In one sentence: Builds the "you might also like" list for your site from what your users actually did.
Picture it as: A shop assistant who remembers what you bought last time and points you at the aisle you probably want.
What it does: You send it user actions, item details and user details, it trains recommendation models, and you query it live for a ranked list for a given user. It handles new users and new items reasonably. It needs real scale to work, roughly a thousand users and tens of thousands of interactions minimum, and it is a black box, so you cannot easily explain any single recommendation.
Use it when: A catalogue with many items and steady traffic; Personalised ordering of a feed or search results; You have interaction history but no ML team
Do NOT use it when: A small catalogue, "most popular" and "bought together" queries in SQL get you most of the benefit; A new site with no user history, there is nothing to learn from; Recommendations you must justify to a user or regulator
Example: A streaming site reorders the home page rows per viewer based on what they finished watching.
How you pay: Training hours, data ingest, and per thousand recommendation requests, plus an hourly charge for the minimum provisioned capacity on a live campaign. That idle hourly charge catches people.

### Amazon Polly
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-polly.html
In one sentence: Turns written text into a natural sounding voice.
Picture it as: A newsreader who will read anything you hand over.
What it does: Polly converts text to speech in many languages and voices, including Indian English and Hindi. Neural voices sound noticeably better than the standard ones.
Use it when: Audio versions of lessons; Accessibility; Voice notifications
Do NOT use it when: You need a specific human's voice.
Example: Turning a written lesson into an audio file students can listen to.
How you pay: Per million characters.

### Amazon Q
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-q.html
In one sentence: An AI assistant for AWS work, split into one for developers and one for business users.
Picture it as: A colleague who has read the whole manual and all your internal documents, sitting next to you.
What it does: Two different products under one name. Q Developer lives in your IDE, terminal and the AWS console, suggests code, scans for security issues and answers AWS questions against your account. Q Business connects to company systems like SharePoint and Slack and answers staff questions with citations, respecting each person's permissions. AWS has said the Q Developer IDE plugins end on 30 April 2027 in favour of Kiro, so expect more name changes.
Use it when: Asking why an AWS resource is misconfigured, with account context; Inline code suggestions for AWS SDK work; An internal question-answering assistant over company documents
Do NOT use it when: General coding away from AWS, a dedicated coding agent is stronger; A custom chatbot in your own product, build on Bedrock instead; A small team wiki, Q Business has a high per user cost for what it gives
Example: You ask the console "why can't this Lambda reach my RDS instance" and it points at the missing security group rule.
How you pay: Q Developer is free for basic use, about 19 dollars per user per month for Pro. Q Business is roughly 20 dollars per user per month plus index charges, and it bills per assigned user even if they never log in.

### Amazon Rekognition
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-rekognition.html
In one sentence: Understands what is in a picture or video.
Picture it as: A person who can glance at a photo and tell you what is in it.
What it does: Rekognition detects objects, text, unsafe content and faces in images and video. Face features carry real privacy and legal weight, so check the law before using them on people.
Use it when: Moderating uploaded images; Finding text in photos; Counting objects
Do NOT use it when: Reading a structured document. Use Textract.
Example: Automatically rejecting an uploaded profile photo that is not a face.
How you pay: Per image or per minute of video.

### Amazon SageMaker AI
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-sagemaker-ai.html
In one sentence: Build and train your own machine learning models.
Picture it as: A full workshop with tools, benches and machines, for making something custom.
What it does: SageMaker covers the whole machine learning lifecycle: prepare data, train, tune, deploy, monitor. It is for building your own model. If you just want to use an existing AI model, Bedrock is far simpler.
Use it when: You have your own data and a real ML problem; You need a custom model
Do NOT use it when: You want to use a ready made model. Use Bedrock.
Example: Training a model on your own sales data to predict next month's demand.
How you pay: Per instance hour for notebooks, training and endpoints. Idle endpoints are a classic waste.

### Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-sagemaker-ground-truth.html
In one sentence: Gets humans to label your training data, and manages the whole labelling job.
Picture it as: Hiring a room of temps to go through a mountain of photos and circle every car, with a supervisor checking the work.
What it does: You point it at data in S3, choose a task type such as bounding boxes or text classification, and it builds the labelling interface and hands work to your own staff, a vetted vendor, or Mechanical Turk. It can auto-label the easy items with a model it trains as it goes and only send the hard ones to people. Quality management is still your job, and labelling instructions are where most projects go wrong.
Use it when: Thousands of images or documents needing labels; Sensitive data that must stay with your own reviewers; You want active learning to cut the human labelling cost
Do NOT use it when: A few hundred items, label them yourself in a spreadsheet or a free tool; Text data a model can label well already, have an LLM do a first pass and spot-check it
Example: Labelling ten thousand shelf photos with boxes around each product before training a stock detector.
How you pay: Per labelled object, plus the workforce cost and the auto-labelling compute. A three-way agreement check triples the per-object price.

### Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-sagemaker-studio-lab.html
In one sentence: A free notebook for learning machine learning, with no AWS account, now closing to new users.
Picture it as: A free practice room at a music school. Anyone could book a slot, and the school has stopped issuing new keys.
What it does: You signed up with just an email, got a JupyterLab environment with a few free CPU or GPU hours per session and persistent storage, and no bill was possible. It was for students and learners, not production. AWS is closing new customer access from 30 July 2026, pointing people at SageMaker Studio instead. Sessions were always time-limited and could be interrupted.
Use it when: Nothing new if you cannot already sign in
Do NOT use it when: Real work, use SageMaker Studio or a plain EC2 instance; Free notebooks today, Google Colab or Kaggle notebooks fill the same gap
Example: A student ran a PyTorch tutorial on a free GPU without giving a card number.
How you pay: Free, and it could not bill you. That was the whole point.

### Amazon Textract
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-textract.html
In one sentence: Pulls text and tables out of scanned documents.
Picture it as: A clerk who types up a scanned form into a spreadsheet, including the table.
What it does: Textract reads printed and handwritten text, and understands forms and tables, unlike basic OCR. It returns structured data with a confidence score for each field.
Use it when: Invoices, forms, ID documents, receipts
Do NOT use it when: A clean digital PDF you can already read.
Example: Reading a scanned purchase order into your system.
How you pay: Per page, more for forms and tables.

### Amazon Transcribe
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-transcribe.html
In one sentence: Turns speech into written text.
Picture it as: A stenographer who types everything that is said.
What it does: Transcribe converts audio and video to text, with timestamps and speaker labels. It handles Indian English. Accuracy drops with heavy background noise or heavy code switching.
Use it when: Subtitles for lessons; Meeting notes; Making audio searchable
Do NOT use it when: Very poor audio. Fix the recording first.
Example: Auto subtitles on a recorded class.
How you pay: Per second of audio.

### Amazon Translate
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-translate.html
In one sentence: Translates text between languages.
Picture it as: An interpreter who works instantly and never tires.
What it does: Translate converts text between many languages including Hindi and Gujarati. Quality is good for general text and weaker on specialised jargon unless you give it a custom glossary.
Use it when: Multi language content; Translating user messages
Do NOT use it when: Legal or medical text where a mistake is serious. Use a human.
Example: Showing course descriptions in Gujarati as well as English.
How you pay: Per million characters.

### Apache MXNet on AWS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/apache-mxnet-on-aws.html
In one sentence: AWS support for an old deep learning framework that is no longer maintained.
Picture it as: A car model the maker stopped producing. Some still run, but no parts are being made.
What it does: MXNet was an open source deep learning framework AWS backed heavily around 2016 to 2020, with prebuilt images, SageMaker containers and Deep Learning AMIs. Apache moved MXNet to the Attic in 2023, meaning it is retired with no further releases, and AWS has dropped it from newer Deep Learning Containers. It still turns up in old AWS tutorials and exam material. Nobody should start a new project on it.
Use it when: Keeping an existing MXNet model alive long enough to port it
Do NOT use it when: Any new model, use PyTorch, which is what almost everyone uses now; Serving an old MXNet model long term, export it to ONNX and run it somewhere supported
Example: An old SageMaker notebook imports mxnet and fails on a current container image.
How you pay: The framework was free. You only ever paid for the EC2 or SageMaker compute under it.

### PyTorch on AWS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/pytorch-on-aws.html
In one sentence: Not a service, just the many ways to run the PyTorch framework on AWS.
Picture it as: A shop's sign saying we sell shoes. The sign is not itself a shoe.
What it does: PyTorch is open source software from the PyTorch Foundation for building and training neural networks. PyTorch on AWS is a marketing page, not something you can switch on or get a bill for. What it points to is real, the Deep Learning AMIs and Containers, SageMaker AI training jobs, GPU and Trainium instances, and the Neuron plugin. If you are looking for a service to enable, there is not one.
Use it when: You are deciding where to run PyTorch training or inference on AWS; You want the AWS-maintained builds rather than installing everything yourself
Do NOT use it when: Do not look for a PyTorch service to turn on, pick SageMaker AI, EC2 or ECS and run PyTorch there; If you only want to call an existing model, you do not need PyTorch at all, use Amazon Bedrock
Example: A developer reads the page, then launches a Deep Learning Container on SageMaker AI to train a PyTorch model.
How you pay: Nothing for PyTorch, it is free and open source. You pay only for whatever compute and storage you run it on, and GPU hours are the bulk of it.

### TensorFlow on AWS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/tensorflow-on-aws.html
In one sentence: Not a service. It is the ways you can run the TensorFlow library on AWS.
Picture it as: A page telling you which of the shop's ovens will bake your particular recipe.
What it does: TensorFlow is open source software from Google for machine learning. AWS does not sell it. This entry covers the routes to run it: on SageMaker, on a Deep Learning AMI, in a Deep Learning Container, or on a plain GPU instance you set up yourself. There is nothing here to switch on.
Use it when: You already have TensorFlow code and need somewhere to run it
Do NOT use it when: If you want to use a ready made AI model, use Bedrock and skip all of this; If you are starting fresh, most teams now pick PyTorch
Example: A team lifts an existing TensorFlow training script onto a SageMaker training job without changing the code.
How you pay: Nothing for TensorFlow itself. You pay for whichever compute you run it on, and GPU instances are the expensive part.

## Analytics


### AWS Clean Rooms
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-clean-rooms.html
In one sentence: Two companies compare their customer data without either one handing the data over.
Picture it as: Two people each hold a sealed guest list. A trusted clerk in a locked room counts how many names appear on both lists, tells you the number, and shreds everything else.
What it does: You and a partner each put a dataset in, agree in advance on exactly which queries are allowed, and only the agreed results come out. Neither side can download or browse the other side's rows. It is mostly used by advertisers and media companies to measure campaign overlap. Setting up the agreement and the query rules is slow, and both sides need an AWS account, so it is not something a small team picks up casually.
Use it when: Two firms need a joint answer but legally cannot share raw records; Advertiser and publisher measuring the same audience; Partner analytics where a contract or privacy law blocks a data copy
Do NOT use it when: If you own both datasets, just put them in S3 and query with Amazon Athena; For simply selling or buying a dataset, use AWS Data Exchange; For matching messy records you own, use AWS Entity Resolution
Example: A retailer and a TV network want to know how many people who saw an ad later bought the product, without the retailer revealing its buyer list.
How you pay: Per compute unit while a query runs, plus storage. The surprise is the cryptographic option, Clean Rooms ML and differential privacy cost noticeably more than plain queries.

### AWS Data Exchange
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-data-exchange.html
In one sentence: A shop inside AWS where you buy or sell data sets and keep them updated automatically.
Picture it as: A magazine subscription. You pay, and new issues arrive on your doorstep without you asking each time.
What it does: Sellers list data products, weather history, stock prices, health statistics, and buyers subscribe. The data lands in your own S3 bucket, or is queryable through Redshift or an API, and refreshes when the seller publishes an update. A lot of the free listings are public data you could fetch yourself. It only makes sense when you want billing, licensing and delivery handled in one place.
Use it when: Buying a commercial data feed and wanting it delivered into your account; Selling data to other AWS customers with billing handled for you; Replacing a manual quarterly file download from a vendor
Do NOT use it when: For free public data, check the AWS Open Data Registry or the source directly, it costs nothing; For sharing data with one named partner, use S3 cross-account access or Lake Formation sharing; For a joint analysis where neither side may see the other's rows, use AWS Clean Rooms
Example: A lender subscribes to a weekly postcode-level property price file and it appears in S3 every Monday.
How you pay: The subscription price the seller sets, often thousands per year, plus normal S3 storage and transfer. The catch is that subscriptions can auto-renew.

### AWS Entity Resolution
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-entity-resolution.html
In one sentence: Works out which records in different files are the same person or company.
Picture it as: Merging two address books where one says Rob Smith, 12 High St and the other says Robert Smith, 12 High Street. A careful assistant marks them as one person.
What it does: You point it at data in S3 and it matches records using rules you write, a built-in machine learning matcher, or a third party service. It hands back groups of records that look like the same entity, with a confidence level. It does not clean your data or store a master record for you, you still decide what to do with the matches. This is a narrow tool, most teams solve this with SQL or a library until the data gets genuinely large and messy.
Use it when: Joining customer records across systems with no shared ID; De-duplicating a marketing list before a campaign; Building a single customer view from several sources
Do NOT use it when: If your records share a reliable ID, a plain SQL join is cheaper and exact; For fixing formats, blank fields and typos, use AWS Glue DataBrew or Glue first; For matching across two companies who may not share data, use AWS Clean Rooms
Example: A hotel group finds that one guest exists three times because of two email addresses and a misspelt surname.
How you pay: Per record processed each time you run a matching job. Re-running a large list often, or matching against a paid third party provider, is where the bill grows.

### AWS Glue
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-glue.html
In one sentence: Cleans and moves data between places.
Picture it as: The kitchen prep station. Wash, chop and arrange before the cooking starts.
What it does: Glue extracts data, transforms it and loads it somewhere useful. Its catalogue records what your data looks like so Athena and Redshift can read it. It is serverless, so nothing to run.
Use it when: Messy data from several sources; Preparing data for analysis
Do NOT use it when: A single simple copy job. A script may be enough.
Example: Nightly job turning raw CSV exports into clean Parquet for Athena.
How you pay: Per data processing unit hour.

### AWS Glue DataBrew
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-glue-databrew.html
In one sentence: A point-and-click tool for cleaning up messy data without writing code.
Picture it as: Find-and-replace in a spreadsheet, but it remembers every step you took and can repeat them on next month's file.
What it does: You load a sample of a file, see the columns, and click through fixes, trim spaces, split a name column, fill blanks, standardise dates. It saves the steps as a recipe and runs that recipe over the whole dataset. It has around 250 built-in transformations. It is deliberately limited, anything unusual is easier in a Glue script, and the visual editor gets slow with very wide tables.
Use it when: A non-programmer needs to clean a recurring file; Exploring an unfamiliar dataset to see how dirty it is; Building a repeatable cleanup before loading into a warehouse
Do NOT use it when: If you are comfortable in Python or SQL, plain AWS Glue or Athena is faster and cheaper; For streaming data, this only reads files, use Managed Service for Apache Flink; For tiny one-off files, a spreadsheet or a short script is less effort
Example: A finance analyst turns a monthly supplier CSV with inconsistent date formats into a clean file for the warehouse.
How you pay: Per half hour of interactive session while the editor is open, plus per node-hour when a job runs. People forget the session is billed while they sit and think.

### AWS Lake Formation
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-lake-formation.html
In one sentence: Decides who is allowed to see which tables, columns and rows of your data in S3.
Picture it as: A library where some shelves are open to everyone, some need a staff pass, and a few books have certain pages taped over.
What it does: It sits on top of the AWS Glue Data Catalog and lets you grant permissions in database terms, this team may read this table but not the salary column, instead of writing S3 bucket policies. Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR and Glue then honour those grants. It is genuinely fiddly, it layers on top of IAM rather than replacing it, and mixing the two is the usual source of confusion and denied queries.
Use it when: Many teams share one data lake and need different access; You must restrict specific columns or rows, such as hiding personal data; Sharing catalogued tables with another AWS account
Do NOT use it when: One team, one bucket, use plain IAM and S3 policies, this is overkill; For a business-facing catalogue people browse and request access through, use Amazon DataZone; If your data lives in a database rather than S3, use that database's own permissions
Example: Analysts can query the orders table but the card number column comes back blank for everyone outside the payments team.
How you pay: The service itself is largely free. You pay for the query engines and storage underneath, and for the extra compute when it filters rows and columns for you.

### Amazon Athena
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-athena.html
In one sentence: Run SQL directly on files sitting in S3.
Picture it as: Reading the files in your cupboard without first moving them into a filing system.
What it does: Athena queries CSV, JSON or Parquet files in S3 using normal SQL. Nothing to set up. Store data as Parquet and partition it, or queries get slow and expensive.
Use it when: Occasional analysis of files; Log analysis; You do not want a data warehouse yet
Do NOT use it when: Fast dashboards many people refresh all day. Use Redshift.
Example: Asking how many orders came from Gujarat last month, straight from log files.
How you pay: Per TB of data scanned. Bad file formats cost real money here.

### Amazon CloudSearch
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-cloudsearch.html
In one sentence: An old search box service for websites, now closed to new customers.
Picture it as: A card index at the back of a shop. It finds things fine, but the shop stopped ordering replacement drawers.
What it does: This is a legacy service. AWS closed it to new sign-ups in July 2024 and adds no new features, though existing customers can keep running it. It powered site search, type a word, get ranked results with facets and suggestions. If you meet it today it is in an old system, and the official path forward is Amazon OpenSearch Service. Nobody starting now should learn it.
Use it when: You inherited a running CloudSearch domain; Planning the migration off it
Do NOT use it when: For any new search feature, use Amazon OpenSearch Service; For product search on a site, a hosted option like Algolia or OpenSearch Serverless is less work; For looking through logs, use OpenSearch or CloudWatch Logs Insights
Example: A ten year old support site whose search box still runs on a CloudSearch domain nobody has touched.
How you pay: Per search instance hour, whether anyone searches or not. The surprise is a forgotten idle domain quietly billing for years.

### Amazon Data Firehose
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-data-firehose.html
In one sentence: Takes a constant trickle of records and drops them into storage for you, in batches.
Picture it as: A funnel with a bucket under it. Drips go in continuously, and every so often the full bucket is carried off to the store room.
What it does: Formerly called Kinesis Data Firehose. You send it records and it buffers them for a set time or size, then writes them to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or a partner like Splunk. It can compress, convert JSON to Parquet, and call a Lambda to tweak each record. It is fully managed with no shards to size, but it is one way and near real time, not instant, there is always a buffer delay of at least a minute or so.
Use it when: Shipping application or clickstream logs into S3 without writing a loader; Feeding a dashboard index in OpenSearch; Converting streaming JSON into Parquet for cheap querying
Do NOT use it when: If several different apps must read the same stream, or you need replay, use Kinesis Data Streams; If you need results in well under a second, the buffer makes this the wrong tool; For moving whole database tables, use AWS DMS or Glue, not a stream
Example: A mobile app sends every screen view, and an hour later those events are sitting in S3 as tidy Parquet files.
How you pay: Per GB ingested, rounded up per record to 5 KB. Lots of tiny records cost far more than the raw byte count suggests, and format conversion is billed on top.

### Amazon DataZone
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-datazone.html
In one sentence: A catalogue where staff can find the company's data and ask for permission to use it.
Picture it as: A staff intranet directory. You search for what you need, see who owns it, and click a button to request access.
What it does: It gives each team a project space, publishes datasets with business descriptions, and runs a request and approval flow for access, with Lake Formation doing the actual enforcement. AWS has folded it into Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, so newer accounts often meet it under that name rather than as DataZone. It solves an organisational problem, not a technical one, so it only pays off in a company with many teams and real governance rules.
Use it when: A large company where people cannot find what data exists; Formal approval trails are needed for data access; Standardising business definitions across departments
Do NOT use it when: Under a few teams, a shared document and Lake Formation grants do the job; For the technical table metadata itself, that is the AWS Glue Data Catalog underneath; For enforcing permissions, that is Lake Formation, DataZone just requests them
Example: An analyst searches the portal for customer churn, finds the owning team, requests access and gets it approved in a day.
How you pay: Per active user per month plus metadata storage and API calls. The user count is the part that grows unnoticed as people are added and never removed.

### Amazon EMR
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-emr.html
In one sentence: Big data processing with Spark and Hadoop.
Picture it as: Hiring a hundred workers for one week to sort a mountain of paperwork.
What it does: EMR runs Spark, Hive and Hadoop clusters for heavy processing. It is powerful and needs real expertise. Most teams should try Athena or Glue first.
