Use it when: Terabytes of data; You already have Spark jobs
Do NOT use it when: Anything Athena can answer.
Example: Reprocessing five years of raw logs in one run.
How you pay: Per instance hour plus an EMR fee.

### Amazon FinSpace
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-finspace.html
In one sentence: A data store built for finance firms, now being shut down.
Picture it as: A specialist trading-floor filing room. Useful to a handful of banks, and the landlord has given notice.
What it does: AWS has ended support for Amazon FinSpace, effective 7 October 2026, and stopped taking new customers a year earlier. It stored and analysed financial time series data, with a Managed kdb Insights option for firms already using the kdb+ database. It was always a niche service for capital markets. Unless you work at a hedge fund or bank that already runs it and is migrating off, you can safely ignore it.
Use it when: You already run FinSpace and must plan the exit before October 2026; Understanding an existing kdb+ workload in AWS
Do NOT use it when: For time series data generally, use Amazon Timestream or Parquet in S3 with Athena; For a normal analytics warehouse, use Amazon Redshift; Do not start anything new here, the service is ending
Example: A trading desk holding years of tick data in FinSpace now has to move it to S3 and rebuild the queries.
How you pay: Per environment hour plus storage, and it was expensive. Migration effort before the end date is the real cost now.

### Amazon Kinesis
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-kinesis.html
In one sentence: Handles data that never stops arriving.
Picture it as: A conveyor belt running all day. You take things off as they pass.
What it does: Kinesis takes continuous streams of events and lets several consumers read them in order. Unlike a queue, data stays for a set window so more than one reader can process it.
Use it when: Clickstreams, sensor data, live logs; Real time dashboards
Do NOT use it when: A handful of events per day. Use SQS or EventBridge.
Example: Every page view on a site, flowing in live for a real time counter.
How you pay: Per shard hour, or per GB with on demand.

### Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-kinesis-data-streams.html
In one sentence: A pipe that holds a stream of events for a while so several programs can read them.
Picture it as: A conveyor belt past several workstations. Each worker reads items as they pass, at their own speed, and the belt keeps them for a day before they fall off the end.
What it does: Producers write records, consumers read them independently, and each keeps its own place in the stream. Records stay for 24 hours by default and up to a year if you pay for it, so you can replay. Order is guaranteed only within a shard, not across the whole stream, which is the thing people get wrong. You either manage shard counts yourself, provisioned mode, or let it scale on demand.
Use it when: Several different systems need the same live event feed; You need to replay recent events after fixing a bug; Ordering matters per user or per device
Do NOT use it when: If you just want events landing in S3, use Amazon Data Firehose, far less work; For a work queue where each message is handled once and then deleted, use Amazon SQS; If you need Kafka APIs or existing Kafka tooling, use Amazon MSK
Example: Every card swipe goes into a stream, read at once by the fraud checker, the ledger, and the analytics loader.
How you pay: Provisioned mode bills per shard hour whether data flows or not, plus per record unit. On-demand is simpler but costs several times more per GB, and long retention adds another charge.

### Amazon Kinesis Video Streams
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-kinesis-video-streams.html
In one sentence: It takes video from cameras and stores it so software can watch it back or analyse it.
Picture it as: A CCTV recorder in a shop back office, except the tape room is rented and never runs out.
What it does: Kinesis Video Streams ingests video from many devices, timestamps it, keeps it for as long as you set, and lets programs read it frame by frame for machine learning or playback. It also has a WebRTC mode for live two way viewing of a camera. It is a pipe and a recorder for machines, not a streaming service for an audience; there is no encoding, packaging or player for viewers.
Use it when: Fleets of cameras, doorbells, dashcams or drones; Feeding video into machine learning such as Rekognition; Letting an app view a camera live from anywhere
Do NOT use it when: Streaming to an audience, use IVS or MediaLive; Storing a handful of finished video files, use S3; Simple motion clips from one camera, an off the shelf camera service is far cheaper
Example: A logistics firm streams dashcam footage from its trucks and runs automatic checks on hard braking events.
How you pay: Per gigabyte ingested, per gigabyte stored per month and per gigabyte consumed. Long retention across many cameras is what makes the bill climb.

### Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-managed-service-for-apache-flink.html
In one sentence: Runs code that does sums over a live stream of events, like a running total per minute.
Picture it as: A shop assistant with a tally counter, keeping a rolling count of customers per hour rather than counting at closing time.
What it does: This was renamed from Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics in 2023. It runs Apache Flink applications, in Java, Scala, Python or SQL, and handles the servers, checkpoints and restarts. Flink is good at windows, counting events per five minutes, and at joining two streams. It is also genuinely hard, the concepts of state, watermarks and late data take real learning, and the service is expensive to leave running.
Use it when: Continuous aggregations, averages or counts over a live stream; Detecting a pattern across events, such as three failures in a minute; Joining two streams as they arrive
Do NOT use it when: For simple per-record work, a Lambda on the stream is far cheaper and simpler; If a five minute delay is fine, land the data with Firehose and query with Athena; For plain delivery with no computation, use Amazon Data Firehose
Example: A delivery app keeps a live count of orders per city per minute and raises an alert when one city stalls.
How you pay: Per Kinesis Processing Unit hour, and the application runs continuously, so you pay around the clock. Durable state storage and the mandatory extra unit for orchestration catch people out.

### Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-managed-streaming-for-apache-kafka.html
In one sentence: AWS runs Apache Kafka for you so you do not have to babysit the servers.
Picture it as: Hiring a managed office building instead of buying one. Same offices, someone else fixes the boiler.
What it does: Kafka is the industry standard event log. MSK runs the brokers, patching and monitoring, in two forms, provisioned, where you pick broker sizes, and Serverless, which scales itself. It is real Kafka, so your existing clients, Connect plugins and tools work unchanged. Note that AWS manages the infrastructure, not your topics, partitions or consumer lag, which are still your job and still the usual source of pain.
Use it when: You already use Kafka and want to stop running brokers; You need Kafka-only features such as Connect, compaction or exactly-once semantics; Moving an on-premises Kafka estate to AWS
Do NOT use it when: Starting fresh on AWS with no Kafka history, Kinesis Data Streams is simpler and cheaper to run; For a simple task queue, use Amazon SQS; For fan-out notifications, use Amazon SNS or EventBridge
Example: A retailer lifts its on-premises Kafka cluster into AWS and its dozens of existing producers keep working untouched.
How you pay: Per broker hour plus storage, billed continuously, and a small cluster across three zones costs real money every month even when idle. Cross-zone data transfer is the line people do not expect.

### Amazon OpenSearch Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-opensearch-service.html
In one sentence: A search engine you can point at your logs or your website content.
Picture it as: The index at the back of a book, rebuilt automatically every time a page changes.
What it does: It runs OpenSearch, the open source fork of Elasticsearch, and gives you full text search, filters, dashboards and vector search for AI features. It is very commonly used for log search. Two flavours exist, managed clusters, where you size and pay for nodes, and Serverless, which scales itself but costs more at small scale. It is not a database, do not treat it as your only copy of the data, reindexing from a real source is a normal part of running it.
Use it when: Searching logs across many services; A search box over products, documents or articles; Vector or semantic search for a retrieval AI feature
Do NOT use it when: For occasional queries over files in S3, Athena is much cheaper than a running cluster; As the primary store for your records, use RDS or DynamoDB and index into OpenSearch; For simple metric alarms, CloudWatch is enough
Example: An engineer types an error message and finds every occurrence across twenty services in the last week.
How you pay: Per instance hour plus storage, running all the time. The classic surprise is Serverless, which has a minimum capacity floor that costs a few hundred dollars a month even with no traffic.

### Amazon Redshift
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-redshift.html
In one sentence: A warehouse built for asking big questions of big data.
Picture it as: A library with a proper index, built for research rather than for borrowing one book.
What it does: Redshift is a data warehouse. It answers analytical queries over billions of rows fast. It is not for running your app. You load data into it from S3 or your database.
Use it when: Business intelligence dashboards; Reporting across years of data
Do NOT use it when: The live database behind your app; Small data. Athena is cheaper.
Example: A dashboard showing revenue by city by month across four years.
How you pay: Per node hour, or per unit with Serverless.

### Amazon SageMaker
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-sagemaker.html
In one sentence: The place to build, train and run your own machine learning models on AWS.
Picture it as: A fully equipped workshop you rent by the hour, with tools, benches and a delivery van, instead of building in your garage.
What it does: A large umbrella of tools, not one thing: notebooks for experimenting, managed training jobs on rented GPUs, endpoints that host a trained model behind an API, plus pipelines, a feature store and a model registry. Confusingly, it now also covers Canvas for no-code models and a unified Studio that includes data and analytics tools. You need to know some ML. It gives you infrastructure, not answers.
Use it when: Training or fine-tuning your own model; Hosting a model you already have behind an API; Team workflows where experiments and models must be tracked
Do NOT use it when: Using an existing large language model, call Bedrock and skip all of this; Common tasks like text or image recognition, the ready-made AI services are far less work; A one-off experiment, a single EC2 GPU instance or Colab is simpler and cheaper
Example: Fine-tuning a model on your own product photos, then hosting it as an endpoint your app calls.
How you pay: Per instance-hour for notebooks, training and endpoints, at a premium over raw EC2. The classic bill shock is a notebook or endpoint left running all month doing nothing.

## Application Integration


### AWS AppSync
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-appsync.html
In one sentence: A managed GraphQL API.
Picture it as: One waiter who brings exactly the dishes you asked for, in one trip.
What it does: AppSync serves a GraphQL API backed by DynamoDB, Lambda or your own database. It supports real time subscriptions and offline sync, which suits mobile apps.
Use it when: You use GraphQL; Real time updates; Mobile apps that go offline
Do NOT use it when: You are happy with REST. API Gateway is simpler.
Example: A chat screen that updates live without polling.
How you pay: Per million queries, plus real time minutes.

### AWS B2B Data Interchange
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-b2b-data-interchange.html
In one sentence: It turns the old-fashioned trading files big companies exchange into JSON your software can read, and back again.
Picture it as: A translator between two companies who insist on writing to each other in a 1980s telex format.
What it does: It handles EDI, the standard format retailers, logistics firms and hospitals use for purchase orders and invoices. You define trading partners and mapping templates, and it converts X12 EDI into JSON or XML on the way in, and back to EDI on the way out. It supports X12, so EDIFACT and HL7 users are mostly out of luck. Only relevant if a partner forces EDI on you.
Use it when: A large retailer will only send you orders as X12 EDI; Replacing an ageing in-house EDI translator; You already handle files in S3 and want the parsing managed
Do NOT use it when: Nobody is asking you for EDI, then you do not need it, use a normal API; You need EDIFACT or HL7 or full partner communications with AS2, a specialist EDI vendor covers more
Example: A supplier receives an 850 purchase order from a supermarket chain and it arrives in their order system as plain JSON.
How you pay: Per transaction processed plus a small charge per active trading partner. Low volumes are cheap, so the real cost is the mapping setup work.

### AWS Express Workflows
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-express-workflows.html
In one sentence: A fast, cheap mode of AWS Step Functions for very high volume, short jobs.
Picture it as: A quick checkout lane at the shop. It moves a lot of people fast, but it is not a different shop.
What it does: This is not a separate AWS service. Express Workflows are one of the two workflow types inside AWS Step Functions. When you create a state machine you pick Standard or Express, and you cannot change it later. Express runs for up to five minutes, has no limit on state transition rate, and is priced by the number of runs, how long they take, and the memory used. Standard runs up to one year and is priced per state transition. Express does not keep an execution history of its own, so you must turn on Amazon CloudWatch Logs to see what happened. Express is at-least-once for the async kind, so a run can happen more than once. The sync kind is at-most-once and returns the result to the caller. Because of this, Express suits steps that are safe to repeat, like writing a record to Amazon DynamoDB. Standard is exactly-once and suits steps that must not repeat, like taking a payment.
Use it when: High volume event processing, like IoT or streaming data, where each run finishes in seconds; Short data transform steps that are safe to run twice; A small chain of steps behind an API call, using the sync mode, so the caller gets the answer back; Cutting Step Functions cost when you run millions of short workflows
Do NOT use it when: Do not use it for work that takes more than five minutes. Use a Standard workflow.; Do not use it for anything that must run exactly once, like charging a card. Use a Standard workflow.; Do not use it if you need human approval steps or long waits. Express does not support the callback or job-run patterns.; Do not use it if you need Distributed Map or Activities. Those are Standard only.; Do not go looking for it as a product to sign up for. You get it by choosing the type when you make a Step Functions state machine.
Example: A sensor sends readings every second. An Express workflow cleans each reading, checks it against a rule, and writes it to DynamoDB. Millions run a day and each takes under a second.
How you pay: You pay per run, plus the run time and the memory it used. There is no charge per step, unlike Standard workflows. Logs sent to CloudWatch cost extra. Check the Step Functions pricing page for current rates.

### AWS Step Functions
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-step-functions.html
In one sentence: Draws your multi step process as a flowchart that actually runs.
Picture it as: A checklist that ticks itself, remembers where it stopped, and retries the step that failed.
What it does: Step Functions coordinates several Lambdas or services in order, with branches, retries and waits. It remembers state, so a long process survives failures. You can see exactly which step failed.
Use it when: A process with several steps; Steps that must retry; Anything that takes minutes or days
Do NOT use it when: A single function call.
Example: Order, then payment, then invoice, then email, with a retry if payment times out.
How you pay: Per state transition. The Express type is cheaper for high volume.

### Amazon AppFlow
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-appflow.html
In one sentence: A managed way to move data between business apps like Salesforce or SAP and AWS, without writing the plumbing.
Picture it as: A courier between two offices that do not speak the same language. You say what to send and how often, and it goes.
What it does: Amazon AppFlow is a real AWS service. It copies data between software as a service apps and AWS. On one side you have apps like Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Slack or Zendesk. On the other side you have AWS stores like Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. You set up a flow: pick the source, pick the target, map the fields, and pick when it runs. It can run on a schedule, on an event in the source app, or when you press run. It can filter rows, mask or drop fields, and combine data before it lands. Traffic can stay off the public internet using AWS PrivateLink. You do not build or run any connector code yourself.
Use it when: Pulling Salesforce or SAP records into Amazon S3 for reporting; Feeding SaaS data into a data lake or warehouse on a schedule; Pushing AWS data back out into a business app so sales or support teams see it; Small to medium data syncs where you do not want to maintain custom API code
Do NOT use it when: Not for moving data between AWS databases. AWS Database Migration Service or AWS Glue fit better.; Not for app to app data that is already in your own systems and needs heavy transformation. AWS Glue gives more control.; Not for real time streaming. AppFlow runs flows, it is not a stream.; Not useful if your source app has no AppFlow connector. Check the supported list first, or write your own integration.; If you need complex joins or business logic in the middle, do that after landing the data, not in AppFlow.
Example: A company copies new Salesforce opportunities into Amazon S3 every hour, then reports on them in Amazon Athena next to their billing data.
How you pay: You pay per flow run, plus per GB of data processed. Prices differ by connector type. There is no monthly fee for keeping a flow that does not run. Check the AppFlow pricing page.

### Amazon EventBridge
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-eventbridge.html
In one sentence: A router for events between services.
Picture it as: A post office that reads the address and delivers only to the right houses.
What it does: EventBridge takes events and sends them to targets based on rules you write. AWS services and some SaaS tools publish into it. It can also run things on a schedule, like a cron.
Use it when: Many events with rules about who cares; Scheduled jobs; Reacting to AWS events
Do NOT use it when: A single simple hand off. SQS is simpler.
Example: Run a report every night at 2am IST.
How you pay: Per million events. Scheduled rules are free.

### Amazon MQ
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-mq.html
In one sentence: It runs ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ for you, so old applications keep talking the way they already do.
Picture it as: Keeping the same post room in a new office building, because everyone already knows how to address the envelopes.
What it does: It is a managed broker for standard protocols such as JMS, AMQP, MQTT and STOMP. The whole point is compatibility: you move an existing message-based application to AWS without rewriting its messaging code. It runs on fixed broker instances, so it does not scale automatically the way SQS does, and you still pick versions and maintenance windows.
Use it when: Lifting an on-premises app that uses JMS or AMQP; You need a protocol SQS and SNS do not speak; Strict message ordering or transactions from an existing broker
Do NOT use it when: Writing something new on AWS, use SQS and SNS or EventBridge, they scale on their own and cost less; Very high throughput streaming, use Kinesis or MSK
Example: A logistics firm moves a Java application that uses JMS queues into AWS without touching the messaging code.
How you pay: Per broker-hour plus storage, whether or not any message flows. A redundant multi-zone deployment doubles it, and idle brokers are the usual waste.

### Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-managed-workflows-for-apache-airflow.html
In one sentence: It runs Apache Airflow for you, so scheduled data pipelines have somewhere to live.
Picture it as: Hiring a caretaker for a machine you already own. Same machine, same controls, you just stop doing the maintenance.
What it does: Airflow is the common open source tool for scheduling data jobs written as Python DAGs. MWAA runs the scheduler, workers and web UI inside your VPC and handles version upgrades. It is still Airflow, so the quirks, the Python dependency conflicts and the learning curve all come with it.
Use it when: Your team already writes Airflow DAGs; Daily data pipelines with dependencies between many steps; You want to stay portable rather than tied to an AWS-only workflow tool
Do NOT use it when: A handful of scheduled tasks, use EventBridge Scheduler with Lambda; Event-driven application logic rather than batch data jobs, use Step Functions
Example: A data team runs a nightly DAG that pulls from three databases, transforms in Glue, and loads into Redshift.
How you pay: Per environment-hour for the scheduler and web server, plus workers and storage. The surprise is the base cost, roughly 350 dollars a month for a small environment even if no DAG ever runs.

### Amazon Simple Notification Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-simple-notification-service.html
In one sentence: Sends one message to many listeners at once.
Picture it as: A WhatsApp group broadcast. One post, everyone in the group sees it.
What it does: SNS publishes a message to a topic. Everything subscribed gets a copy: queues, Lambda functions, emails, SMS. SQS is one to one, SNS is one to many.
Use it when: One event must trigger several things; Alerts to a team
Do NOT use it when: You need a durable work queue. Use SQS.
Example: A payment succeeds, so an email goes out, stock updates and analytics record it.
How you pay: Per million publishes, plus SMS charges which are not cheap.

### Amazon Simple Queue Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-simple-queue-service.html
In one sentence: A waiting line for tasks.
Picture it as: A ticket counter. Work is dropped in the queue and picked up when someone is free.
What it does: SQS holds messages until a worker takes them. If the worker crashes the message comes back. It protects you from traffic spikes. Standard queues can deliver a message twice, so your worker must handle that.
Use it when: Slow work that should not block the user; Absorbing spikes; Separating parts of a system
Do NOT use it when: You need an instant answer back to the user.
Example: Order placed, a message goes in the queue, invoices are generated in the background.
How you pay: Per million requests. Very cheap.

## Blockchain


### Amazon Managed Blockchain
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-managed-blockchain.html
In one sentence: Runs blockchain networks so you do not have to operate the nodes yourself.
Picture it as: Renting a seat at a shared ledger that several companies all write into, with someone else maintaining the room.
What it does: Two separate things sit under this name. One creates and runs a private Hyperledger Fabric network between named members. The other gives you access to public blockchain nodes, mainly Ethereum and Bitcoin, so you can read and write without running your own node. Very few business problems actually need a blockchain, and a shared database with good audit logging solves most of them.
Use it when: Several companies that do not trust each other must share one record; You need public chain node access without operating nodes
Do NOT use it when: Keeping an audit trail inside one company, an append only table with row level security is far simpler and cheaper; Anything where one organisation owns the data, a normal database is the honest answer
Example: Three logistics firms record container handovers on one shared ledger that none of them alone can rewrite.
How you pay: Per node hour and per GB of data written, or per request for node access. Idle nodes keep billing, which is the usual surprise.

## Business Applications


### AWS AppFabric
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-appfabric.html
In one sentence: It pulls the activity logs out of your SaaS apps and puts them in one place.
Picture it as: Every shop in a mall keeps its own visitor book in its own format. AppFabric collects all the books nightly and rewrites them in one common format so security can actually read them.
What it does: You connect SaaS tools like Slack, Zoom, Okta or Asana, and AppFabric fetches their audit logs, converts them to the OCSF standard schema and drops them in S3 or sends them to a security tool. It is read-only plumbing for logs and user lists, not a way to control those apps. The catch is the connector list: if your app is not on it, AppFabric does nothing for you.
Use it when: You run many SaaS apps and want their audit logs in one SIEM; Security asks who did what across tools; You want a user inventory across SaaS apps
Do NOT use it when: Your apps are not on the supported connector list, write to the vendor APIs or use your SIEM vendor's own connectors; You want to sync data or automate actions between SaaS apps, that is a job for EventBridge or an iPaaS like Workato
Example: A 300 person company sends Slack, Zoom and Okta audit logs through AppFabric into Splunk so one query can find every login from a new country.
How you pay: Charged per GB of log data ingested, plus the S3 storage and the SIEM ingestion cost on the other side. The SIEM bill is usually the bigger surprise.

### AWS End User Messaging
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-end-user-messaging.html
In one sentence: It sends SMS, voice calls and phone push notifications from your code.
Picture it as: A post office counter that will send a text, place a recorded call or ping someone's phone for you, and handles the paperwork with the phone companies.
What it does: This is the SMS, MMS, voice and mobile push part of Amazon Pinpoint, renamed in 2024 and kept alive while the rest of Pinpoint is retired. It handles phone numbers, sender IDs, carrier registration and one-time passcodes. It sends messages, it does not decide who to message or track campaigns, that logic is yours. Note the API and SDK clients are still called pinpoint, which confuses people.
Use it when: Sending one-time passcodes or login codes; Order and delivery alerts by SMS; Push notifications to your iOS or Android app
Do NOT use it when: You want email, use Amazon SES instead; You want campaign scheduling, segments and journeys, that was Pinpoint and it ends 30 October 2026, look at Amazon Connect outbound campaigns or a third party like Braze
Example: A food delivery app texts a six digit login code and later pushes a notification when the rider is two minutes away.
How you pay: Per message, and the price varies a lot by destination country. What surprises people is the per number monthly rental plus one-off carrier registration fees, for example US 10DLC registration.

### AWS Supply Chain
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-supply-chain.html
In one sentence: It reads your existing ERP data and warns you when stock is about to run short.
Picture it as: A shop manager who walks the stockroom every morning, checks what is arriving, and tells you which shelf will be empty on Thursday.
What it does: It connects to SAP, Oracle or flat files, builds a data lake of your inventory, orders and suppliers, and then runs demand forecasting, supply planning and risk alerts on top. It is a finished application, not a toolkit. Honestly, it is a niche product with few users, and its value depends almost entirely on how clean your ERP data is. Getting the data mapped in is most of the work.
Use it when: You already run SAP or Oracle and want forecasting without a new full system; You want one view of inventory across warehouses; You need supplier lead time risk alerts
Do NOT use it when: You are small or your data lives in spreadsheets, a normal inventory tool or even Excel is cheaper and faster; You want to build your own supply chain logic, use Glue, Athena and SageMaker instead of a closed app
Example: A mid sized electronics maker sees an alert that a component's lead time doubled and a build slot in six weeks is now at risk.
How you pay: Priced per module per unit hour, so you pay for demand planning, supply planning and insights separately, plus data lake storage. The surprise is that turning on several modules multiplies the bill.

### AWS Wickr
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-wickr.html
In one sentence: An end-to-end encrypted chat and calling app for organisations that need messages to stay secret.
Picture it as: A sealed envelope service where only the sender and the named receiver have a key, and the envelope can be set to burn itself after an hour.
What it does: Messaging, voice, video and file transfer with end-to-end encryption, plus expiry timers and optional compliant archiving for regulators. It is used mostly by government, defence and public safety, and there is a FedRAMP High and DoD authorised version. The free consumer app Wickr Me was retired at the end of 2023, so what remains is the enterprise product. Most ordinary companies do not need this.
Use it when: Government, defence or law enforcement communications; Incident response chat that must stay out of the compromised systems; Work where message content is genuinely sensitive
Do NOT use it when: You just want team chat, Slack or Teams are far better tools for daily work; You want customers to talk to your business, use Amazon Connect or a normal support tool
Example: A security team runs its ransomware response in a Wickr room because the corporate email and Teams may be in the attacker's hands.
How you pay: Per user per month, with tiers. The surprise is the minimum user count on enterprise plans, you pay for the floor whether or not you fill it.

### Amazon Chime
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-chime.html
In one sentence: Amazon's own video meetings app, which is being switched off.
Picture it as: A meeting room that the building owner has announced will be locked up for good, so nobody is booking it any more.
What it does: A Zoom style meetings and business calling product. It is retired: no new customers are accepted, and after 20 February 2026 you cannot schedule or host meetings or use Business Calling. Do not build anything on it. The separate Amazon Chime SDK is not affected and continues.
Use it when: Nothing new, it is closing; Only relevant if you still have meetings or numbers to migrate off it
Do NOT use it when: Any new meeting need, use Zoom, Teams, Google Meet or Webex; Any new voice or video in your own app, use the Amazon Chime SDK
Example: An IT team exports its Chime Business Calling numbers and ports them to another provider before the February 2026 cutoff.
How you pay: Was per user per month plus per minute calling. Not worth planning around now.

### Amazon Chime SDK
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-chime-sdk.html
In one sentence: Building blocks for putting video calls, audio and chat inside your own app.
Picture it as: Buying the engine and gearbox rather than the whole car, you still have to build the vehicle around it.
What it does: Gives you meeting sessions, audio and video streams, WebRTC clients for web, iOS and Android, live transcription, noise reduction and phone dial-in via SIP. You build the entire user interface yourself, which is a lot more work than people expect. It survives the shutdown of the Chime app, but the market is competitive and Twilio, Daily, LiveKit and Agora are common alternatives.
Use it when: Your product needs calls inside it, like telehealth or online tutoring; You want call audio piped into transcription or an AI agent; You need meetings under your own brand
Do NOT use it when: You just want staff meetings, use a finished app like Zoom, not an SDK; You want a full contact centre with queues and agent screens, use Amazon Connect
Example: A telemedicine site opens a doctor patient video call in the browser with no app install, and records the audio for notes.
How you pay: Per attendee minute for meetings, extra per minute for recording, transcription and phone dial-in. The surprise is that a one hour call with five people is five attendee hours, not one.

### Amazon Connect
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-connect.html
In one sentence: A ready-made call centre you set up in a browser instead of buying phone hardware.
Picture it as: Renting a fully staffed reception desk with phone lines, hold music and a queue, instead of installing a switchboard in your building.
What it does: You get phone numbers, a drag and drop call flow builder, agent and supervisor screens, queues, routing, recording and reports, plus chat, email and outbound campaigns. It also has AI add-ons for transcription, agent assist and self service bots. It is genuinely a full contact centre, but configuring flows, routing and reporting well is real work, and reporting is often the weak point people complain about.
Use it when: You need agents answering customer calls or chats; You want an IVR phone menu that reads from your own database; You are replacing an old on-premise phone system
Do NOT use it when: You just need to place or receive a few automated calls, use AWS End User Messaging voice; You need internal staff telephony and meetings, that is Teams Phone or a normal UCaaS product, not Connect
Example: A bank's caller enters a card number, a Lambda checks the account, and the call routes straight to the fraud queue with the details already on the agent's screen.
How you pay: Per minute of usage plus per number per day, with no per seat licence. The surprise items are the AI add-ons like Contact Lens and Amazon Q in Connect, which are charged per minute or per message on top.

### Amazon Pinpoint
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-pinpoint.html
In one sentence: A marketing messaging service that AWS is closing down.
Picture it as: A mailroom that still delivers, but the landlord has posted the date it shuts, so nobody moves in.
What it does: It combined message sending with audience segments, campaigns, journeys and analytics. AWS stopped taking new customers in May 2025 and support ends on 30 October 2026, after which the console, segments, campaigns, journeys and analytics stop working. The sending channels live on as AWS End User Messaging, and confusingly the API is still named pinpoint. If you are on it, plan the move now.
Use it when: Nothing new; Only for planning an exit if you already run campaigns on it
Do NOT use it when: New campaign and journey work, use Braze, Iterable, Klaviyo or Amazon Connect outbound campaigns; Plain SMS, push or voice sending, use AWS End User Messaging; Email, use Amazon SES
Example: A retailer exports its Pinpoint segments and journey definitions and rebuilds them in Braze ahead of the October 2026 cutoff.
How you pay: Was per targeted endpoint per month plus per message. The migration effort, not the bill, is the cost that matters now.

### Amazon Pinpoint APIs
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-pinpoint-apis.html
In one sentence: The older set of Pinpoint APIs for customer messaging, most of which stop working in October 2026.
Picture it as: A phone line that is being switched off, with the useful calls moved to a new number.
What it does: Amazon Pinpoint was a service for talking to your customers by email, SMS, push and voice, with campaigns, journeys and analytics on top. AWS has announced end of support for Amazon Pinpoint on 30 October 2026. After that date the Pinpoint console and Pinpoint resources such as endpoints, segments, campaigns, journeys and analytics stop being available. The parts that survive are the sending APIs. AWS says the APIs for SMS, voice, mobile push, OTP and phone number validate are not affected, and those now live under AWS End User Messaging. So "Amazon Pinpoint APIs" today means two different things. The campaign and analytics APIs are going away. The message sending APIs continue under a new name.
Use it when: You already have an app calling Pinpoint APIs and need to plan the move before October 2026; You want to send SMS, push, OTP or voice from your own code, in which case you use AWS End User Messaging; You are checking which of your API calls survive the end of support date
Do NOT use it when: Do not start a new project on Pinpoint APIs. The service has an end of support date. For SMS, push, voice and OTP use AWS End User Messaging. For email use Amazon SES.; If you only send transactional email such as receipts and password resets, Amazon SES is the better fit and always was.; If you want marketing campaigns and customer journeys with a console, AWS no longer offers that here. You will need a third party tool.
Example: A shopping app sends order updates by SMS and push. The sending calls keep working through AWS End User Messaging. The campaign that used to send a weekly offer from the Pinpoint console has to move somewhere else before October 2026.
How you pay: You pay per message sent, by channel, with the price depending on the country for SMS and voice. There is no charge for the API itself. Pinpoint campaign and analytics features carried their own charges, and those go away with the service.

### Amazon Quick
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-quick.html
In one sentence: The new umbrella name for Amazon QuickSight plus AI agents that answer questions about your business data.
Picture it as: A business analyst who reads all your reports and answers your questions, instead of just handing you the reports.
What it does: On the AWS site, QuickSight is now presented as part of Amazon Quick, also written as Amazon Quick Suite. Quick is the wider product. Amazon Quick Sight is the business intelligence part inside it, the dashboards and charts that QuickSight always did. Around it, Quick adds research and automation agents, connections to many other applications, and no code app building. The pitch is answers grounded in your own business data rather than a general chatbot. This is recent, so treat the naming as still settling. The QuickSight dashboards, APIs and pricing you may already use are not gone. They sit under a new brand.
Use it when: You already use QuickSight and want to know why the branding changed; You want people to ask questions in plain English about company data instead of reading a dashboard; You want dashboards plus an agent that can pull from other business apps in one place
Do NOT use it when: If you just want charts over a database and nothing more, plain QuickSight dashboards, or Athena with any BI tool, is a simpler answer.; If your data is not in AWS and not in a connected app, there is nothing for the agent to ground its answers in.; If you need an AI agent inside your own application rather than a business tool, Amazon Bedrock is the right layer.
Example: A sales head asks "why did revenue drop in the west region last month" and gets an answer built from the company's own sales data, with the chart behind it, instead of opening six dashboards.
How you pay: QuickSight has always charged per user per month, split between authors who build and readers who view, with a capacity option for large reader counts. The agent and automation parts of Quick are new and priced separately, so check the current pricing page before committing.

### Amazon Simple Email Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-simple-email-service.html
In one sentence: Sends email from your app, cheaply and at scale.
Picture it as: A bulk post office for letters your system writes.
What it does: SES sends transactional and bulk email. New accounts start in a sandbox and must be approved for real sending. You must set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC or your mail lands in spam.
Use it when: Invoices, receipts, password resets; Newsletters
Do NOT use it when: A handful of manual emails a week.
Example: Emailing an invoice PDF the moment a payment succeeds.
How you pay: Per thousand emails. Very cheap.

### Amazon WorkDocs
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-workdocs.html
In one sentence: Amazon's file storage and sharing service for staff, now switched off.
Picture it as: An office filing cabinet that the company has already emptied and taken away.
What it does: It was a Dropbox or Google Drive style service with sync clients, sharing links and commenting on documents. AWS stopped new sign-ups in April 2024 and ended support on 25 April 2025, after which data was purged. The site, the APIs and WorkDocs Drive are all gone. Listed here only so you recognise the name in old documentation.
Use it when: Nothing, it is closed
Do NOT use it when: Team file sharing, use Google Drive, SharePoint, OneDrive or Dropbox; File storage for an application, use Amazon S3, or Amazon FSx or EFS for a network drive
Example: An admin ran the bulk export in early 2025 and moved the company's shared folders to SharePoint before the purge.
How you pay: Nothing, it is closed.

### Amazon WorkDocs SDK
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-workdocs-sdk.html
In one sentence: The programming interface to Amazon WorkDocs, a file sharing service AWS has closed to new customers.
Picture it as: A key to a building that is being emptied. Useful for carrying your things out, not for moving in.
What it does: Amazon WorkDocs was a managed file storage and sharing service for companies, with commenting, versions, sharing controls and desktop and mobile apps. AWS documentation now carries a notice that new customer sign ups and account upgrades are no longer available for Amazon WorkDocs, and points customers at instructions for migrating their data out. The WorkDocs SDK is the set of API calls for that service, available through the normal AWS SDKs in Python, Java, Go and so on. It lets code upload documents, list folders, manage users and read comments. Because the service itself is being wound down, the SDK matters mainly for one job now, which is getting existing data out in bulk. I could not confirm a final shutdown date from an official page, so verify that before planning a migration.
Use it when: You are an existing WorkDocs customer and need to export documents, folders and metadata in bulk; You need to list what is stored in WorkDocs before deciding where it should move to; You are auditing old code that still calls WorkDocs APIs
Do NOT use it when: Almost nobody needs this now. Do not build anything new on it. The service is closed to new customers.; For file storage from an application, use Amazon S3.; For shared team file storage that people use like a drive, use Amazon FSx or a non AWS product such as Google Drive, SharePoint or Dropbox.
Example: A company with ten years of documents in WorkDocs writes a script that walks every folder, downloads each file with its latest version, and writes it into an S3 bucket before the service closes.
How you pay: WorkDocs charged per active user per month with a storage allowance. There was no separate charge for API calls. Since sign ups are closed, pricing only matters to existing customers.

### Amazon WorkMail
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-workmail.html
In one sentence: AWS business email and calendar. It is being shut down on 31 March 2027.
Picture it as: A company post room that is closing. It still sorts your post today, but you have been told the date it stops.
What it does: Amazon WorkMail is a managed business email and calendar service. It gives your staff mailboxes on your own domain, with shared calendars and contacts. People can use Microsoft Outlook on Windows or Mac, phone mail apps, IMAP clients, or a web browser. It can link to Active Directory and it encrypts mail using keys you control in AWS KMS. The important fact comes first though. AWS has said it will stop supporting Amazon WorkMail on 31 March 2027. After that date you will not be able to get into it. AWS has published migration guidance. So this is not a product to start a new business on.
Use it when: Almost nobody should start with this now, because of the 2027 end date; Existing WorkMail customers, who should be planning a move off it; Reading up on it only to understand a system you have inherited
Do NOT use it when: Do not pick this for new email. It ends on 31 March 2027. Use Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace instead.; Do not use it to send bulk or app email. That is Amazon Simple Email Service, which is a different thing and is not going away.; Do not confuse it with Amazon Simple Email Service. WorkMail is staff mailboxes. SES is mail your software sends.; If you are on it today, start the migration now rather than near the date.
Example: A 30 person firm gave every person a mailbox on their own domain and used Outlook as usual. That firm now needs to move to another mail provider before March 2027.
How you pay: 4 US dollars per user per month, including 50 GB of storage per user. That price is still listed, but the service ends in March 2027, so the real cost to you includes a migration.

## Compute


### AWS App Runner
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-app-runner.html
In one sentence: Give it your code or container, it runs a web service.
Picture it as: A vending machine for web apps. Put the code in, a running URL comes out.
What it does: App Runner builds from your repository or image, runs it, scales it and gives you HTTPS. No VPC or load balancer to configure. Less control than ECS, far less to learn.
Use it when: A containerised web app, quickly; Small teams with no ops person
Do NOT use it when: Complex networking needs.
Example: A Node API live from a GitHub repo in minutes.
How you pay: Per vCPU and GB while running, with a lower idle rate.

### AWS Batch
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-batch.html
In one sentence: Runs large numbers of background jobs.
Picture it as: A night shift that works through a pile of tasks while you sleep.
What it does: Batch queues your jobs and starts the right amount of compute to work through them, then shuts it down. It handles dependencies and retries. Good with Spot instances for cheap compute.
Use it when: Rendering, simulations, bulk processing; Thousands of independent jobs
Do NOT use it when: A few small tasks. Use Lambda.
Example: Generating ten thousand certificate PDFs overnight.
How you pay: Free service. You pay for the compute it starts.

### AWS Compute Optimizer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-compute-optimizer.html
In one sentence: Looks at how hard your servers actually work and tells you which ones are too big.
Picture it as: A friend who checks your wardrobe and says you only ever wear three of these coats.
What it does: It reads CloudWatch metrics from the last 14 days and rates resources as over provisioned, under provisioned or fine, with a suggested size. It covers EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda and ECS on Fargate. Without the CloudWatch agent it cannot see memory usage, so advice for memory heavy workloads can be wrong. It only recommends, it never changes anything.
Use it when: Cutting a bill that grew without anyone watching; Choosing a Lambda memory setting with evidence; A quarterly right sizing review
Do NOT use it when: Workloads with a big monthly or seasonal peak, 14 days of data will mislead you; Deciding whether to buy Savings Plans, use Cost Explorer for that
Example: It shows 40 EC2 instances sitting under 10 percent CPU and suggests a smaller size, saving a few thousand a month.
How you pay: The basic recommendations are free. Enhanced infrastructure metrics, which extend the lookback to three months, carry a small per resource hourly charge that quietly applies to every resource once enabled.

### AWS Elastic Beanstalk
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elastic-beanstalk.html
In one sentence: Upload your code and AWS sets up the servers for you.
Picture it as: A serviced office. Bring your laptop, the desk and internet are ready.
What it does: Beanstalk takes your application and creates the EC2 servers, load balancer and scaling behind the scenes. You can still reach in and change things. It is an older service and newer options often fit better.
Use it when: A traditional app you want online fast; You want servers without configuring them
Do NOT use it when: A brand new project. Look at App Runner or containers first.
Example: Deploying a Django app without touching a load balancer setting.
How you pay: Free. You pay for the resources it creates.

### AWS Lambda
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-lambda.html
In one sentence: Run a small piece of code without owning a server.
Picture it as: A taxi instead of a car. You pay for the trip, not for parking it all night.
What it does: You upload a function. AWS runs it when something triggers it, then shuts it down. Nothing to patch, nothing running idle. It sleeps between requests, so the first call after a quiet spell can be slower.
Use it when: Short jobs that run on an event; Traffic that comes in bursts; You do not want to manage a server at all
Do NOT use it when: Jobs that run longer than 15 minutes; Something that must respond instantly every single time
Example: Someone uploads a photo, a function makes a thumbnail, then stops.
How you pay: Per request and per millisecond of run time. Nothing when idle.

### AWS Local Zones
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-local-zones.html
In one sentence: Small AWS outposts in extra cities, so your servers sit closer to users there.
Picture it as: A corner shop your chain opens in a suburb, stocking the few items people need urgently, while the big warehouse stays across town.
What it does: A Local Zone is an extension of an AWS Region placed in a metro area like Los Angeles or Mumbai, giving single digit millisecond latency to users there. Only a small subset of services is available in each one, and you still lean on the parent Region for the rest. Most applications do not need this, CloudFront gets you most of the benefit for content.
Use it when: Real time gaming or trading where a few milliseconds matter; Live video or media editing for a specific city; Data that must stay inside a particular geography
Do NOT use it when: General web speed, use Amazon CloudFront instead; Anything needing the full AWS service catalogue, stay in the Region; Mobile network edge latency, look at AWS Wavelength
Example: A game studio puts match servers in the Los Angeles Local Zone so local players see under 10 ms ping.
How you pay: EC2 in a Local Zone costs more per hour than the same instance in the parent Region, and data moving between the zone and the Region is charged.

### AWS Nitro Enclaves
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-nitro-enclaves.html
In one sentence: A sealed side room on your server where secret data can be processed and nobody, not even you, can look in.
Picture it as: A bank's night safe drop slot. Things go in through one narrow opening, nothing else reaches inside, not even the branch staff.
What it does: An enclave is an isolated virtual machine carved out of an EC2 instance, with no network, no persistent storage and no shell access. The only way in or out is a local secure channel from the parent instance. It can prove what code it is running through attestation, and KMS can be told to release a key only to that proven code. This is a specialist tool, most teams never need it.
Use it when: Processing card numbers or health records where even admins must be excluded; Holding private keys for signing, with proof of the code using them; Regulated multi-party data where each side must not see the other's raw data
Do NOT use it when: Ordinary secret storage, use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store; Just encrypting data, use KMS on its own; Any workload needing disk or direct network access, it has neither
Example: A payments firm decrypts card data only inside an enclave, so its own engineers can never read a full card number.
How you pay: No extra charge for the enclave. You pay for the parent EC2 instance, which must be large enough to donate CPU and memory to the sealed room, so you buy capacity you cannot otherwise use.

### AWS Outposts family
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-outposts-family.html
In one sentence: AWS ships actual racks or small boxes of its own hardware to your building and runs them for you.
Picture it as: A coffee chain installing one of its own branded machines in your office lobby, still serviced by their staff, still on their system.
What it does: Outposts come as full 42U racks or as 1U and 2U servers. They run a subset of AWS services on your premises, managed by AWS and connected back to a Region. You need real datacentre conditions, power, cooling and a solid network link, and if that link drops your control plane goes with it. The service list is much shorter than a Region's.
Use it when: Data legally required to stay in a specific building or country; Factory or hospital systems that need very low latency to local machines; Migrating slowly while old hardware still sits on site
Do NOT use it when: Just wanting things nearer users, use Local Zones or CloudFront; Short projects, these are multi-year commitments; Small offices without proper power, cooling and network
Example: A hospital runs its imaging application on an Outposts rack in its own basement so scans never leave the building.
How you pay: You buy or commit for one or three years, upfront or monthly, per rack. The surprise is that the commitment runs whether you use the capacity or not, plus the cost of the network link home.

### AWS Outposts rack
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-outposts-rack.html
In one sentence: Puts a full rack of AWS hardware inside your own building.
Picture it as: Renting a branch of the bank and having it built in your office lobby.
What it does: AWS ships a 42U rack, installs it in your data centre, and keeps running it. You use the same AWS console and APIs, but the machines sit on your floor. Only a subset of AWS services run on it, and you need real data centre space, power and cooling.
Use it when: Data must stay inside your building by law; An app needs very low delay to machines on site; You are moving off a data centre slowly and want one control plane
Do NOT use it when: If you just want cloud servers, use amazon-ec2 in a normal Region.; If you only need a small box at a shop or factory, use AWS Outposts servers instead.; If you only need a private network link back to AWS, use aws-direct-connect.; Most companies never need this. It is for large regulated or latency bound workloads.
Example: A hospital runs its imaging app on an Outposts rack in its own basement so patient scans never leave the site.
How you pay: You pay per rack for a 3 year term, billed monthly, whether you use it or not. The surprise is that it is a long commitment, not pay as you go, and you still pay for data going back to the Region.

### AWS Outposts servers
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-outposts-servers.html
In one sentence: A single AWS server box you put in a shop, clinic or factory.
Picture it as: A vending machine AWS drops off, refills and services, but it lives in your shop.
What it does: This is the small version of Outposts. A 1U or 2U server arrives, you or a contractor rack it, and AWS provisions it remotely. It runs far fewer services than the rack, mainly EC2, ECS and local storage, and there is no local block storage service or database service.
Use it when: A retail store needs compute on site when the internet drops; A factory floor needs fast local processing of sensor data; Hundreds of small sites need the same setup managed centrally
Do NOT use it when: If you have real data centre space and need databases or large capacity, use the Outposts rack.; If you just need to process data on a small device at the edge, aws-iot-greengrass is far cheaper and simpler.; If latency is fine, use a normal Region with amazon-ec2.; Very few teams need this.
Example: A supermarket chain puts one 1U Outposts server in each store to run checkout software that must keep working offline.
How you pay: Per server, on a 3 year commitment, paid up front or monthly. Capacity is fixed, so you pay the same whether the box is busy or idle.

### AWS Parallel Cluster
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-parallel-cluster.html
In one sentence: Sets up a cluster of machines that run scientific jobs in a queue.
Picture it as: Hiring a shift manager who opens extra counters when the queue grows and closes them when it empties.
What it does: It is an open source command line tool, not a hosted service. You give it a config file and it builds the head node, the Slurm scheduler, the shared file system and the compute nodes. You still own and operate the cluster, including patching and upgrades.
Use it when: Running engineering simulations or genomics pipelines; Moving an existing on-site Slurm cluster to AWS; You want machines to start only while jobs are waiting
Do NOT use it when: AWS Parallel Computing Service (PCS) is the newer managed Slurm option. Pick that if you do not want to run the cluster yourself.; For ordinary batch work that is not HPC, aws-batch or aws-step-functions is simpler.; If your work is containers, use amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service.; Nobody outside HPC and research computing needs this.
Example: A drug research team submits 2000 molecule simulations; the cluster grows to 500 instances, then shrinks back to zero.
How you pay: The tool is free. You pay for the EC2 instances, the shared storage and the network. The surprise is the head node and shared file system run 24/7 and cost money even with no jobs.

### AWS Parallel Computing Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-parallel-computing-service.html
In one sentence: It runs a proper scientific computing cluster for you, using the Slurm scheduler researchers already know.
Picture it as: A university workshop with a booking sheet. You write your job on the sheet, the technician assigns benches and tools, and work starts when there is room.
What it does: PCS is AWS's managed Slurm service, launched in 2024. It runs the controller for you and scales compute nodes up and down, so researchers keep submitting jobs with the same sbatch and squeue commands. It is for genuine HPC with many nodes working on one problem together, which is a narrow audience. It replaces the hand-built approach of ParallelCluster with something AWS operates.
Use it when: Existing Slurm workflows you want to move to the cloud; Simulations spanning many nodes that must talk to each other; A research group wanting a cluster without an HPC admin
Do NOT use it when: Independent jobs that do not talk to each other, AWS Batch is simpler and cheaper; Machine learning training, use SageMaker; Full control over every cluster detail, use AWS ParallelCluster
Example: A weather research team submits a 200-node Slurm job for a regional forecast run and the cluster grows to fit, then shrinks.
How you pay: An hourly charge for the managed controller plus all the EC2, storage and networking underneath. The controller charge continues even when no jobs are running.

### AWS Serverless Application Repository
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-serverless-application-repository.html
In one sentence: A catalogue of ready-made small AWS apps you can deploy into your own account in a few clicks.
Picture it as: A recipe card box. You pick a card, and the whole dish gets cooked in your kitchen, with your ingredients.
What it does: It holds SAM templates published by AWS and third parties, mostly small Lambda based utilities. Deploying one creates the resources in your account, so you own and pay for them. It is quiet and lightly maintained, many listings are years old, and most teams now copy a template from GitHub or use CDK constructs instead. Read the template before deploying anything from a publisher you do not know.
Use it when: Grabbing a known AWS-published helper like a log forwarder; A quick one-off utility you do not want to write; Publishing an internal template for your own organisation
Do NOT use it when: Anything production critical, write the template yourself with SAM or CDK; Reusable building blocks in code, use CDK constructs or Terraform modules; Trusting an unknown publisher's stale template with IAM permissions
Example: A team deploys the published Datadog log forwarder Lambda straight from the repository instead of writing one.
How you pay: The catalogue is free. You pay normal charges for whatever the template creates, which can include resources you did not notice in the template.

### AWS SimSpace Weaver
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-simspace-weaver.html
In one sentence: A retired service that used to spread one huge simulated world across many servers.
Picture it as: A shop that has closed down. Worth knowing what it sold, but you cannot buy there any more.
What it does: SimSpace Weaver ran large spatial simulations, like a city of millions of people, by splitting the world across several machines that kept each other in step. It closed to new customers in January 2025 and support ended on 20 May 2026, so the console and resources are gone. AWS points people to AWS Batch for containerised simulation work instead. Include it only so nobody wastes time looking for it.
Use it when: Understanding an old architecture diagram that mentions it; Planning a migration off a legacy simulation setup
Do NOT use it when: Any new simulation project, it no longer exists, use AWS Batch; Large agent-based models, use AWS Batch or a self-managed cluster on EC2
Example: A city planning demo once simulated a million pedestrians across several servers, work that now goes to Batch or EC2.
How you pay: Not applicable any more. While it ran, you paid per simulation hour and per worker instance.

### AWS Wavelength
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-wavelength.html
In one sentence: AWS servers placed inside mobile phone networks, so phone apps reach them without crossing the wider internet.
Picture it as: A first aid post inside the stadium instead of a hospital across town. Help arrives fast, but it only does a few things.
What it does: Wavelength Zones sit in telecom operators' 5G sites, so traffic from a phone on that network reaches your servers in very few hops. It only helps devices on that specific operator's network, availability varies by country and operator, and only a small set of services runs there. Almost nobody needs this.
Use it when: AR or VR on phones where latency is visible to the user; Connected vehicles or drones on a specific carrier network; Live video processing from mobile devices
Do NOT use it when: Users on home broadband or WiFi, it does not help them, use CloudFront; General low latency in a city, use Local Zones; Anything needing the full AWS service list, stay in the Region
Example: An AR game puts its physics server in a Verizon Wavelength Zone so headset movement feels immediate.
How you pay: EC2 in a Wavelength Zone costs more than in the Region, plus data transfer between the zone and the Region.

### Amazon DCV
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-dcv.html
In one sentence: Lets you use a graphics heavy desktop that is running somewhere else.
Picture it as: A very good live video link to a computer in another room, with your mouse and keyboard attached.
What it does: Amazon DCV is the renamed NICE DCV, the remote display protocol AWS bought in 2016. It streams the screen of a remote Linux or Windows machine to a laptop or browser. It is software you install, not a managed service, and it is the same protocol underneath WorkSpaces and AppStream.
Use it when: A designer needs a CAD or 3D app that will not run on a laptop; Viewing simulation results that live next to the data; Giving engineers access to a shared GPU workstation
Do NOT use it when: If you want a finished managed desktop, use amazon-workspaces instead of building your own.; For plain server admin, SSH or Systems Manager is enough.; If the app is a normal web app, none of this is needed.
Example: An architect opens a 40 GB building model on a GPU instance in Mumbai and works on it from a thin laptop.
How you pay: No charge for the DCV server when it runs on an EC2 instance. You pay the normal EC2 and GPU cost. Running DCV outside AWS needs a paid licence, which catches people out.

### Amazon EC2
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-ec2.html
In one sentence: A computer you rent in Amazon's data centre.
Picture it as: Renting a flat instead of buying a house. You pick the size, you get the keys, you install what you want.
What it does: EC2 gives you a full server. You choose how much CPU, memory and disk. You install the operating system and your software. You control everything, so you also maintain everything.
Use it when: You need full control of the machine; You are moving an existing server to the cloud; Your software must run all the time
Do NOT use it when: You just want to run a small piece of code now and then. Use Lambda.; You do not want to patch servers. Use Fargate or App Runner.
Example: A shop's billing software that must run 24 hours a day on one server.
How you pay: Per second the machine is on, by size. Stopped machines cost nothing for compute but the disk still costs.

### Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-ec2-auto-scaling.html
In one sentence: Adds servers when busy, removes them when quiet.
Picture it as: Calling in extra staff on a festival weekend and sending them home on Monday.
What it does: You set a minimum, a maximum and a rule. Auto Scaling adds or removes EC2 machines to match. It also replaces any machine that fails a health check.
Use it when: Traffic rises and falls; You want automatic recovery from a dead server
Do NOT use it when: Steady, predictable traffic on one machine.
Example: Two servers normally, six during a live class, back to two after.
How you pay: The feature is free. You pay for the servers it starts.

### Amazon EC2 Image Builder
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-ec2-image-builder.html
In one sentence: It builds your standard server image for you, on a schedule, with your software and patches baked in.
Picture it as: A bakery that makes the same loaf to the same recipe every morning, so every shop gets an identical one.
What it does: You define a recipe: a base OS image plus components that install software and settings. Image Builder runs it on a temporary instance, tests the result and publishes an AMI or container image to the accounts and regions you choose. It is slow, a build takes many minutes, and debugging a failed component is awkward because the test instance disappears.
Use it when: A hardened golden AMI your organisation must use; Monthly patched images without a person doing it; Sharing one image across many accounts and regions
Do NOT use it when: Container images, use a Dockerfile and a normal CI pipeline; Config that changes often, use user data or a config tool at boot; One-off images, just snapshot an instance
Example: A security team publishes a patched, CIS-hardened Amazon Linux AMI on the first of every month to twelve accounts.
How you pay: The service is free. You pay for the temporary build instance, the snapshots and the storage of every AMI version. The surprise is dozens of old AMIs and snapshots quietly accruing storage charges.

### Amazon Elastic VMware Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elastic-vmware-service.html
In one sentence: It runs VMware Cloud Foundation on AWS hardware, inside your own network.
Picture it as: Renting the same machinery you already know how to operate, in somebody else's factory, so none of your staff need retraining.
What it does: Launched in August 2025 as the AWS answer after VMware Cloud on AWS changed hands. It runs VMware Cloud Foundation on EC2 bare metal inside your VPC, so your IP addresses, vCenter habits and runbooks carry over. You bring your own VMware licence from Broadcom, and you or a partner manage the VMware layer, not AWS.
Use it when: A data centre lease ends and you must move VMware workloads fast; You cannot change IP addresses or rewrite applications; Your team's skills and tooling are all VMware
Do NOT use it when: You have time to replatform, plain EC2 or containers cost less and need no VMware licence; You have a few dozen VMs, the minimum host count makes this very expensive, use Application Migration Service to move them to EC2
Example: A manufacturer moves 500 VMs out of an expiring data centre in weeks, keeping vCenter and the same addresses, and modernises later.
How you pay: Per bare metal host hour, plus storage and network, plus your own VMware licence from Broadcom. The surprise is the minimum number of hosts and the separate licence bill, so this is not a small monthly number.

### Amazon Lightsail
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-lightsail.html
In one sentence: A simple server at a fixed monthly price.
Picture it as: A prepaid mobile plan. One price, known limits, no bill shock.
What it does: Lightsail gives a small server, a fixed price and a simple console. It hides most of AWS. Good for learning and small sites. You outgrow it once you need real AWS features.
Use it when: A small website or WordPress; Learning; You want a predictable bill
Do NOT use it when: Anything that will need to scale properly.
Example: A WordPress site for a small business.
How you pay: A fixed price per month, from a few dollars.

### Amazon Lightsail for Research
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-lightsail-for-research.html
In one sentence: A simple rented desktop in the cloud with research software like RStudio or JupyterLab already installed.
Picture it as: A hotel room with the kettle and iron already there. You do not shop for anything, you just check in.
What it does: You pick a size and an application, and get a browser accessible virtual computer with that software set up, at a flat monthly price. It is aimed at academics and students who do not want to learn EC2. It is a niche corner of Lightsail, the software choices are few and fixed, and serious labs outgrow it quickly.
Use it when: A student needing RStudio on a bigger machine than their laptop; A short research project with a predictable budget; Teaching, where everyone needs the same environment
Do NOT use it when: Multi-node or GPU heavy research computing, use EC2 or AWS Parallel Computing Service; Shared team notebooks with data governance, use Amazon SageMaker; Anything needing VPC or IAM control, it is deliberately simplified
Example: A masters student runs a month of R analysis on a 16 GB Lightsail for Research machine instead of their old laptop.
How you pay: Flat hourly or monthly by size, with an idle shutdown option. The surprise is being billed for a machine left running after the term ends, since flat pricing hides the waste.

### Bottlerocket
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/bottlerocket.html
In one sentence: A stripped down operating system for machines that only run containers.
Picture it as: A kitchen with nothing in it but the one oven you need, so there is less to clean and less to break.
What it does: Bottlerocket is a free, open source Linux distribution from AWS. It has no package manager and no SSH by default, and updates are applied as one whole image that can roll back. That minimalism is the point, but it also means you cannot install agents the normal way.
Use it when: Running EKS or ECS nodes and wanting a smaller attack surface; You want node updates that are atomic and reversible; A security team asks for a hardened container host
Do NOT use it when: If you run normal software on the host, not containers, use Amazon Linux.; If you use aws-fargate, there is no host to choose, so this is irrelevant.; If your tooling depends on SSH and yum, expect friction.
Example: An EKS cluster runs Bottlerocket nodes, and a bad update rolls back automatically on reboot.
How you pay: The OS is free. You pay only the usual EC2 charges for the instances.

### Elastic Fabric Adapter
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/elastic-fabric-adapter.html
In one sentence: A special network card for EC2 that lets many servers talk to each other extremely fast.
Picture it as: Swapping a queue at the post office for a hatch between two adjoining rooms. The message goes straight across, no counter in between.
What it does: EFA is a network interface option on certain EC2 instance types. It lets applications bypass the operating system's networking and talk directly between machines, which matters for MPI and for spreading model training across GPUs. Your software has to be written for it, a normal web app gains nothing. Instances using EFA must sit in the same subnet and ideally the same placement group.
Use it when: MPI simulations across many nodes; Distributed GPU training with NCCL; Any job where nodes exchange data constantly
Do NOT use it when: Ordinary application traffic, plain networking is fine; Independent jobs that never talk, it adds nothing; Instance types that do not support it, check first
Example: A 64-node fluid dynamics run finishes in a third of the time once EFA replaces standard networking.
How you pay: No charge for EFA itself. The cost is being forced onto larger, pricier instance types that support it, and keeping the cluster together in one placement group.

## Containers


### AWS Fargate
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-fargate.html
In one sentence: Runs containers without you owning any servers.
Picture it as: Ordering food instead of renting a kitchen. You get the meal, not the gas bill.
What it does: Fargate is not a separate service you visit. It is a way to run ECS or EKS where AWS supplies the machine. No patching, no capacity planning. It costs more per unit than raw EC2.
Use it when: You want containers with no servers to manage; Uneven workloads
Do NOT use it when: Very heavy steady workloads where EC2 is cheaper.
Example: A background worker that runs for ten minutes each night.
How you pay: Per vCPU and per GB of memory, per second.

### Amazon ECS Anywhere
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-ecs-anywhere.html
In one sentence: Lets AWS run and manage containers on servers you own, not AWS servers.
Picture it as: A cleaning company that also sends staff to your own house, while still running the schedule from their office.
What it does: It is a feature of ECS, not a separate product. You install an agent on your own machine, it registers as an external instance, and ECS schedules containers onto it. The control plane is still in AWS, so you need a working network link to AWS, and some ECS features that depend on AWS networking or load balancers do not apply.
Use it when: Data must stay in your own building for legal reasons; Factory or shop floor hardware that must keep working close to the machines; You want one way of deploying containers across cloud and on site
Do NOT use it when: Normal cloud workloads, plain ECS on Fargate is simpler and cheaper to run; Sites with no reliable internet link, the agent needs to reach AWS
Example: A retailer runs the same stock counting container in AWS and on a small server in each shop, deployed from one ECS console.
How you pay: A small hourly charge per registered external instance. The hardware, power and network are yours and are the bigger cost.

### Amazon EKS Anywhere
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-eks-anywhere.html
In one sentence: Runs AWS style Kubernetes clusters on your own servers.
Picture it as: Getting the restaurant's recipe and kit so you can cook the same dish in your own kitchen.
What it does: EKS Anywhere is software you install on your own hardware or VMware to create and update Kubernetes clusters. AWS does not operate these clusters, you do. The control plane is not in AWS, so cluster uptime is your problem, and support is a paid add on.
Use it when: Kubernetes must run in your own data centre; You want the same tooling on site and in AWS; Air gapped or regulated environments
Do NOT use it when: If the workload can run in AWS, use amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service and let AWS run the control plane.; If you only want the tested open source parts, use Amazon EKS Distro.; If you do not already run Kubernetes, do not start here.
Example: A bank runs EKS Anywhere on vSphere in its own data centre and uses the same Helm charts as its AWS clusters.
How you pay: The software is free. Enterprise support for it costs per cluster per year. You also pay for your own hardware.

### Amazon EKS Distro
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-eks-distro.html
In one sentence: The exact Kubernetes build AWS itself runs, handed to you as open source.
Picture it as: Buying the same flour and yeast the bakery uses, then baking the bread yourself.
What it does: EKS Distro is a set of tested Kubernetes binaries and container images on GitHub, with AWS security patches. It is parts, not a product. It does not install, run or upgrade anything for you, and there is no console and no support ticket.
Use it when: You already have your own cluster build process; You want versions patched after upstream support ends; Building a Kubernetes product of your own
Do NOT use it when: If you want clusters created and managed for you on your hardware, use EKS Anywhere.; If you want a managed cluster, use amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service.; This is for platform teams. Almost no application team should touch it.
Example: A platform team builds its own cluster images from EKS Distro so its on-site clusters match the AWS ones.
How you pay: Free. You pay only for wherever you run it.

### Amazon Elastic Container Registry
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elastic-container-registry.html
In one sentence: A private store for your container images.
Picture it as: Your own locked shelf for the blueprints your factory builds from.
What it does: ECR keeps Docker images privately in your account. ECS, EKS and Lambda pull from it. It can scan images for known vulnerabilities.
Use it when: You build containers and do not want them public
Do NOT use it when: Open source images that are fine on Docker Hub.
Example: Pushing a new build image, then telling ECS to use it.
How you pay: Per GB stored, plus data transfer.

### Amazon Elastic Container Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elastic-container-service.html
