In one sentence: Runs your app in containers, the simple AWS way.
Picture it as: Standard shipping containers. Any port can handle them because the shape is always the same.
What it does: ECS runs Docker containers for you. It restarts them if they crash and can scale them. It is simpler than Kubernetes and only works on AWS.
Use it when: You already use Docker; You want containers without learning Kubernetes
Do NOT use it when: You need to run the same setup on other clouds too. Use EKS.
Example: A Node.js API running as three containers behind a load balancer.
How you pay: Free control plane. You pay for the EC2 or Fargate capacity underneath.

### Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elastic-kubernetes-service.html
In one sentence: Managed Kubernetes.
Picture it as: The international standard plug socket. It works the same everywhere, and the wiring is complicated.
What it does: EKS runs Kubernetes so you do not have to run the control plane. Kubernetes is powerful and genuinely hard. It is the right answer for large teams and the wrong answer for small ones.
Use it when: You already know Kubernetes; You must stay portable across clouds; Large, complex systems
Do NOT use it when: A small team shipping one app. ECS or App Runner will hurt less.
Example: A company running forty microservices across several teams.
How you pay: An hourly fee for each cluster, plus the compute underneath.

### Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/red-hat-openshift-service-on-aws.html
In one sentence: Red Hat's OpenShift, run for you inside your AWS account.
Picture it as: Renting a branded kitchen from a restaurant chain. Same fittings and rules you already trained on, but somebody else does the plumbing.
What it does: OpenShift is a Kubernetes platform with extra developer tools and stricter defaults. This version is installed, patched and supported jointly by AWS and Red Hat. It is mostly bought by companies that already run OpenShift in their own data centres and want the same thing in the cloud. It costs noticeably more than plain Kubernetes on AWS.
Use it when: You already run OpenShift on premises and want a matching cloud setup; Your team's skills and tooling are OpenShift specific; You want Red Hat support included
Do NOT use it when: A team new to Kubernetes, EKS is cheaper and simpler; A small app that does not need Kubernetes at all, use ECS Fargate or Lambda
Example: A bank running OpenShift in its own data centre moves a few workloads to AWS without retraining its platform team.
How you pay: Hourly per worker node plus a control plane fee, on top of the EC2, storage and network charges. The OpenShift licence sits inside that hourly rate, so it is meaningfully pricier than EKS.

## Cost and Billing


### AWS Billing Conductor
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-billing-conductor.html
In one sentence: It lets you send someone a different AWS bill than the one AWS actually produced.
Picture it as: A landlord who pays one electricity bill for the whole building, then works out what each flat owes, with his own rates and a service charge added.
What it does: You group accounts into billing groups and set your own prices, discounts or flat fees. It produces a second, made-up bill for that group, while AWS still charges you the real amount. It is for resellers, managed service providers and big companies that charge internal departments. Almost nobody else needs it.
Use it when: You resell AWS to customers and need to bill them your own rates; You charge internal business units for their cloud use; You must hide AWS discounts from the people you invoice
Do NOT use it when: You only want to see which team spent what, use cost allocation tags with Cost Explorer; You just want a spending limit, use AWS Budgets
Example: An IT company hosts 12 clients in separate AWS accounts and invoices each one at list price plus 15 percent, generated automatically each month.
How you pay: A fee per account per month in each billing group. The surprise is that you still pay AWS the real bill in full, so this is pure extra cost on top.

### AWS Budgets
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-budgets.html
In one sentence: It emails you when your AWS spending passes a number you picked.
Picture it as: A limit alert on your bank card. It does not stop the card, it just texts you.
What it does: You set a monthly amount and it warns you at thresholds, for example at 80 percent and 100 percent. It can warn on forecast spend too, so you hear about it before the month ends. Important limitation: by default it only alerts, it does not stop anything, though you can attach an action that applies a restrictive IAM policy or stops instances.
Use it when: Your first week on AWS, before anything can run up a bill; Capping a side project or a client account; Tracking whether a team stays inside its allowance
Do NOT use it when: You want to understand why the bill grew, use Cost Explorer instead; You want a hard spending cap that cannot be exceeded, AWS does not really offer that, so use alerts plus tight IAM limits
Example: A student sets a 20 dollar budget and gets an email at 16 dollars, finds a forgotten NAT gateway, and deletes it.
How you pay: Two budgets are free. After that a few cents per budget per day. Budget actions and forecasted alerts cost a little more.

### AWS Cost Explorer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cost-explorer.html
In one sentence: Shows where your AWS money is going.
Picture it as: A bank statement with charts, so you can see what you actually spend on.
What it does: Cost Explorer breaks the bill down by service, tag and time, and forecasts next month. Tag everything from day one or the breakdown is useless. Set a budget alert on day one too.
Use it when: Always. From the first day.
Example: Spotting that a forgotten test server has cost 4,000 rupees this month.
How you pay: The console view is free. The API has a small per request charge.

### AWS Cost and Usage Report
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cost-and-usage-report.html
In one sentence: It drops a giant spreadsheet of every line of your AWS bill into an S3 bucket.
Picture it as: An itemised phone bill, except every call is listed hour by hour, so the file is far too big to read by eye.
What it does: It is the most detailed billing data AWS gives you, one row per resource per hour, delivered as compressed files a few times a day. You are meant to query it with Athena or load it into a data tool, not open it. The newer version, CUR 2.0, is created through the Data Exports console and has a cleaner, more stable column layout.
Use it when: You need exact per-resource costs for chargeback; You are building your own cost dashboard; Cost Explorer does not slice the data the way you need
Do NOT use it when: You just want to see where the money went, Cost Explorer already shows that with no setup; You want alerts, use AWS Budgets
Example: A finance team queries the report in Athena to find every S3 bucket that cost more than 100 dollars last month.
How you pay: The report itself is free. You pay for the S3 storage and for every Athena query you run against it, and the files get big fast.

### AWS FinOps Agent
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-finops-agent.html
In one sentence: An AI agent that watches your AWS bill, investigates cost spikes and answers cost questions in plain English.
Picture it as: A finance person who notices the bill jumped, finds out who changed what, and tells the right engineer.
What it does: AWS FinOps Agent is an agent you create in your own AWS account to monitor cost, investigate anomalies and surface savings. It reads cost and usage data from AWS Cost Explorer, listens for alerts from AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, pulls recommendations from Cost Optimization Hub and Compute Optimizer, and uses AWS CloudTrail to find the change that caused a spike. It then writes an investigation summary with a likely root cause and the owner, and can open a Jira ticket or post to Slack. Engineers can also just ask it questions such as why cost went up last month. You can upload context files, for example which account belongs to which team, so it answers in your own terms. Each agent is a separate instance with its own permissions, context, memory and integrations. It is in preview and starts in the US East N. Virginia region, so expect changes.
Use it when: A cost spike appears and nobody wants to dig through CloudTrail to find which change caused it; You want engineers to self serve cost answers instead of pinging the finance team; You want anomaly alerts to arrive as a Slack message or Jira ticket with a cause already attached, not just a number
Do NOT use it when: If your AWS bill is small and one person reads Cost Explorer once a month, this is more machinery than you need. Cost Explorer plus AWS Budgets is enough.; If you only want to be told when spend crosses a limit, AWS Budgets does that on its own.; It is in preview, so do not put a process that must not break on top of it yet.
Example: Cost Anomaly Detection flags a 900 dollar jump overnight. The agent correlates it with CloudTrail, finds a team launched a large GPU instance and left it running, and posts that in Slack with the owner named, by the time people log in.
How you pay: Preview pricing should be checked on the AWS page before use. The data sources it reads, Cost Explorer, Cost Anomaly Detection and Compute Optimizer, are largely free or low cost on their own, so the agent's own charge is what to look at.

### Reserved Instance Reporting
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/reserved-instance-reporting.html
In one sentence: It is the screen that tells you whether the capacity you pre-paid for is actually being used.
Picture it as: Checking a gym membership you paid for a year upfront, to see how many sessions you actually attended.
What it does: This is not a separate service, it is a pair of reports inside Cost Explorer: utilization, how much of what you bought you used, and coverage, how much of your usage is protected by a reservation. It covers EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, MemoryDB, OpenSearch and Redshift. You can set a target percentage and be alerted when you fall below it.
Use it when: You bought Reserved Instances and want to know if they are wasted; Deciding whether to buy more reservations before renewal; Proving savings to finance
Do NOT use it when: You use Savings Plans instead of Reserved Instances, look at the Savings Plans reports; You have not committed to anything yet, start with Cost Explorer's recommendations
Example: A team sees RI utilization at 62 percent, finds an instance type was changed after buying, and modifies the reservation.
How you pay: The reports are free. The cost is the reservation itself, paid whether or not you use it, which is exactly what these reports expose.

### Savings Plans
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/savings-plans.html
In one sentence: A pricing commitment, not a service. You promise to spend a set amount per hour for one or three years and pay less per hour.
Picture it as: A yearly train pass instead of buying a ticket each day. Cheaper per trip, but you pay for the pass whether you travel or not.
What it does: Savings Plans is a way of paying, not something you switch on and use. You commit to spend a fixed amount of money per hour, for one year or three years, and in return AWS charges you lower rates, up to about 72 percent below on demand. The discount is applied to your bill automatically each hour, across your accounts in AWS Organizations. There are different plans. Compute Savings Plans are the most flexible and cover Amazon EC2, AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate across instance families, sizes, operating systems and Regions. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give a bigger discount but lock you to one instance family in one Region. There are also plans for Amazon SageMaker AI. You can pay all up front, part up front, or nothing up front, with a better rate the more you pay early. Once bought, a plan cannot be cancelled or refunded.
Use it when: You have steady baseline usage that runs all year and is not going away; You want a discount without picking exact instance types, so a Compute Savings Plan fits; You already know your lowest monthly compute spend and can commit to a part of it safely; You run Lambda or Fargate a lot, since Reserved Instances do not cover those but Compute Savings Plans do
Do NOT use it when: Not for short lived or spiky workloads. You pay the commitment even on quiet hours.; Not for a new workload you cannot size yet. Run on demand first, look at AWS Cost Explorer, then commit.; Not a fault tolerance or batch discount. For interruptible work, Spot Instances are cheaper.; Do not commit to 100 percent of your usage. Cover the floor, not the peak.; Do not buy one expecting to change your mind. There is no cancel and no refund.
Example: A team always runs at least 20 servers day and night. They look at Cost Explorer, commit to the spend those 20 cover for three years, and their bill for that part drops sharply. The extra servers they add in busy weeks stay on demand.
How you pay: There is no fee for a Savings Plan itself. You pay the hourly amount you committed to, every hour of the term, used or not. Usage above the commitment is billed at normal on demand rates. Paying more up front lowers the rate.

## Customer Enablement


### AWS Activate
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-activate.html
In one sentence: Free AWS credits and help for new startups.
Picture it as: A voucher book a shopping mall hands new tenants so they try the place out.
What it does: A programme that gives startups AWS credits, plus some technical guidance and free support plan time. The Founders tier gives a small amount, around $1,000. The big numbers, up to $200,000 or more for AI startups, come through the Portfolio tier, which you can only reach if a VC, accelerator or partner refers you. Credits expire, usually in a year or two.
Use it when: You are a startup under about 10 years old and new to AWS; Your investor or accelerator is an AWS Activate provider; You want to test an idea without paying the first bills
Do NOT use it when: You are an established business, there is no credit programme for you, ask an AWS account manager or a reseller for a discount instead; You want a big grant without a referral, applying direct gets you the small tier, go through your accelerator or VC
Example: A two person startup applies through their accelerator, gets credits, and runs their first year of EC2 and RDS bills for free.
How you pay: Nothing to join. The surprise is the expiry date, and the fact that credits often do not cover Marketplace software or reserved capacity, so those charges hit your card while you think you are on credits.

### AWS IQ
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iq.html
In one sentence: A retired marketplace where you hired freelance AWS experts by the project.
Picture it as: A noticeboard for local handymen that the shop has now taken down.
What it does: AWS IQ let you post a small project and get proposals from vetted independent AWS experts, billed through your AWS account. It is being shut down. New expert sign ups stopped in May 2025, new projects stopped in August 2025, and access ends on 28 May 2026. AWS points people to AWS Marketplace Professional Services instead.
Use it when: Basically never now, it is closing; Only relevant if you have an old engagement still running on it
Do NOT use it when: You need short term AWS help, use AWS Marketplace Professional Services, an AWS Partner, or hire a contractor normally; You need deep ongoing help from AWS itself, that is AWS Professional Services
Example: A small firm used to post "set up our VPC and a backup plan" and pick a freelancer for a few hundred dollars. That route no longer exists.
How you pay: Per project, on your AWS bill. Moot now, since you cannot start new work on it.

### AWS Managed Services
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-managed-services.html
In one sentence: You pay AWS staff to run your AWS infrastructure operations for you.
Picture it as: Hiring a managing agent for a building. They handle repairs, inspections and the fire alarm checks, you still own the building.
What it does: It is a service offering with people behind it, not a console feature. AWS handles patching, backups, incident response, monitoring and change requests under an agreed process. Changes usually go through a request workflow, which can feel slow to teams used to deploying themselves. It is aimed at large enterprises, often ones migrating off a data centre.
Use it when: A large migration with no in house AWS operations team; Regulated workloads needing documented 24/7 operations; Buying time while you hire and train
Do NOT use it when: Small or mid sized teams, the minimum spend is large, hire or use a partner; Fast moving product teams, the change process will slow you down
Example: A bank moves its core estate to AWS and AWS engineers handle patching windows and night time incidents.
How you pay: A percentage of your managed AWS spend, plus the AWS resources themselves, with a substantial monthly minimum.

### AWS Professional Services
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-professional-services.html
In one sentence: AWS consultants you pay to come and build or advise on a project with you.
Picture it as: Calling in the manufacturer's own engineers to install a machine, rather than a local fitter.
What it does: A paid consulting team inside AWS that works alongside your staff on migrations, big architecture jobs and modernisation programmes. They are consultants, not support, so they do not answer tickets. They are usually more expensive than an AWS Partner doing the same work, and most projects run through Partners instead.
Use it when: A large, high risk migration where you want AWS itself involved; You need expertise on a very new AWS service nobody else knows yet; An executive wants AWS accountable on the project
Do NOT use it when: You have a bug or an outage, that is AWS Support, not this; You want normal delivery work at a normal price, use an AWS Partner or your own contractors
Example: An airline hires ProServe for a year to help move a core booking system off a data centre.
How you pay: Time and materials or fixed fee, quoted per engagement, usually six figures. The surprise is that it does not come out of credits and is not included in any support plan.

### AWS Support
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-support.html
In one sentence: A paid plan that lets you raise a ticket and get a human at AWS to help.
Picture it as: An extended warranty with a phone number, where the price decides how fast somebody picks up.
What it does: Four paid tiers above the free Basic account help. Developer is cheap and business hours only. Business gives 24/7 technical help and one hour response for a production outage. Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise add faster response and a named technical account manager. Support covers AWS services, not bugs in your own code.
Use it when: You run anything in production; You need somebody to call during an outage; You want a service limit raised quickly
Do NOT use it when: You just want a general question answered, re:Post is free; You want somebody to write or debug your application, support will not do that, hire a Partner or Professional Services
Example: Your RDS instance fails over at midnight and you open a severity one case that gets a reply in under an hour.
How you pay: Developer starts around $29 a month, Business around $100 a month, but both are really a percentage of your AWS spend once it grows, which is the bit that surprises people. Enterprise On-Ramp starts around $5,500 a month and Enterprise around $15,000 a month.

### AWS Training Certification
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-training-certification.html
In one sentence: AWS courses and exams, some free, that prove you know the services.
Picture it as: Driving lessons and a driving licence. The lessons help, the licence is what employers ask to see.
What it does: Free digital courses on AWS Skill Builder, paid classroom and lab training, and exams such as Cloud Practitioner, Solutions Architect Associate and the specialty certs. The exams test recall of AWS specifics, so passing one is not the same as having built anything. Certifications expire after three years.
Use it when: You are new to AWS and want a structured path; Your employer or a partner tier needs certified staff; You want the hands on labs rather than reading docs
Do NOT use it when: You want to actually learn to build, do a real small project alongside, certification alone does not teach you that; You want vendor neutral cloud knowledge, this is AWS specific by design
Example: A developer does the free Cloud Practitioner course in a week, then sits the exam for $100 to satisfy a client requirement.
How you pay: Much of Skill Builder is free. Exams cost roughly $100 to $300 depending on level. Instructor led classes and the paid Skill Builder subscription cost extra.

### AWS rePost
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-repost.html
In one sentence: A free public question and answer site for AWS, run by AWS.
Picture it as: A public library help desk. Free, useful, but you wait for whoever is around to answer.
What it does: The replacement for the old AWS Forums. You ask a question in public and community members or AWS staff may answer. Answers are not guaranteed and not a support commitment. Quality varies, and for a specific account problem it is usually slower than a support ticket.
Use it when: A general how do I question about a service; You want to search what others already asked; You have no paid support plan
Do NOT use it when: Your production system is down, open an AWS Support case, do not post in public; The question involves account numbers, billing detail or anything private, it is a public site
Example: You ask why a Lambda function times out reaching RDS, and somebody points you at the VPC subnet setup.
How you pay: Free.

### AWS rePost Private
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-repost-private.html
In one sentence: A private version of the re:Post question site, just for your company. It is being shut down.
Picture it as: An internal staff noticeboard instead of a public one.
What it does: A private knowledge and question space for large AWS customers, where your own engineers and AWS support staff answer internal questions. It is closed to new customers and reaches end of service on 30 June 2027, after which all private spaces are removed. Very few organisations ever used it.
Use it when: Almost never, it is closing; Only if you already have a space and need to plan an exit
Do NOT use it when: You want an internal knowledge base, use Confluence, Notion, SharePoint or a wiki, not a service with an end date; You want expert answers from AWS, that is your Enterprise Support plan and your technical account manager
Example: A large enterprise ran an internal space where staff asked AWS questions without going public. Those spaces now need moving elsewhere before mid 2027.
How you pay: Tiered, tied to Enterprise or Enterprise On-Ramp Support. Not worth pricing now given the shutdown.

## Databases


### AWS Database Migration Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-database-migration-service.html
In one sentence: Moves a database into AWS with almost no downtime.
Picture it as: Shifting house while still living in it. Things move across one room at a time.
What it does: DMS copies an existing database into AWS and keeps replicating changes until you switch over. It can also change engine, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL, paired with the conversion tool.
Use it when: Moving an on premise database to AWS; Changing database engine
Do NOT use it when: A small database you can dump and restore in an hour.
Example: Moving a live MySQL server to RDS with minutes of downtime, not days.
How you pay: Per replication instance hour.

### Amazon Aurora
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-aurora.html
In one sentence: Amazon's faster version of MySQL and PostgreSQL.
Picture it as: The same car, tuned. It drives the same way, it just goes faster and recovers better.
What it does: Aurora speaks MySQL and PostgreSQL, so your code usually works unchanged. Storage grows on its own and copies data across three availability zones. Serverless versions can scale down when quiet.
Use it when: You outgrew RDS; You need more read copies; Traffic goes up and down a lot
Do NOT use it when: A tiny app. Plain RDS is cheaper.
Example: A growing LMS where thousands of students log in at exam time.
How you pay: Per hour, plus storage used, plus reads and writes. Serverless charges by capacity used.

### Amazon DocumentDB
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-documentdb.html
In one sentence: It is a database that speaks MongoDB's language but is built and run by AWS.
Picture it as: A coffee shop that makes a drink tasting like a famous chain's, close enough for most people, not identical.
What it does: You point a MongoDB driver at it and store JSON-like documents, and AWS handles backups, patching and failover. It is compatible with the MongoDB API up to version 5.0, not with MongoDB itself, so some commands, aggregation stages and features are missing. Check compatibility before committing, because migrations away from it are painful.
Use it when: Moving an existing MongoDB app onto managed AWS infrastructure; You want document storage without running database servers; You need the MongoDB query style rather than SQL
Do NOT use it when: You need the full modern MongoDB feature set, use MongoDB Atlas which also runs on AWS; You are starting fresh with simple key lookups, DynamoDB is cheaper and scales better
Example: A content platform moves its self-hosted MongoDB cluster to DocumentDB so nobody has to patch servers at midnight.
How you pay: Per instance-hour plus storage, I/O and backups. The surprise is that it runs on always-on instances, so a small idle cluster still costs over 200 dollars a month, and I/O charges can exceed the instance cost.

### Amazon DynamoDB
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-dynamodb.html
In one sentence: A very fast database with no tables to join.
Picture it as: A cloakroom. You hand over a ticket, you get your coat instantly. You cannot ask it which coats are blue.
What it does: DynamoDB gives single digit millisecond reads at any scale. You must know how you will look data up before you design it. Queries it was not designed for are slow or impossible.
Use it when: Huge scale, simple lookups; Sessions, carts, device data; You want zero database administration
Do NOT use it when: You need flexible reporting queries; Your access patterns keep changing
Example: Storing which lesson each student is currently on, looked up by student id.
How you pay: Per read and write, or a fixed capacity. Plus storage.

### Amazon ElastiCache
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elasticache.html
In one sentence: Keeps frequently used data in memory so it is fast.
Picture it as: Keeping the tools you use most on the bench, not in the store room.
What it does: ElastiCache runs Redis or Memcached. It holds results in memory so your database is not asked the same question a thousand times. Memory is not permanent, so never keep the only copy here.
Use it when: Slow repeated queries; Session storage; Leaderboards and counters
Do NOT use it when: Data you cannot afford to lose.
Example: Caching the course list so the database is hit once a minute, not once a click.
How you pay: Per node hour.

### Amazon Keyspaces
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-keyspaces.html
In one sentence: It stores data the way Apache Cassandra does, without you running any Cassandra servers.
Picture it as: Renting a self-drive car that has the same controls you already learned, so you can drive off without lessons.
What it does: It accepts Cassandra CQL queries and drivers, and scales storage and throughput on its own. It is API compatible, not real Cassandra, so some features such as materialized views and certain consistency options behave differently or are missing. It is a narrow service, mainly useful if you already have Cassandra code.
Use it when: You have a Cassandra application and do not want to operate a cluster; You need wide-row, high-write workloads with a known access pattern; Your team already knows CQL
Do NOT use it when: You are starting a new project on AWS with no Cassandra history, DynamoDB is the better default; You depend on Cassandra internals or unusual features, run Cassandra yourself on EC2
Example: A telecom team lifts an existing CQL-based event store off a self-managed cluster and keeps the same client code.
How you pay: Per read and write request plus storage, or provisioned capacity. Costs climb fast with large rows, because you are billed by data size per operation, not per row.

### Amazon MemoryDB
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-memorydb.html
In one sentence: It is a very fast in-memory store that, unlike a normal cache, does not lose your data.
Picture it as: A whiteboard that quietly photocopies itself every time you write on it, so wiping it by accident costs nothing.
What it does: It is compatible with Valkey and Redis, so existing clients work, but every write is also stored in a durable multi-zone log before it is acknowledged. That makes it safe to use as the main database, which plain ElastiCache is not. The trade-off is slower writes than a pure cache and a much higher bill, since everything lives in RAM.
Use it when: You need microsecond reads and cannot lose the data; Replacing a cache plus database pair with one system; Session or leaderboard data that must survive a node failure
Do NOT use it when: You only need a cache in front of a real database, use ElastiCache, it is cheaper; Your data set is large or cold, RAM pricing will hurt, use DynamoDB
Example: A payments service keeps live fraud counters in MemoryDB so a node restart does not reset them.
How you pay: Per node-hour by memory size, plus a charge per gigabyte written to the durable log. The write charge is the part people do not expect.

### Amazon Neptune
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-neptune.html
In one sentence: It is a database for things that are connected to other things, and for the connections themselves.
Picture it as: A family tree on a wall. The lines between the names matter as much as the names.
What it does: You store nodes and the relationships between them, and ask questions like who is two steps away from this person, using Gremlin, openCypher or SPARQL. There is also Neptune Analytics for running graph algorithms over a loaded data set. Graph databases are a genuinely small niche, and most problems people bring to them are better handled by SQL joins.
Use it when: Fraud rings, recommendations or identity resolution; Knowledge graphs where relationships are the main data; Queries that would need many levels of joins in SQL
Do NOT use it when: Your relationships are only one or two joins deep, use RDS or Aurora; You want a graph for the sake of it, the operating cost and learning curve are real
Example: A bank finds accounts that share a phone number with an account that shares an address with a known fraudster.
How you pay: Per instance-hour plus storage and I/O, or serverless capacity units. There is no cheap idle mode on provisioned instances, so a test cluster left running is an expensive mistake.

### Amazon RDS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-rds.html
In one sentence: A normal SQL database, run for you.
Picture it as: A rented flat with a cleaner included. It is still your flat, someone else does the chores.
What it does: RDS runs MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle or SQL Server. AWS handles backups, patching and standby copies. You still design the tables and write the queries.
Use it when: You already know SQL; Normal business data: orders, users, invoices
Do NOT use it when: You need one database serving the whole world at once. Look at Aurora or DynamoDB.
Example: The orders table for a shop, with an automatic nightly backup.
How you pay: Per hour the database is on, by size, plus storage and backups.

### Amazon Timestream
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-timestream.html
In one sentence: It stores readings that arrive with a timestamp, like sensor or metric data.
Picture it as: A logbook where every entry is stamped with the time and you mostly ask what happened between two times.
What it does: Read the status carefully, because the name covers two different things now. Timestream for LiveAnalytics, the original AWS-built engine, was closed to new customers on 20 June 2025, so you cannot start using it unless you already do. The version still open is Timestream for InfluxDB, which is AWS running the open source InfluxDB for you.
Use it when: You already use InfluxDB and want it managed; IoT device readings or application metrics kept for a long time; Queries that are almost always time ranges and roll-ups
Do NOT use it when: You are new to AWS and want time series storage, do not plan on LiveAnalytics, it is closed to new customers; You only want dashboards and alarms on your own systems, CloudWatch already does that
Example: A solar company stores per-minute output from 5,000 inverters and charts the last 90 days.
How you pay: Timestream for InfluxDB bills per instance-hour and storage, like a database. Idle instances still cost money, so it is not a cheap parking spot for old data.

### Oracle Database at AWS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/oracle-database-at-aws.html
In one sentence: Runs real Oracle Exadata databases inside an AWS data centre, next to your apps.
Picture it as: Oracle renting a locked room inside AWS's building, with a door straight into your office.
What it does: This is a joint Oracle and AWS offering, also branded Oracle AI Database@AWS. Oracle's own hardware sits in an AWS Availability Zone and you link it to your VPC over an ODB network. You create the network and infrastructure in AWS, but you manage the databases themselves in the Oracle Cloud console, so you work in two clouds.
Use it when: You have Oracle Exadata workloads that cannot be rewritten; Apps on EC2 need very low latency to an Oracle database; You want Oracle licence benefits without your own data centre
Do NOT use it when: If your database is not Oracle, ignore this completely.; If you can move to PostgreSQL or MySQL, amazon-rds or Aurora is far cheaper and simpler.; For plain Oracle Database without Exadata, RDS for Oracle is the normal choice.; Buying is through a private offer, so this is enterprise only.
Example: An insurer keeps its Exadata core system in Oracle Database@AWS and points its EC2 application servers at it over a peered ODB network.
How you pay: Bought through AWS Marketplace as a private offer negotiated with Oracle, on committed terms. It is not pay as you go pricing, and it is expensive.

## Developer Tools


### AWS Cloud Control API
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloud-control-api.html
In one sentence: One set of five commands to create, read, update, delete and list almost any AWS thing.
Picture it as: A universal remote. Instead of a different remote for the TV, the fan and the lights, one remote with the same five buttons works on all of them.
What it does: Normally every AWS service has its own API with its own command names. Cloud Control API puts a single CRUDL interface in front of hundreds of resource types, so tool builders write one piece of code instead of hundreds. It is mostly used by people building infrastructure tools, like the Terraform Cloud Control provider. Coverage is not total, and it can lag behind a service's own API by a while.
Use it when: You are building a tool that manages many AWS resource types; You want new resource support without writing per service code; You already use CloudFormation resource types and want them callable directly
Do NOT use it when: You just want to create a few resources, use the AWS CLI or CDK; You need a service feature that is new or unusual, call that service's own API
Example: A small internal tool that can create an S3 bucket, a DynamoDB table or an SNS topic using the same function, just with a different type name.
How you pay: No charge for the API itself. You pay for whatever resources it creates, and those bills are easy to forget because the tool hides which service it touched.

### AWS Cloud Development Kit
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloud-development-kit.html
In one sentence: Write your AWS setup as normal code instead of a long config file.
Picture it as: A recipe you write in your own handwriting, which a machine then turns into the official form the kitchen requires.
What it does: CDK lets you describe infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Java, Go or C#. It converts that code into a CloudFormation template and deploys it. You get loops, variables and reuse, but you still inherit CloudFormation's behaviour underneath, including slow stack updates and awkward rollbacks. The generated template is often much bigger than one a person would write.
Use it when: Your setup repeats a lot and you want loops and functions; Your team already writes in one of the supported languages; You want sensible defaults instead of hand writing every property
Do NOT use it when: A handful of resources you will rarely change, plain CloudFormation or the console is simpler; Your team already runs on Terraform, adding CDK gives you two sources of truth
Example: Ten near identical Lambda functions defined with a for loop over a list of names, rather than ten copied blocks of YAML.
How you pay: CDK itself is free. The surprise is the deploy bucket and the bootstrap stack it creates in every account and region, plus charges for whatever it builds.

### AWS Cloud9
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloud9.html
In one sentence: A code editor that ran in your browser, now closed to new customers.
Picture it as: A shared workshop that stopped taking new members. The people already inside can keep working, but nobody new gets a key.
What it does: Cloud9 was a browser based IDE with a terminal attached to an EC2 machine. AWS stopped accepting new customers in mid 2024 and is not adding features. Existing users still have it. If you want a browser terminal today, use CloudShell, and for a full editor use VS Code on your own machine or a remote dev environment.
Use it when: You are an existing Cloud9 user and it still works for you; You are reading old tutorials and need to know why the button is missing
Do NOT use it when: You want a quick terminal in the browser, use CloudShell; You want a real IDE, use VS Code locally with the AWS Toolkit
Example: An old workshop tells you to open a Cloud9 environment, and your account has no option to create one.
How you pay: You paid for the EC2 instance behind it, not the editor. People were billed for idle environments they forgot to stop.

### AWS CloudShell
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloudshell.html
In one sentence: A terminal inside the AWS website that already knows who you are.
Picture it as: A courtesy phone in a hotel lobby. It is already connected, you just pick it up and use it.
What it does: Click the shell icon in the AWS console and you get a Linux command line with the AWS CLI installed and your console login already applied. It gives you a small home directory that persists, around 1 GB. The machine itself resets after about 20 minutes of no use, so anything installed outside your home directory disappears.
Use it when: You need to run one or two AWS commands without setting up keys locally; You are on a machine where you cannot install the CLI; You want to test what permissions your console role actually has
Do NOT use it when: You are running long builds or heavy jobs, use EC2 or CodeBuild; You need access to something inside a private VPC, it does not sit in your VPC by default
Example: Checking why an S3 bucket policy is blocking you, by running one CLI command from the console without touching your laptop.
How you pay: Free. The catch is the small home directory, which is deleted if you do not use that region for about 120 days.

### AWS CodeArtifact
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-codeartifact.html
In one sentence: A private store for the code libraries your team installs.
Picture it as: A company stockroom. Common parts are pulled in from the outside supplier once, and your own in house parts sit on the same shelves.
What it does: CodeArtifact hosts private npm, pip, Maven, NuGet and similar packages, and can also mirror public registries so builds do not break when a public package vanishes. Authentication uses a token that expires, up to 12 hours, so build scripts must fetch a fresh one. It supports fewer package formats than JFrog Artifactory.
Use it when: You publish internal libraries that must not be public; You want a cached copy of public packages so builds are repeatable; You already run builds in AWS and want package access controlled by IAM
Do NOT use it when: You only use public packages and builds are fine, this is extra work for nothing; You need Docker images, use ECR instead; You need a format it does not support, use Artifactory or GitHub Packages
Example: An internal Python utility library that every team installs with pip, without it ever being published to PyPI.
How you pay: Per GB stored, per request, and per GB transferred out of the region. The request charges add up when many build agents install the same packages repeatedly.

### AWS CodeBuild
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-codebuild.html
In one sentence: A machine AWS starts for you to compile and test your code, then throws away.
Picture it as: Hiring a kitchen by the hour. You bring the ingredients and the recipe, cook, and leave nothing behind.
What it does: You give CodeBuild a buildspec.yml listing the commands to run. It starts a clean container, runs them, keeps the logs and output files, then shuts down. Every build starts fresh, so dependency downloads repeat unless you turn on caching. Builds default to no VPC access, which surprises people trying to reach a private database.
Use it when: You want CI without running your own build servers; Your build must reach AWS resources using IAM instead of stored keys; You need a specific container image or large build machine on demand
Do NOT use it when: Your code lives on GitHub and the team is happy there, GitHub Actions is usually simpler; You need long running or always on build agents, use EC2 or ECS
Example: On every push, install dependencies, run the test suite, build a Docker image and push it to ECR.
How you pay: Per build minute, by machine size. The surprise is slow builds with no cache, and ARM or GPU sizes costing far more per minute.

### AWS CodeCommit
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-codecommit.html
In one sentence: AWS's own private Git repository hosting.
Picture it as: A filing cabinet in your own office rather than a shared one down the street.
What it does: CodeCommit stores Git repositories inside your AWS account with IAM controlling access. AWS closed it to new customers in 2024, then reversed that in late 2025 and made it generally available again with new features planned. It has no pull request review culture, issues, or actions comparable to GitHub or GitLab, so it is a bare repository host.
Use it when: Your rules say source code must stay inside your AWS account; You want repository access controlled by IAM roles, not separate accounts; You need a repo in a restricted region such as GovCloud
Do NOT use it when: You want code review, issues and a community, use GitHub or GitLab; Your CI already lives on GitHub, connecting AWS to it is easier than moving
Example: A bank keeping its deployment scripts in an account that has no route to the public internet.
How you pay: Free for the first five active users per month, then a flat fee per active user, with extra for storage and requests above the included amount.

### AWS CodeDeploy
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-codedeploy.html
In one sentence: Puts a new version of your app onto servers gradually, and rolls back if it breaks.
Picture it as: Changing the menu in one branch of a restaurant first. If customers complain, the other branches never get the new menu.
What it does: CodeDeploy pushes code to EC2 or on premises servers, or shifts traffic for Lambda and ECS. You get canary and linear rollouts, and automatic rollback on a CloudWatch alarm. On EC2 it needs an agent installed and an appspec.yml with lifecycle hooks, which is the fiddly part. It moves traffic, it does not build anything.
Use it when: You run on EC2 and want staged rollouts instead of replacing everything at once; You want an automatic rollback tied to an error alarm; You need blue green traffic shifting for ECS or Lambda
Do NOT use it when: You deploy containers and already use ECS rolling updates, that is often enough; Your infrastructure is defined in CDK or CloudFormation and deploys with the stack; You want the whole pipeline, that is CodePipeline
Example: Sending 10 percent of traffic to a new Lambda version for five minutes, then all of it if no errors fire.
How you pay: Free for Lambda and ECS deployments. On premises instance deployments cost per instance update, and EC2 deployments are free but you still pay for the instances.

### AWS CodePipeline
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-codepipeline.html
In one sentence: Joins the steps from code change to live release into one automatic chain.
Picture it as: A conveyor belt. Something is placed at one end, each station does its job, and it comes out finished at the other end.
What it does: CodePipeline watches a source, then runs stages in order: build, test, approve, deploy. It does not do the work, it calls CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CloudFormation and others. Version 2 added better triggers, branch filters and variables. It is rigid compared with a script, and approvals and cross account deploys take real setup.
Use it when: You want a visible chain of stages with manual approval gates; Your deploy steps already use AWS build and deploy services; You need separate dev, staging and production accounts in one flow
Do NOT use it when: Everything you need is in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, do not run two CI systems; You have one small app, a build job that deploys directly is simpler
Example: A push to main runs tests, waits for a human to click approve, then deploys the CloudFormation stack to production.
How you pay: A small monthly fee per active pipeline, free if unused that month. The real cost is the CodeBuild minutes each run burns.

### AWS Command Line Interface
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-command-line-interface.html
In one sentence: Type AWS commands in a terminal instead of clicking around the website.
Picture it as: Ordering by phone with an exact list, instead of walking every aisle of the shop.
What it does: The AWS CLI is one program that can call almost every AWS service. You install it, configure credentials, and run commands like aws s3 cp. Version 2 is the current one, version 1 reached end of support. Output is JSON by default, and the --query and --output flags are what make it usable. Some services have long, unfriendly command names.
Use it when: You want to script something you do repeatedly; You need a feature the console has not exposed yet; You are debugging permissions and want the exact error
Do NOT use it when: You are writing an application, use the SDK for your language, not shell calls; You want repeatable infrastructure, use CloudFormation or CDK, not a pile of CLI commands
Example: Copying a folder of files to S3 with one command instead of dragging them in the browser.
How you pay: Free. The trap is a command like a full S3 listing or a wide CloudWatch query running up request or scan charges.

### AWS Fault Injection Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-fault-injection-service.html
In one sentence: Deliberately breaks parts of your system so you can see how it copes.
Picture it as: A fire drill. You set off the alarm on purpose, on a day you choose, to find out whether people know the way out.
What it does: Formerly called AWS Fault Injection Simulator. It runs controlled experiments such as stopping EC2 instances, adding network latency, throttling an API, or failing over a database. You define stop conditions using CloudWatch alarms so the experiment aborts if real damage starts. This is a niche tool, useful mainly to teams that already have good monitoring and a real availability target.
Use it when: You claim multi AZ resilience and want proof; You are preparing for a game day or a disaster recovery test; You want to check that alarms and failover actually fire
Do NOT use it when: You have no monitoring yet, you will break things and learn nothing, fix observability first; You want to test application logic under load, use a load testing tool
Example: Stopping every instance in one availability zone for ten minutes to confirm the load balancer keeps serving traffic.
How you pay: Per action minute during an experiment. The real cost is the outage you cause if you skip stop conditions, so never start in production without them.

### AWS Infrastructure Composer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-infrastructure-composer.html
In one sentence: Draw your AWS setup on a canvas and get the config file out of it.
Picture it as: Sketching a floor plan by dragging furniture around, and the builder's drawing is produced from your sketch.
What it does: Renamed from AWS Application Composer in October 2024. You drag services onto a canvas in the console or in VS Code, connect them, and it writes a CloudFormation or SAM template. It also draws a diagram from an existing template, which is often the more useful direction. It covers a limited set of resource types well, and hand edits and canvas edits can fight each other.
Use it when: You are new to CloudFormation and want to see the shape of a template; You want a diagram of a template someone else wrote; You are sketching a small serverless app before writing code
Do NOT use it when: Your infrastructure is large or written in CDK, this will not help; You need full control over every property, write the template by hand
Example: Dragging an API Gateway, a Lambda and a DynamoDB table onto the canvas and exporting a working SAM template.
How you pay: Free to use. You pay for whatever the generated template deploys, which is easy to underestimate from a picture.

### AWS Tools and SDKs
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-tools-and-sdks.html
In one sentence: The official libraries that let your program talk to AWS.
Picture it as: The set of adapters that come with an appliance, one for each country's socket.
What it does: This is not one service, it is the collection: SDKs for Python (boto3), JavaScript, Java, Go, .NET, Rust and more, plus IDE plugins, the SAM CLI and toolkits. They handle signing requests, retries and credential lookup so you do not write that yourself. Each SDK has its own idea of defaults, especially around retries and timeouts, so check those rather than assuming.
Use it when: Your application needs to read or write AWS resources; You want credentials picked up automatically from a role; You want retries and request signing handled for you
Do NOT use it when: A one off task from your terminal, use the CLI; Managing infrastructure, use CDK or CloudFormation, not SDK calls in a script
Example: A Python Lambda using boto3 to write a record into DynamoDB, with no keys in the code because the role supplies them.
How you pay: Free to use. The surprise is aggressive default retries turning one failure into several billed API calls.

### AWS X Ray
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-x-ray.html
In one sentence: Follows one request through all your services and shows where the time went.
Picture it as: A parcel tracking page. You see every depot the parcel passed through and how long it sat at each one.
What it does: X-Ray collects traces from instrumented applications and draws a service map plus a timeline of each request. You must instrument your code or run an agent, it does not appear on its own. It samples by default, so a rare slow request may never be recorded. AWS now points new work toward OpenTelemetry and CloudWatch Application Signals, with X-Ray as the storage behind them.
Use it when: A request is slow and you do not know which service caused it; You have several services calling each other and need a map; You want to see downstream AWS call latency per request
Do NOT use it when: You have one small service, logs and CloudWatch metrics are enough; You already run Datadog, Honeycomb or another tracing tool, do not double instrument
Example: Finding that a 3 second API response was actually 2.6 seconds spent on one DynamoDB query, not on your code.
How you pay: Per trace recorded, per trace retrieved and per trace scanned. Turning sampling up to 100 percent on a busy service is the bill shock.

### Amazon CodeCatalyst
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-codecatalyst.html
In one sentence: AWS's all in one place for repos, pipelines and issues, now in maintenance mode.
Picture it as: A serviced office where the desks, phones and meeting rooms all came together. The landlord has stopped refurbishing it.
What it does: CodeCatalyst bundled Git hosting, CI workflows, issue tracking and dev environments into one product with project blueprints. AWS has moved it to maintenance mode, meaning it still runs but is not getting new development. Do not start new projects on it. Use GitHub or GitLab for the repo and issues, with CodePipeline or GitHub Actions for the pipeline.
Use it when: You already have projects on it and need to keep them running; You are evaluating it and need to know its status before committing
Do NOT use it when: You are starting a new project, use GitHub or GitLab; You want AWS native CI, use CodePipeline and CodeBuild
Example: An existing CodeCatalyst space still building an app, with a plan being written to move it to GitHub.
How you pay: There was a free tier, with charges for build minutes, storage and dev environment hours. The dev environments billed for uptime, not use.

### Amazon Corretto
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-corretto.html
In one sentence: Amazon's free version of Java, which they keep patched for years.
Picture it as: A generic medicine. Same formula as the branded one, made by someone else, and cheaper to keep taking.
What it does: Corretto is a build of OpenJDK that Amazon supports at no cost, with long term security updates for versions 8, 11, 17, 21 and newer. It runs anywhere, not only on AWS. It is not a service, it is a download, and it behaves like standard Java because it is certified against the Java standard. Most people switch to it purely to avoid Oracle's licence terms.
Use it when: You want free long term security patches for an old Java version; You want to avoid Oracle JDK licensing questions; You run Java on AWS and want the build AWS already tests against
Do NOT use it when: You need a feature only a commercial JDK offers, such as a specialist garbage collector; Your build is pinned and tested against another JDK, changing it for no reason adds risk
Example: A Java 11 service still in production, pulling Corretto 11 security updates years after Oracle's free updates stopped.
How you pay: Free, including the updates. No AWS account needed, and nothing appears on your bill.

## End User Computing


### Amazon WorkSpaces
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-workspaces.html
In one sentence: Gives each person a Windows or Linux desktop they open from any device.
Picture it as: A locker at work. Your things stay in it, and you can open it from any branch.
What it does: AWS runs the desktop in the cloud and streams the screen to a client app or browser. The desktop keeps your files and settings between sessions. Performance depends heavily on the user's internet, and Windows licensing rules can be awkward if you bring your own.
Use it when: Contractors need access without company laptops; Staff must work from home on a locked down machine; Data must never sit on a personal device
Do NOT use it when: If you only need one application, not a whole desktop, AppStream 2.0 is cheaper.; If people only need a safe browser, use WorkSpaces Secure Browser.; For developers who just need a Linux shell, an amazon-ec2 instance is simpler and cheaper.; With bad or high latency internet, this feels terrible. Do not force it.
Example: A support team of 200 contractors in another country logs into WorkSpaces each morning, and no customer data leaves AWS.
How you pay: Monthly per desktop, or hourly plus a smaller monthly fee. The surprise is the monthly option charges a full month even if someone logs in once, and idle desktops keep billing until you delete them.

## Front End Web and Mobile


### AWS Amplify
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-amplify.html
In one sentence: The quickest way to put a web or mobile front end online.
Picture it as: A ready made kitchen fitted in a day, instead of building one.
What it does: Amplify hosts your front end, connects to GitHub and deploys on every push. It can also generate a backend with auth, API and storage. Great to start, restrictive once your needs grow.
Use it when: React, Next.js or Vue front ends; Quick prototypes and MVPs
Do NOT use it when: Complex custom backends.
Example: Pushing to GitHub and the site is live two minutes later.
How you pay: Per build minute and per GB served, with a free tier.

### AWS Device Farm
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-device-farm.html
In one sentence: Lets you test your app on real phones and tablets sitting in an AWS data centre.
Picture it as: A shop display of a hundred different phones you can borrow one at a time, remotely.
What it does: You upload your app and either run automated tests on many devices at once, or take manual remote control of one device and tap through it yourself. It covers real hardware, not just simulators, which is the point. Device availability varies, and the newest handsets are not always there. Note that its desktop browser testing feature was retired, so it is now mobile devices only.
Use it when: Checking an app on Android models you do not own; A bug that only appears on one manufacturer's phone; Automated test runs across many devices before a release
Do NOT use it when: Testing a website across browsers, use Playwright yourself or a browser testing service; A team with a shelf of test phones already, this adds cost and latency; Unit tests, run those in CI
Example: A release candidate is run on 25 Android models overnight and crashes on two older Samsung handsets.
How you pay: Per device minute, or a flat monthly fee for unlimited testing slots. Long automated suites across many devices multiply minutes quickly.

### Amazon Location Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-location-service.html
In one sentence: Maps, address lookup, routes and location tracking for your app, without a Google Maps contract.
Picture it as: An A to Z street atlas with a ruler and an index, available to your app as it runs.
What it does: It bundles map tiles, geocoding, routing, geofences and a tracker for moving devices, using map data from Esri, HERE and others. The pricing is usually cheaper than Google Maps at volume, which is the main reason teams pick it. The map styles and place data are less rich than Google's, and the SDK ecosystem is smaller, so expect more work in the front end.
Use it when: Showing a map or tracking vehicles in your own app; Turning addresses into coordinates in bulk; Alerting when a delivery driver enters or leaves an area
Do NOT use it when: Rich place details, reviews and street imagery, Google Maps is far ahead; A simple static map image on a web page, an image from a tile provider is less setup; Indoor positioning or precise asset tracking in a building, this is not built for that
Example: A delivery app draws each driver on a map and fires an alert when a van enters the customer's street.
How you pay: Per thousand map tile loads, geocoding requests, route calculations and tracked position updates. A map heavy screen that reloads tiles on every pan is what inflates the bill.

## Games


### Amazon GameLift Servers
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-gamelift-servers.html
In one sentence: Runs and scales the game servers for a multiplayer game.
Picture it as: A sports centre that opens more courts as more players turn up, and closes them when people leave.
What it does: This is the current name for what was called Amazon GameLift. The GameLift brand now covers several products, and this one is the server hosting part. It places players into game sessions, scales fleets up and down, and includes FlexMatch matchmaking. Your game server has to be built against its SDK, so it is not a drop in.
Use it when: A session based multiplayer game needs servers near players; Player numbers swing wildly between launch and quiet hours; You want matchmaking without writing it yourself
Do NOT use it when: If the game is turn based or not real time, a normal API on amazon-api-gateway and aws-lambda is much cheaper.; If you already run your own orchestration, use amazon-elastic-container-service or EKS and skip the SDK work.; Only game studios need this.
Example: A shooter launches worldwide; fleets in 12 Regions scale on player demand and FlexMatch groups players by skill and ping.
How you pay: Per instance hour for the fleet, plus data transfer. Spot instances cut cost a lot. The surprise is that you pay for spare capacity you keep warm for demand spikes.

### Amazon GameLift Streams
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-gamelift-streams.html
In one sentence: Runs a game on an AWS machine and streams the video to a player's browser or device.
Picture it as: A television channel where the console is in the broadcaster's building and only the picture reaches your screen.
What it does: Launched in 2025. The game runs on GPU machines in AWS, and the player's device just shows the video and sends back controller input. It means a player with weak hardware can play a heavy game, and it can run in a browser with no install. It is separate from GameLift Servers, which hosts multiplayer logic rather than pictures. Streaming quality depends heavily on the player's network latency.
Use it when: Playable demos in a browser with no download; Reaching players on low powered devices; Letting people try a PC game before buying
Do NOT use it when: Ordinary multiplayer hosting, that is GameLift Servers; Players on slow or high latency connections, the experience will be poor; Mobile friendly casual games that run fine on the device itself
Example: A studio puts a Try it now button on its website and the full PC game starts in the visitor's browser in seconds.
How you pay: Per hour of GPU streaming capacity, plus data transfer for the video. Idle capacity held ready so players start instantly is charged too, and video egress adds up fast.

### Open 3D Engine
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/open-3d-engine.html
In one sentence: A free 3D game and simulation engine you download and build with.
Picture it as: A free workshop full of tools. Nobody charges rent, but you still have to build the furniture.
What it does: O3DE is not an AWS service. It is open source software under the Linux Foundation, built from the code of the retired AWS Lumberyard. AWS is one member of the foundation, not the owner. It is far less used than Unreal or Unity, so tutorials, assets and hiring are thin.
Use it when: You want a 3D engine with no royalties and full source; Robotics simulation, where its ROS support is used; You need to change engine internals
Do NOT use it when: For most games, Unreal or Unity has a far bigger ecosystem. Pick those unless royalties or source access are the deciding issue.; There is nothing to buy or switch on in the AWS console.; If you need hosted game servers, that is Amazon GameLift Servers, a different thing.
Example: A robotics team simulates a warehouse robot in O3DE before running the same code on real hardware.
How you pay: Free, with no royalties. You pay only for whatever machines you run it on.

## General


### AWS Marketplace Dark
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-marketplace-dark.html
In one sentence: Not a service. It is the dark background version of the AWS Marketplace icon.
Picture it as: The white version of a company logo used on a black poster. Same logo, different sheet.
What it does: This is an entry from the AWS Architecture Icons set, where many icons ship in a light and a dark variant. There is no product called AWS Marketplace Dark, nothing to sign up for and nothing to pay. The real thing is AWS Marketplace, an online store for software you can buy and run on AWS, billed through your AWS account.
Use it when: Drawing an architecture diagram on a dark slide; Building a diagram tool's icon library
Do NOT use it when: If you wanted the store, that is AWS Marketplace, not this icon file.; Do not put this in a service list or a cost estimate. It is an image asset.; Nobody needs to learn this.
Example: A solutions architect drops the dark Marketplace icon into a diagram that uses a black background.
How you pay: Nothing. It is an image. AWS Marketplace itself adds the vendor's software charges to your normal AWS bill.

### AWS Marketplace Light
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-marketplace-light.html
In one sentence: Not a product. It is the light-background version of the AWS Marketplace icon.
Picture it as: A shop sign printed in two colours, one for a white wall and one for a black wall.
What it does: This is not a service. It is an icon variant from the AWS architecture icon set, where AWS Marketplace is drawn twice, once light and once dark, so diagrams look right on either background. The real thing behind the icon is AWS Marketplace, an online store where you buy software and data from other companies and the cost lands on your AWS bill. Nothing runs when you 'use' this icon.
Use it when: Drawing an architecture diagram on a dark slide or a light slide; Picking the correct icon file from the AWS icon pack; Showing that part of your stack is bought software, not built in-house
Do NOT use it when: If you actually want to buy software, go to AWS Marketplace itself, not this icon.; If you want to sell software on AWS, that is AWS Marketplace seller listings, managed through AWS Partner Central.; Nobody needs to 'learn' this. It is a picture file.
Example: You are drawing your VPC diagram in a dark theme, so you drop in the dark icon and leave the light one alone.
How you pay: Nothing. Icons are free. AWS Marketplace purchases themselves are charged by the seller and appear on your normal AWS bill, often as a monthly or hourly software fee on top of the EC2 cost.

## Internet of Things


### AWS IoT Core
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-core.html
In one sentence: It is the front door where your gadgets connect to AWS and send messages.
Picture it as: A post office for machines. Every device has its own registered address, drops off letters, and picks up letters left for it, even if it was switched off for a while.
What it does: Devices connect over MQTT, WebSockets or HTTPS using certificates, and publish messages to named topics. A rules engine then forwards those messages to other AWS services like Lambda, S3 or a database. It also keeps a 'device shadow', a stored copy of each device's last known and wanted state, so your app can read or set values while the device is offline. It handles the plumbing, not your application logic, and you still have to design topics, certificates and data format yourself.
Use it when: Many small devices sending small readings; You need per device identity and certificates; You want device data to land in AWS services automatically
Do NOT use it when: A handful of devices you control, where a plain HTTPS API behind API Gateway is simpler and cheaper; Phone or browser apps, use API Gateway or AppSync instead of pretending they are IoT devices; High volume telemetry that only needs to be streamed and stored, Kinesis Data Streams is a better fit
Example: Two thousand water meters each publish a reading every fifteen minutes, and a rule writes each reading into DynamoDB.
How you pay: Per million messages, plus separate charges for connection minutes, rules engine actions and device shadow reads and writes. The surprise is that one incoming message can be billed several times over as it passes through each part.

### AWS IoT Device Defender
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-device-defender.html
In one sentence: It watches your connected devices for signs that one has been tampered with.
Picture it as: A building security guard who knows the normal routine. If a door that opens twice a day suddenly opens forty times at three in the morning, the guard raises it.
What it does: It has two parts. Audit checks your AWS setup for weak settings, like certificates that are shared between devices, expiring, or policies that are too open. Detect watches device behaviour against rules or a learned baseline and alerts on odd traffic. Note that Device Defender Detect moves to maintenance and access is restricted from 31 August 2026, so do not build new work on Detect; Audit is unaffected.
Use it when: A fleet where a stolen device could be used to attack you; You need evidence of security checks for an auditor; Certificate and policy hygiene across many devices
Do NOT use it when: Small fleets, where reading CloudWatch metrics yourself is enough; Account wide threat detection, that is GuardDuty; New behaviour monitoring work, since Detect is being retired, build alerting on CloudWatch and your own rules
Example: An alert when one smart lock starts opening two hundred MQTT connections an hour instead of its usual one.
How you pay: Per device per month for audit checks, and per behaviour metric checked for Detect. Costs grow with the number of behaviours you define, not just device count.

### AWS IoT Device Management
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-device-management.html
In one sentence: It helps you keep track of and update a large number of devices at once.
Picture it as: A fleet manager for a delivery company. It keeps the list of every van, groups them by depot, and rolls out a change to one group at a time instead of all at once.
What it does: It sits on top of IoT Core and adds bulk registration, searchable device groups, over the air software update jobs, and secure tunnelling so you can open a remote shell to a device behind a firewall. Jobs can be rolled out gradually and stopped automatically if too many devices fail. It manages devices, it does not run your device software.
Use it when: Thousands of devices in the field needing firmware updates; You need to find devices by attribute, like model or region; You need remote access to a device for support
Do NOT use it when: Under a hundred devices, the plain IoT Core registry and your own scripts are enough; Servers or containers, use Systems Manager instead; Devices you can physically reach to update
Example: Pushing a firmware update to five thousand vending machines, ten percent at a time, pausing if failures pass five percent.
How you pay: Per device registered, per bulk registration, per search query, and per minute of secure tunnelling. Tunnelling sessions left open are a common unwanted charge.

### AWS IoT Events
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-events.html
In one sentence: A service, now being retired, that watched device readings and reacted when a pattern appeared.
Picture it as: A checklist on the wall that says: if the light stays red for ten minutes, ring the bell. It is being taken down.
What it does: IoT Events let you define a state machine in the console, for example normal, warning and fault, with the conditions that move a device between states and the actions to take, such as sending an SNS message. It is being retired. New customers were cut off on 20 May 2025 and support ends on 20 May 2026. AWS suggests rebuilding the logic with IoT Core, Lambda, DynamoDB for state, and EventBridge.
Use it when: Nothing new, it is closing; Only if you already run it and are planning the move off it
Do NOT use it when: Any new alerting logic, use IoT Core rules into Lambda with state in DynamoDB; Simple threshold alarms, a CloudWatch alarm is enough; Complex workflow across steps, use Step Functions
Example: A rule that raised a ticket if a freezer stayed above minus fifteen degrees for twenty minutes now runs as a Lambda with state kept in DynamoDB.
How you pay: Charged per message evaluated and per detector. Becomes irrelevant after May 2026.

### AWS IoT ExpressLink
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-expresslink.html
In one sentence: A ready made connectivity chip, so a simple product can reach AWS without you writing network code.
Picture it as: A pre paid mobile dongle for a machine. You plug it in, send it plain text commands, and it handles the phone network and the security for you.
What it does: ExpressLink is not really a service you switch on, it is a specification that hardware makers such as Espressif and u blox build modules to. Your microcontroller talks to the module over a serial link with simple AT style commands, and the module handles Wi-Fi or cellular, TLS, certificates and the MQTT connection to IoT Core. It saves firmware effort at the cost of buying a specific module and accepting what it supports.
Use it when: A small product team with no embedded security experience; A microcontroller too small for a full TLS and MQTT stack; You want to get a connected product to market quickly
Do NOT use it when: A device already running Linux, just use the AWS IoT device SDK; Anything needing unusual protocols or fine control of the connection; Cases where the extra hardware cost per unit at scale outweighs the saved development time
Example: A battery powered water leak alarm whose small chip sends one MQTT message by writing a single command line to the module.
How you pay: There is no AWS charge for ExpressLink itself. You pay for the module in your bill of materials and for the IoT Core messages it sends.

### AWS IoT FleetWise
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-fleetwise.html
In one sentence: It collects data from vehicles, choosing what to send so you do not pay for every signal.
Picture it as: A dashcam that only saves the clip when something interesting happens, rather than filming the whole journey and posting you the tapes.
What it does: You describe a vehicle's signals from its CAN bus or other network, then write campaigns that say which signals to collect and under what conditions, for example brake pressure only when speed is over eighty. An agent in the vehicle applies that and uploads to AWS. It is a narrow service for carmakers and fleet operators, and it needs access to the vehicle's signal database, so most people cannot use it at all.
Use it when: You build or operate vehicles and control their software; Mobile data costs make sending everything impossible; Engineering teams investigating faults across a model range
Do NOT use it when: Tracking where vehicles are, a GPS tracker into IoT Core is far cheaper; Non vehicle machinery, use IoT SiteWise; Anyone without access to the vehicle bus and signal definitions
Example: Collecting battery cell temperatures from ten thousand electric cars, but only during fast charging.
How you pay: Per vehicle per month plus per signal message collected. Campaigns that trigger more often than expected drive the cost up quickly.

### AWS IoT Greengrass
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-greengrass.html
In one sentence: It runs AWS style code on your own hardware, near the machines, even without internet.
Picture it as: A branch office that can keep serving customers when the phone line to head office goes down, then sends the paperwork up later.
What it does: You install the Greengrass runtime on a Linux device such as an industrial PC or gateway. It runs components, which can be Lambda functions, containers or plain programs, caches messages while offline, talks to nearby devices, and syncs with IoT Core when the link returns. Version 1 is being retired, so use version 2. You are responsible for the hardware, the operating system and keeping it patched.
Use it when: Unreliable or expensive connectivity at the site; Decisions that must happen in milliseconds, locally; Data too bulky or too sensitive to send raw to the cloud
Do NOT use it when: Devices with a solid always on connection, plain IoT Core is far less work; Tiny microcontrollers that cannot run Linux, use FreeRTOS or ExpressLink; A single site where an ordinary local server and your own code would do
Example: A gateway on a factory floor that reads a conveyor sensor, stops the line locally on a fault, and uploads a summary each hour.
How you pay: Per active device per month, plus the IoT Core messages it sends. The hidden cost is the field engineering to install and maintain hundreds of edge boxes.

### AWS IoT SiteWise
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-sitewise.html
In one sentence: It collects readings from factory machines and stores them in a way that matches how the plant is laid out.
Picture it as: A meter reading book for a whole factory, where each page is a machine and each machine belongs to a line, and a line belongs to a site.
What it does: An edge gateway reads industrial protocols such as OPC UA and sends the values to AWS. You then model your equipment as assets with properties and hierarchies, and define metrics computed from raw readings, for example machine uptime per shift. It comes with a simple dashboard tool called Monitor. Setting up the asset model is real work and the service only pays off in a plant with a lot of equipment. The SiteWise Edge data processing pack reached end of support in October 2025.
Use it when: Existing factory equipment speaking OPC UA or Modbus; You want equipment metrics like OEE without writing a pipeline; Many sites you want to compare on the same model
Do NOT use it when: Consumer or one off devices, use IoT Core and a time series database; Plain time series storage with no equipment hierarchy, Timestream is simpler; A handful of sensors, where CloudWatch metrics are enough
Example: Reading temperature and cycle count from twelve injection moulding machines and showing downtime per shift.
How you pay: Per message ingested, per computed metric, per data storage tier and per Monitor user. Computed metrics recalculating often is the usual bill shock.

### AWS IoT TwinMaker
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iot-twinmaker.html
In one sentence: Builds a live 3D model of a real factory or building that updates from its sensors.
Picture it as: A doll's house of your factory where the tiny lights turn on when the real lights turn on.
What it does: It takes a 3D model you already have, then wires each part of it to live data from sensors, cameras and business systems. Operators see the building on screen with real readings attached. The honest limitation is that it does not create the 3D model or the sensors for you, and the viewing layer is a Grafana plugin, so you need both before it is useful.
