Use it when: Plant operators need one screen showing equipment status in physical context; You already have CAD or 3D models of a site and live sensor data; Diagnosing which machine on a line is causing a problem
Do NOT use it when: If you only need charts and alarms, use Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Grafana. A 3D scene is a lot of work for a line graph.; If you just need to collect and store sensor readings, use AWS IoT Core and a database.; Most companies never need this. It suits large industrial sites with existing 3D models.
Example: A cookie factory shows its oven in 3D, and the oven turns red on screen when its real temperature sensor goes out of range.
How you pay: You pay per query against the digital twin and per GB of data stored, plus the cost of every underlying service. The surprise is that the bill is mostly the other services, the sensors, storage and the Grafana users, not TwinMaker itself.

### FreeRTOS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/freertos.html
In one sentence: A tiny free operating system that runs on very small chips inside devices.
Picture it as: The brain of a washing machine, not the brain of a laptop.
What it does: FreeRTOS is open source software you compile into a microcontroller, the sort of chip in a thermostat or a sensor. It handles running several small tasks on time. AWS looks after the project and adds libraries for talking to AWS IoT securely. It was briefly called Amazon FreeRTOS, then renamed back to FreeRTOS. It is not a cloud service and nothing of it runs in AWS.
Use it when: Writing firmware for a battery powered sensor or small device; You need several jobs on one small chip to run on a fixed schedule; Connecting a microcontroller to AWS IoT with TLS and over-the-air updates
Do NOT use it when: If your device runs Linux, such as a Raspberry Pi or a gateway, use AWS IoT Greengrass instead.; If you are not writing embedded C, this has nothing for you.; If you only want the cloud side of IoT, that is AWS IoT Core. FreeRTOS is the device side.
Example: A water meter with a small chip runs FreeRTOS, wakes hourly, reads the meter, and publishes one message to AWS IoT Core.
How you pay: Nothing. It is MIT licensed and free, including for commercial products. You pay only for the AWS services the device talks to, such as AWS IoT Core messages.

## Management and Governance


### AWS AppConfig
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-appconfig.html
In one sentence: Changes a setting in your running app without redeploying the code.
Picture it as: The dimmer switch on the wall. You change the brightness without rewiring the lamp.
What it does: You store settings, like feature flags or limits, outside your app. The app checks for the current value and picks up changes within about a minute. AppConfig can roll a change out slowly and roll it back automatically if alarms fire. It is part of AWS Systems Manager, not a separate console, which confuses people. It is for small config values, not for secrets and not for large data.
Use it when: Turning a feature on for 5 percent of users first; Changing a timeout or rate limit without a deploy; Config changes that need a safe, staged rollout
Do NOT use it when: Storing passwords or API keys, use AWS Secrets Manager; Plain static settings nobody changes at runtime, a Parameter Store value or an environment variable is simpler
Example: You flip a flag to turn off a slow search feature during a traffic spike, with no deploy and no restart.
How you pay: Per configuration request your app makes. The surprise is polling: an app that checks every second across many instances adds up, so you cache and poll less often.

### AWS Application Auto Scaling
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-application-auto-scaling.html
In one sentence: Adds and removes capacity automatically for AWS services other than plain servers.
Picture it as: A cafe that opens extra tills when the queue gets long and closes them when it is quiet.
What it does: It watches a metric, like CPU or queue length, and changes how much capacity a service has. It covers things like ECS tasks, DynamoDB tables, Aurora read replicas and SageMaker endpoints. It does not scale EC2 instances, that is EC2 Auto Scaling, and the similar names cause real confusion.
Use it when: Scaling the number of ECS or Fargate tasks; Scaling DynamoDB read and write capacity; Scaling a machine learning endpoint by traffic
Do NOT use it when: Scaling EC2 virtual machines, use EC2 Auto Scaling groups; Traffic that spikes in seconds, scaling takes minutes, so use a queue or serverless like AWS Lambda
Example: Your order service runs 3 containers overnight and 30 at lunchtime, with nobody touching it.
How you pay: The scaling itself is free. You pay for whatever capacity it turns on, which is the whole point and also the bill.

### AWS Auto Scaling
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-auto-scaling.html
In one sentence: One screen to set up scaling across several services at once.
Picture it as: A master thermostat for the whole house instead of one dial per room.
What it does: It is a front end over EC2 Auto Scaling and Application Auto Scaling. You pick an app, say whether you care more about cost or availability, and it sets scaling policies on the pieces. Most engineers skip it and configure the underlying services directly, often through infrastructure as code. It gets little attention and is easy to mistake for EC2 Auto Scaling, which is the one people actually mean.
Use it when: A first, quick scaling setup across a small stack; Wanting one plan covering EC2 and DynamoDB together
Do NOT use it when: Anything defined in Terraform or CloudFormation, set the underlying policies directly; A single service, go straight to EC2 Auto Scaling or Application Auto Scaling
Example: You point it at a web app and it puts target tracking on both the EC2 group and the DynamoDB table.
How you pay: Free. You pay only for the capacity that gets added.

### AWS Backint Agent
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-backint-agent.html
In one sentence: Backs up an SAP HANA database straight into S3 using SAP's own backup screens.
Picture it as: A plug adapter, so SAP's existing backup button works with an Amazon cupboard.
What it does: It is a small program you install on the EC2 machine running SAP HANA. It is certified by SAP and implements SAP's Backint interface, so backups triggered from SAP HANA Cockpit, Studio or SQL land in Amazon S3 or AWS Backup. It supports full, incremental, differential and log backups. It only works for SAP HANA. It does nothing for any other database.
Use it when: You run SAP HANA on EC2 and want backups in S3 rather than on disk; Your SAP team wants to keep using their own backup tools and schedules; You need log backups going to durable storage continuously
Do NOT use it when: If your database is not SAP HANA, this is the wrong tool. Use Amazon RDS backups or AWS Backup.; If you use SAP HANA Cloud or RISE, backups are handled for you and this does not apply.; If you only want EBS volume snapshots, use AWS Backup directly and skip the agent.
Example: Your SAP admin runs the usual nightly full backup from HANA Cockpit, and the files quietly arrive in an S3 bucket instead of a local disk.
How you pay: The agent itself is free. You pay for S3 storage, requests and any AWS Backup charges. The surprise is log backups, which are small but constant, so request counts add up.

### AWS Chatbot
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-chatbot.html
In one sentence: Sends AWS alerts into Slack or Microsoft Teams, and lets you run some commands from the chat.
Picture it as: A pager that posts into the team group chat instead of buzzing one person.
What it does: It was renamed to Amazon Q Developer in chat applications in February 2025. The API, the console URL and the IAM names are still chatbot, so you will see both names. Alarms and events go to an SNS topic, and it posts them to a channel. You can also type read only AWS commands in chat. It is not a conversational bot for your customers.
Use it when: Getting CloudWatch alarms into a team channel; Letting on-call check a resource without opening the console; Posting deploy or budget events to chat
Do NOT use it when: Building a chatbot for your own users, use Amazon Lex or Amazon Bedrock; Serious incident paging with escalation, use PagerDuty or similar
Example: A CloudWatch alarm on database CPU posts to the #ops Slack channel, and someone types a command there to check the instance.
How you pay: The service is free. You pay for the SNS messages and CloudWatch behind it, which is small.

### AWS CloudFormation
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloudformation.html
In one sentence: Writes your whole setup as a file, so you can rebuild it exactly.
Picture it as: An IKEA instruction sheet for your infrastructure. Same sheet, same result, every time.
What it does: You describe what you want in YAML or JSON. CloudFormation creates it, updates it, and can delete it all cleanly. No more clicking in the console and forgetting what you did.
Use it when: You want staging and production to match; You want a record of your infrastructure
Do NOT use it when: A one off experiment you will delete tomorrow.
Example: One file that builds a VPC, two servers, a load balancer and a database.
How you pay: Free. You pay for what it creates.

### AWS CloudTrail
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloudtrail.html
In one sentence: Records who did what in your AWS account.
Picture it as: A CCTV log of the building. Not what the machines did, what the people did.
What it does: CloudTrail records every API call: who, when, from where. It is how you answer 'who deleted that database'. CloudWatch watches your app. CloudTrail watches your account.
Use it when: Always. Turn it on the first day.; Any compliance requirement
Example: Finding out which user turned off a security setting last Tuesday.
How you pay: One free trail of management events. Extra trails and data events cost.

### AWS Config
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-config.html
In one sentence: Records how your AWS setup changes over time.
Picture it as: A logbook of every change made to the building, with the rules it must follow.
What it does: Config records the configuration of your resources and checks them against rules. It can tell you what changed and when, and flag anything that drifts out of policy.
Use it when: Compliance; You need change history; Many people have access
Do NOT use it when: A single tiny project.
Example: Alerting the moment a security group is opened to the whole internet.
How you pay: Per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation. It adds up.

### AWS Console Mobile Application
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-console-mobile-application.html
In one sentence: The official AWS app for your phone, for checking things while away from a laptop.
Picture it as: A mobile banking app. Enough to check the balance and stop a card, not enough to run the bank.
What it does: It shows alarms, billing, and the status of common resources, and lets you do a few actions like restarting an instance. It covers a small slice of what the web console does. Sign in works with a device passcode or biometrics after the first setup. Most people install it, use it during one incident, then forget it.
Use it when: Checking an alarm while you are out; Seeing current spend quickly; Restarting or stopping an instance in a pinch
Do NOT use it when: Real work like configuring a service, use the web console; Team incident response, chat alerts through AWS Chatbot reach more people
Example: A billing alert fires on a Sunday, you open the app and see one forgotten large instance running.
How you pay: Free. You only pay for whatever the underlying resources cost.

### AWS Control Tower
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-control-tower.html
In one sentence: Sets up a tidy, rule enforced group of AWS accounts for a company.
Picture it as: An estate with a gatehouse and rules. Every new house gets the same wiring, the same locks and the same inspections.
What it does: It creates a multi account setup with a management account, logging and audit accounts, single sign on, and guardrails that block or detect risky actions. New accounts come out of a factory already set up. It is opinionated, hard to unwind later, and it turns on AWS Config broadly, which drives cost. It is for organisations, not for one person with one account.
Use it when: A company standardising dozens of AWS accounts; Needing audit logging and rules applied everywhere by default; Giving teams their own accounts safely
Do NOT use it when: One or two accounts, use AWS Organizations and service control policies directly; A setup already built in Terraform, Control Tower will fight your existing structure
Example: A new product team asks for an account and gets one within an hour, already logging to the central bucket with guardrails on.
How you pay: Control Tower itself is free. The surprise is AWS Config recording every resource in every account, plus CloudTrail and S3 storage, which can run to hundreds of dollars a month.

### AWS DevOps Agent
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-devops-agent.html
In one sentence: An AI assistant that digs into why your system broke and suggests the fix.
Picture it as: An on-call colleague who reads all the logs before you wake up.
What it does: It connects to your logs, metrics, code repositories and deployment pipelines, then works out what changed and what is failing. It went generally available in March 2026 and also looks at Azure and on-premises systems. It is new, so treat its conclusions as a strong first draft, not a verdict, and it needs real access to your telemetry and code before it is any use.
Use it when: An incident is live and nobody knows which deploy caused it; You want preventive advice from past incidents rather than a fresh guess each time; A small team has no dedicated SRE
Do NOT use it when: If you have no logs or metrics wired up yet, fix that first with Amazon CloudWatch. The agent has nothing to read otherwise.; If you want simple threshold alerts, a CloudWatch alarm is cheaper and more predictable.; If your rules require a human to approve every production change, keep it as an advisor and do not let it act.
Example: Latency jumps at 2am, and by morning it has pointed at a config change in yesterday's deploy and named the pull request.
How you pay: Charged for use, with monthly credits included depending on your AWS Support plan. The surprise is that heavy investigation of large log volumes also raises your CloudWatch and data transfer bills.

### AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-distro-for-opentelemetry.html
In one sentence: AWS's own build of the standard open source tool that collects traces and metrics from your app.
Picture it as: A generic medicine sold under a shop's own label. Same formula, packaged and supported by that shop.
What it does: OpenTelemetry is an industry standard for instrumenting code. ADOT is AWS's tested distribution of it, with the AWS exporters already included and AWS support behind it. It sends data to X-Ray, CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Prometheus, or to non AWS tools like Datadog. It is a packaging choice, not a new capability, and upstream OpenTelemetry works on AWS too.
Use it when: Instrumenting apps without locking into one vendor; Sending the same telemetry to AWS and a third party tool; Wanting AWS support on your collector build
Do NOT use it when: A pure AWS shop happy with the CloudWatch agent and X-Ray SDK, that is less work; Just wanting logs, CloudWatch Logs is far simpler
Example: Your Kubernetes services run an ADOT collector that ships traces to X-Ray and metrics to Managed Prometheus.
How you pay: The distribution is free. You pay for what receives the data, and trace and custom metric ingestion in CloudWatch and X-Ray is the part that surprises people at volume.

### AWS Health Dashboard
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-health-dashboard.html
In one sentence: Tells you when AWS itself has a problem, including ones that affect only your account.
Picture it as: The notice board at the station. General delays for everyone, plus a message about your specific train.
What it does: There are two views. The public one shows broad service issues. Your account view shows events that touch your resources, such as a scheduled reboot of your instance or a certificate about to expire. The account level API and the organisation view need a Business or Enterprise support plan, so basic accounts see less. It reports, it does not fix.
Use it when: Checking whether an outage is AWS or your code; Finding scheduled maintenance on your instances; Getting warnings about deprecations that affect you
Do NOT use it when: Monitoring your own application health, use CloudWatch alarms; Fast public outage news, the public dashboard is often slow, and your own metrics tell you sooner
Example: Your app slows down, and the dashboard shows raised error rates for a service in your region, so you stop hunting your own code.
How you pay: The dashboard is free. The Health API and organisation view require a paid support plan, which is the real cost.

### AWS Launch Wizard
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-launch-wizard.html
In one sentence: A guided form that builds the AWS setup for a few specific packaged applications.
Picture it as: The setup wizard on a new printer. It asks a few questions and does the fiddly bits for you.
What it does: You answer questions about size and availability, and it generates and deploys a CloudFormation stack sized for that application. It supports a short list, mainly SQL Server, SAP and Active Directory. It is narrow, and outside that list it is no help at all. What it produces is a normal stack you can then manage yourself.
Use it when: A first SQL Server Always On cluster on EC2; Standing up an SAP landscape without deep AWS knowledge
Do NOT use it when: Anything not on its short supported list, write CloudFormation or Terraform; Infrastructure your team will keep changing, own the templates from the start
Example: A Windows admin answers ten questions and gets a highly available SQL Server cluster across two availability zones.
How you pay: The wizard is free. You pay for the EC2, storage and any Windows or SQL licensing it turns on, which is not small.

### AWS License Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-license-manager.html
In one sentence: Keeps count of software licences you own so you do not go over what you paid for.
Picture it as: A library ticket system. Only so many copies exist, so it tracks who has one out.
What it does: You describe a licence rule, such as 100 Windows Server cores, and it counts usage across accounts and can block launches that would break the limit. It also manages bring your own licence hosts and user based subscriptions for things like Office on AppStream. Most people only meet it because a vendor audit or a Microsoft agreement forced them to.
Use it when: Bringing your own Windows or Oracle licences to AWS; Proving licence compliance in an audit; Stopping teams launching more licensed instances than allowed
Do NOT use it when: Everything running on open source or AWS supplied licences, you do not need it; Tracking SaaS seats like Slack or Figma, it does not do that
Example: A launch of an eleventh Oracle instance is blocked because the rule says you own ten.
How you pay: The core tracking is free. User based subscriptions carry a per user monthly charge, and dedicated hosts for bring your own licence are the expensive part.

### AWS Management Console
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-management-console.html
In one sentence: The AWS website where you click around to see and change your stuff.
Picture it as: The dashboard of a car. Everything is reachable, but you still need to know what each dial does.
What it does: It is the browser interface covering every AWS service, plus search, billing and a built in shell called CloudShell. It is the right place to learn and to look at things. It is the wrong place to build production infrastructure, because clicks are not recorded, not repeatable, and nobody can review them. Experienced teams read here and write with code.
Use it when: Learning what a service does; Checking a resource or a bill quickly; One off emergency action during an incident
Do NOT use it when: Creating production infrastructure, use CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform; Anything repeated more than twice, script it with the AWS CLI or an SDK
Example: You open the S3 page to check why a bucket is bigger than expected, then fix the lifecycle rule in Terraform.
How you pay: Free to use. Everything you click into costs whatever that service costs, and forgotten resources created here are a classic surprise bill.

### AWS Organizations
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-organizations.html
In one sentence: Manages many AWS accounts as one company.
Picture it as: A head office with branch offices. One policy, one bill, separate premises.
What it does: Organizations groups accounts under one payer, applies rules that even account admins cannot override, and keeps production separate from development. Separate accounts are the strongest blast radius control AWS offers.
Use it when: More than one project or client; You want production isolated
Do NOT use it when: A single personal learning account.
Example: Separate accounts for dev, staging and production, one combined bill.
How you pay: Free.

### AWS Partner Central
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-partner-central.html
In one sentence: The website AWS resellers and software vendors use to manage their AWS partnership.
Picture it as: The staff entrance of a shopping centre, not a shop you buy from.
What it does: This is a business portal, not a technical service. Companies in the AWS Partner Network sign in here to list products on AWS Marketplace, register sales deals with AWS, claim partner benefits and get training. It has now absorbed the old AWS Marketplace Management Portal. It runs nothing and stores none of your application data.
Use it when: Your company sells software or consulting and wants to list it on AWS Marketplace; You need to register a customer deal so AWS sales will co-sell with you; Tracking your partner tier and required certifications
Do NOT use it when: If you are an AWS customer rather than an AWS partner, you will never open this.; If you only want to buy software, use AWS Marketplace.; If you want technical support on a service, use AWS Support, not this portal.
Example: A consultancy logs in to register a deal with a retail client so AWS sales does not compete with them on the same account.
How you pay: Free to use. Some partner programmes have their own annual fees or spend requirements, and Marketplace takes a cut of what you sell through it.

### AWS Proton
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-proton.html
In one sentence: A way for a platform team to publish ready made deployment templates for developers, now being shut down.
Picture it as: A canteen with fixed menu sets. The kitchen decides what combinations exist, you pick one.
What it does: Platform engineers defined environment and service templates, developers picked one and got infrastructure plus a pipeline. AWS is discontinuing it. New customers were closed off on 7 October 2025 and support ends on 7 October 2026. It never caught on widely. Do not build on it now.
Use it when: Only if you already run it and are planning the exit
Do NOT use it when: Any new platform work, use Terraform or CDK with a module library, or Backstage for the developer portal; Simple app deployment, use ECS or Lambda with a normal pipeline
Example: An existing Proton user plans migration of its service templates to CDK before the October 2026 cut off.
How you pay: No charge for Proton itself, you paid for the resources. Now the real cost is the migration work before support ends.

### AWS Resilience Hub
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-resilience-hub.html
In one sentence: Scores how well your app would survive a failure, and tells you what is missing.
Picture it as: A home safety inspection. Someone checks the smoke alarms and the fire exit, then hands you a list.
What it does: You describe an application and your recovery targets, how much downtime and data loss you can accept. It inspects the resources, compares them against those targets, gives a score and lists fixes such as missing backups or a single availability zone. It can also run fault injection tests. It checks your setup, it does not make your app resilient.
Use it when: Before a compliance or disaster recovery review; Checking whether recovery targets are actually met; Finding single points of failure in a known stack
Do NOT use it when: Small or non critical apps, the per application charge is not worth it; Actually testing failure behaviour deeply, use AWS Fault Injection Service directly
Example: It flags that your database has no cross region backup, so your four hour recovery target is not achievable.
How you pay: A flat monthly charge per application assessed, around 15 dollars, which surprises teams that register dozens of small apps.

### AWS Resource Explorer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-resource-explorer.html
In one sentence: Search across all your AWS resources in every region at once.
Picture it as: The search box on your phone that looks through every app instead of you opening each one.
What it does: You turn on an index, then search by name, tag or type and see matches across regions. Before this you had to visit each service in each region. It needs to be enabled with an aggregator region first, and results lag behind reality by minutes. Not every resource type is indexed, so an empty result is not proof something does not exist.
Use it when: Hunting a resource when you forgot the region; Finding everything tagged with an old project name; Cleaning up before a cost review
Do NOT use it when: A precise inventory for audit or compliance, use AWS Config; Cross account search, it is per account, so use Config aggregators or Organizations tooling
Example: You search a project tag and find a load balancer still running in a region nobody remembered using.
How you pay: Free. The value is the resources you find and switch off.

### AWS Service Catalog
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-service-catalog.html
In one sentence: An internal menu of approved setups that staff can deploy without free rein.
Picture it as: A vending machine in the office. Only the approved items are inside, and you press one button.
What it does: An admin publishes CloudFormation or Terraform products, and users launch them with a few inputs. The launch runs under a role the admin defines, so the user does not need broad permissions. It works well for standard, stable items and poorly when teams want to change templates often, because every change goes through the catalog. Mostly seen in larger, governed organisations.
Use it when: Letting non experts create approved infrastructure safely; Enforcing tagging and standards on every new resource; Handing out sandbox or project stacks on request
Do NOT use it when: Engineering teams that own their own infrastructure code, it just slows them down; One team, one repository, plain CloudFormation or Terraform in a pipeline is simpler
Example: A data analyst clicks one item and gets an approved, encrypted, correctly tagged S3 bucket plus a notebook.
How you pay: Free for normal use. Charges apply to very heavy API usage above a monthly allowance, and you pay for whatever the products create.

### AWS Service Management Connector
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-service-management-connector.html
In one sentence: Retiring. It let ServiceNow or Jira users request and see AWS resources from their own ticket tool.
Picture it as: A hatch between two offices, now being bricked up.
What it does: This is being shut down. It closed to new customers on 31 March 2026 and support ends on 31 March 2027, after which it stops working. It was a plugin for ServiceNow, Jira Service Management and Jira Cloud that surfaced AWS Service Catalog products, AWS Config data, Security Hub findings and Support cases inside those tools. AWS now tells customers to use partner ITSM integrations or write their own with the SDK.
Use it when: Nothing new. Existing users should be planning their exit; Understanding an old diagram or runbook that mentions it; Deciding what replaces it before March 2027
Do NOT use it when: Do not start a new project on it. It is being switched off. Use a partner ITSM integration or build a direct SDK integration.; If you only need a self-service catalogue inside AWS, use AWS Service Catalog on its own, which is not affected.; If you want AWS events pushed into a ticket tool, EventBridge plus a webhook does that and is not going away.
Example: A staff member used to raise a ServiceNow ticket for a test server and get an approved EC2 instance, and that path now needs rebuilding.
How you pay: The connector was free. You paid only for the AWS resources it created. The real cost now is the migration work before the 2027 cutoff.

### AWS Sustainability
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-sustainability.html
In one sentence: Not a service. It is AWS's environment programme, with one real tool for your carbon numbers.
Picture it as: A company's recycling policy, plus a single electricity meter you can actually read.
What it does: There is no service you can switch on called AWS Sustainability. The name covers AWS's own renewable energy commitments, the Sustainability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework, which is guidance, and one concrete tool, the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool in the Billing console. That tool shows estimated emissions from your AWS usage, by month, region and service.
Use it when: Your company has to report cloud emissions for an ESG disclosure; You want to compare the carbon cost of regions before choosing one; Reviewing a design against the Well-Architected sustainability guidance
Do NOT use it when: If you want live, detailed, per-resource carbon data, this is too coarse. It is monthly and estimated.; If your real goal is to spend less money, use AWS Cost Explorer. Less waste usually means less carbon anyway.; Do not expect an API to call. Most of it is documents and a billing dashboard.
Example: Your finance team downloads last quarter's carbon report from the Billing console for the annual ESG statement.
How you pay: Free. The surprise is the delay and the coarseness. Data appears about three weeks after month end, and anything under half a kilo of CO2e shows as zero.

### AWS Systems Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-systems-manager.html
In one sentence: Manage all your servers from one place.
Picture it as: A facilities team with a master key and a maintenance schedule.
What it does: Systems Manager patches servers, runs commands on all of them at once, stores configuration in Parameter Store, and gives shell access without opening SSH to the internet.
Use it when: More than a couple of servers; You want to stop opening port 22
Do NOT use it when: Fully serverless setups with no servers to manage.
Example: Applying a security patch to twenty servers with one command.
How you pay: Most of it is free. Some advanced features are paid.

### AWS Telco Network Builder
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-telco-network-builder.html
In one sentence: Deploys and manages mobile network software for phone companies running 5G on AWS.
Picture it as: Assembly instructions and a crew for building a phone network, rather than a shelf.
What it does: Known as AWS TNB. Telecom operators package network functions in a standard telecom format called TOSCA, and TNB turns that into running infrastructure on EC2 and EKS, then handles upgrades. It is still active and still getting updates. Almost nobody needs it. If you are not a mobile network operator or a telecom vendor, this service is not for you.
Use it when: A mobile operator running 5G core functions on AWS; A telecom vendor automating network function delivery
Do NOT use it when: Any normal application, use ECS, EKS or plain CloudFormation; Networking between your own VPCs, use Transit Gateway
Example: An operator rolls out a new version of its 5G core across regions from one package definition.
How you pay: No charge for TNB itself. You pay for the EC2, EKS and networking it creates, and 5G workloads use large instances.

### AWS Trusted Advisor
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-trusted-advisor.html
In one sentence: Checks your account and suggests fixes.
Picture it as: A yearly service for your car. It lists what needs attention.
What it does: Trusted Advisor checks for wasted money, security holes, missing redundancy and hitting limits. A few checks are free on every account, the full set needs a paid support plan.
Use it when: Regular account health checks
Example: Flagging an S3 bucket that is open to the public.
How you pay: Some checks free. Full set needs Business support or above.

### AWS User Notifications
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-user-notifications.html
In one sentence: One place to decide which AWS events reach you, and where they land.
Picture it as: The notification settings screen on your phone, for the whole of AWS.
What it does: You set rules like send me EC2 state changes and CloudWatch alarms in these regions, and choose email, chat, or push to the mobile app. It gives a single inbox in the console instead of scattered per service settings. It is a router over EventBridge events, so if an event does not exist in EventBridge, it cannot notify you. It is fairly new and still thin on options.
Use it when: Wanting one consistent place for AWS alerts; Cross region and cross account alerting without wiring each service; Push notifications to the mobile console app
Do NOT use it when: Notifying your own end users, use SNS or Pinpoint; Complex routing, filtering and retries, build on EventBridge and SNS directly
Example: You get one email whenever any account in the organisation has a security finding, instead of per account rules.
How you pay: The service is free. You pay for the underlying delivery, and a noisy rule sending high volume email is what annoys people.

### AWS Well Architected Tool
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-well-architected-tool.html
In one sentence: A questionnaire about your system that produces a list of the risks you have not handled.
Picture it as: A building safety checklist you fill in yourself. The form does not inspect the building, it just makes sure you thought about the fire exits.
What it does: You answer questions across six areas such as security, cost and reliability, and it produces a scored report of high and medium risks with links to guidance. Every answer comes from you, so the output is only as honest as your answers. It is mostly used by consultants and by teams doing a formal review before a big launch.
Use it when: A structured review before a major launch; Partner or audit work that needs a documented review; Getting a team to agree on where the weak spots are
Do NOT use it when: Finding real problems in a live account, use Trusted Advisor, Security Hub or Compute Optimizer which actually look at your resources; A small side project, the review takes hours and tells you little
Example: A team answers the reliability questions, realises nobody has ever tested the database restore, and logs it as a high risk.
How you pay: The tool is free. The cost is the time, and any consultant you pay to run the review.

### Amazon CloudWatch
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-cloudwatch.html
In one sentence: Watches your systems and tells you when something is wrong.
Picture it as: The dashboard of a car. Speed, fuel, engine warning light.
What it does: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms. An alarm can email you or trigger scaling. Log storage grows quietly, so set a retention period or the bill creeps up.
Use it when: Always. If you cannot see it, you cannot run it.
Example: Alert on WhatsApp when CPU stays above 80 percent for five minutes.
How you pay: Per metric, per GB of logs, per alarm. Log retention is the usual surprise.

### Amazon Managed Grafana
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-managed-grafana.html
In one sentence: Runs Grafana dashboards for you so nobody has to patch a Grafana server.
Picture it as: Renting a noticeboard that someone else keeps clean and locked.
What it does: Grafana is popular open source dashboard software. This is AWS hosting it, with logins through your existing identity provider and ready-made connections to CloudWatch, Prometheus, OpenSearch and outside sources. You get the normal Grafana experience. You do not get full server access, so some plugins and tweaks are not possible.
Use it when: Several teams share dashboards and you do not want to run the server; You want one dashboard mixing AWS metrics with non-AWS sources; You need single sign-on and per-team dashboard permissions
Do NOT use it when: If you only look at AWS metrics, CloudWatch dashboards are already there and cost less.; If you have dozens of casual viewers, self-hosting Grafana on a small EC2 instance is usually cheaper.; If you need an unusual plugin or deep server config, run your own Grafana.
Example: An on-call engineer opens one dashboard showing EKS pod health from Prometheus next to RDS metrics from CloudWatch.
How you pay: Per active user per workspace per month, roughly nine dollars for an editor and five for a viewer. The surprise is that anyone who logs in once in a month counts as active for the whole month, and API keys and service accounts are billed as users too.

### Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-managed-service-for-prometheus.html
In one sentence: Stores and queries Prometheus metrics for you, without running Prometheus servers.
Picture it as: A warehouse for your meter readings, instead of a filing cabinet you have to keep buying shelves for.
What it does: Prometheus is the standard way Kubernetes and containers expose metrics. Running it yourself means managing storage and scaling as metric volume grows. This takes the metrics in, keeps them, and answers PromQL queries. It stores and queries only. It draws no dashboards, so pair it with Grafana.
Use it when: You run EKS or ECS and already emit Prometheus metrics; Your self-hosted Prometheus keeps running out of disk or memory; You want metrics kept longer than a local Prometheus can hold
Do NOT use it when: If you are not using Prometheus metrics today, use Amazon CloudWatch. Do not adopt Prometheus just to have this.; If you have a handful of containers, a single self-hosted Prometheus is simpler and cheaper.; If you want dashboards, this is not it. Add Amazon Managed Grafana.
Example: Your EKS cluster ships pod metrics here, and Grafana queries them to show memory use per service over six months.
How you pay: You pay per metric sample taken in, per GB stored, and per billion samples processed by queries. The surprise is the query charge. A dashboard on auto-refresh in front of a wall screen can quietly cost more than the storage.

## Media


### AWS Deadline Cloud
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-deadline-cloud.html
In one sentence: It runs your 3D renders and other heavy creative jobs on rented computers.
Picture it as: A print shop for animation frames. You drop off the job, they run hundreds of machines overnight, you pick up the finished pictures.
What it does: You submit a render job from software like Maya, Blender, Houdini, Nuke or Unreal, and Deadline Cloud spreads the frames across a fleet of machines it starts and stops for you. It handles the queue, the job dependencies and the licences for some paid renderers. It is aimed at studios; the hard parts are still getting your assets and plugin versions onto the render machines, which the service does not do for you.
Use it when: Rendering animation or VFX frames faster than your own machines can; You already use a render farm manager and want burst capacity; Studio pipelines with deadlines and many artists
Do NOT use it when: A single quick render, just use your own workstation; General batch computing that is not rendering, use AWS Batch instead; You want a cheap hobby farm, the per-machine-hour fee plus licence fees adds up fast
Example: A small animation studio pushes 4,000 frames of a commercial to Deadline Cloud on Friday and has them back Saturday morning.
How you pay: Per minute of machine time on the render workers, plus a smaller per-minute service fee per worker, plus usage-based licence charges for renderers you get through AWS. The service fee on top of the machine cost is the part people miss.

### AWS Elemental Appliances & Software
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-appliances-software.html
In one sentence: It is the name for the video encoding boxes and software AWS sells you to run in your own building.
Picture it as: Buying the oven instead of ordering from the bakery. Same recipes, but it sits in your kitchen and you maintain it.
What it does: This is not a cloud service you switch on. It is a catalogue: physical appliances and licensed software (Live, Server, Conductor, Delta) that broadcasters install in their own machine rooms, usually to work alongside AWS video services. Almost nobody outside television and live sports operations buys this. AWS now pushes MediaLive Anywhere for new on-premises work, which runs the cloud service on your hardware with cloud control.
Use it when: A broadcast facility that must keep video processing on site; Latency or contract rules stop you sending the feed to the cloud; You are extending an existing Elemental on-premises setup
Do NOT use it when: Any normal streaming need, use MediaLive or MediaConvert in the cloud; New on-premises projects, look at MediaLive Anywhere first; You do not have staff who rack and maintain hardware
Example: A national broadcaster keeps encoders in its playout centre and sends only the finished streams to AWS.
How you pay: You buy or license it through AWS sales, not by the hour. Support contracts and hardware refresh are the ongoing cost.

### AWS Elemental Conductor
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-conductor.html
In one sentence: It is the control panel that manages a room full of Elemental encoders.
Picture it as: A shift supervisor on a factory floor. The machines do the work, the supervisor decides which machine gets which job and shouts when one stops.
What it does: Conductor sits on top of several AWS Elemental Live or Elemental Server units in your own building and gives one place to set up channels, balance work and fail over when a box dies. It is legacy on-premises broadcast software, sold with appliances, and very few organisations run it. In the cloud the equivalent controls are simply built into MediaLive and MediaConvert.
Use it when: You already run a cluster of on-premises Elemental encoders; You need redundancy across those boxes with automatic failover; A broadcast facility with an operations team watching channels
Do NOT use it when: Anything cloud based, MediaLive already manages itself; A single encoder, Conductor adds cost and no benefit; New builds, prefer MediaLive Anywhere
Example: A sports network runs twelve Elemental Live boxes and uses Conductor so a failed unit is replaced by a spare without anyone going off air.
How you pay: Licensed with the appliance purchase, not metered. Cost sits in licences and support, not usage.

### AWS Elemental Delta
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-delta.html
In one sentence: It stores and hands out live video in your own building so thousands of viewers can watch it.
Picture it as: A newsagent who keeps the last hour of newspapers on the counter, so everyone arriving late can still take a copy.
What it does: Delta is on-premises software that packages a live feed into the formats players need, keeps a rolling window so viewers can pause or rewind, and serves it to a CDN. It is the older, self-hosted cousin of MediaPackage. It is legacy and rare; new work of this kind goes to MediaPackage in the cloud.
Use it when: An existing on-premises broadcast chain that already uses it; Time shift and catch up recording that must stay on site; Serving your own network of viewers without cloud delivery
Do NOT use it when: Anything new, use MediaPackage; Video on demand files, that is MediaConvert plus S3 and CloudFront; Small audiences, a plain origin server is cheaper
Example: A cable operator lets subscribers rewind the last two hours of a channel from equipment in its own head end.
How you pay: Sold as software licences with appliances, not per stream. No hourly bill, but support and hardware are yours.

### AWS Elemental Link
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-link.html
In one sentence: A small box you plug a camera into, and the video goes straight to AWS.
Picture it as: A prepaid postbox for video. Plug in the cable, and whatever the camera sees is posted to AWS with no settings to fiddle with.
What it does: Link is a piece of hardware about the size of a paperback. One end takes HDMI or SDI from a camera or vision mixer, the other takes network, and it appears as an input inside MediaLive. There is nothing to configure on the device itself; you control it from the AWS console. It only feeds MediaLive, so it is useless on its own, and if it is lost or broken you buy another.
Use it when: Sending a camera feed to the cloud without an encoding PC; Fixed installations like a church, lecture hall or stadium; Events where you want a setup that non technical staff can plug in
Do NOT use it when: Streaming from software you already run, use RTMP into MediaLive directly; A one off event, hiring an encoder or using OBS is cheaper than buying hardware; You need the feed to go somewhere other than AWS
Example: A university plugs a Link into the lecture theatre camera so every session streams without an operator.
How you pay: A one time purchase for the device, a few hundred dollars. The video it sends is then billed by MediaLive as normal, which is the recurring cost people forget.

### AWS Elemental Live
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-live.html
In one sentence: Software or a box in your building that turns a live camera feed into internet streams.
Picture it as: A translator standing beside the camera, turning what it says into every language the audience speaks, right there in the room.
What it does: Elemental Live is the on-premises live encoder: it takes SDI, ST 2110 or IP feeds and produces multiple bitrates and formats for broadcast and streaming. It is the product MediaLive was built from. It is still sold for facilities that must process video on site, but for most new work AWS points people at MediaLive, or MediaLive Anywhere if the processing has to stay local.
Use it when: Broadcast facilities with baseband SDI infrastructure; Feeds that legally or practically cannot leave the building; Very low latency contribution inside a venue
Do NOT use it when: Cloud streaming, use MediaLive and skip the hardware; Recorded files, that is MediaConvert or Elemental Server; Teams without broadcast engineers
Example: A stadium encodes the in-house camera feeds on site and sends only the finished streams out to the internet.
How you pay: Appliance or software licence bought through AWS, with a support contract. Not hourly.

### AWS Elemental MediaConnect
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-mediaconnect.html
In one sentence: It moves a live video feed from one place to another without losing quality.
Picture it as: A courier for a single fragile parcel. Not a shop, not a warehouse, just careful delivery from A to B, with a spare van following.
What it does: MediaConnect carries broadcast grade live feeds over the internet using protocols that recover lost packets, such as Zixi, SRT and RIST, and it can encrypt the stream and fan it out to several receivers. It only transports; it does not encode, package or store anything. Broadcasters use it to replace satellite links between sites.
Use it when: Sending a live feed between studios, partners or regions; Replacing a satellite or fibre contribution link; Handing a feed to another company without giving them AWS access
Do NOT use it when: Delivering video to viewers, that is MediaPackage plus CloudFront; Changing resolution or format, MediaConnect does not encode; File transfer, use S3
Example: A news agency sends a reporter's live feed from a remote city into its main studio's MediaLive channel.
How you pay: Per hour for each flow plus per gigabyte transferred, and each extra output of a flow is billed too. Redundant flows double the cost.

### AWS Elemental MediaConvert
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-mediaconvert.html
In one sentence: It converts video files you already have into the formats players can stream.
Picture it as: A photo lab that takes one negative and prints it in every size the customer asked for.
What it does: You put a video file in S3, submit a job, and MediaConvert writes out new files: different resolutions, codecs, subtitles, thumbnails, and the playlists streaming players need. It is for files, not live feeds. Jobs are queued, so a long film takes real time to process, and getting the output settings right is fiddly the first time.
Use it when: Preparing recorded video for a website or app; Making one upload play on phones, TVs and browsers; Adding captions, watermarks or audio tracks to a library of files
Do NOT use it when: Live streaming, use MediaLive; Simple, low volume conversions, a script running ffmpeg on EC2 can be cheaper; Real time conversion while a user waits, jobs are not instant
Example: A training company uploads a 2 hour recorded session and gets back three quality levels plus an HLS playlist.
How you pay: Per minute of output video, per output. Six renditions of one hour means six hours of billed output, which is why bills come out higher than expected. Professional tier features like HEVC and HDR cost more per minute.

### AWS Elemental MediaLive
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-medialive.html
In one sentence: It takes a live camera or stream and turns it into something viewers can watch.
Picture it as: The control room at a TV station. The camera feed comes in, and it goes out in the shapes every screen in the country can show.
What it does: MediaLive is the live encoder. You point a feed at it, it produces several quality levels, inserts ad markers, adds captions and overlays, and passes the result to MediaPackage or your own destination. Channels are billed while they are running whether or not anyone is watching, and stopping a channel is a manual step people forget.
Use it when: Live events, sport, worship services, conferences; 24/7 channels that need broadcast features like ad insertion; Live feeds that must go out in several bitrates
Do NOT use it when: Simple low latency streaming with chat, Amazon IVS is far less work; Recorded files, use MediaConvert; Occasional casual streams, a third party service is cheaper than running a channel
Example: A football club streams home matches, with MediaLive producing 1080p, 720p and 480p versions live.
How you pay: Per hour of channel running time, by input and output class, plus data out. The surprise is being charged for a channel left running after the event ended.

### AWS Elemental MediaPackage
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-mediapackage.html
In one sentence: It hands your live video to viewers in whatever format their player wants, and can record it.
Picture it as: A waiter who takes one dish from the kitchen and serves it on the plate each table asked for.
What it does: MediaPackage sits between the encoder and the viewer. It takes one incoming stream and outputs HLS, DASH or CMAF, applies content protection, and keeps a recent window so viewers can pause, rewind or start the programme again. It can also save a finished event as a video on demand asset. It does not encode, so it always needs MediaLive or a similar source in front of it.
Use it when: Live streaming where viewers use many kinds of device; You want pause, rewind or catch up on a live channel; You need DRM applied to a live stream
Do NOT use it when: Static video files, use S3 with CloudFront; Low latency chat style streaming, look at Amazon IVS; If your players all take one format, you may not need the extra layer
Example: A conference stream lets someone joining an hour late rewind to the opening keynote.
How you pay: Per gigabyte in and out, plus storage for any recorded window. Each extra output format multiplies the outbound gigabytes.

### AWS Elemental MediaStore
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-mediastore.html
In one sentence: It was fast storage made for live video, and AWS has now shut it down.
Picture it as: A kiosk that was closed and boarded up. The nearby supermarket sells the same thing now.
What it does: MediaStore was storage tuned for live video origination, with lower delay than S3 had at the time. AWS discontinued it on 13 November 2025; the console and the resources are gone. S3 improved to the point where it is both faster and cheaper for this job, so AWS told customers to move to S3 or MediaPackage. Do not design anything around MediaStore.
Use it when: Nothing, the service is retired; Only relevant if you are reading old architecture diagrams; Migrating legacy documentation that mentions it
Do NOT use it when: Any live origin need, use Amazon S3; Live packaging with catch up, use MediaPackage; Do not follow old tutorials that still show MediaStore containers
Example: An old 2019 reference architecture shows MediaLive writing to MediaStore; today that arrow points to S3.
How you pay: No longer billable. When it ran, it charged per gigabyte stored and per request, and the request charges were the expensive part for live workloads.

### AWS Elemental MediaTailor
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-mediatailor.html
In one sentence: It slips adverts into a video stream so they play like part of the programme.
Picture it as: A radio presenter reading a different advert to each listener, in the same gap, without the music stopping.
What it does: MediaTailor stitches personalised ads into live and on demand streams on the server side, so ad blockers and player quirks do not break them, and it reports what was actually watched. It can also build a 24/7 linear channel out of a list of files. It needs an ad decision server to tell it which ad to play, which you bring yourself, and getting ad breaks to line up exactly is the hard part.
Use it when: Making money from streaming through advertising; Free ad supported channels built from a content library; You need ads that client side blockers cannot strip out
Do NOT use it when: You have no advertising, it adds cost and complexity for nothing; Simple pre roll in your own player, a client side ad SDK is simpler; Small audiences, ad revenue will not cover the effort
Example: A free film channel plays a different local advert to a viewer in Mumbai and one in Manchester, in the same break.
How you pay: Per thousand ad requests, plus per gigabyte for the channel assembly feature. Heavy channel assembly use is the surprise line.

### AWS Elemental Server
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elemental-server.html
In one sentence: Software in your own building that converts recorded video files into streaming formats.
Picture it as: Your own photocopier in the office instead of walking to the copy shop.
What it does: Elemental Server is the on-premises file transcoder, the local version of what MediaConvert does in the cloud. It runs on appliances or your own servers and is used where the source files must not leave the building, or where a facility already owns the hardware. It is legacy broadcast kit, and very few new buyers pick it over MediaConvert.
Use it when: Media archives that cannot legally leave the premises; A facility with spare hardware and steady, predictable volume; Existing Elemental installations being extended
Do NOT use it when: Cloud workflows, MediaConvert needs no hardware; Bursty volumes, you pay for capacity you are not using; Small teams, there is nobody to maintain it
Example: A broadcaster converts its master tapes to streaming files on machines inside its own archive facility.
How you pay: Licence and appliance purchase through AWS sales, plus support. Your own power, space and staff are the real running cost.

### AWS Thinkbox Deadline
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-thinkbox-deadline.html
In one sentence: Free software you install yourself to manage a render farm.
Picture it as: A job board pinned up in a workshop. Everyone takes the next ticket when they are free.
What it does: Deadline is the long established render farm manager AWS bought with Thinkbox. You run the database and the scheduler on your own machines, and it hands frames out to whatever computers you have, including EC2 machines when you want extra. AWS made it free of charge in 2022 and put it into maintenance mode on 7 November 2025, so it gets critical fixes and DCC integration updates but no new features. Deadline Cloud is the managed successor.
Use it when: You already own render machines and want to schedule them; An existing studio pipeline built around Deadline; You want a free scheduler and will run it yourself
Do NOT use it when: Starting fresh with no hardware, use AWS Deadline Cloud; You want AWS to run it for you, this one you install and maintain; Long term bets, it is in maintenance mode and will not gain features
Example: An architecture visualisation studio runs Deadline on its own 20 workstations overnight and bursts to EC2 at deadlines.
How you pay: The software is free. You pay for the machines it runs on, and for the EC2 capacity if you burst to the cloud.

### AWS Thinkbox Frost
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-thinkbox-frost.html
In one sentence: A 3ds Max plugin that turns clouds of particles into a solid surface you can render.
Picture it as: Taking a bowl of tiny beads and shrink wrapping them, so it looks like one smooth blob of liquid instead of beads.
What it does: Frost is a mesher for 3ds Max: it builds geometry around particle simulations so splashes, mud, snow or crowds of objects can be rendered. It is a niche artist tool with nothing to do with cloud computing. AWS made it free in 2022 and published the source on GitHub, but has not updated it since; a community developer maintains builds for newer 3ds Max versions. Almost nobody outside 3ds Max VFX work needs it.
Use it when: 3ds Max artists meshing fluid or particle simulations; Scattering geometry over particle positions; Existing pipelines already built on Frost
Do NOT use it when: Any non 3ds Max software, use that package's own mesher such as Houdini's VDB tools; Anything to do with AWS infrastructure, it is a desktop plugin; New work, be aware AWS is not developing it
Example: An artist turns a 3ds Max water splash simulation into a renderable mesh for a drinks advert.
How you pay: Free, with no AWS account needed. The cost is the 3ds Max licence and the machines you render on.

### AWS Thinkbox Krakatoa
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-thinkbox-krakatoa.html
In one sentence: Free desktop software that renders huge clouds of particles, like smoke, dust and fire.
Picture it as: A camera that can photograph every grain in a sandstorm.
What it does: This is desktop software, not a cloud service. AWS bought Thinkbox and now gives all Thinkbox products away at no cost, with parts of Krakatoa released as open source. It is a renderer plugin for 3ds Max, Maya, Cinema 4D and similar tools, built for scenes with billions of particles. It is effectively in maintenance. Do not expect active development.
Use it when: Rendering dust, smoke, fire or magic effects in a film or advert; Visualising very large point cloud or particle data sets; You already work in 3ds Max or Maya and hit limits on particle counts
Do NOT use it when: If you are not doing 3D visual effects, this is irrelevant.; If you want rendering to run on AWS machines, that is AWS Deadline Cloud, which schedules the jobs. Krakatoa is just the renderer.; If you are starting fresh, check whether your DCC tool's own particle renderer is enough before adopting maintenance-mode software.
Example: A studio renders a collapsing building's dust cloud from a hundred million particles, spread over a render farm.
How you pay: Free to download and use, including the licences. You pay only for whatever machines you render on, such as EC2 instances or your own workstations.

### AWS Thinkbox Stoke
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-thinkbox-stoke.html
In one sentence: Free 3ds Max plugin that simulates particles moving through fields of motion.
Picture it as: Dropping confetti into a wind tunnel and watching where it goes.
What it does: This is desktop software for Autodesk 3ds Max only, not a cloud service. It generates and simulates particles driven by velocity fields, and reads simulation data from FumeFX, Particle Flow, thinkingParticles and RealFlow. It is free now, along with every Thinkbox product, and is in maintenance rather than active development. It is usually used to feed Krakatoa.
Use it when: Adding drifting debris or spray on top of an existing smoke simulation in 3ds Max; Reusing velocity field data from another simulation tool; You need particle counts beyond what 3ds Max handles natively
Do NOT use it when: If you use Maya, Houdini or Blender, this does not apply. It is a 3ds Max plugin.; If you need full fluid or smoke simulation, use a dedicated solver. Stoke moves particles, it does not simulate the fluid.; Almost nobody outside 3ds Max visual effects work has a use for this.
Example: An artist takes a FumeFX explosion and uses Stoke to send sparks tumbling along its motion, then renders them with Krakatoa.
How you pay: Free, licence included. Your only cost is the 3ds Max licence and the machines you simulate and render on.

### AWS Thinkbox XMesh
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-thinkbox-xmesh.html
In one sentence: Saves moving 3D animation to disk so an artist can replay it fast.
Picture it as: Recording a stage rehearsal on video, so you can watch it again without calling the actors back.
What it does: This is not a cloud service. It is a plugin for 3ds Max and Maya on an artist's own computer, from Thinkbox, a company AWS bought. It writes animated geometry to XMesh files that load quickly, which helps with heavy crowd or simulation scenes. AWS made all Thinkbox tools free in 2022, and the Maya version was released as open source. It is a niche visual effects tool, and almost nobody outside a VFX or animation studio will ever touch it.
Use it when: A 3D scene is so heavy that scrubbing the timeline crawls; A studio wants to hand a baked animation to render machines without the original rig; Crowd or particle work needs to be cached once and reused
Do NOT use it when: You are not doing 3D animation in 3ds Max or Maya. Then this is simply not for you.; You want cloud rendering. That is Deadline plus EC2, not XMesh.; You want to store files in the cloud. Use amazon-simple-storage-service.
Example: An animator bakes a 200 million polygon crowd shot to XMesh so the scene opens in seconds.
How you pay: Nothing. The software is free with an AWS account, and the Maya plugin is open source.

### Amazon Interactive Video Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-interactive-video-service.html
In one sentence: It gives you live streaming with chat, like a Twitch style channel, with very little setup.
Picture it as: A walkie talkie set you take out of the box and use. No wiring, no engineer.
What it does: IVS takes an RTMP stream from software like OBS and delivers it to viewers in a few seconds, with a player, a chat service and viewer counts included. There is a real time mode for stages where several people appear on screen together with sub second delay. You give up control: fewer broadcast features than MediaLive, and the channel types and limits are fixed by AWS.
Use it when: Live shopping, creator streams, classes, gaming style channels; You want chat and low latency without building a video stack; Small teams with no broadcast experience
Do NOT use it when: Broadcast channels needing ad insertion and DRM, use MediaLive with MediaPackage and MediaTailor; Recorded video libraries, use MediaConvert with CloudFront; Very high hour counts, per hour delivery pricing gets expensive at scale
Example: A jewellery seller runs a nightly live sale where viewers ask questions in chat and buy as they watch.
How you pay: Per hour of input and per hour of video delivered to viewers, plus chat messages. Delivery hours multiply by audience size, which is where the bill grows.

## Migration and Transfer


### AWS Application Discovery Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-application-discovery-service.html
In one sentence: It surveys the servers in your data centre so you know what you actually have before moving.
Picture it as: Walking through a warehouse with a clipboard and writing down every box, its size and who uses it, before you hire the removal van.
What it does: Collects inventory and performance data from on premises servers, either agentless through a VMware appliance or with an agent on each machine. It records CPU, memory, disk and network connections, which helps you see which servers talk to each other. It does not move anything, and the agentless mode only works properly with VMware vCenter.
Use it when: Planning a data centre migration and you do not trust your own inventory; You need to work out which servers must move together; You want real usage data to size EC2 instances
Do NOT use it when: You already have a good CMDB or a small, well known server list, just export what you have; You are moving a handful of servers, the setup effort is not worth it, size them by hand
Example: Before a migration, a team runs the collector for a month and finds 40 of their 300 servers have no network traffic at all, so they are switched off instead of moved.
How you pay: The service is free. You pay for the data it stores in your account and for the agentless appliance running on your own hardware.

### AWS Application Migration Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-application-migration-service.html
In one sentence: It copies your existing servers, as they are, onto EC2 and lets you cut over.
Picture it as: Moving house by lifting every room exactly as it is onto the new plot, rather than repacking each cupboard.
What it does: Known as MGN, and the replacement for the retired CloudEndure and Server Migration Service. You install an agent on each source server, it replicates the disks continuously to AWS, then you launch a test instance and finally cut over with minutes of downtime. It is a lift and shift tool, so it copies your problems too, and it does not modernise anything.
Use it when: Moving physical or virtual servers to EC2 with little downtime; A data centre exit with a hard deadline; You want to test the migrated server before committing
Do NOT use it when: The workload is a plain database, use DMS or a native restore instead of copying the whole machine; You want to end up on containers or serverless, replatform properly, a lifted server stays a server you have to patch
Example: A company replicates 60 Windows servers over three weeks, tests each one, then cuts over on a Saturday night with 15 minutes of downtime.
How you pay: Free for 90 days per source server, which is the trap. Replication is not free, because staging EBS volumes, snapshots and data transfer are charged from day one, and servers left replicating past 90 days start costing per server per hour.

### AWS Data Transfer Terminal
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-data-transfer-terminal.html
In one sentence: Lets you drive your hard drives to an AWS building and copy them in over a very fast cable.
Picture it as: Taking a suitcase of photos to a print shop instead of emailing them one by one.
What it does: It is a real physical room you book by the hour. You bring your own storage device, plug into two 100 Gbps fibre links, and copy data straight into AWS. It launched in late 2024 and there are only a few sites, starting with New York and Los Angeles, so it is useless unless you can physically reach one.
Use it when: You have tens or hundreds of terabytes and a slow office internet line; Film footage or vehicle sensor logs need to land in AWS the same day; You do not want to post a device and wait for it to be loaded
Do NOT use it when: There is no terminal near you. Then use aws-direct-connect or an online copy tool instead.; The data is small, a few terabytes or less. A normal internet upload is cheaper and simpler.; You need ongoing daily transfers. Book a permanent link with aws-direct-connect, not a one off visit.
Example: A film crew back from a shoot books two hours in Los Angeles and pushes 400 TB of camera files into S3.
How you pay: Per port per hour, roughly 300 USD for US uploads and more for cross continent. The surprise is that you also pay for travel and staff time, and you pay for the booked slot even if your copy runs slow.

### AWS DataSync
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-datasync.html
In one sentence: It copies large amounts of files from one place to another, and checks they arrived.
Picture it as: A removals firm. They pack the boxes, drive them over, and tick each one off the list at the other end.
What it does: DataSync moves data between on-premises NFS, SMB, HDFS or object stores and AWS services such as S3, EFS and the FSx family, and between AWS services or other clouds. It runs much faster than a plain copy, handles retries, keeps file metadata and verifies content afterwards. For on-premises sources you deploy an agent VM. It is task-based and scheduled, so it is not continuous replication and not a live sync.
Use it when: A one-off migration of millions of files into AWS; A nightly copy from an office NAS into S3; Moving data between S3 and EFS or FSx
Do NOT use it when: For continuous, near-live replication, use S3 Replication or NetApp SnapMirror; For ongoing local access to cloud storage, use Storage Gateway; For a few small files, the AWS CLI is enough
Example: A media company schedules DataSync to pull each night's camera footage from the studio NAS into S3, with verification on.
How you pay: Per GB copied, around 0.0125 USD. The surprise is that request and retrieval charges on the destination, and the EC2 or VMware cost of running the agent, sit on top, and re-running a task on unchanged data still scans everything.

### AWS Mainframe Modernization
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-mainframe-modernization.html
In one sentence: Tools to move old mainframe programs to AWS, either running them as they are or rewriting them into Java.
Picture it as: An old factory machine that still works. You either build a new shed around it so it keeps running, or you rebuild it from scratch in modern parts.
What it does: Offers two paths, replatform with Rocket Software so COBOL and JCL keep running mostly unchanged, or refactor with AWS Blu Age which converts the code to Java or .NET. The managed runtime is closed to new customers, and the self managed experience moves to maintenance status on 30 July 2026, closing to new customers. AWS now steers new mainframe work to AWS Transform. Very few organisations ever need this.
Use it when: You already use it and are continuing an existing programme; You are studying the replatform versus refactor choice
Do NOT use it when: You are starting a mainframe migration now, look at AWS Transform first, this one is closing to new customers; You have an old server but not a mainframe, this is for IBM z/OS, use Application Migration Service
Example: An insurer converts decades of COBOL batch jobs into Java Spring Boot services that produce the same output, checked line by line against the old system.
How you pay: Charged per compute hour for the runtime plus storage. Real cost is the multi year project and the testing, not the AWS line item.

### AWS Migration Evaluator
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-migration-evaluator.html
In one sentence: Looks at the servers you own today and estimates what they would cost on AWS.
Picture it as: A removal company walking through your house and quoting the van size before you pack.
What it does: You run a small collector program in your own data centre for a few weeks. It measures how busy each server really is, then AWS produces a report matching each one to an EC2 size, with a cost estimate including licences. It is an assessment report, not something that moves any workload, and the useful version comes through an AWS team rather than fully self service. It came from TSO Logic, a company AWS bought in 2019.
Use it when: Management wants a number before approving a move to AWS; You suspect your servers are far bigger than the work needs; You need a licence cost comparison for Windows or SQL Server
Do NOT use it when: You only have a handful of servers. Price them by hand with aws-cost-explorer style guesses instead.; You already decided to move and want the actual migration tooling. This only produces a business case.; You want ongoing cost control after you are on AWS. Use aws-cost-explorer and aws-budgets.
Example: A company finds 300 servers averaging 8 percent CPU and the report shows a far smaller EC2 bill than expected.
How you pay: No charge for the assessment itself. The real cost is the weeks of data collection and the people time.

### AWS Transfer Family
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-transfer-family.html
In one sentence: An SFTP server that saves files straight into S3.
Picture it as: An old style letterbox bolted onto a modern warehouse.
What it does: Transfer Family gives partners a normal SFTP, FTPS or AS2 endpoint, while the files actually land in S3. Useful when a bank or vendor will only send files the old way.
Use it when: A partner insists on SFTP; Bank or government file exchange
Do NOT use it when: You control both ends. Use the S3 API.
Example: A bank drops a daily settlement file by SFTP, it appears in S3.
How you pay: Per hour the endpoint exists, plus per GB. The hourly charge runs even when idle.

### AWS Transform
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-transform.html
In one sentence: An AI agent that reads your old applications and rewrites them for AWS.
Picture it as: A translator who reads an old handwritten ledger and types out a modern version, then you still have to check every page.
What it does: An agentic AI service for large modernisation jobs, covering mainframe COBOL to Java, .NET Framework to modern .NET, and VMware workloads to EC2. It assesses the code, writes documentation, converts it and helps test. It is new, aimed at big enterprise programmes, and the output still needs human review, so treat it as a fast first draft rather than a finished migration.
Use it when: Thousands of files of legacy code that nobody understands any more; Upgrading old .NET Framework applications at scale; You need a documented assessment before committing to a migration
Do NOT use it when: A handful of applications, a developer with Amazon Q or Claude will be quicker and cheaper; You expect a working system with no review, the converted code must be tested against the old system's output
Example: A team points it at a .NET Framework application and gets a ported .NET 8 version plus a list of the parts it could not convert.
How you pay: Varies by workload type and has been offered free for some transformation paths. The real cost is the engineering time spent checking what it produced.

## Networking and Content Delivery


### AWS App Mesh
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-app-mesh.html
In one sentence: A retired traffic controller that used to sit next to each of your services.
Picture it as: A telephone switchboard operator who sat between every pair of departments in an office. The company has now removed the switchboard and told everyone to call each other directly.
What it does: App Mesh is being shut down. AWS stopped letting new customers sign up in September 2024, and support ends on 30 September 2026, after which the console and resources go away. It ran a small proxy (Envoy) beside every one of your services so traffic between them could be routed, retried and measured in one place. AWS points existing users to Amazon ECS Service Connect or Amazon VPC Lattice.
Use it when: Only if you already run it and are planning the exit; Reading old blog posts or Terraform and wondering what it was
Do NOT use it when: Starting anything new, use Amazon VPC Lattice or ECS Service Connect; Wanting a service mesh you control yourself, use Istio or Linkerd on Kubernetes
Example: A team with forty ECS services on App Mesh spent 2026 moving them to ECS Service Connect before the cutoff.
How you pay: There was no charge for App Mesh itself. The cost was the Envoy sidecar on every task, which quietly added CPU and memory to every service you ran.

### AWS Client VPN
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-client-vpn.html
In one sentence: Lets staff on laptops anywhere dial into your private AWS network.
Picture it as: A staff side door with a key card, for people working from home.
What it does: You set up an endpoint, users install an OpenVPN style client, and once connected their laptop can reach private servers as if it were in the office. It handles logins through certificates, Active Directory or a federated identity provider. It is per user remote access, and it is not cheap once you have many people online.
Use it when: Developers need to reach a private database that has no public address; Staff work from home and need internal tools; A contractor needs limited access for a short project
Do NOT use it when: You are joining two networks, an office to AWS, not individual people. Use aws-site-to-site-vpn.; You just want to reach one EC2 box for admin. Session Manager needs no VPN at all.; You want per app access without a network tunnel. A zero trust proxy fits better than this.
Example: Twenty engineers connect each morning and can reach the private RDS instance from their laptops.
How you pay: About 10 cents per hour for the endpoint in each subnet, plus about 5 cents per connected user per hour. The surprise is the subnet charge ticks along all night even when nobody is connected.

### AWS Cloud Map
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloud-map.html
In one sentence: A phone book your services look things up in instead of hard coding addresses.
Picture it as: An office directory on the wall. You look up "Accounts" and it tells you which room they are in today, so nobody has to memorise room numbers that keep changing.
What it does: You register a resource under a friendly name, and your code asks Cloud Map for the current address. It also removes entries that fail health checks. Most people never call it directly, because ECS service discovery and Kubernetes create Cloud Map records for you behind the scenes.
Use it when: Services on ECS that need to find each other by name; Registering things DNS cannot describe well, like a queue URL or a table name
