Do NOT use it when: Public websites and domains, use Amazon Route 53; Service to service calls where you also want auth and routing rules, use Amazon VPC Lattice
Example: An order service asks Cloud Map for "payments" and gets the IPs of the healthy payment containers running right now.
How you pay: Cents per registered resource per month, plus a charge per lookup. Chatty apps that look up on every single request can run up the call count, so cache the answer.

### AWS Cloud WAN
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloud-wan.html
In one sentence: One place to build and see your whole global network instead of wiring regions together by hand.
Picture it as: Managing a rail network from a single control room with one map, rather than each station agreeing its own connections with its neighbours.
What it does: You describe your network as a policy document, which regions connect, which sites connect, who may talk to whom, and AWS builds it. It joins AWS regions and your own offices and data centres into one network with a shared dashboard. It is aimed at large companies with many regions and many physical sites, and it is overkill and expensive for anyone smaller.
Use it when: Many VPCs across several AWS regions plus branch offices; You want one policy file to define global connectivity; Replacing a tangle of peerings and Transit Gateways
Do NOT use it when: A handful of VPCs in one region, use AWS Transit Gateway; Two VPCs that need to talk, use VPC peering
Example: A retailer with stores in twelve countries defines one policy so every store reaches the regional AWS network nearest to it.
How you pay: A monthly charge per core network edge in each region, plus per attachment and per GB of data. The per edge fee applies whether or not traffic flows, so idle regions still cost money.

### AWS Direct Connect
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-direct-connect.html
In one sentence: A private cable from your building or data centre into AWS, instead of going over the internet.
Picture it as: A private road from your warehouse to the motorway, so your lorries never sit in public traffic.
What it does: A dedicated fibre link between your network and AWS, ordered through a partner at a location where AWS has equipment. It gives steadier speed and lower delay than the internet, and it lowers the price of data leaving AWS. It is not encrypted by itself, and setup takes weeks or months, not minutes.
Use it when: Moving large amounts of data in and out every day; Applications that break when latency jitters; Rules that say your traffic must not cross the public internet
Do NOT use it when: You need something working today, use AWS Site-to-Site VPN; Small or occasional traffic, the internet is cheaper and fine; Only want privacy, not speed, a VPN gives you that at far less cost
Example: A media firm pushes a terabyte of daily footage to S3 over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link instead of saturating its office line.
How you pay: An hourly port charge whether you use it or not, plus per GB out at a reduced rate. The surprise is the separate bill from the telecom partner for the last stretch of fibre to your building, which AWS does not include.

### AWS Global Accelerator
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-global-accelerator.html
In one sentence: Gets users onto the AWS network early so their traffic takes a faster path to your servers.
Picture it as: A fast lane entrance that gets you onto the motorway right away, rather than crawling through town first.
What it does: You get two fixed IP addresses that work worldwide. A user's traffic enters AWS at the nearest edge location and then travels over the AWS network to your application, which is usually faster and steadier than the open internet. It also fails over between regions in seconds. It does not cache anything, so it helps live and dynamic traffic, not static files.
Use it when: Games, chat, video calls, APIs where delay matters; You need fixed IP addresses that never change; Running the same app in several regions with automatic failover
Do NOT use it when: Websites, images and video files, use Amazon CloudFront which also caches; One region and one country of users, a load balancer alone is enough
Example: A multiplayer game gives players two static IPs, and a player in Mumbai is routed to the Singapore servers over the AWS backbone.
How you pay: A fixed hourly fee per accelerator, about 18 dollars a month, plus a per GB charge on top of normal data transfer. The fixed fee runs even with zero traffic, and the data premium is easy to miss.

### AWS Interconnect
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-interconnect.html
In one sentence: Orders a private cable between AWS and another cloud or your office, in a few clicks.
Picture it as: Asking the phone company for a dedicated line instead of running the wire yourself.
What it does: It is a newer managed connectivity service that arranges private, fixed bandwidth links from AWS to Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, or to your own sites through a network partner. The point is that AWS handles the paperwork and router setup that used to take weeks. It is aimed at large multicloud setups, so most teams will never open it.
Use it when: You run workloads in AWS and another cloud and want them talking privately; Setting up a cross connect by hand with a carrier is taking weeks; You need encrypted, predictable bandwidth between providers
Do NOT use it when: You only need AWS to your own data centre. Plain aws-direct-connect is the well worn path.; Your traffic is small or occasional. A aws-site-to-site-vpn over the internet costs far less.; You only use one cloud. Then there is nothing here for you.
Example: A bank links its AWS region to its Azure tenancy with a 10 Gbps private path instead of routing over the internet.
How you pay: By the link, on capacity and how long you keep it. Fixed bandwidth means you pay whether or not traffic flows.

### AWS PrivateLink
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-privatelink.html
In one sentence: Lets your private network reach an AWS service or a partner's service without touching the internet.
Picture it as: A service hatch built straight through the wall into the shop next door, so deliveries never go out onto the street.
What it does: It puts a private address inside your own VPC that points at a service somewhere else, an AWS service like S3, or software sold by another company, or another team's application. Traffic stays on the AWS network. The link is one way, the consumer calls the provider, and the provider cannot call back.
Use it when: Servers with no internet access that still need to call AWS APIs; Buying SaaS that must not be reached over the internet; Exposing one internal API to another AWS account without peering
Do NOT use it when: Two VPCs that need full two way access, use peering or AWS Transit Gateway; Reaching your own office network, use Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect
Example: A database server in a private subnet writes to S3 through a VPC endpoint, with no NAT gateway and no route to the internet.
How you pay: An hourly charge per endpoint per availability zone, plus per GB. Teams create endpoints for a dozen services across three zones and are surprised by the hourly fees, which add up before any data moves.

### AWS RTB Fabric
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-rtb-fabric.html
In one sentence: Carries advertising bid requests between ad companies in a few milliseconds.
Picture it as: A private courier lane between trading floors, because the public road is too slow.
What it does: A private network built for real time bidding, the auctions that decide which advert you see while a web page loads. Those auctions must finish in tens of milliseconds, so it connects ad platforms to partners like Amazon Ads directly. It is only useful if your business is programmatic advertising. Everyone else has no reason to look at it.
Use it when: You run a demand side or supply side ad platform; Bid timeouts are losing you auctions; Cross network data transfer for bid traffic is a large part of your bill
Do NOT use it when: You buy adverts but do not run bidding infrastructure. This is not for you.; You want general low latency networking. Use amazon-virtual-private-cloud with placement groups, or amazon-cloudfront for content.; Your traffic tolerates 100 ms or more. Ordinary networking is far cheaper.
Example: An ad exchange routes bid requests to partners over the fabric and sees fewer timed out bids.
How you pay: Per transaction, with no upfront commitment. It is pitched as much cheaper than paying normal cross network data transfer for the same bid volume.

### AWS Site to Site VPN
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-site-to-site-vpn.html
In one sentence: An encrypted tunnel over the internet joining your office network to your AWS network.
Picture it as: Sending post in a locked box through the normal postal service. Same roads as everyone else, but nobody can read what is inside.
What it does: You set up a tunnel between AWS and a router or firewall at your site, and the two networks can then reach each other by private address. It is quick to create and cheap. Because it rides the public internet, speed and delay vary with the day, and a single tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps.
Use it when: Connecting an office or data centre to AWS this week; A backup path in case a Direct Connect link fails; Small or occasional traffic between sites
Do NOT use it when: Steady high throughput or predictable latency, use AWS Direct Connect; Giving individual laptops access, use AWS Client VPN or AWS Verified Access
Example: A company's finance server in its own server room reads an RDS database in AWS over a VPN tunnel.
How you pay: Around 5 cents per hour per connection, plus data out. The catch is that AWS gives two tunnels for redundancy but many routers are configured to use only one, so you pay for resilience you do not actually have.

### AWS Transit Gateway
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-transit-gateway.html
In one sentence: A central hub that connects all your networks so you stop wiring each pair together.
Picture it as: An airport hub. Instead of a direct flight between every pair of towns, everything routes through one airport.
What it does: You attach VPCs, VPN tunnels and Direct Connect links to one gateway, and it routes between them using route tables you control. It replaces the mess of peering connections that grows unmanageable past about five VPCs. Every packet passing through is charged, so it is a real line on the bill, not a free convenience.
Use it when: More than a handful of VPCs that need to talk; Sharing one VPN or Direct Connect across many VPCs; You want route tables that separate environments, like prod and test
Do NOT use it when: Two VPCs only, VPC peering is free and simpler; Just calling a service in another VPC, use AWS PrivateLink; Many regions and physical sites, look at AWS Cloud WAN
Example: Twelve team VPCs and the office VPN all attach to one Transit Gateway, and only some route tables let teams reach the shared services VPC.
How you pay: An hourly fee per attachment plus a per GB charge on all traffic crossing it. Cross zone and cross region traffic is charged again on top, so a chatty app between two VPCs can cost more than the servers.

### AWS Verified Access
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-verified-access.html
In one sentence: Staff reach internal apps over the internet without a VPN, and every request is checked.
Picture it as: A doorman who checks your ID and that your coat is buttoned, every single time you walk in, instead of one lock on the front door.
What it does: Verified Access puts a policy in front of an internal application. Each request is evaluated against who the user is, from IAM Identity Center or an OIDC provider, and optionally the device's health from a tool like CrowdStrike or Jamf. It is AWS's take on zero trust access. It only covers applications you host inside AWS, so it does not replace a VPN that also reaches on-premise networks or non-HTTP services.
Use it when: Replacing a VPN for internal web apps hosted in AWS; You want device posture checked on every request; Per-application access rules instead of full network access
Do NOT use it when: Not for public, customer-facing apps, use Cognito or your own login plus WAF; If staff need SSH, RDP or on-premise networks, keep a VPN or use Client VPN; Small teams with one internal tool will find Cognito plus a load balancer simpler
Example: A contractor opens the internal dashboard in a browser, and access is denied because their laptop disk is not encrypted.
How you pay: Per application per hour, plus per gigabyte of data processed. The hourly charge runs per application whether anyone uses it or not.

### Amazon API Gateway
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-api-gateway.html
In one sentence: The front door for your API.
Picture it as: A reception desk. It checks who you are, stops rude visitors, then sends you to the right room.
What it does: API Gateway takes HTTP requests and passes them to Lambda or your servers. It handles authentication, rate limits, keys and versions. It adds a little delay and a per request cost.
Use it when: A public API; You are building with Lambda; You need rate limiting
Do NOT use it when: A simple website. A load balancer is cheaper.
Example: A mobile app calling /orders, which triggers a Lambda function.
How you pay: Per million requests, plus data out.

### Amazon Application Recovery Controller
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-application-recovery-controller.html
In one sentence: Big red switches that move your traffic away from a broken region or zone, and checks that the backup is really ready.
Picture it as: A fire drill plus a clearly labelled master switch. Someone checks every month that the second exit actually opens, and there is one lever to send everyone that way.
What it does: Formerly called Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller, renamed to Amazon Application Recovery Controller in late 2024. It has three parts: readiness checks that compare your standby region against production and warn when they drift, routing controls that are simple on and off switches with a safety rule so you cannot switch everything off at once, and zonal shift and autoshift, which pull traffic out of one unhealthy availability zone. Zonal shift is free and useful to many people. The routing control part is expensive and aimed at banks and similar.
Use it when: A multi region setup where failover must work under pressure; Draining a single bad availability zone quickly; Proving to auditors that the standby is genuinely ready
Do NOT use it when: Simple DNS failover on health checks, plain Amazon Route 53 does that; One region only, use zonal shift and skip the rest; Backup and restore of data, use AWS Backup
Example: An availability zone starts timing out, and an operator triggers a zonal shift so the load balancer stops sending traffic there.
How you pay: Zonal shift and autoshift are free. Routing control costs roughly 3,000 US dollars a month per cluster, which shocks people who find it while browsing, plus per readiness check. Turn a cluster on and you pay even in a quiet month.

### Amazon CloudFront
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-cloudfront.html
In one sentence: Keeps copies of your files near your users so pages load fast.
Picture it as: A local warehouse in every city instead of shipping everything from one factory.
What it does: CloudFront is a CDN. It caches your content at locations around the world. Users get served from the nearest one. It also absorbs traffic spikes and shields your servers.
Use it when: Any public website; Images and video; Global audience
Do NOT use it when: An internal tool used by ten people in one office.
Example: A course video watched from Ahmedabad is served from an Indian location, not from Virginia.
How you pay: Per GB delivered and per request. There is a generous free tier.

### Amazon Route 53
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-route-53.html
In one sentence: The phone book that turns your domain name into an address.
Picture it as: Saving a contact by name so you never memorise the number.
What it does: Route 53 is DNS. It points yourdomain.com to your server or CloudFront. It can also register domains, check if your site is healthy, and send users to the closest region.
Use it when: You own a domain and it points at AWS
Do NOT use it when: Your DNS is already fine at GoDaddy or Cloudflare and you have no reason to move.
Example: kwickprep.com points at CloudFront, which points at S3.
How you pay: A small monthly fee per hosted zone, plus per million queries.

### Amazon VPC Lattice
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-vpc-lattice.html
In one sentence: Connects your services to each other by name, with permissions and routing handled for you.
Picture it as: An office receptionist who knows every department, checks whether you are allowed to speak to them, and puts the call through. You never need their extension number.
What it does: You register services into a service network and they call each other by a stable name, across VPCs and AWS accounts, without peering or Transit Gateway. It applies IAM permissions per request and handles retries and traffic splitting. It is AWS's recommended replacement for App Mesh, and it is still fairly new with a smaller community than Kubernetes service meshes.
Use it when: Services spread across several VPCs or accounts that need to call each other; You want per request authorisation between services, not just network rules; Moving off AWS App Mesh before it shuts down
Do NOT use it when: Everything in one VPC, a load balancer and security groups are simpler and cheaper; You need deep mesh features and portability, use Istio on EKS
Example: A checkout service in one account calls an inventory service in another, by name, with an IAM policy allowing only that caller.
How you pay: An hourly fee per service and per service network, plus per GB and per request. The standing hourly fees mean a network of many small services costs money before it serves a single request.

### Amazon Virtual Private Cloud
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-virtual-private-cloud.html
In one sentence: Your own private section of the AWS network.
Picture it as: A gated plot inside a big township. You decide the roads, the gates and who gets in.
What it does: A VPC is where your servers live. You split it into subnets. Public subnets can reach the internet, private ones cannot. Security groups act as a firewall on each machine.
Use it when: Always. Anything you run sits in a VPC.
Example: Web servers in a public subnet, the database in a private one so it can never be reached from the internet.
How you pay: The VPC is free. NAT gateways and data transfer cost money and surprise people.

### Elastic Load Balancing
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/elastic-load-balancing.html
In one sentence: Shares incoming traffic across several servers.
Picture it as: A queue manager at a bank sending you to whichever counter is free.
What it does: A load balancer sits in front of your servers. If one dies, it stops sending traffic there. It also handles HTTPS so your servers do not have to.
Use it when: More than one server; You want zero downtime deploys; You want HTTPS handled in one place
Do NOT use it when: A single small server with little traffic. It is an extra monthly cost.
Example: Three web servers behind one address. One reboots, nobody notices.
How you pay: Per hour, plus a usage unit based on traffic.

## Quantum


### Amazon Braket
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-braket.html
In one sentence: Lets you send programs to real quantum computers, or to simulators of them, and get results back.
Picture it as: Booking time on a telescope at an observatory. You submit when you want to look, and you wait your turn.
What it does: It gives one interface to quantum machines from several makers, plus simulators that run on ordinary AWS hardware. Today's quantum machines are small and noisy, so almost all useful work is research, learning or simulation, not production. Almost nobody needs this service for a real business problem yet, and it is honest to say so.
Use it when: Academic or corporate research into quantum algorithms; Learning quantum programming against real hardware; Comparing results across different quantum machines
Do NOT use it when: Any current business workload, classical computing will be faster and far cheaper; Optimisation or machine learning problems, use normal solvers and SageMaker; Claiming quantum benefit in a product, the hardware is not there yet
Example: A university group runs the same small circuit on a simulator and on a trapped ion machine to compare error rates.
How you pay: Per task and per shot on real hardware, plus a per hour charge for simulators. Per shot charges on real devices climb quickly, since meaningful runs need thousands of shots.

## Satellite


### AWS Ground Station
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-ground-station.html
In one sentence: Rents you time on satellite dishes to talk to your satellite, by the minute.
Picture it as: A pay by the hour recording studio, except the studio is a large dish pointed at the sky.
What it does: AWS owns antennas at sites around the world. You book a contact window when your satellite passes overhead, and the data it sends down lands in your AWS account ready to process. This only applies if you or your customer actually operate a satellite, which is a very small group of organisations. You still need your own satellite, licences and radio approvals.
Use it when: You operate satellites and do not want to build ground stations; Earth observation data that must be processed immediately after downlink; Extra antenna coverage on top of your own stations
Do NOT use it when: Anyone who does not operate a satellite, which is nearly everyone; Buying satellite imagery, buy it from a provider such as an Open Data set or a commercial vendor; GPS or location features in an app, use Amazon Location Service
Example: An imaging satellite passes over Sweden, downlinks through an AWS antenna, and the images are in S3 minutes later.
How you pay: Per minute of antenna contact, with different rates for narrowband and wideband, plus a monthly reserved option. Data egress and the processing instances are extra.

## Security and Identity


### AWS Artifact
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-artifact.html
In one sentence: A self-service download page for AWS's own audit and compliance reports.
Picture it as: The filing cabinet at the back of the office where the landlord keeps the fire safety certificates. You go and take a copy when someone asks for proof.
What it does: Artifact holds AWS's third-party audit reports, like SOC 1, SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI, plus agreements such as the HIPAA BAA and GDPR terms. You download them and hand them to your auditor or customer. The thing people get wrong: these reports cover AWS's side of the line only. They say nothing about whether your own setup is secure or compliant.
Use it when: An auditor or enterprise customer asks for AWS compliance evidence; You need to accept a legal agreement like a HIPAA BAA; Filling in a security questionnaire
Do NOT use it when: Do not use it to prove YOUR system is compliant, that is Audit Manager or Security Hub CSPM; Not a place to store your own documents, use S3
Example: A hospital asks your startup for proof AWS is HIPAA eligible. You open Artifact, accept the BAA, and download the SOC 2 report.
How you pay: Free. No charge at all.

### AWS Audit Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-audit-manager.html
In one sentence: It collects evidence about your AWS setup automatically so an audit is less painful.
Picture it as: A clerk who quietly photocopies every receipt all year, so at tax time the shoebox is already sorted into folders.
What it does: Audit Manager runs against a framework, like SOC 2, PCI DSS or HIPAA, and keeps pulling evidence from CloudTrail, Config and Security Hub into an assessment you can export. It gathers and organises evidence. It does not decide you passed, and it does not fix anything. A human auditor still reads the report, and plenty of controls still need manual evidence you upload yourself.
Use it when: You are going through a real, repeated compliance audit; You need a paper trail of control evidence over time; Many accounts and you cannot collect evidence by hand
Do NOT use it when: Not for finding or fixing security problems, use Security Hub CSPM and Inspector; Overkill if you have no actual audit coming, it costs money and attention for nothing; Not proof of AWS's own compliance, that is Artifact
Example: A fintech enables the PCI DSS framework, and a year of evidence for each control is ready when the assessor arrives.
How you pay: Charged per resource assessment, so cost rises with how many resources each control touches. Enabling many frameworks at once across a big account is the surprise.

### AWS Certificate Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-certificate-manager.html
In one sentence: Free HTTPS certificates that renew themselves.
Picture it as: A licence that renews automatically so it never expires on you.
What it does: ACM issues and renews TLS certificates at no cost for use with CloudFront, load balancers and API Gateway. Automatic renewal removes the classic outage of a certificate expiring at midnight.
Use it when: Any site with HTTPS on AWS
Do NOT use it when: You need the certificate file to install on your own server. ACM public certs cannot be exported.
Example: HTTPS on your domain through CloudFront, renewing itself forever.
How you pay: Free for public certificates used with AWS services.

### AWS CloudHSM
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-cloudhsm.html
In one sentence: A dedicated tamper-proof box that holds your encryption keys, and only you can open it.
Picture it as: Renting the actual safe deposit box at the bank, with the only key, instead of asking the bank to look after your valuables.
What it does: CloudHSM gives you single-tenant hardware security modules, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, where you control the keys completely. AWS cannot see or recover them. That last part is the real point and the real danger: lose your credentials and the keys are gone, with no AWS support ticket that gets them back. Most people who think they need CloudHSM actually need KMS. It exists for regulators who demand sole custody of keys.
Use it when: A regulator or contract demands you hold the keys with no cloud provider access; You need an HSM for a specific standard KMS does not meet; Running your own certificate authority or custom crypto offload
Do NOT use it when: For almost all encryption, use KMS instead, it is far cheaper and simpler; Do not use it for payment card PIN and EMV work, use Payment Cryptography
Example: A bank keeps its signing keys in a CloudHSM cluster because the regulator will not accept a shared service.
How you pay: Per HSM, per hour, and you are told to run at least two or three for reliability. That runs into thousands of dollars a month whether you use it or not.

### AWS Directory Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-directory-service.html
In one sentence: It runs Microsoft Active Directory for you, or connects AWS to the one you already have.
Picture it as: The office staff list that decides whose badge opens which door. This is AWS running that list for you.
What it does: There are three quite different things under one name. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real Active Directory that AWS patches and backs up. AD Connector is a pass-through to your existing on-premise AD, storing nothing. Simple AD is a small Samba-based stand-in and is the weakest option. You pick one by what you need, and mixing them up is the usual mistake.
Use it when: Windows servers, SQL Server or file shares on EC2 that need domain join; Amazon WorkSpaces or RDS SQL Server with Windows authentication; You want AWS to reach your existing corporate AD
Do NOT use it when: Not for signing in to the AWS console, that is IAM Identity Center; Not for your app's own user accounts, use Cognito; If you have no Windows or AD in the picture, you do not need this at all
Example: A company joins its EC2 Windows file servers to AWS Managed Microsoft AD so staff use the same office login.
How you pay: Per hour, per directory, always on. A Managed Microsoft AD standard edition runs a few hundred dollars a month even if idle, and you need two of them for a second region.

### AWS Firewall Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-firewall-manager.html
In one sentence: It pushes the same firewall rules to every account in your company automatically.
Picture it as: A head office rule that every branch must lock the back door, applied centrally so a new branch is locked on day one.
What it does: Firewall Manager sits above WAF, Shield Advanced, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall and security groups, and applies your policies across all accounts in an AWS Organization, including accounts created later. It is a policy distributor, not a firewall itself. It needs AWS Organizations, a nominated admin account and, for some policies, Shield Advanced, so it is useless to a single-account setup.
Use it when: Many AWS accounts under an Organization; You must guarantee a new account cannot ship without WAF; Auditing for stray, overly open security groups across accounts
Do NOT use it when: Pointless with one or two accounts, just configure WAF or Network Firewall directly; It does not inspect traffic itself, the underlying services do that and bill separately
Example: Security mandates that every public ALB in the company has the managed WAF rule set, and Firewall Manager applies it to accounts opened next month too.
How you pay: A monthly fee per policy, per region, on top of the full cost of every WAF, Network Firewall or Shield resource it creates. The underlying services are the big number.

### AWS IAM Identity Center
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-iam-identity-center.html
In one sentence: One login that gets your staff into all your AWS accounts, with the right permissions.
Picture it as: A single office badge that opens the doors you are allowed through, instead of a separate key for every room.
What it does: Formerly AWS Single Sign-On, and still called that in older docs. It gives each person one sign-in, often from Okta, Entra ID or Google Workspace, and hands out short-lived credentials for each AWS account and role. This is the current recommended way for humans to access AWS. Long-lived IAM users with access keys are the old way and are discouraged.
Use it when: More than one AWS account, or more than about two people; You want to stop creating IAM users and access keys; You already have a company identity provider to plug in
Do NOT use it when: Not for applications or servers, they should use IAM roles; Not for your product's end users, use Cognito; Not a replacement for IAM policies, it hands them out, it does not define what they mean
Example: A new engineer is added to one group in Okta and instantly has read-only access to production and admin in the sandbox account.
How you pay: Free. You pay for nothing here, which is why there is no excuse not to use it.

### AWS Identity and Access Management
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-identity-and-access-management.html
In one sentence: Decides who can do what in your AWS account.
Picture it as: Keys for a building. The cleaner's key opens the store room, not the safe.
What it does: IAM holds users, roles and policies. A policy is a list of allowed actions. Give the least access that still works. Never use the root account for daily work, and turn on MFA.
Use it when: Always. From day one.
Example: A role that lets one Lambda function read one S3 bucket and nothing else.
How you pay: Free.

### AWS Key Management Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-key-management-service.html
In one sentence: Creates and guards the keys that encrypt your data.
Picture it as: The master key cutting machine, kept in a locked room. You can use the keys, you can never take them out.
What it does: KMS holds encryption keys. S3, RDS, EBS and others call it to encrypt your data. The key never leaves KMS. Every use is logged in CloudTrail.
Use it when: Encrypting anything; Compliance requirements
Example: All backups encrypted with a key only two roles may use.
How you pay: Per key per month, plus per request.

### AWS Network Firewall
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-network-firewall.html
In one sentence: A firewall that inspects traffic going in and out of your private network in AWS.
Picture it as: A guard at the estate gate who checks where each van is going, not just whether it has a pass.
What it does: Network Firewall is a managed, stateful firewall for a VPC. It can filter by domain name, match Suricata intrusion detection rules, and block outbound traffic to places you did not approve. Security groups and network ACLs already do simple allow and deny far more cheaply, so this earns its place mainly when you need deep inspection or outbound domain control. Getting the routing right, with traffic forced through firewall endpoints, is the hard part.
Use it when: You must control which domains your servers can reach outbound; A compliance rule demands intrusion detection on network traffic; A central inspection VPC for many accounts
Do NOT use it when: For ordinary port and source rules, security groups are free and enough; For filtering HTTP attacks on a public web app, use WAF; For blocking DNS lookups only, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall is much cheaper
Example: A regulated workload may only call api.stripe.com outbound, and Network Firewall drops every other destination.
How you pay: An hourly charge per firewall endpoint in each availability zone, plus a charge per gigabyte inspected. The per-zone hourly fee adds up before you pass any traffic.

### AWS Payment Cryptography
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-payment-cryptography.html
In one sentence: It does the card-industry encryption work that bank payment systems need.
Picture it as: The sealed machine in a bank branch that turns a typed PIN into something nobody can read, rented by the hour instead of bought.
What it does: A very narrow service for payment processors, card issuers, acquirers and banks. It handles PIN translation, card verification values, EMV and key exchange under PCI PIN and PCI P2PE rules, replacing the physical payment HSMs those firms used to rack in a data centre. Almost nobody needs this. If you are not personally handling raw card PINs or issuing cards, it is not for you.
Use it when: You process or translate card PINs yourself; You issue cards and need EMV key handling; You are replacing physical payment HSMs in a colocation cage
Do NOT use it when: Taking card payments on a website does not need it, use Stripe or a payment provider; For general encryption keys, use KMS; For your own custom crypto with sole key custody, use CloudHSM
Example: A card issuer verifies an ATM PIN block without ever having the clear PIN in its own application.
How you pay: Per API call plus per active key, per hour. Keys you created and forgot keep billing.

### AWS Private Certificate Authority
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-private-certificate-authority.html
In one sentence: It lets you issue your own certificates for things inside your own network.
Picture it as: Printing your own staff ID cards. They work everywhere inside your building, and mean nothing outside it.
What it does: Private CA, formerly ACM Private CA, runs a certificate authority you own, so you can issue TLS certificates for internal services, containers, devices and users. Browsers and the public internet will not trust these unless you install your root on every machine, which is the point people miss. It is the right tool for mutual TLS between services and for IoT fleets.
Use it when: Mutual TLS between internal services or in a service mesh; Certificates for IoT devices or company laptops; An internal domain a public CA will not issue for
Do NOT use it when: Never for a public website, use ACM public certificates, which are free; Small setups can often self-sign or use cert-manager instead, this is expensive for a handful of certs
Example: A Kubernetes cluster issues short-lived certificates to each pod so services only talk to each other over verified TLS.
How you pay: A few hundred dollars per month for each CA, whether idle or not, plus a per-certificate charge. Spinning up a CA to try it and leaving it running is the classic bill shock.

### AWS Resource Access Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-resource-access-manager.html
In one sentence: Lets one AWS account share a specific resource with another account.
Picture it as: Giving a neighbour a key to your garage. They can use that one space, not the whole house.
What it does: Known as RAM. It shares certain resource types across accounts, most often VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 resolver rules and License Manager configurations. The other account uses the resource as if it were theirs, while you keep ownership and pay for it. Only some resource types can be shared, and it works best inside one AWS Organization.
Use it when: Many accounts using one shared network; Sharing a Transit Gateway across the company; Central DNS resolver rules for every account
Do NOT use it when: Sharing files or data, use an S3 bucket policy; Giving someone access to act in your account, use an IAM cross account role
Example: The network account shares its private subnets, so each team's account launches workloads into the shared VPC.
How you pay: Free. The owning account keeps paying for the shared resource, which is the part that catches out billing.

### AWS Secrets Manager
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-secrets-manager.html
In one sentence: A safe for passwords and API keys.
Picture it as: A bank locker. Only the right person gets in, and there is a record of every visit.
What it does: Secrets Manager stores database passwords and keys encrypted. Your app fetches them at runtime instead of keeping them in code. It can rotate database passwords automatically.
Use it when: Any password or key; Anything you would hate to see on GitHub
Do NOT use it when: Plain non secret settings. Parameter Store is cheaper.
Example: The database password is fetched at startup, never written in the repo.
How you pay: Per secret per month, plus API calls.

### AWS Security Agent
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-security-agent.html
In one sentence: An AI helper that attacks and reviews your own application to find holes.
Picture it as: Hiring someone to try the locks on your house and write you a list.
What it does: A very new AI agent, now presented under AWS Continuum. It does on demand penetration testing, which is generally available, plus code scanning and threat modelling which are still in preview. Because parts are preview and it is so recent, treat its findings as a first pass, not as a replacement for a human security review or a compliance audit.
Use it when: You want a security check before a release without booking a testing firm; You need a threat model drafted for a new design; You want repeated cheap scans between real audits
Do NOT use it when: You need a signed penetration test report for a customer or auditor. Use an accredited human firm.; You want to find threats in your running account, like odd API calls. That is GuardDuty and aws-cloudtrail.; You want to manage who can access what. That is aws-identity-and-access-management.
Example: A team runs it against a new API and gets a list of injection risks in hours instead of weeks.
How you pay: Not clearly published. Expect usage based charging, and expect preview features to change or be priced later.

### AWS Security Hub
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-security-hub.html
In one sentence: One screen that gathers security problems from all your AWS security tools.
Picture it as: A hospital nurses' station where every ward's alarms come to one desk, instead of ringing in rooms nobody is standing in.
What it does: Careful, the name moved. In 2025 the original service was renamed Security Hub CSPM, which runs best-practice checks against standards like CIS and AWS Foundational Security Best Practices. A newer service took the plain name Security Hub and focuses on correlating findings into prioritised exposures using the OCSF format. Both pull in findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partners. Older blog posts and docs saying just Security Hub usually mean the CSPM one.
Use it when: More than one AWS security service switched on and too many alerts; You need a compliance score against CIS or PCI controls; Sending security findings to a ticketing system or SIEM
Do NOT use it when: It does not detect threats itself, GuardDuty and Inspector do that; It does not fix anything, you still need automation or people; With one tiny account and no compliance need, the check charges may not be worth it
Example: GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings for twelve accounts land in one place, and a critical one opens a Jira ticket automatically.
How you pay: Per security check run and per finding ingested. Turning on every standard across many accounts multiplies the check count quickly.

### AWS Security Incident Response
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-security-incident-response.html
In one sentence: AWS security experts help you handle a breach, and the service triages alerts in between.
Picture it as: A plumber on retainer. Day to day they check the meter, and when a pipe bursts at midnight you have a number that answers.
What it does: Launched at re:Invent 2024. It does two things: automatic triage of GuardDuty and Security Hub findings to cut noise, and, when something real happens, access to the AWS Customer Incident Response Team with a case workflow and communications. It is help with an AWS-side incident. It is not a full managed security operations centre, and it does not cover your code, your laptops or your SaaS.
Use it when: You have no security team of your own and AWS is where your risk lives; You want a defined path to AWS experts before an incident, not during; GuardDuty noise nobody triages
Do NOT use it when: Not a replacement for detection, you still need GuardDuty switched on; If you already have a mature SOC or an MDR vendor, this overlaps; Not for non-AWS incidents like a compromised laptop
Example: GuardDuty flags credentials used from an unusual country, and the service escalates a real case to AWS responders instead of it sitting unread.
How you pay: Originally a large monthly subscription with a high minimum. It now bills per finding ingested, with the first 10,000 a month free, and it is included with Enterprise Support.

### AWS Shield
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-shield.html
In one sentence: Protection against attacks that try to flood your site.
Picture it as: Flood barriers around the building.
What it does: Shield Standard is automatic and free on CloudFront and load balancers. Shield Advanced is a paid tier with a response team and bill protection. Most small projects only ever need Standard.
Use it when: You are a likely target; You need the bill protection
Do NOT use it when: A small site. Standard is already on and free.
Example: A flood of fake traffic is absorbed before it reaches your servers.
How you pay: Standard is free. Advanced is a large fixed monthly fee.

### AWS Signer
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-signer.html
In one sentence: It digitally signs your code so the thing running it can check nobody tampered with it.
Picture it as: A wax seal on a letter. If the seal is broken when it arrives, you do not read it.
What it does: Signer manages the signing keys and certificates, and produces signatures for Lambda deployment packages, container images in ECR using Notation, and IoT and FreeRTOS firmware. The runtime, such as Lambda's code signing configuration, is what actually refuses unsigned code. Signer only makes the signature, so on its own it enforces nothing until you turn on enforcement at the other end.
Use it when: A rule says only approved, signed Lambda code may run; Signing container images so a cluster rejects unsigned ones; Firmware updates to devices in the field
Do NOT use it when: Not for signing documents or emails, that is a different world entirely; Not needed for ordinary app deploys where your pipeline is already the only way in; It does not scan code for problems, use Inspector or a SAST tool
Example: A Lambda function is configured to reject any package that was not signed by the release pipeline's signing profile.
How you pay: No charge for the signing service itself. You pay for the underlying storage and, where used, a Private CA.

### AWS WAF
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-waf.html
In one sentence: A filter that blocks bad web traffic before it reaches you.
Picture it as: A security guard at the gate who turns away known troublemakers.
What it does: WAF sits in front of CloudFront, a load balancer or API Gateway. It blocks SQL injection attempts, bad bots and abusive IPs, and can rate limit. It is a filter, not a fix for insecure code.
Use it when: Any public site; Login pages being attacked
Do NOT use it when: Internal tools behind a VPN.
Example: Blocking an IP that tries two hundred logins a minute.
How you pay: Per rule per month, plus per million requests.

### Amazon Cloud Directory
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-cloud-directory.html
In one sentence: Stores objects like people and devices in several overlapping trees at once.
Picture it as: A staff list you can view by manager, by office, or by project, from one set of records.
What it does: Closed to new customers and it reaches end of support on 24 July 2027. Do not start anything on it. It was a directory store where one object could sit in many hierarchies at the same time, useful for device registries and product catalogues. AWS points people to amazon-dynamodb or Neptune instead. It was never a login directory for IT admins.
Use it when: Nothing new. It is on its way out; Only relevant if you already run it and need an exit plan before 2027
Do NOT use it when: You are building anything new. Use amazon-dynamodb, or a graph database, from the start.; You want staff logins and Active Directory. That is AWS Directory Service or IAM Identity Center.; You want app permissions. Use amazon-verified-permissions.
Example: An existing customer plans a move of its device registry from Cloud Directory to DynamoDB before the 2027 cutoff.
How you pay: Per gigabyte stored and per request, but the real cost now is the migration you must fund before support ends.

### Amazon Cognito
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-cognito.html
In one sentence: Sign up and log in for your app's users, ready made.
Picture it as: Hiring a receptionist who checks ID, instead of building your own front desk.
What it does: Cognito handles user sign up, login, password reset, MFA and Google or Apple login. Your app gets a token. Do not confuse it with IAM. IAM is for your team, Cognito is for your customers.
Use it when: Your app needs customer accounts; You do not want to store passwords yourself
Do NOT use it when: You only need internal staff access. Use IAM Identity Center.
Example: Students logging into a learning app with email or Google.
How you pay: Per monthly active user, with a free tier.

### Amazon Detective
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-detective.html
In one sentence: After an alert, it shows you the story of what actually happened.
Picture it as: CCTV footage you scrub back through after the alarm goes off, to see who came in and where they went.
What it does: Detective pulls CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings into a linked graph, so you can follow a suspicious role or IP across time and accounts without writing queries. It is for investigating, not detecting: it finds nothing on its own and is only useful once GuardDuty or Security Hub has raised something. Teams that never investigate alerts get no value from it.
Use it when: You get GuardDuty findings and have to work out the blast radius; Tracing what one compromised role touched across accounts; You do not want to hand-write Athena queries over CloudTrail
Do NOT use it when: Useless without GuardDuty, turn that on first; If nobody investigates alerts, this is money for a screen nobody opens; For ad hoc log searching across many sources, Security Lake plus Athena is more flexible
Example: An EC2 instance is flagged for talking to a known bad IP, and Detective shows it also assumed a role and listed every S3 bucket.
How you pay: Per gigabyte of log data ingested per account, per month. Chatty accounts with high VPC flow log volume drive it.

### Amazon GuardDuty
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-guardduty.html
In one sentence: Watches for signs that someone has broken in.
Picture it as: A burglar alarm that has learned what normal looks like in your house.
What it does: GuardDuty reads your logs and flags suspicious activity: a key used from a strange country, a server talking to a known bad address, crypto mining. It only tells you, it does not block.
Use it when: Any account holding real data; You want intrusion detection without effort
Do NOT use it when: A throwaway learning account, unless you want to see how it works.
Example: An alert that your access key is suddenly being used from another continent.
How you pay: By the volume of logs analysed. Watch this one.

### Amazon Inspector
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-inspector.html
In one sentence: It keeps checking your servers, containers and functions for known security holes.
Picture it as: A building inspector who comes back every time you change something, not once a year.
What it does: Inspector scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, Lambda functions and code for known vulnerabilities, and scores them by whether they are actually reachable. It runs continuously rather than on a schedule you start. Note the name confusion: the old Amazon Inspector Classic is a different, retired product, and AWS ends support for it on 20 May 2026. Anything new is the current Inspector.
Use it when: You run EC2, containers or Lambda and need CVE scanning; Blocking a vulnerable image before it reaches production; A compliance requirement for vulnerability management
Do NOT use it when: Not for misconfiguration like a public S3 bucket, that is Security Hub CSPM or Config; Not for active threats and intrusions, that is GuardDuty; If you build images in a pipeline that already scans them, this may duplicate what you have
Example: A base image in ECR is flagged for a critical OpenSSL flaw, and the build pipeline refuses to promote it.
How you pay: Per EC2 instance per month, per container image scan, and per Lambda function. Rebuilding images many times a day multiplies the image scan charges.

### Amazon Macie
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-macie.html
In one sentence: It looks through your S3 buckets for personal data you did not know was there.
Picture it as: Someone going through every filing cabinet in the office looking for stray photocopies of passports.
What it does: Macie uses pattern matching and machine learning to find sensitive data such as card numbers, passport numbers and credentials in S3 objects, and reports which buckets are public or unencrypted. It only covers S3, not databases, not EBS, not other stores. Its bucket inventory is cheap, but the actual content scanning is priced per gigabyte, so scanning everything blindly is the mistake.
Use it when: You suspect personal data has leaked into log or export buckets; A privacy law makes you prove you know where personal data sits; Before opening a bucket more widely
Do NOT use it when: Does not cover RDS, DynamoDB or anything outside S3, use Glue plus custom checks there; If you already know exactly what is in each bucket, you are paying to be told; For encryption and access control problems only, S3 Block Public Access and Config are free or cheaper
Example: Macie finds full card numbers sitting in a debug log bucket that an old application wrote three years ago.
How you pay: A per-bucket monthly charge for inventory, plus per gigabyte of objects actually inspected. Pointing it at a multi-terabyte data lake is the expensive mistake.

### Amazon Security Lake
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-security-lake.html
In one sentence: It puts all your security logs in one place, in one standard format.
Picture it as: Everyone in the company finally agreeing to write dates the same way, so the records can actually be read together.
What it does: Security Lake collects CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 logs, findings and third-party sources into your own S3 bucket, converted to the OCSF standard schema and stored as Parquet. The value is the normalisation, since you can then query everything with Athena or feed one clean feed to Splunk or OpenSearch. It is plumbing. It shows you no dashboards and raises no alerts by itself.
Use it when: Many accounts and several log sources you cannot join today; Feeding a SIEM without building a converter per source; Keeping years of security logs cheaply for investigations
Do NOT use it when: Not a detection tool, use GuardDuty and Security Hub for that; Not worth it for one or two accounts, just query CloudTrail with Athena; If your SIEM already ingests everything happily, this adds a layer for nothing
Example: A responder runs one Athena query across three years of flow logs and CloudTrail from forty accounts, without joining formats by hand.
How you pay: Per gigabyte of data converted and ingested, plus the ongoing S3 storage and Athena query costs you would pay anyway. Flow logs are usually the biggest volume.

### Amazon Verified Permissions
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-verified-permissions.html
In one sentence: Decides whether a user is allowed to do a thing in your app, so you do not code it yourself.
Picture it as: A doorman with the guest list, instead of every room checking names itself.
What it does: You write the rules in a language called Cedar, store them here, and your app asks a yes or no question for each action. It keeps permission rules out of your application code, so they can be changed and reviewed on their own. It is for permissions inside your own application, not for who can touch AWS resources.
Use it when: A SaaS app where each customer sets their own sharing rules; Rules keep changing and you are tired of editing if statements; Auditors want to see the permission rules written down in one place
Do NOT use it when: You want to control access to AWS itself, like who may stop an EC2 instance. That is aws-identity-and-access-management.; Your app has three simple roles. A table in your own database is simpler and free.; You cannot afford an extra network call in a hot path. Cache decisions or check locally instead.
Example: A document app asks whether Priya may share a folder, and the answer comes back from a Cedar rule, not app code.
How you pay: Per authorization call, fractions of a cent each. The surprise is volume. If you check permissions on every item in a list, calls multiply fast, so use the batch call.

## Storage


### AWS Backup
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-backup.html
In one sentence: One place to schedule backups of everything.
Picture it as: One alarm clock for the whole house instead of one in every room.
What it does: AWS Backup sets backup rules across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and more, from a single policy. It handles retention and can copy backups to another region. A backup you have never restored is not a backup.
Use it when: More than one thing needs backing up; Any compliance rule
Do NOT use it when: A single database whose own backups are enough.
Example: Daily backups kept 30 days, monthly kept a year, copied to Mumbai.
How you pay: Per GB of backup stored.

### AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-elastic-disaster-recovery.html
In one sentence: It keeps a live copy of your servers in AWS so you can start them if the originals die.
Picture it as: A spare car kept fuelled in the garage. It is not driven every day, but you can turn the key and go.
What it does: An agent on each server copies disk changes continuously into cheap staging storage in AWS. When you declare a disaster, it boots real EC2 instances from that data, usually in minutes, and can roll back to a point in time from before the problem. It replaces CloudEndure Disaster Recovery, which AWS retired. It protects whole machines, not application state, so databases still need their own consistency thinking, and you must run drills or you will not know it works.
Use it when: On-premises or other-cloud servers that need a cloud fallback; Recovery time measured in minutes, not hours; Ransomware rollback to a point in time before the infection
Do NOT use it when: For serverless or container apps, deploy the same stack in a second region instead; For long-term archival copies, use AWS Backup, this is not a backup archive; For a one-off move to AWS, AWS Application Migration Service is the matching tool
Example: A hospital's 40 on-premises Windows servers replicate to AWS, and a quarterly drill boots them all in a test VPC in about 15 minutes.
How you pay: A flat fee per source server per hour, about 0.028 USD. The surprise is everything underneath, the staging EC2 instances, EBS volumes and snapshots are billed separately at normal rates.

### AWS Snowball
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-snowball.html
In one sentence: AWS posts you a rugged box, you copy data onto it and post it back.
Picture it as: Posting a hard drive instead of emailing a huge file, because the post office is faster than your broadband.
What it does: Snowball Edge devices hold tens of terabytes and also run EC2 and Lambda locally, which made them useful at ships, mines and army bases. The family is closing down. Snowmobile, the truck, is gone, Snowcone was discontinued in 2024, and as of late 2025 Snowball Edge is open only to existing customers, with support ending in commercial regions on 31 December 2026. Treat it as retired and do not plan new work on it.
Use it when: Almost never now, the service is being withdrawn; Only if you already have devices under an existing arrangement
Do NOT use it when: For bulk transfer over a network, use AWS DataSync; For a permanent fast private link, use AWS Direct Connect; For edge compute in a remote site, use AWS Outposts servers or ordinary hardware
Example: A research ship used to fill a Snowball Edge with sonar data at sea and ship it home at port. Today that team would plan for DataSync over satellite or a Direct Connect at dock.
How you pay: Historically a per job fee plus per day device rental, with shipping. Moot now, since new orders are closed.

### AWS Snowball Edge
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-snowball-edge.html
In one sentence: A rugged box AWS posts you, which you fill with data and post back.
Picture it as: Posting a hard drive instead of uploading over a slow line.
What it does: No longer available to new customers. AWS now points new users to DataSync for online copies, aws-data-transfer-terminal for physical drop off, and aws-outposts-family for edge computing. The device held large amounts of data, could run EC2 instances and Kubernetes offline, and shipped with an E Ink label. It is still supported for existing customers, but it is not something to plan around.
Use it when: Nothing new. New sign ups are closed; Existing users finishing an in flight migration or edge deployment
Do NOT use it when: You are a new customer with a bulk transfer. Use aws-data-transfer-terminal or an online copy service.; You need compute at a remote site. Use aws-outposts-family.; You want normal cloud storage. Use amazon-simple-storage-service.
Example: A ship at sea collected sensor data on a device and the box was posted ashore on arrival.
How you pay: A per job device fee plus daily rental after a free window, plus shipping. The classic surprise was the daily charge while the device sat unused on a loading dock.

### AWS Storage Gateway
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/aws-storage-gateway.html
In one sentence: A small piece of software in your office that makes AWS storage look like a local drive.
Picture it as: A post box on your street. You drop letters in as if it were local, and the van takes them to the sorting office.
What it does: You run a virtual appliance on-premises. It presents an NFS or SMB share, an iSCSI disk, or a virtual tape drive, keeps recent data cached locally, and stores everything in S3, EBS snapshots or Glacier behind the scenes. Reads of cached data are fast, reads of anything else go over your internet link and feel slow. The Tape Gateway variant is popular because it lets old backup software keep thinking it has a tape library.
Use it when: Old backup software that only understands tape; An office file share that should live in S3; Slowly retiring a NAS without changing how users work
Do NOT use it when: For applications running inside AWS, mount Amazon EFS or FSx directly, a gateway adds nothing; For one-time or scheduled bulk copying, AWS DataSync is faster and simpler; For low latency shared storage across an office, keep a local NAS
Example: An accounting firm points its Veeam backups at a Tape Gateway, and the tapes quietly become objects in Glacier Deep Archive.
How you pay: Per gateway per month, plus the underlying S3 or Glacier storage, plus request charges. The surprise is retrieval, pulling old virtual tapes back out of Deep Archive costs real money and takes hours.

### Amazon EFS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-efs.html
In one sentence: A shared folder that many servers can read and write at the same time.
Picture it as: A filing cabinet in the middle of an office. Anyone can open a drawer, and everyone sees the same papers.
What it does: EFS is managed NFS storage. It grows and shrinks on its own, spans multiple availability zones, and mounts on EC2, ECS, EKS and Lambda. It is a network file system, so per file latency is higher than a local disk, and small random writes are noticeably slower. It is Linux only, there is no SMB support.
Use it when: Several machines need the same files, such as uploads or shared config; A web app you cannot rewrite that expects a normal filesystem; Lambda functions needing more than the small temp space
Do NOT use it when: For a single machine's fast disk, use EBS, it is cheaper and quicker; For Windows and SMB shares, use FSx for Windows File Server; For storing objects an app fetches by key, S3 costs far less
Example: Three WordPress servers behind a load balancer all mount the same EFS volume so an image uploaded on one appears on the others.
How you pay: Per GB stored per month, with a standard and a cheaper infrequent access tier. The surprises are the per GB charge for reading infrequent access data, and Elastic throughput mode billing per GB transferred.

### Amazon Elastic Block Store
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-elastic-block-store.html
In one sentence: The hard disk attached to your EC2 server.
Picture it as: The hard drive inside a computer, except you can unplug it and attach it to another computer.
What it does: EBS is a disk volume for one EC2 instance. It survives when the instance stops. You can take snapshots for backup. Type gp3 is the sensible default.
Use it when: Any EC2 server needs a disk; Databases running on EC2
Do NOT use it when: Sharing one disk across many servers. Use EFS.; Storing files for a website. Use S3.
Example: A 100 GB disk holding the application and its data.
How you pay: Per GB per month, whether or not you use the space. Snapshots cost extra.

### Amazon FSx
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-fsx.html
In one sentence: The family name for AWS's managed versions of four real file systems.
Picture it as: A shop that sells four brands of filing cabinet. FSx is the shop, not the cabinet.
What it does: FSx is not one product you buy. It is the umbrella over FSx for Windows File Server, FSx for Lustre, FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS. AWS runs the servers, backups and patching, and you pick the type by the protocol and features you need. Choosing wrongly is the common mistake, since you cannot convert one type into another later, you migrate the data.
Use it when: You need a specific filesystem's behaviour, not generic storage; Moving an existing NetApp, Windows or ZFS estate to AWS; Workloads needing SMB, NFS with snapshots, or parallel throughput
Do NOT use it when: If you have no strong requirement, EFS is simpler and cheaper for Linux sharing; For object storage accessed by key, use S3; For one server's disk, use EBS
Example: A team lists its needs, SMB shares plus Active Directory, and that answer points them at FSx for Windows File Server rather than the other three.
How you pay: Each type bills differently, generally per GB of provisioned capacity plus provisioned throughput. The surprise across all of them is that capacity is provisioned in advance, so you pay for empty space.

### Amazon FSx for Lustre
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-fsx-for-lustre.html
In one sentence: A file system built for hundreds of machines reading the same data very fast.
Picture it as: A motorway with fifty lanes. Useless for one car, excellent when a whole city leaves at once.
What it does: Lustre is the parallel filesystem used in scientific supercomputing, and FSx runs it for you. It can link to an S3 bucket, so objects appear as files and new files can be written back to S3. Throughput scales with the size you provision, into hundreds of GB per second. It is POSIX and Linux only, and it is tuned for large sequential reads, not for lots of tiny files or long-lived general storage.
Use it when: Machine learning training reading a large dataset from many GPUs; Genomics, seismic or simulation workloads; You need S3 data to look like files with high throughput
Do NOT use it when: For general shared files, use EFS, Lustre is costly and specialised; For Windows or SMB clients, use FSx for Windows File Server; For long-term storage, keep the data in S3 and create the Lustre filesystem only while a job runs
Example: A training job on 64 GPU instances mounts an FSx for Lustre filesystem linked to the S3 bucket holding 20 TB of images, then the filesystem is deleted when training ends.
How you pay: Per GB per month by deployment type, with throughput tied to size. An Intelligent-Tiering class now exists on Persistent_2. The surprise is provisioning capacity you do not need just to reach the throughput you do need.

### Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-fsx-for-netapp-ontap.html
In one sentence: Real NetApp storage, run by AWS, with the same tools your storage team already knows.
Picture it as: Moving house but taking your own kitchen with you, so you still know where everything is.
What it does: This is genuine ONTAP software running as a managed service, so you get NFS, SMB and iSCSI at once, plus NetApp features like snapshots, cloning, deduplication, compression and SnapMirror replication from an on-premises NetApp. Cold data tiers automatically to cheaper capacity storage. It is the most feature-rich and the most complex of the FSx types, and it really pays off only if you already use NetApp or need those features.
Use it when: An existing NetApp estate moving to AWS with SnapMirror; You need NFS and SMB against the same data; Instant zero-copy clones of large volumes for test environments
Do NOT use it when: If you have never used NetApp, FSx for OpenZFS or EFS is far less to learn; For pure Windows shares, FSx for Windows File Server is simpler; For extreme parallel throughput, use FSx for Lustre
Example: A bank mirrors volumes from its on-premises NetApp into FSx for ONTAP nightly, then clones one instantly to give developers a full-size test copy.
How you pay: Per GB of SSD capacity, per GB of capacity pool storage, plus provisioned throughput capacity per hour. The surprise is the throughput capacity charge, which is a separate line from storage and is easy to over-provision.

### Amazon FSx for OpenZFS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-fsx-for-openzfs.html
In one sentence: A fast Linux file share with snapshots, run by AWS.
Picture it as: A notebook with carbon copies. Every time you change a page, you can still flip back to yesterday's version.
What it does: This runs the OpenZFS filesystem as a managed service over NFS. It gives very low latency, cheap instant snapshots and clones, plus compression, and is the simplest way to lift an on-premises ZFS or general NFS server into AWS. It speaks NFS only, so Windows clients are not the target. A single-AZ filesystem is not protected against a zone failure, you choose Multi-AZ for that.
Use it when: Replacing a Linux NFS server with something managed; Databases or build servers needing sub-millisecond file latency; You want frequent cheap snapshots and instant test clones
Do NOT use it when: If you do not need snapshots or low latency, EFS grows on its own and needs less thought; For SMB and Active Directory, use FSx for Windows File Server; For hundreds of parallel readers, use FSx for Lustre
Example: A CI system stores its build workspace on FSx for OpenZFS and clones a snapshot per pull request so each build starts from a clean tree in seconds.
How you pay: Per GB provisioned, plus provisioned IOPS and throughput. An Intelligent-Tiering class exists for Multi-AZ. The surprise is that snapshots consume the same provisioned capacity, so heavy snapshot retention forces you to buy more space.

### Amazon FSx for WFS
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-fsx-for-wfs.html
In one sentence: A Windows file share, the kind with drive letters, run by AWS.
Picture it as: The shared drive at work that everyone calls the P drive, except nobody has to look after the server.
What it does: It gives you SMB shares with real Windows behaviour, NTFS permissions, Active Directory integration, shadow copies for user self-restore, and DFS namespaces. It is the natural home for Windows workloads and for file shares users map from their laptops. It is Windows-protocol first, Linux clients can mount SMB but it is not the smooth path, and it needs an AD directory, either your own or AWS Managed Microsoft AD.
Use it when: Moving an on-premises Windows file server to AWS; SharePoint, SQL Server or .NET apps wanting an SMB share; User home directories and department shares
Do NOT use it when: For Linux workloads, use EFS or FSx for OpenZFS; If you have no Active Directory and do not want one, this is heavy going; For app data accessed by key, S3 costs much less
Example: A 300-person firm retires its old file server and maps P: to an FSx for Windows share joined to their existing Active Directory.
How you pay: Per GB provisioned, SSD or cheaper HDD, plus provisioned throughput capacity per MBps and backup storage. The surprise is the separate throughput charge and the fact that HDD has a minimum size.

### Amazon File Cache
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-file-cache.html
In one sentence: A temporary fast copy of files that actually live somewhere slower.
Picture it as: Bringing a few library books to your desk for the week, instead of walking to the shelves each time you need a page.
What it does: File Cache links to an S3 bucket or an NFS server and presents those files as one high speed filesystem inside AWS, built on Lustre. Files are pulled in the first time they are read and dropped when unused. It is a cache, not a home for data, so you size it for the working set, not the whole dataset. Very few teams need it, it exists for heavy compute bursts reading from on-premises or S3 data.
Use it when: A big compute job in AWS reading data that lives on-premises; Bursty rendering or simulation that reads the same files repeatedly; You need one namespace over several scattered data sources
Do NOT use it when: If the data already lives in S3 and the job is in one region, FSx for Lustre linked to S3 does the same job for a steady workload; For everyday shared files, use EFS; For a permanent store, use S3 or FSx, a cache is not durable storage
Example: A visual effects studio bursts 500 render nodes into AWS and points them at a File Cache backed by the NFS server in the London office.
How you pay: Per GB of cache capacity per hour while it exists, and it is expensive. The surprise is that you pay for the cache even on idle days, so it is meant to be created and deleted around a job.

### Amazon S3 on Outposts
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-s3-on-outposts.html
In one sentence: Gives you S3 buckets on AWS hardware sitting in your own building.
Picture it as: Having the same brand of filing cabinet at home as the one at head office.
What it does: It is S3 buckets running on an Outposts rack in your data centre, so the data never leaves your premises. Your code uses the normal S3 API through an access point. The limits matter, there is only one storage class, capacity is fixed by the hardware you bought, and features like versioning and cross region replication are not the same as in a Region.
Use it when: A law or contract says the data must stay in your building; An application on the Outpost needs local storage with very low latency; You want one S3 style codebase across cloud and on premises
Do NOT use it when: You have no regulatory or latency reason to keep data local. Plain amazon-simple-storage-service is cheaper and has far more features.; You need shared file access rather than object storage. Use amazon-efs style file storage on the Outpost.; You just want a one off bulk transfer. That is not what this is.
Example: A hospital keeps scan images in an S3 bucket on an Outpost rack in its own basement.
How you pay: You pay for the Outpost rack up front or over a term, and the storage capacity is bought with it. The surprise is that you pay for the whole capacity whether or not you fill it.

### Amazon Simple Storage Service
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-simple-storage-service.html
In one sentence: A place to keep files, as many as you want.
Picture it as: An unlimited cupboard. You put a file in, you get a link to it.
What it does: S3 stores files, called objects, in buckets. It is built for very high durability. It is not a disk you can mount and edit in place. You put a whole file and get a whole file.
Use it when: Images, videos, PDFs, backups; Website files; Data before you analyse it
Do NOT use it when: A database. It cannot search inside your data.; A file share your server edits live. Use EFS.
Example: All product photos for an online shop, served through CloudFront.
How you pay: Per GB stored per month, plus requests, plus data going out.

### Amazon Simple Storage Service Glacier
URL: https://aws.4bittechnology.com/s/amazon-simple-storage-service-glacier.html
In one sentence: Very cheap storage for files you almost never open.
Picture it as: A deep basement archive. Cheap to keep things, slow to fetch them.
What it does: Glacier classes store data at a fraction of normal S3 cost. Retrieval can take minutes or hours depending on the tier, and costs extra. It is for archives, not for anything you serve live.
Use it when: Records you must keep for years; Old backups
Do NOT use it when: Anything a user might open today.
Example: Seven years of invoices kept for audit.
How you pay: Very low per GB per month. You pay to retrieve.

===============================================================================
PART 3. WHAT TO ACTUALLY BUILD, BY SITUATION
===============================================================================
Each entry starts from the reader's own situation rather than from a service list.
All cost figures are rough teaching estimates.


### A website that just shows information
Sounds like you if you would say: "I just need my business online and nobody will be logging in."
The situation: You need a site for your business, your docs, or your portfolio. Nobody logs in. You change it by uploading new files when the prices or the words change.
The answer: Keep the files in S3, which is AWS storage, and put CloudFront in front of it so the pages load fast everywhere.
Cost: About $0.50 to $2 a month at 10,000 visits, and still about $1 to $3 a month at 100,000 visits. The domain name record costs a fixed $0.50 a month.
How far it gets you: This does not run out. 10,000 to 100,000 visits a month is nothing, and the same setup serves millions. The limit is how fast you can publish new files, not AWS.
What breaks first: Not the traffic. Two things go wrong. You publish a change and some visitors keep seeing the old site for hours, so it works in one city and not another. Or someone changes a setting so every visit goes back to the storage instead of the fast copy, and the bill and the load jump.
Move on when: Move on the day you need to store something a visitor typed, like a contact form or a signup, or you need logins, or you need a secret key that must not sit in the browser.
Do not add yet: Do not build a private network. This setup does not use one at all. The gateway people add for that costs about $32 a month for one, and about $65 a month for the usual pair, which is thirty times the cost of this whole site, for a site that has no servers. Do not add the AWS firewall either. That is $5 a month per rule set plus $1 per rule plus $0.60 per million visits, and there is nothing here to attack.
Components: Amazon S3 (Origin. Holds the built HTML/CSS/JS/images. Not a website endpoint - a plain private bucket accessed via the REST endpoint.); Amazon CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC) (The only public front door. TLS termination, global edge cache, compression, security headers, SPA routing.); AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) (Free public TLS certificate for example.com and www.example.com, auto-renewed.); Amazon Route 53 (DNS. Alias A and AAAA records at the apex and www pointing to the distribution.); Deployment: GitHub Actions with OIDC, `aws s3 sync` then targeted invalidation (Build, upload, bust the cache.)

### A real app with logins for your first 1,000 users
Sounds like you if you would say: "I have paying users and logins, and I cannot afford an ops person yet."
The situation: You have a product with logins, a database, and some work that runs in the background. Up to about 1,000 signed up users. A few minutes down during a release is fine. Losing a day of data is not.
The answer: Run the app on one right sized server or one ECS service, keep the data in managed Postgres, keep passwords in Secrets Manager, and watch it with CloudWatch.
Cost: About $25 to $120 a month, not counting the domain. A small server is about $18 to $20 a month, and the managed database on top of that.
How far it gets you: About 1,000 users, 10 to 30 requests a second at peak, a database under 20 GB and under 2,000 writes a minute. One machine with 2 CPUs and 4 GB does this with room to spare.
