What breaks first: You get a mention somewhere, three times as many people show up at once, and every page starts returning errors at the same moment. The confusing part is that the CPU on both the app and the database is under 30 percent, so every chart you are looking at says everything is fine.
Move on when: When the database connections sit above 70 percent of the limit, or the small server runs out of its CPU credit more than once a week, or slow pages happen while the database is under half busy, or users start complaining about downtime during releases.
Do not add yet: Do not build a custom private network with gateways. Each gateway is about $32.85 a month plus $0.045 per GB, so the standard pair is about $66 a month before you send a single byte. That is two to three times the cost of everything else here, to give your app an internet exit it mostly uses for software updates and one API call. Use the default network with tight rules instead.
Components: Compute: pick ONE — ECS Express Mode (containerised team) or a single EC2/Lightsail instance (non-containerised team) (Runs the application process.); Database: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, db.t4g.micro or db.t4g.small, SINGLE-AZ (The system of record.); Connection pooling: PgBouncer sidecar or RDS Proxy — but only if you went serverless (Keeps the database from being the ceiling.); Edge + TLS: CloudFront in front of the app, ACM certificate in us-east-1, Route 53 alias (HTTPS on your domain, static asset caching, one place to add WAF later.); Secrets: AWS Secrets Manager (or SSM Parameter Store SecureString) (Database password, API keys, signing keys.); Backups + a proven restore (Recovery.); Minimum viable monitoring: CloudWatch Logs + 5 alarms + one synthetic check (Knowing it is broken before a user tells you.)

### Two copies of everything so one reboot is not an outage
Sounds like you if you would say: "One bad reboot takes my whole business offline and customers notice."
The situation: You run the app and the database on one box. Revenue is real, maybe 1,000 to 10,000 users. A reboot or a bad release is a visible outage and someone emails you about it.
The answer: Put a load balancer in front of a small group of servers that grows and shrinks, and move the database to a managed one that keeps a standby copy in a second data centre.
Cost: About $450 to $900 a month. The two things that drive the bill are the standby database copy and the network gateway, not the servers.
How far it gets you: About 1,000 to 20,000 signed up users, 50 to 300 requests a second with peaks near 600, a database under 500 GB and under 1 TB of traffic out a month. The app side can keep growing. The single database that accepts writes is the wall.
What breaks first: The database. Under load you add more app servers, each one opens its own set of connections, and you cross the limit. The app logs fill with too many clients messages and users see errors, while the database CPU looks fine, which is exactly why people add more app servers and make it worse.
Move on when: When the database CPU stays above 70 percent for a week of work hours, or connections sit above 60 percent of the limit at peak, or pages take over half a second while the servers are under half busy, or the server group hits its maximum more than twice a week.
Do not add yet: Do not add Kubernetes. It is $73 a month before a single thing runs, and the real cost is that one of your two to eight engineers becomes a part time cluster operator, roughly 20 to 30 percent of a salary, which is $30,000 to $60,000 a year to save maybe $100 a month. Do not add a read only copy of the database until you have proved your load is mostly reads and your code can live with that copy being slightly behind.
Components: Application Load Balancer (Single public entry point, TLS termination with an ACM certificate, health checks that actually remove bad instances); EC2 Auto Scaling group (2-6 app instances across 2 AZs behind the ALB); VPC: 2 public + 2 private subnets, one NAT gateway (App instances and RDS in private subnets; ALB in public; egress for package installs, webhooks and third-party APIs); Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL or MySQL), Multi-AZ (The primary datastore, on gp3 storage, in private subnets); Connection pooling in the application (PgBouncer/HikariCP/pgx pool), not RDS Proxy yet (Keep total DB connections well under max_connections as the ASG scales); S3 + CloudFront (Static assets, and all user uploads; CloudFront in front of both the asset bucket and the ALB); SQS + a small worker ASG (or the same AMI with a different role) (Email, PDF generation, webhook delivery, image processing, anything over ~300ms that the user does not have to wait for); CI/CD: GitHub Actions (or CodePipeline) -> build AMI/artifact -> deploy to staging -> manual approval -> production (One deploy path for code, migrations, and config); Secrets Manager (or SSM Parameter Store SecureString) + CloudWatch Logs + a small set of alarms (Config, logs, and being told when it breaks); Backups you have restored (Automated RDS snapshots plus a quarterly restore drill)

### Containers, a spare copy of the data, and releases that are not scary
Sounds like you if you would say: "The database is the bottleneck and I dread every deploy."
The situation: The database is now the obvious bottleneck and releasing new code has become the scary part of the week. 10,000 to 100,000 users. You have more than one service, and one engineer is losing a day a week to infrastructure they never wanted.
The answer: Run the app as containers on Fargate, add one read only copy of the database and an ElastiCache memory cache, and build a real release pipeline with a staging copy that matches production.
Cost: About $1,800 to $5,000 a month. The main pieces are the containers at $250 to $600, the main database around $700 to $800, the read copy about $350 and the cache about $300.
How far it gets you: About 10,000 to 100,000 users, 500 to 2,000 requests a second with peaks, and 100 to 500 GB of hot data. You can keep adding containers almost forever. You cannot keep adding writes. The wall is around 2,000 to 4,000 requests a second.
What breaks first: One popular row or table, like a counter or a jobs table, gets written by everyone at once. Writes start taking much longer for a small share of users while the CPU and disk both look fine. Separately, the read only copy falls behind during the nightly batch, so anything reading from it shows people stale data.
Move on when: When writes pass 60 percent of what you measured the database can take, or your biggest table passes about 500 GB and a schema change becomes a multi hour event, or the read copy is regularly more than 10 seconds behind, or one customer's traffic can slow down every other customer, or your team says out loud that they are afraid to run a migration.
Do not add yet: Do not split the database into shards. It is about a year of engineering and you lose the ability to join or transact across the pieces. Almost everyone who did it at this size could have bought two bigger instances and an archiving job instead. Do not go multi region, and do not add Kubernetes for portability you will never use.
Components: ECS on Fargate (The web service and the worker service as separate ECS services, same image, different command); RDS primary (larger, Multi-AZ) + one read replica (Writes and read-your-writes go to the primary; reporting, search, exports and analytics-shaped reads go to the replica); ElastiCache (Valkey or Redis OSS), replication group with automatic failover (Cache the three or four things you measured, plus sessions and rate-limit counters); SQS + dead-letter queues + worker autoscaling, with backpressure discipline (All async work, with queues separated by job class and by tenant where one tenant can flood); S3 + CloudFront with an upload pipeline (All user uploads via presigned POST direct to S3; processing triggered by S3 event -> SQS -> worker); CI/CD with a real staging environment and an approval gate (Build once, promote the same image through staging to production); Centralised logging, metrics and traces (Structured JSON logs to CloudWatch, Container Insights on, and X-Ray or an OTel collector for traces)

### Keeping production separate so one mistake cannot wipe it
Sounds like you if you would say: "Someone could delete production from a laptop and nothing would stop them."
The situation: Everything runs in one AWS account and that is now the risk. Someone can delete production from a laptop. A test under load slowed down real customers. A customer asks how your environments are separated and the honest answer is not good.
The answer: Split into separate AWS accounts under AWS Organizations, sign in through IAM Identity Center, and fence off what each account may do with service control policies.
Cost: About $50 to $250 a month extra. The accounts, the sign in system and the policies cost nothing. The extra money is duplicated basics per account, mainly a $33 a month network gateway in each one and about $20 for a second load balancer for staging.
How far it gets you: Well past 100,000 users and into hundreds of accounts. The limit is your organisation, not the technology.
What breaks first: The joins between accounts. Most often a release pipeline can read a file from another account but cannot unlock it, and the error just says access denied with no hint about the key. Or someone reconnects the networks between environments and quietly undoes the separation you just spent a week building.
Move on when: When you need a dedicated account for a single large customer, or you run in more than two regions, or you are creating accounts by hand more than once a month, or an auditor wants evidence of rules you are only enforcing by habit.
Do not add yet: Do not create fifteen accounts on day one. Start with four, which are management, log archive, production and non production, and add more when you feel the specific pain. Every account is another network, another gateway and another place for things to drift. Do not adopt Control Tower before you have four accounts, and do not write clever deny policies you cannot explain.
Components: AWS Organizations with a Production OU and a Non-Production OU (A hard boundary between environments, not a policy one); IAM Identity Center (SSO) with permission sets (How humans get access, everywhere, with no long-lived keys); Service Control Policies (Guardrails that even an account admin cannot escape); Cross-account CI/CD from a shared services account (The pipeline lives in one account and assumes a deploy role in each target account); Centralised logging to a log archive account (CloudTrail (organisation trail), VPC Flow Logs and application logs land in an account nobody can write to); Per-account cost visibility and budgets (Each environment's bill is a number, not an estimate)

### One well built app in three data centres in one region
Sounds like you if you would say: "An hour of downtime means refunds, and I have no platform team."
The situation: 100,000 to 1,000,000 users and 10 to 40 engineers. Five minutes down is a customer email and an hour is a refund. You have an on call rota but no platform team. Most teams who say they need to scale are actually here.
The answer: Run one well organised app across three data centres behind CloudFront and a load balancer, put the data in one Aurora cluster with two read copies, and push everything slow onto SQS queues and background workers.
Cost: About $12,000 to $45,000 a month. The order of spend is the database at $4,500 to $7,000, the app at $3,000 to $10,000, the cache at $800 to $2,500, network transfer at $1,000 to $4,000 which is almost always unbudgeted, and logs at $0.50 per GB which easily reaches $2,000 if you log full requests.
How far it gets you: 100,000 to 1,000,000 registered users, 20,000 to 150,000 daily actives, 2,000 to 8,000 reads a second at peak and 200 to 800 writes a second, with 1 to 10 TB of data. The one writing database typically holds 3,000 to 6,000 writes a second before it bites.
What breaks first: Not the CPU. Pages get slow for the unlucky few while the database CPU sits at 40 percent, because the app is queueing for a free database connection. Adding more connections makes it slower, not faster. The other common one is background cleanup falling behind on your biggest table until disk activity flatlines.
Move on when: When the writing database stays above 60 percent CPU at daily peak, or writes have doubled in a quarter, or you are adding your fifth read copy, or the read copies fall more than a second behind and support tickets show people not seeing what they just saved, or your biggest table passes about 500 GB and cleanup no longer finishes overnight.
Do not add yet: Do not go multi region. AWS's own guidance says start with multiple data centres in one region and be honest about whether you really need more. Multi region roughly doubles your infrastructure, adds cross region transfer, and gives you a failover path you will not practise enough to trust. At this size it costs 2 to 2.5 times as much and eats a senior engineer for two quarters, to protect against an event rarer than your own bad releases. Do not shard the database.
Components: CloudFront in front of an ALB (TLS termination, cacheable-GET offload, absorbs bot long tail.); ALB + ECS Fargate (or an EC2 ASG), one service, three AZs (Runs the modular monolith. Horizontal, stateless, autoscaled.); Aurora PostgreSQL, writer + 2 readers across AZs, behind RDS Proxy (System of record. Reads split onto the reader endpoint, writes to the writer.); ElastiCache (Valkey/Redis), cluster mode disabled, 1 primary + 1 replica (One cache layer only: hot object cache and session/rate-limit counters.); SQS standard queues + a separate worker service, fed by a transactional outbox table (Everything the user does not wait for: email, webhooks, PDF generation, search indexing, analytics fan-out.); CloudWatch + a structured log pipeline, with a heartbeat per scheduled job (Observability and proof that background work actually ran.)

### Many identical copies so one bad customer cannot sink everyone
Sounds like you if you would say: "One bad deploy or one heavy customer takes down every customer I have."
The situation: 1,000,000 to 10,000,000 users, or a platform with many customers where one bad release or one heavy customer takes down every other customer. 40 to 150 engineers with a platform team. The trigger is not traffic, it is that a single failure hits 100 percent of your customers and the board has noticed.
The answer: Run several complete independent copies of the stack, called cells, spread customers across them, and split the reading side from the writing side so each scales on its own.
Cost: About $80,000 to $400,000 a month. The cells dominate, because four cells each with their own database, cache and servers cost about four times the fixed floor of one cell, so that floor is the number to attack.
How far it gets you: 1,000,000 to 10,000,000 users, 200,000 to 2,000,000 daily actives and 20,000 to 150,000 requests a second in total. One cell tops out around 10,000 to 25,000 requests a second and tens of thousands of customers before it hits the same database wall as the tier below.
What breaks first: The small piece that decides which cell a customer belongs to. It is the one part that is not duplicated, so a bug or a bad release there hits everyone, and you spent a year of work to still have one of those. The other one is a single customer growing bigger than a whole cell, which your design may not allow you to split.
Move on when: When one customer's traffic alone approaches the stated limit of a cell, or you have more cells than your automation can deploy in one working day, or a full load test of a cell has become too expensive to run, which means the cell is too big.
Do not add yet: Do not add multi region because cells worked and it looks like the next box. Multiple data centres already survive a data centre failure and cells already survive bad code. Multi region only survives a whole region failing, which is rarer than the outage your own failover practice will cause. Do not shard the database if moving search to OpenSearch and sessions to DynamoDB would take the pressure off instead, which it often does and for less money.
Components: A thin cell router (Route 53 / CloudFront Function / API Gateway) plus a control plane (Maps a partition key to exactly one cell and presents one endpoint. Nothing else.); The cell: a complete, independent copy of the stack (compute + DB + cache + queues) (Serves a fixed subset of tenants. Shares no state with any other cell.); Shuffle sharding on top of the cells (or on the worker/queue tier) (Gives each tenant a near-unique combination of workers so that two tenants rarely share their full set.); Read path and write path as separate, separately scaled services (Writes go to the system of record; reads go to purpose-built read stores fed asynchronously.); EventBridge for routing, Kinesis Data Streams for volume, SQS for work (The asynchronous spine. Outbox writes to the spine; consumers do the work.); Load shedding and backpressure at the front door, backed by fairness quotas (Protects goodput when offered load exceeds capacity.); Sampled tracing + aggregate metrics + full logs only on error (Observability that does not cost more than the service.)

### Running in more than one part of the world, and what it really costs
Sounds like you if you would say: "A signed contract or a data residency law says one region is not enough."
The situation: Only three things genuinely buy this. A contract or regulator names a recovery target one region cannot meet. A law says the data must stay in a country. Or your users are truly global and the speed of light, not your capacity, is the slowness. If none of that is written down and signed, you are buying insurance against something rarer than your own releases.
The answer: Run cells in each region, route people with Route 53, and replicate data with DynamoDB global tables or Aurora Global Database, with each region owning its own writes.
Cost: 1.8 to 2.5 times the single region build, so realistically $200,000 to $900,000 a month or more. The forgotten lines are cross region transfer on every replication stream, a full duplicate test environment, duplicate monitoring, and the biggest one, two senior engineers for more than two quarters.
How far it gets you: 5,000,000 to 10,000,000 plus users across continents, or any size with a hard legal driver, at 50,000 to 500,000 requests a second in total, aiming at 99.99 percent uptime with penalties attached. You have removed the technical ceiling and replaced it with how fast you can safely change anything. Teams routinely see their pace of change drop 30 to 50 percent.
What breaks first: The switchover itself, because it is the only part normal traffic never exercises. The classic story is a limit, a setting or a permission that exists in one region and not the other, found at 3am in the middle of an incident. The other one is a hidden single thing everywhere depends on, like one login provider or one hand edited DNS zone.
Move on when: There is no next step up. From here you subtract things, and the job is to make cost per user fall while users rise. If a quarterly real failover drill is not boring, you do not have multi region, you have a second region and a hope.
Do not add yet: Do not add a third region because two worked. Each one adds another replication link and, when all regions accept writes, a conversation about consistency that grows with every pair. Do not build automatic cross region failover without a human in the loop until you have run at least four successful manual drills, because automatic failover on partial signals is a known way to turn a slowdown into an outage. Do not write your own replication layer.
Components: Route 53 (latency or geoproximity records) + Application Recovery Controller routing controls (Sends users to a region and, critically, lets a human take a region out of rotation with one deliberate action.); Active-active with per-region ownership of the write key, not global writes (Each partition key has one home region that owns its writes; other regions read locally and forward writes.); DynamoDB global tables, or Aurora Global Database, depending on the consistency you can defend (Cross-region data replication.); Region-scoped cells, and a global control plane that can fail regionally (Cells do not span regions. The control plane is regional with a designated leader.); Idempotency and exactly-once-effect discipline, enforced globally (Makes retries, replays and failovers safe.)

### A known big moment, like a match or a ticket drop
Sounds like you if you would say: "I know the exact minute millions of people will arrive at once."
The situation: You run live streaming or ticketing. The rush is on the calendar, like a match starting or a sale opening at 09:00. People watching can go from 2 million to 25 million in the minutes around a wicket. You know the minute. You do not know the multiple.
The answer: Turn on the servers before the crowd arrives using pre warmed auto scaling groups, send the video through more than one CDN, and keep a panic switch that turns off the nice to have features.
Cost: A normal day is small. The event is the bill. Expect 10 to 40 times a normal day's cost on event days, because you hold capacity for the peak you forecast, not the peak you get. Video delivery dominates everything else.
How far it gets you: Hotstar published 25.3 million people watching at once during the 2019 India versus New Zealand World Cup semi final, up from 18.6 million at the IPL 2019 final and 10.3 million at the IPL 2018 final. The real limit is not a request rate, it is one step of growth. You absorb the peak you pre booked plus your spare, and nothing more, for about 90 seconds, because you cannot add machines faster than that.
What breaks first: The check that says whether a viewer is allowed to watch. Everyone hits it at the same instant, it usually talks to a database or a billing company, and it was sized for a normal day. It stalls, playback stops being allowed, and every app retries, which doubles the load on the thing that is already stuck.
Move on when: When your peak forecast is wrong by more than your spare capacity more than once, or a new machine takes longer than 120 seconds to be ready to serve, or one country's video traffic passes what a single CDN will commit to in writing, or the entitlement check is slower than about 200 milliseconds at only half your forecast peak, or you had to flip panic mode to stay alive.
Do not add yet: Do not go multi region for this. A live event for one country is a single region problem plus a global CDN, and a second live region buys nothing against the failure you actually have, which is your own dependency stalling, while adding cross region consistency to your incident list. Do not add a service mesh before the event, because it adds a hop and a brand new failure mode on the exact path you cannot afford surprises on. Do not move to Kubernetes for the pre warming story.
Components: Multi-CDN for the video data plane (CloudFront plus at least one non-AWS CDN) (Carries essentially all bytes. Origin sees manifest and segment misses only.); EC2 Auto Scaling groups, pre-warmed on a manual ladder (API plane: playback authorization, subscription checks, metadata, social/engagement.); Application Load Balancer, pre-warmed and over-provisioned by count (Ingress for the API plane.); A purpose-built load generator and a scheduled game day (Rehearsal. Face the real game before the actual game.); Panic mode: a runtime feature-flag plane with tiered service classes (Designed degradation. P0 services stay up; everything else is switched off by an operator or a trigger.)

### Running your whole service in three places at once
Sounds like you if you would say: "One AWS region going down would end my company, and I have the traffic to justify paying three times over."
The situation: If one whole AWS region goes dark, our business is over. We are big enough that spare capacity in other places would not sit idle for nothing.
The answer: Run a full live copy in three regions, send users to the nearest one with Route 53, and copy data between them all the time so any one region can serve the whole world.
Cost: Each region runs at about 33% use, so you pay roughly 3 times the compute you actually use, plus cross region data transfer charged per gigabyte.
How far it gets you: Netflix runs this in three regions and can lose two and still serve everyone. Region evacuation dropped from close to an hour to under 10 minutes.
What breaks first: A user updates something in one region and sees the old value, because copies are about a second behind and the last write wins. Money balances, stock counts and entitlements come out wrong in a way people notice.
Move on when: When the revenue lost in one minute of a regional outage is more than a year of the extra region. Or when your evacuation drill takes longer than the recovery time you promised.
Do not add yet: Do not do this before you have squeezed multi AZ. Multi AZ in one region costs about 1.5 times instead of 3 times, and AZ failures are far more common than region failures. Also do not call it active active if only one place can accept writes, that is active passive and you will find out during the incident.
Components: Route 53 latency-based or geolocation routing, plus Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls (Steers users to a region; the ARC routing control is the on/off switch that evacuates one.); A cross-region-capable edge proxy (Netflix's is Zuul; AWS-native equivalent is ALB plus a proxy tier you own) (Progressive traffic shifting during evacuation, and load shedding at the edge.); Asynchronously replicated, multi-master data (Cassandra-style, or DynamoDB global tables in MREC mode) (The same data readable and writable in every region.); Statically stable regional capacity (Each region carries enough standing capacity to absorb its share of an evacuation without launching anything.); Chaos Kong-style scheduled regional failure (Proof that the evacuation works, run regularly, in production.)

### Splitting users into separate self contained copies
Sounds like you if you would say: "I hold tens of millions of live connections and one shared component failing for everyone is unacceptable."
The situation: Millions of people stay connected to my app all the time. Right now one shared piece breaking knocks out every single user at once, and I cannot live with that.
The answer: Split the whole stack into independent cells, each a full copy, and put a thin router in front that decides which cell a user belongs to.
Cost: Mostly memory and connection slots on the connection servers, plus data transfer for fan out. Each cell needs its own cache, queue and database, so N cells cost noticeably more than one big system of the same total size.
How far it gets you: WhatsApp reported 147 million connections at once, 342,000 messages in and 712,000 out per second, on about 550 servers with roughly 10 people. Each node holds hundreds of thousands up to about 1 million connections.
What breaks first: One server dies and a million people all try to log back in at the same second. The sign in path chokes and people stare at a reconnecting spinner long after the original server is gone.
Move on when: When one incident hits more than the share of customers you said was acceptable, or one cell is close to an AWS account limit, or a cell is too big to load test properly.
Do not add yet: Do not build cells at the start. Below roughly a few million users, a well run single region multi AZ setup wins on everything that matters to a small team, one deploy, one dashboard, one runbook. The cost is not money, it is that you now have N of everything to deploy, watch and debug with the same people.
Components: A thin cell router (Route 53, API Gateway, or a small EC2/ECS proxy tier reading a cell map from S3) (Maps a partition key — user ID — to a cell, and does nothing else.); Independent cells, each a complete self-contained copy of the stack (App tier, cache, queues and data — no state shared across cells.); Connection-tier instances tuned for concurrent sockets, not CPU (Holds the long-lived TCP/WebSocket connections.); Regional write-locality with queued asynchronous cross-region writes (Keeps a user's writes in their own region; propagates asynchronously.); Load shedding as designed behaviour, at the edge of every cell (Protects goodput when demand exceeds capacity.)

### Paid video library that people watch on demand
Sounds like you if you would say: "I sell access to recorded videos and I need people who did not pay to be unable to watch."
The situation: I have a course or media library people pay to watch. Videos get uploaded, not streamed live, and only paying members should be able to play them.
The answer: Store the files in S3, convert them into multiple quality versions with MediaConvert, and deliver them through CloudFront using signed cookies so only paying members can play.
Cost: About 200 to 400 dollars a month for 2 TB of viewing. About 9,000 to 12,000 dollars at 100 TB a month. Delivery is 85 to 95 percent of the bill, roughly 8,500 dollars for 100 TB.
How far it gets you: Comfortable to roughly 200 to 300 TB a month and thousands of people watching at once, because the heavy work is not on your servers.
What breaks first: Not the video. Your own members only check breaks first. Everyone hits play on a new release, that check dies somewhere around 300 to 600 requests a second, and players spin forever at 0:00 while the delivery network sits idle.
Move on when: When delivery passes 150 TB a month, or conversion costs more than about 3,000 dollars a month, or fewer than 90 percent of video chunks are served from cache.
Do not add yet: Do not build a second delivery network. Below 100 TB a month it saves nothing because you have no committed rate yet. Do not build your own conversion farm on day one, teams spend six weeks on it to save 400 dollars a month. Do not add studio grade copy protection until a contract demands it, that is about a month of work per platform.
Components: Amazon S3 (two buckets: source and output) (Ingest of the mezzanine file and storage of the packaged HLS/DASH renditions.); AWS Elemental MediaConvert (Transcode the mezzanine into an adaptive bitrate ladder and package it as CMAF/HLS plus DASH.); Amazon CloudFront with signed cookies and OAC (Delivery to players, and the authorization boundary for paid content.); AWS Lambda plus EventBridge (Orchestration: S3 upload event starts the job, MediaConvert completion event writes the record and notifies the app.); DRM via SPEKE (only where required) (Widevine/PlayReady/FairPlay key delivery for content whose licence demands it.)

### Streaming a live event to a big audience
Sounds like you if you would say: "I have one live channel and losing it mid event would be a disaster."
The situation: I am streaming something live, a conference, a match, a shopping channel. It has to stay up for the whole event and the event will not wait for me.
The answer: Send the camera feed into MediaLive, package it with MediaPackage, and deliver it through CloudFront at a latency setting you pick on purpose.
Cost: A 1080p dual pipeline MediaLive channel is about 1.50 to 3.00 dollars an hour, so a 24/7 channel is roughly 1,100 to 2,200 dollars a month before any viewer watches. Delivery is the variable part and it is the one that hurts.
How far it gets you: One channel serves 500,000 viewers as easily as 500, and this shape holds to a few hundred thousand watching at once on a single delivery network.
What breaks first: The internet line at the venue goes first, which is why you run two from two providers. After that, viewers get errors while the encoder dashboard looks perfectly fine, and one small hiccup makes every player retry at the same moment.
Move on when: When you pass about 200,000 viewers at once, or over 100,000 in one country, or under 95 percent of video chunks come from cache, or more than 1 percent of viewing time is buffering.
Do not add yet: Do not chase low latency by default. Normal streaming gives about 20 to 30 seconds delay and is very hard to break. Getting to about 5 seconds triples the requests per viewer, shrinks the player buffer so every network hiccup becomes a visible freeze, and costs you more in delivery and support.
Components: AWS Elemental MediaConnect or a MediaLive RTP/SRT push input (Get the contribution feed from the venue or encoder into AWS reliably.); AWS Elemental MediaLive, channel class STANDARD (Decode the contribution feed and produce the adaptive bitrate ladder in real time.); AWS Elemental MediaPackage v2 (Just-in-time packaging into HLS/DASH, origin endpoints, DVR window, and the SPEKE integration point.); Amazon CloudFront, tuned for live (Fan-out. One segment is fetched from the origin once and delivered to every viewer from the edge.)

### A national live event with millions watching at once
Sounds like you if you would say: "My event will pull millions of people in the same five minutes and the date is already on the calendar."
The situation: A cricket final or election night. Millions of people arrive within minutes, the date has been known for months, and I get exactly one chance.
The answer: Buy capacity across several delivery networks in advance, steer traffic between them live, and build in a panic mode that switches off nice to have features under load.
Cost: Priced per event and it is huge. 20 million viewers at 2.5 Mbps is 22.5 petabytes for one 3.5 hour match, about 2.4 million dollars at India list rates for a single evening.
How far it gets you: JioHotstar reached over 61 million watching at once in 2023, after 10 million in 2018 at 5.7 Tbps and about 1 million requests a second. Growth runs at roughly 500,000 extra viewers per minute.
What breaks first: Load follows the drama, not the clock. A wicket or a push notification sends it near vertical within 90 seconds. The video usually survives, the personalised parts of the app do not, so the stream plays while the rest of the app stops responding.
Move on when: This is the top tier. You arrive here when you pass roughly 500,000 viewers at once, or when one failed event costs more than a year of extra delivery contracts. Inside it, act when the forecast comes within 20 percent of the capacity you bought in any one country.
Do not add yet: None of this belongs in a product that has never run a million viewer event. Three delivery contracts with minimum commitments and a steering service buy nothing at 50,000 viewers. Pre buying peak capacity instead of scaling up on demand means paying for the peak all the time.
Components: Multi-CDN with a real-time steering layer (Deliver the video, and route each viewer cohort to whichever CDN is healthiest right now.); Pre-provisioned compute with reactive autoscaling explicitly disabled (Serve the app, entitlement, metadata and playback-start APIs during a load curve that is nearly vertical.); Panic mode and tiered graceful degradation (Decide in advance, in code, what gets sacrificed when saturation arrives — so that the video keeps playing.); Network and cluster plumbing sized for the event (The unglamorous layer that is usually the real ceiling.)

### Chat or live updates without running a server
Sounds like you if you would say: "I need chat inside my app and we are too small to babysit servers."
The situation: I want chat, a support inbox or live notifications inside my product. We are a small team and nobody wants a 3am page about a connection server.
The answer: Use API Gateway WebSockets for the live connections, store messages in DynamoDB, and let DynamoDB Streams with Lambda push them out.
Cost: About 150 to 900 dollars a month at 10,000 people connected and 5 million messages a day. Holding 10,000 connections all month is about 108 dollars on API Gateway, or about 35 dollars on AppSync Events.
How far it gets you: 5,000 to 50,000 people connected at once, 50 to 500 messages a second with bursts near 2,000, rooms up to about 500 people. That fits a product with 200,000 to 1,000,000 registered users.
What breaks first: Messages start arriving 8, then 30, then 90 seconds late for some people and instantly for others. Nobody sees an error, sending still works, delivery just falls behind.
Move on when: When delivery lag stays over 10 seconds for 5 minutes, or the WebSocket bill passes about 800 dollars a month, or one conversation needs more than 800 write units, or time to first message goes over 1 second.
Do not add yet: Do not add Kafka, it costs about 500 dollars a month before it moves a single byte, and DynamoDB Streams already gives you the same ordered log for almost nothing here. Do not add a cache, it drags Lambda into a VPC and adds NAT charges of about 33 dollars per month per AZ to fix a speed problem you do not have. Do not build end to end encryption yet, it kills server side search.
Components: Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API (Terminates every client WebSocket. Routes $connect, $disconnect, $default and custom routes (sendMessage, markRead, typing) to Lambda. Server-to-client delivery is the separate @connections POST endpoint, called with the stored connectionId.); DynamoDB — connections table (Maps connectionId to userId, and userId to the set of connectionIds (a user has three devices). Written on $connect, deleted on $disconnect.); DynamoDB — messages table (The durable ordered message log. Source of truth for history, offline delivery and read receipts.); DynamoDB Streams + Lambda fan-out worker (Reads new message rows off the stream and does delivery: look up room members, look up live connections, POST via @connections, and for members with no live connection enqueue a push.); SQS FIFO + Amazon SNS mobile push (APNs/FCM) (Anything not delivered over a live socket becomes a push notification; SQS holds the retry and the dedupe.)

### Running your own live connection servers
Sounds like you if you would say: "My message bill is out of hand and I need presence, typing and huge rooms that managed services will not give me."
The situation: Paying per message stopped making sense, or I need things the managed services will not give me, like rooms with tens of thousands of people, presence and typing indicators, or live counters.
The answer: Run your own connection servers on ECS behind a Network Load Balancer, with ElastiCache for Valkey as the pub sub spine and Kafka or Kinesis as the durable log.
Cost: About 4,000 to 25,000 dollars a month at 500,000 connections. Budget 40,000 to 80,000 idle connections per node, so about 10 nodes for 500,000, but run 2 to 3 times that for headroom, roughly 1,500 to 4,000 dollars, plus about 1,100 dollars for the pub sub spine.
How far it gets you: 200,000 to 2,000,000 connections across 20 to 100 nodes, 10,000 to 100,000 incoming messages a second. Roughly 1 to 2 million connections in one region before the pub sub spine, not the servers, becomes the limit.
What breaks first: Messages get slower, not broken. Delivery creeps from 40 milliseconds to 400 to 4 seconds over about twenty minutes, while one busy room pins a single shard and everything else looks idle. Nothing throws an error.
Move on when: When any Valkey shard sits above 70 percent CPU, or delivery time measured at the client passes 250 milliseconds, or reconnecting everyone after a test failure takes more than 2 minutes.
Do not add yet: Do not go multi region active active for chat before you actually have users in a second country. It forces you to answer what order two simultaneous messages happened in, and teams spend two quarters on it only to pin each conversation to a home region, which they could have done on day one. Do not put Kafka in the live delivery path.
Components: ECS on EC2 (not Fargate) behind a Network Load Balancer (The connection tier: long-lived stateful nodes terminating TLS and WebSocket, holding per-connection state (subscriptions, auth claims, last-ack sequence, send buffer).); ElastiCache for Valkey (cluster mode) as pub/sub spine and presence store (Routes a message from the gateway node that received it to the gateway nodes holding recipients; also holds presence, typing state and live counters.); Presence, typing indicators and live counters — the ephemeral tier (The state nobody wants to pay for but everyone expects: who is online, who is typing, how many are watching.); MSK (Kafka) or Kinesis Data Streams as the durable spine (Every message that matters is appended here alongside the live hop. Consumers: persistence writer, push worker, search indexer, analytics, moderation.); Message ordering and delivery guarantees (protocol, not a service) (What makes this feel correct rather than merely fast.)

### A follow based feed that survives famous accounts
Sounds like you if you would say: "I am building a follow based feed and I know one popular account will eventually break it."
The situation: People follow each other and see a feed of posts. It works fine until someone with a huge following posts, and then everything crawls.
The answer: Write most posts straight into each follower's ready made timeline in Redis, but leave famous accounts out and merge their posts in when the feed is read.
Cost: About 300 to 1,200 dollars a month at 100,000 users, roughly 220 dollars for one Redis group and 100 to 400 dollars for the database. At 10 million users with 1 million daily actives, 15,000 to 60,000 dollars, mostly Redis memory.
How far it gets you: Works from 100,000 users on one Redis node up to the published Twitter scale of about 150 million active users, 300,000 feed reads a second against only about 6,000 writes a second.
What breaks first: One famous person posts, the worker spends 40 seconds on it, and everyone whose post landed behind theirs shows up in friends' feeds two minutes late. Support says posting is broken while every dashboard stays green.
Move on when: When fan out takes more than 5 seconds, or any account crosses about 100,000 followers, or building a feed takes more than 200 milliseconds, or Redis memory passes 70 percent.
Do not add yet: Do not build fan out at all below roughly 10,000 users or 100 posts an hour. One indexed database query for the latest 50 posts from people you follow runs in single digit milliseconds and gives you correct deletes and unfollows with no cache bugs. Teams routinely spend six weeks building fan out for a feed two hundred people read.
Components: ElastiCache for Valkey/Redis — the materialized timeline (One capped list per active user holding post IDs (not bodies). Reading a feed is one LRANGE.); Fan-out-on-write worker (SQS + Lambda, or ECS consumers on Kafka) (On a post from a normal account, page the follower list and LPUSH the post id onto each follower's timeline.); The celebrity path — read-time merge (Accounts above a follower threshold are NOT fanned out; their posts stay in their own author timeline and are pulled and merged when a follower loads their feed.); Aurora PostgreSQL (or DynamoDB) — post store and follow graph (Source of truth for posts and edges; hydrates post IDs into bodies.); Ranking and caching layer (Turns a chronological merge into a ranked feed and caches the result briefly.)

### One database, with an automatic spare copy
Sounds like you if you would say: "I have paying users, one team, and I just need storage that will not page me at night."
The situation: I have real users and one team. I need somewhere safe to keep the data that will not wake me up at 3am.
The answer: Run one Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database with Multi AZ on, keep it in private subnets, and put the password in Secrets Manager.
Cost: About 120 to 450 dollars a month. The standby copy doubles the instance cost, storage and backups are the rest.
How far it gets you: Roughly 200 to 500 requests a second and low tens of gigabytes. A db.m7g.large allows around 800 to 900 connections at once.
What breaks first: It looks like a complete outage, not a slowdown. Once connection slots run out even your health checks are refused, so the load balancer kills healthy app tasks, they restart, each opens fresh connections, and it gets worse.
Move on when: When connections stay above 70 percent of the limit for 5 minutes, or write time passes 20 milliseconds while CPU is under 50 percent, or free memory keeps falling all week with no deploy.
Do not add yet: No read copy, no cache, no connection proxy, no separate analytics database. Each one answers a problem you do not have and hands you a new one, stale reads, cache invalidation, session pinning. Teams that add all three in month one spend about 600 dollars a month extra and debug three distributed systems problems instead of shipping.
Components: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (The single source of truth for all operational data.); Private subnets + security group (The database is not on the internet.); AWS Secrets Manager with rotation (Database credentials.); CloudWatch alarms (The three alarms that actually matter at this stage.)

### Rent a bigger database machine
Sounds like you if you would say: "My database is the bottleneck and I need breathing room this week, not a rebuild."
The situation: Your app is slow and the database is the thing struggling. You have about a week to fix it, not three months.
The answer: Move the database to a bigger machine size, and watch the few numbers that tell you when bigger stops working.
Cost: About 450 dollars a month at the small end, and over 12,000 dollars at the big end. Cost goes up almost in line with size. Keeping a standby copy in a second data centre doubles it. Above the db.r7g.4xlarge size, paying for one year up front cuts 30 to 40 percent, and you should, because you will sit at that size for at least a year.
How far it gets you: Roughly 5,000 to 15,000 reads a second and 1,000 to 3,000 writes a second, if your data is well organised, with a few thousand gigabytes of data.
What breaks first: Pages that used to open instantly start taking half a second, then longer. The database has an internal clean up job that falls behind on very large tables, and the proper fix needs a lock that freezes the table, which you cannot do while customers are using it. Notion hit exactly this.
Move on when: When you are two sizes from the biggest machine on offer. Or when the database's internal clean up has been running for hours and the dead rows on your biggest table outnumber the live ones. Or when the disk is at its speed limit during normal traffic. Or when the next size up costs more per month than a week of an engineer's time.
Do not add yet: Do not split your data across many databases yet. That takes 6 to 9 months, Figma needed nine months just for the first table, and it is close to impossible to undo. Do not add a second kind of database for one busy table before you have tried splitting that table into date ranges inside the same database, which takes days instead of months. Do not add a cache to hide a missing index, you will store a wrong answer and then have two problems.
Components: RDS instance class change, memory-optimised family (More RAM so the working set stays in shared_buffers; more vCPU for connections.); gp3 with provisioned IOPS, or io2 Block Express (Storage that is not the bottleneck.); Parameter group tuning (The settings that actually move the needle after a resize.); pg_stat_statements + Performance Insights (Find the three queries causing 80% of load before buying hardware to hide them.)

### Extra copies of the database for reading
Sounds like you if you would say: "Reads are ten times my writes and the database is drowning in them."
The situation: People read from your app far more than they write to it, and the one database is worn out just answering read requests.
The answer: Run extra read only copies of the database, and send some reads to them.
Cost: Each copy costs the same as the main database, so plus 100 percent each, plus a small charge for shipping the data between data centres. Two copies of an r7g.2xlarge is about 1,400 dollars a month extra.
How far it gets you: Each copy adds roughly 2 to 5 times more read capacity. In practice 2 to 5 copies before the copying itself starts costing the main database.
What breaks first: The copies fall behind the main database, usually right in the middle of a big data change when you are already stressed. Users start seeing old information, a price or a post that is minutes stale, and if you are not watching for it, a customer tells you first.
Move on when: When the lag on the copies goes past what your users can tolerate during normal traffic. Or when you are about to add a fourth copy just to get more reading power. Or when the total number of open connections across the main database and all copies is nearing the limit.
Do not add yet: Do not flip one setting that sends all reads to the copies. Choose them one place at a time, starting with pages that can safely show slightly old data, like search, listings and dashboards. A global switch turns every save then read in your code into a hidden bug on the same day. Do not put reports on a copy and call it analytics, a 30 second report still causes trouble there.
Components: RDS read replicas (async physical/streaming replication) (Serve SELECTs that tolerate staleness.); Replica lag monitoring and fencing (Know how stale each replica is, and stop serving from it when it is too stale.); Explicit read-after-write handling in the application (Stop the class of bug where a user saves and the next page shows the old value.)

### A traffic controller in front of the database
Sounds like you if you would say: "My database keeps running out of connections whenever traffic scales up."
The situation: Your app runs on many copies of itself, or on Lambda, and the database keeps refusing new connections and falling over.
The answer: Put a connection pooler like RDS Proxy in front, so thousands of app connections share a few hundred real database ones.
Cost: RDS Proxy is about 22 dollars a month per processor core of your database, so roughly 175 dollars a month on an 8 core r7g.2xlarge. Running PgBouncer yourself on Fargate is about 30 to 60 dollars a month for two small tasks, plus your time.
How far it gets you: One database can serve thousands of app connections. A common result is 5,000 app connections collapsed onto 200 to 400 real database connections.
What breaks first: Something called pinning. It all works in testing. Then one piece of code uses a feature that needs its own private connection, the sharing collapses from 20 to 1 down to 1 to 1, and you are out of connections again, with an extra piece in the path that you trust and so do not suspect.
Move on when: When connection counts are finally low and steady, and processor use or disk speed becomes the new pinned number. That means the plumbing is fixed and the next problem is real capacity.
Do not add yet: Do not add the pooler and raise the connection limit at the same time, you will not know which helped, and the raised limit costs you memory forever. Do not put a pooler in front of a database whose real problem is one query missing an index, you will have spent 175 dollars a month to make a bad query wait more politely. Do not run PgBouncer as a single task for now, a pooler with no backup in front of a two data centre database makes your uptime worse, not better.
Components: Amazon RDS Proxy (Connection pool and multiplexer between the app and the database; also preserves application connections across failover.); Application-side pool sizing, deliberately computed (Stop the app from asking for connections it cannot use.); Session pinning awareness (Know what silently turns multiplexing back off.); Lambda + RDS Proxy, or Aurora Data API (Serverless compute against a connection-oriented database.)

### Keep popular answers in fast memory
Sounds like you if you would say: "The same few thousand things get read over and over and my database is doing it all again each time."
The situation: The same information gets read thousands of times before it ever changes: sessions, product listings, user profiles, permission checks.
The answer: Put ElastiCache in front of the database and keep hot answers in memory, with a written plan for clearing them when things change.
Cost: 50 to 800 dollars a month. Two cache.r7g.large nodes across two data centres is about 250 dollars a month. The serverless option is cheaper below about one gigabyte and spiky traffic. What drives the price is memory size and node count, not how much traffic it handles.
How far it gets you: Takes 60 to 95 percent of reads off the database. A cache answer takes about 0.5 to 1 millisecond against 5 to 50 milliseconds from the database, so slow pages get faster too.
What breaks first: Correctness, and your dashboards will look fine while it happens. Everything is fast, and a user sees a deleted document or an old price. The other trap is that the database can no longer survive the cache going away. Turn the cache off during a load test on purpose. If the database falls over, it was never a cache, it was a hidden part of your database.
Move on when: When the hit rate drops below 80 percent because the data no longer fits in memory, then grow the cache, not the database. Or when the database is still busy after caching, which means writes are the load and caching cannot help. Or when you find yourself caching things that must never be out of date.
Do not add yet: Do not cache before you have added the right indexes. A cache over a slow query hides it until the cache misses, and then the outage is worse. Do not use the cache as your only copy of anything unless you deliberately chose that and tested getting it back. Do not turn on cluster mode on day one, the code changes it forces will cost you a week for capacity you do not need.
Components: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey (or Redis OSS) (Low-latency key/value in front of the database.); Cache-aside (lazy loading) as the default pattern (Read: check cache, miss -> read DB -> write cache with TTL. Write: write DB, then DELETE the key.); Invalidation strategy, written down (The part everyone skips and then pays for.); Stampede protection (Stop a cold key from becoming a thundering herd.)

### Teach your app which database to talk to
Sounds like you if you would say: "I have replicas and a cache and the main database is still the wall."
The situation: You already have read copies and a cache, and the main database is still the thing holding you back.
The answer: Change the app so each query knowingly goes to the writer or to a reader, with a rule for what may be slightly old.
Cost: No new AWS bill. The cost is engineering time, realistically 2 to 6 weeks on an established codebase, because the work is checking every single query.
How far it gets you: Gives you the full reading power of all your copies, usually 3 to 8 times more total reads than using one address for everything.
What breaks first: Someone builds a new feature, points a query at the wrong place, and a user finds it. Nothing errors. That is why the shadow checking you build for the rollout should stay in the code forever, running on a small sample.
Move on when: When the main database sits above 70 percent busy even with reads moved off. Or when write times get worse while read times stay flat. Or when you need more than about 5 copies, or making a new copy takes hours because the data is so large. Those three together are the case for Aurora.
Do not add yet: Do not build a smart proxy that reads your queries and routes them. It becomes a service you have to keep alive in the path of every single query, and it will cause an outage before it prevents one. Do not split the data across many databases to fix a reading problem, that technique is for writes and is a painfully expensive way to get reads. Do not split reads and writes into separate services now, that is a bigger and worse change wearing the same clothes.
Components: Two connection pools in the application (writer pool, reader pool) (Make the destination of every query an explicit decision.); Transaction-aware routing rule (One rule that prevents most of the bugs.); Per-request freshness contract (Every endpoint declares how stale it may be.); Dark-read verification during rollout (Prove the reader path returns the same answers before you trust it.)

### Switch to Amazon's own database engine
Sounds like you if you would say: "My database is fine, but making copies and doing failovers has become an operations problem."
The situation: Making a new database copy takes hours, failovers are slow, and you are close to the storage limit. Operations, not speed, is the pain.
The answer: Move to Aurora PostgreSQL, using Blue/Green Deployments for the switch over.
Cost: Usually 20 to 40 percent more than the same setup on RDS for steady traffic, and unpredictably more if your work is heavy on disk activity, because the standard plan charges per disk request. The I/O-Optimized plan removes those charges for about 30 percent higher base rate, and is the better deal once disk charges pass roughly 25 percent of your Aurora bill.
How far it gets you: Up to 15 read copies per cluster, and storage up to 128 TiB, or 256 TiB on current versions. Still only one machine accepting writes.
What breaks first: The bill, if you did not plan for it. On the standard plan a workload that scans a lot of data can run up a disk charge bigger than the machine charge. The other failure is people assuming Aurora removed the write limit, so they stop planning, and arrive at the hard decision with no runway.
Move on when: When the writer is on the biggest machine in its family and stays busy on writes. Or when one table clearly is not a normal table, an append only log, time series, files, full text search. Move those to fitting tools before splitting the database, it is ten times cheaper. Or when the one writer limit is now the named blocker with a date on it.
Do not add yet: Do not put Aurora Serverless v2 under your main production cluster without measuring it. It does not grow instantly, and sharp spikes get throttled while it ramps. Do not turn on Global Database for disaster recovery without a rehearsed plan and a named owner. Do not expect Aurora to make your queries faster, it makes your operations faster. A bad query is just as bad on Aurora, and moving is not a replacement for reading your slow query stats.
Components: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster (Same engine, different storage architecture: compute separated from a distributed cluster volume spanning multiple AZs.); RDS Blue/Green Deployments for the cut-over (Near-zero-downtime migration and, afterwards, near-zero-downtime major version upgrades forever.); Aurora Global Database (only if you need it) (Cross-region read scaling and disaster recovery.)

### Move one odd workload to a tool built for it
Sounds like you if you would say: "One table is eating my database and it does not really behave like a table."
The situation: One table or one thing your app does is creating most of the load, and when you describe it out loud it does not sound like a normal table at all.
The answer: Move that one workload to the tool that fits it, DynamoDB, OpenSearch, S3, or date range partitioning, and keep the rest where it is.
Cost: Depends on the tool, but each is far cheaper for its own kind of work than forcing it into Postgres. DynamoDB on demand for a write heavy table is often a fifth of the database capacity it replaces. Budget 200 to 2,000 dollars a month per tool plus the move itself.
How far it gets you: Usually takes 30 to 70 percent of writes or storage off the main database, buying 1 to 3 years of room for a few weeks of work.
What breaks first: The two copies stop agreeing. Once a fact lives in both places and your app writes to both, a crash between the two writes, a retry or an out of order update makes them differ. Fix the pattern everywhere, not the one case: write to one place and let the other be built from its change feed, using DynamoDB Streams, Aurora logical replication or an outbox table drained by a worker.
Move on when: When you have moved the obvious things out and what is left is still hitting the write limit on the biggest machine. Only then does splitting the database make sense. Most teams never get here, which is the whole point of this step.
Do not add yet: Do not move everything. Move one workload, prove the whole pattern including how you rebuild it, then move the next. Do not adopt a tool you cannot back up and restore on demand, run the restore drill before real data goes in. Do not build a general purpose wrapper over several tools, it will leak and it makes each tool worse than using it directly.
Components: Amazon DynamoDB (High-volume, key-access, append-or-overwrite workloads: sessions, idempotency keys, feature flags, device state, audit/event logs, per-user timelines, rate-limit counters.); Amazon OpenSearch Service (after Postgres tsvector/pg_trgm, not before) (Full-text search, faceting, fuzzy matching, relevance ranking.); Amazon S3 (+ a pointer column) (Blobs, attachments, exports, generated documents, anything over ~100 KB.); Time-series store: Postgres declarative RANGE partitioning, or Amazon Timestream (Metrics, IoT readings, high-frequency append-only series.); Amazon ElastiCache / Valkey for ephemeral counters and locks (Rate limits, distributed locks, leaderboards, presence.)

### Split the data across many databases
Sounds like you if you would say: "One machine takes all my writes and I have genuinely run out of other options."
The situation: You have tried everything else, bigger machines, read copies, caching, routing, Aurora, moving odd workloads out, and one machine taking all the writes is still the wall.
The answer: Split the data across many databases by a chosen key, with a routing layer, after first splitting tables by area onto separate clusters.
Cost: Roughly your current database cost times the number of pieces, plus the routing layer, plus the thing that dominates everything, 6 to 12 months of a dedicated team. Figma's first split table took nine months. Treat the engineering time as the real number.
How far it gets you: Notion runs 480 logical pieces across 32 physical Postgres machines. Figma uses several keys across about a dozen databases and has grown roughly 100 times since 2020.
What breaks first: One piece gets far more traffic than the rest. A single customer is 100 times bigger than the average, lands on one piece, and that piece is maxed out while the other 31 sit idle. Adding machines does not fix it. Spreading keys evenly helps but it cannot split one huge key, so plan how to split your biggest customers before you need to.
Move on when: This is near the end of the path. What comes next is not more splitting but specialisation, separating read and write models where they have truly diverged, or a purpose built engine. Discord moving from Cassandra to ScyllaDB is the reference: 177 machines down to 72, 9 TB per machine instead of 4 TB, and slow historical reads dropping from 40 to 125 milliseconds down to 15.
Do not add yet: Do not split the database to fix a reading problem, a storage size problem or a clean up problem. Read copies, fitting tools and date range partitioning each solve one of those for a fraction of the cost. Do not adopt a distributed SQL engine like CockroachDB, Vitess or a Spanner style system without honestly costing the move. Figma looked at exactly that and built their own instead, because the data migration was complex and they would have had to learn a whole new system from scratch with only months of runway.
Components: Vertical partitioning FIRST (split tables by domain onto separate clusters) (Buy years before you shard horizontally.); The shard key (The irreversible decision.); Many logical shards on few physical hosts (Make future rebalancing a data move, not a rewrite.); A routing layer (Turn a shard key into a connection.); Double-write, backfill, verify, cut over (The migration, without downtime.)

### Store every change, build views from it
Sounds like you if you would say: "One save in my product has to feed many different views, and I need the full history too."
The situation: In one part of your product, one save has to update many different views, or you must be able to show not just how things are now but every step they passed through.
The answer: Record changes to a log, using an outbox table to start, and build separate read views from that log.
Cost: 300 to 3,000 dollars a month for the stream and the view builders and their stores, plus a permanent tax on every feature in that area, because new engineers need weeks to become useful in it.
How far it gets you: Apply it to one area of the product, not the whole system. Typically 1,000 to 100,000 changes a second into the log, with several views that scale on their own.
What breaks first: A view quietly falls behind, or chokes on one bad record and stops. Nothing shows an error. Users see stale or missing data, and because the saved data is correct, everyone investigates the wrong place first. Track how far behind each view is and alarm on it as hard as you alarm on the database, and send bad records to a side queue with an alert.
Move on when: You do not move on from this one. It is a tool for one area, not a rung on a ladder. The sign you did it right is that one or two areas use it and everything else stays boring.
Do not add yet: Do not apply this across the whole system. It is the most expensive mistake available to a small team: everything becomes slightly out of date, debugging turns into digging, and you pay for it on every feature forever, usually for no measured gain. Do not use it for an area whose events your team cannot list on a whiteboard in a meeting. Do not use it as a stand in for an audit log, an append only audit table is the simpler answer.
Components: The transactional outbox (start here, and often stop here) (Reliably publish events derived from database writes, without a dual write.); Change Data Capture instead of an outbox, where the writes are not all yours (Derive the event stream from the database's own WAL.); Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK as the log (The ordered, replayable event stream.); Projections into purpose-fit read stores (One write model, many read models, each shaped for its queries.); Full event sourcing (the log IS the system of record) (Reserved for domains where history is the product.)

### Reports that do not slow down the live app
Sounds like you if you would say: "Our reports keep hurting the live app, and I want them somewhere else."
The situation: Someone on my team runs a big report over months of data, and the live app slows down or falls over. It always seems to happen at month end.
The answer: Keep a second copy of the data just for reports, either in Redshift fed automatically from Aurora, or as files in S3 that you query with Athena.
Cost: About $150 to $3,000 a month. S3 plus Athena can be under $100 a month at modest volumes. A small Redshift cluster is roughly $200 to $900 a month. The automatic Aurora to Redshift copy has no charge of its own.
How far it gets you: It can scan terabytes to petabytes, amounts the live database could never handle, and it removes a whole class of outage.
What breaks first: Before you do this, the live database dies during month end close when finance runs the big report. After you do this, the copying quietly stops after a schema change, nobody notices, and analysts spend a week making decisions on old numbers.
Move on when: This is the end of the road, not a step. The sign you left it too late is a postmortem where the cause was a report. Do it before that.
Do not add yet: Do not build a data lake, dbt, Airflow and hire a data team before you have three analysts and a question they cannot answer. The smallest useful version is the automatic copy, or a nightly file export to S3, plus Athena, and it is a day of work. Do not copy every table by default. Do not let the words real time analytics become an excuse to query the live database. Real time means a running counter kept in the live database, not a big ad hoc query.
Components: Aurora zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift (Continuously replicate operational tables into a warehouse with no pipeline to maintain.); S3 + Glue Catalog + Athena (the cheap tier, and often the right one) (Query exported and archived data with SQL, paying only per scan.); A hard boundary: no BI tool credentials on the operational database (The control that actually prevents the outage.); Amazon QuickSight (or your existing BI tool), pointed only at the warehouse (Where the humans actually go, with exactly one permitted data source.)

### Deciding how long you keep data, and where
Sounds like you if you would say: "Data goes into our system and never leaves, and that is starting to scare me."
The situation: Our database keeps growing and nothing is ever deleted. A customer has asked us to delete their data and I am not sure we can actually find all of it.
The answer: Split big tables by date, move old rows out to S3 and down into Glacier storage tiers, and keep one written list of every place data lives so deletion can reach all of them.
Cost: This usually saves money. Moving cold rows from RDS storage at about $0.115 per GB a month, to S3 at $0.023, to Glacier Instant at $0.004, to Deep Archive at $0.00099, is a 20 to 100 times cut on the archived part.
How far it gets you: It decides whether your live database is 200 GB or 5 TB at the same number of users, which sets your backup time, replica setup time and how long a restore takes.
What breaks first: A customer asks to be deleted and you cannot fully do it, and you find out in an audit or a security review, because the data had been copied into a store that was added after the deletion job was written.
Move on when: It never ends. Review it whenever you add a data store, add a region, or take on a customer with different rules.
Do not add yet: Do not buy a data governance product before you have a one page written list of where data lives. The product will only catalogue your confusion faster. Do not set retention to forever because deciding is hard. Forever is a decision, it is usually the wrong one, and it makes every other problem here arrive sooner and hurt more. Do not encrypt everything so you can delete by throwing away keys, across the whole system, for safety. It turns key management into a new single point of failure.
Components: Declarative time-based partitioning on every append-heavy table (Make expiry a metadata operation instead of a vacuum problem.); S3 Lifecycle policies + Glacier tiers (Tiered archive for detached partitions, blobs, logs and exports.); S3 Object Lock, where a regulator requires immutability (WORM storage that even the root account cannot delete.); Deletion machinery for data-subject erasure requests (Actually erase a person's data, everywhere it went.); Restore rehearsal, on a schedule (Prove the backup is a backup.); Data residency as an architecture input (Where the bytes are legally allowed to live.)

### Two servers instead of one, so a reboot is not an outage
Sounds like you if you would say: "One server runs everything, and a reboot takes my business offline."
The situation: My whole app runs on one server. If it reboots, the site is down. I also cannot deploy without taking the site off for a minute.
The answer: Put an Application Load Balancer, which is a traffic splitter, in front of two servers in two different data centres, and keep login sessions in Redis instead of on the server.
Cost: About $18 to $25 a month for the load balancer, plus the second server. A second m7g.large is about $60 a month, or about $35 on a one year Savings Plan. The duplicate server is the real cost, not the balancer.
How far it gets you: Roughly 2,000 to 5,000 requests a second across two m7g.large servers before the database, not the app, is the limit. Typical starting point is 50 to 800 requests a second and a few thousand users a day.
What breaks first: The database connection pool, nearly always. Two servers each holding 20 connections is 40, and a small database starts struggling long before its stated limit. It looks like the site is slow while the database CPU looks fine.
Move on when: When p99 response time at the balancer is over 500ms for 5 minutes while the servers are under 50% busy, or database connections are over 70% of the maximum, or you have had to add a third server by hand more than once in a month.
Do not add yet: Do not add auto scaling, CloudFront, a read replica, containers or a service mesh in this same move. A team that bundles containers into the add a load balancer project turns a two week change into a two month one and can no longer tell which change caused a problem. No auto scaling until you have run with exactly two servers for a month and know what one server can take. No CloudFront until your images and files are actually on S3.
Components: Application Load Balancer (The new stable front door and the thing DNS points at from now on); EC2 Auto Scaling group (min 2, max 2 at first) (Holds the instances so replacement is automatic and identical); Route 53 weighted A/ALIAS records (The gradual traffic move from the old EIP to the ALB); ElastiCache for Redis (or DynamoDB) for session state (Removes the one thing that actually blocks two instances: local session/file state); EFS or S3 for user uploads (The second hidden blocker: files written to local disk)

### Packaging the app so deploys are fast and identical
Sounds like you if you would say: "Deploys take too long and our servers are no longer identical."
The situation: Every deploy takes over 12 minutes, I cannot run production properly on my laptop, and our servers have slowly drifted apart from each other.
The answer: Move each service, one at a time, into ECS on Fargate, keep the same load balancer, and store the packaged images in ECR.
Cost: Fargate costs about 20 to 50% more per CPU hour than equivalent EC2, but usually removes 1 to 2 person weeks a month of server patching. A 1 vCPU, 2GB task running all day is about $36 a month. Fargate Spot cuts that by about 70% for work that can be interrupted.
How far it gets you: Hundreds of services and low thousands of tasks per cluster. Typical range is 10 to 60 servers, 5 to 40 deployable pieces, 500 to 10,000 requests a second.
What breaks first: You run out of private IP addresses. Each task takes its own IP, a /24 subnet holds 251, and a deploy briefly doubles the count. You see it as tasks stuck starting with an error about not being able to attach a network card. Next, anything that lived on the old server and not in the container, like the log shipper or the cron jobs, just stops happening.
Move on when: When deploys are consistently over 10 minutes, or you have had more than two drift incidents in a quarter, or you cannot reproduce a production bug locally, or you are running more than about 8 deployable pieces on shared servers.
Do not add yet: Do not add a service mesh, do not split the monolith while you containerise it, and do not move the database. Package what you already have, unchanged, with the same process, config and ports. Teams that rewrite while containerising cannot answer whether new slowness came from the container or the rewrite, and that question costs weeks. Skip service discovery until you have more than one service that actually needs it.
Components: ECS on Fargate (Runs the containerized service without you owning hosts); The SAME Application Load Balancer, with a second target group (The seam that lets EC2 and Fargate serve the same hostname simultaneously); ECR with immutable tags and a lifecycle policy (Image storage); AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store via task definition secrets (Config that no longer lives in a file baked into the AMI)

### Paying per request instead of per hour, and how to undo it
Sounds like you if you would say: "We pay all day for servers that are busy for an hour."
The situation: Our traffic comes in bursts and sits idle in between, so we pay all day for servers doing nothing. Or we went all in on Lambda and now the bill grows faster than our traffic.
The answer: Move one route to Lambda behind API Gateway, add RDS Proxy if it touches a relational database, and keep the same container image so you can go back.
Cost: A 1 vCPU, 2GB Fargate task at about $36 a month equals roughly 36 million Lambda calls at 128MB and 100ms, or about 300,000 at 1GB and 1 second. A 1GB function running 200ms is about $3.50 per million requests. Above roughly 1.5 to 2 million GB seconds a month on one busy path, containers are cheaper.
How far it gets you: Good under about 200 requests a second per endpoint, or bursty traffic with long quiet gaps. Default limit is 1,000 running at once per region, raisable, with a hard 15 minute timeout and 10GB memory.
What breaks first: Going in, database connections run out, then the cost on your busiest endpoint. With heavy work, a batch job nobody timed hits the 15 minute cutoff. Coming back, nothing breaks technically. What breaks is the belief that the move was reversible, because the code now depends on the Lambda event shape everywhere.
Move on when: To Lambda when average Fargate CPU is under 15% for a month, or a path is called fewer than about 50,000 times a day. Back to containers when one function's monthly run cost exceeds two Fargate tasks, or p99 is over 1 second with over 20% of it startup, or you are paying for warm capacity on more than two functions.
Do not add yet: Do not move everything. Move one route with a clear shape, background, bursty or scheduled, and live with it for a month. Do not adopt Step Functions in the same change. Teams reach for it to dodge the 15 minute limit and end up with business logic split across a state machine nobody can test locally. Do not go event driven at the same time either. You lose your stack traces and your ability to answer what happened to this one request.
Components: AWS Lambda behind API Gateway HTTP API (or a Lambda Function URL) (The new execution path for one route at a time); ALB with a Lambda target group, OR API Gateway stage weighting (The per-route seam for shifting traffic); RDS Proxy (or Data API) if the function touches a relational DB (Stops Lambda concurrency from becoming database connections); Provisioned Concurrency or SnapStart — only where measured (The cold start fix, applied surgically); The return path: the same container image, run as both (The escape hatch that makes the experiment reversible)

### Extra copies of the database for reading
Sounds like you if you would say: "Our database is maxed out on reading and reports are hurting checkout."
The situation: Our database is pegged during business hours, reporting queries slow down checkout, and buying a bigger machine is no longer an option.
The answer: Add Aurora read replicas, send read only queries to them through a feature flag in the app, and check replica lag before trusting a read.
Cost: Each Aurora replica costs the same as the main database, about $210 a month for a db.r6g.large on demand, with no extra storage charge. RDS replicas duplicate storage too. Aurora Serverless v2 replicas drop to about $43 a month when idle.
