How far it gets you: Good when reads outnumber writes by about 5 to 1, at 2,000 to 50,000 reads a second. Aurora allows up to 15 replicas, but reading scales well only to about 5 to 8. It does nothing at all for writes.
What breaks first: You save something, then immediately read it back and get the old value, in the exact paths nobody flagged. It shows up as odd support tickets, not errors. Then connections run out, because each replica has its own limit and the pool settings get copy pasted, so three replicas quietly triples the total.
Move on when: Add replicas when read queries are over 60% of database time and the writer is over 70% busy. Move past this when the writer is still over 70% busy with reads already moved off, or you are at 5 or more replicas, or write speed is your top wait.
Do not add yet: Do not add replicas before you add a cache. One ElastiCache node in front of the 10 hottest read queries often removes 60 to 80% of read load for $15 to $40 a month, against $210 a month per replica, and takes a day. Do not add replicas before you run your five slowest queries through EXPLAIN. A missing index has taken down more databases than a lack of replicas. And do not let a driver or proxy split reads automatically as your first step. The stale read bugs it creates are expensive.
Components: Aurora reader endpoint (or RDS read replica endpoints) (Where read traffic goes); Application-level read/write splitting behind a feature flag (Deciding, per query, which endpoint to use); A lag-aware guard in the routing helper (Automatic fallback to the writer when replicas fall behind); Performance Insights + a slow query baseline, captured BEFORE the change (The way you prove the replicas helped)

### Switching database software without going offline
Sounds like you if you would say: "We have to change databases under a system that cannot go down."
The situation: We need to move off our old database, or do a big version upgrade, and we cannot take an hour of downtime to do it.
The answer: Use RDS Blue/Green for same engine upgrades, or DMS full load plus ongoing change capture for an actual engine change, with a read only comparison harness checking both sides.
Cost: A DMS replication instance, dms.r5.large, is about $180 a month for the 2 to 8 weeks of the move, plus double database cost during overlap. The real cost is people time. A same engine major upgrade is 2 to 6 weeks. An engine change like Oracle to PostgreSQL is 6 to 18 months.
How far it gets you: 50GB to 20TB. Below about 50GB, if you can take a maintenance window, a dump and restore at 3am is genuinely the better call and takes a night instead of a quarter. DMS loads roughly 30 to 100 GB an hour.
What breaks first: Tables with no primary key, which cannot be copied reliably. Then large text or file columns, which get cut off past your configured limit without telling you. Then auto numbering counters that do not carry over and collide on the first write after the switch.
Move on when: You may cut over when change capture lag stays under 5 seconds for 24 hours, the validation task reports zero failed rows, shadow reads match exactly for 7 days, every counter reset step is scripted and rehearsed, and you have tested replicating backwards at least once.
Do not add yet: Do not change the schema, the engine and the application version in the same cutover. Move the data with the schema identical, ugly column names and all, then clean up afterwards. Otherwise when something is wrong you cannot tell which change did it, and your rollback is not really a rollback. Do not switch on new engine features before cutover. And do not delete the old database for at least 30 days.
Components: RDS/Aurora Blue/Green Deployments — for SAME-engine version upgrades (Managed staging copy plus a guarded switchover); AWS DMS full load + CDC — for engine CHANGES and anything blue/green cannot cover (Continuous replication from old engine to new while both are live); AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) + DMS Schema Conversion (Converts DDL and tells you what it cannot convert); A read-only shadow comparison harness (Verifying correctness DURING the move, not after)

### A second copy of everything in another part of the world
Sounds like you if you would say: "We have a contract or regulator that says one region is not enough."
The situation: We have promised a customer we can recover fast from a disaster, or our users on another continent wait too long for every page.
The answer: Run a warm standby in a second region using Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables, with Route 53 recovery controls to switch traffic.
Cost: A warm standby realistically costs 30 to 60% of your main region spend. Active in both regions costs 100 to 130%. Add cross region transfer at $0.02 per GB. The real cost is 3 to 9 months of a team's attention plus a permanent tax on every future change.
How far it gets you: Aurora Global Database allows up to 5 secondary regions. The honest threshold is money, about $50,000 to $100,000 of lost revenue per hour of downtime, or a regulator saying so. Below that, multi AZ plus a tested restore is the better spend.
What breaks first: The things you forgot were tied to one region. Queued messages are stranded, the last few minutes of uploaded files never copied over, the standby's cache is empty so the sudden rush knocks the database over, and permissions nobody ever used show up as access errors under load.
Move on when: You need this when you have a written recovery target under 1 hour that a restore cannot meet, or measured page load over 150ms for a large group of users, or a regulator. You are not ready if you have not restored a backup this quarter, have no runbook for one region, or deploy by hand.
Do not add yet: Do not go multi region until multi AZ is genuinely right and you have proven a restore. A backup nobody restored is not a backup. Far more outages come from a bad deploy, a full disk, an expired certificate or a bad migration than from a region failing, and multi region makes each of those harder to fix. Do not add a global accelerator, a global cache, or calls between regions in this phase. Synchronous cross region calls turn two regions into one system.
Components: Aurora Global Database (single writer) OR DynamoDB Global Tables (multi-active) (The data layer, and the decision that determines everything else); Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing controls (The failover switch, and the thing that makes failover a decision rather than an inference); Pre-provisioned capacity in the standby region (warm, not pilot-light) (Making sure the standby can actually take the traffic); Region-scoped deployment pipeline with a mandatory bake (Preventing your own deploy from being the correlated failure)

### Slicing one big app into parts, slowly
Sounds like you if you would say: "Four teams share one deploy and we are always waiting on each other."
The situation: Every deploy has to be coordinated across teams, one team's change breaks another's, and the merge queue is where work goes to wait.
The answer: Put API Gateway or your existing load balancer in front, move out one capability at a time behind a feature flag, run both sides side by side and compare, and split the database last.
Cost: Infrastructure barely changes. The routing layer adds about $20 to $50 a month. The real cost is duplicated work while both versions exist. Plan for 15 to 25% ongoing drag on capacity, over 12 to 24 months. Anyone promising a quarter has not done one.
How far it gets you: The trigger is team count, above about 4 teams sharing one deploy, not code size. A 30 engineer organisation can hold about one extraction per team in flight, two or three in total.
What breaks first: Shared data that both sides write to, found after the flag reaches 50%. Then operations that used to be one safe database transaction now span two services, so a half finished state appears that your code has never seen. Then speed, because a call that took 0.1ms inside the app now takes 2 to 10ms over the network, and a loop doing 200 of them becomes a 2 second page.
Move on when: Extract the next piece when the old code path is deleted and the new service has run a month without an incident. Stop when the teams that needed independent deploys have them, not when the monolith is gone. A small stable core is a fine end state.
Do not add yet: Do not add Kubernetes, a service mesh, gRPC, event sourcing or a new language in the same programme. Each is a separate multi month learning curve, and together they guarantee that when something is slow nobody can say why. Put new services on the same runtime the monolith already uses. Do not build a shared internal platform before you have three services, because you will build it for a shape you have not learned yet. And do not split the database first.
Components: Amazon API Gateway or the existing ALB as the interception facade (The seam: everything enters here, and this is where a route stops going to the monolith); Branch-by-abstraction inside the monolith (The seam INSIDE the code, for logic that is not reachable as an HTTP route); Shadow / parallel-run comparison (Proving the new service is correct BEFORE it serves anyone); The database boundary: keep it shared, then split it LAST (The decision that determines whether this succeeds); Per-capability ownership and an explicit kill list (Making 'eliminate' actually happen)

### Moving your live system to AWS safely
Sounds like you if you would say: "We have a real system running somewhere else and we need it on AWS without a scary big bang weekend."
The situation: Our app runs somewhere else, like Heroku or our own servers, and we have to move it to AWS. I am scared we will break it all in one weekend.
The answer: Link the old place and AWS with a VPN, copy the servers with AWS Application Migration Service, keep the database copying over with DMS, then shift traffic slowly using DNS.
Cost: You pay for both places for 1 to 3 months. A Site to Site VPN is about 36 dollars a month plus data, and that is enough for most app moves. A serious colo move with Direct Connect starts at 300 dollars a month for a 1Gbps link plus port hours. Shipping a Snowball box is worth it above roughly 10 to 20TB.
How far it gets you: Your link is the limit, not AWS. A 1Gbps link moves about 10TB a day in theory and really 4 to 6TB a day. Above about 50TB, shipping a physical box, about a week door to door, is faster than the wire.
What breaks first: While the app is in the old place and the database is already in AWS, every page feels slow. A 20 to 40ms gap gets multiplied by every small query, so pages crawl. Then your emails start landing in spam from the new addresses. Then a payment partner blocks you because they had your old IP address on an allow list and nobody remembered.
Move on when: Switch over only when a test server has passed a full run through twice, the database copy is caught up and checked, the parity checklist has no unassigned items, and you have practised the rollback, DNS back to zero plus reversing the database copy, at least once end to end.
Do not add yet: Do not redesign anything while moving. Same runtime, same instance sizes rounded up, same single app, same database engine. Teams that also adopt containers, new infrastructure code, a new CI system and microservices at the same time are the ones still migrating two years later. Move as is, be stable for a month, then improve one thing at a time. Also do not switch off the old place on cutover day. Keep it paid and bootable for 30 days.
Components: Site-to-Site VPN (or Direct Connect) between old and new (Makes the two environments one network so a service can move without its callers changing); AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) for lift-and-shift servers (Block-level continuous replication of existing VMs/servers into EC2); DMS or native replication for the database, with the app still on the old provider (Moving the state separately from the compute); DNS with short TTL and weighted records across providers (The gradual traffic shift, provider to provider); A parity checklist built from what the old provider did for you (Catching the invisible services)

### Splitting one AWS account into several
Sounds like you if you would say: "One AWS account holds everything we have and a dev slip can now take down our live system."
The situation: Everything lives in one AWS account. A dev mistake can hit our live system, the permissions are a mess nobody wants to touch, and I cannot tell which team spent what.
The answer: Turn on AWS Organizations with Control Tower, sign in through IAM Identity Center, and start with about four accounts instead of one.
Cost: Organizations, Control Tower basics and IAM Identity Center are effectively free. The cost is the repeated baseline in each account. A NAT Gateway per account per zone is 32 dollars a month each plus 0.045 dollars per GB, which is the line that surprises people, so shared exit networking or VPC endpoints matter.
How far it gets you: You can have a lot of accounts. The real limit is people. Past roughly 20 to 30 accounts, doing anything by hand per account stops working and you need an account factory, shared networking and shared logging already in place. Retrofitting that at 40 accounts is a year of work.
What breaks first: Restores fail. An encrypted database snapshot or file will not open in the new account because the encryption key was not shared in all three needed places, and the error message does not tell you that. Next, things break because account numbers were typed into policies, image addresses and CI settings. Then you hit limits, because a fresh account starts at default caps.
Move on when: Split when a non production action has already hurt production at least once, or you cannot tie more than about 70 percent of spend to a team, or an auditor asks for a boundary. Move the next workload only after the last one ran a month with no permission incidents.
Do not add yet: Do not make an account per service, per environment and per team all at once. Start with three or four: management, security and log archive, production, non production. Adding accounts later is cheap, removing them is not, because each one collects networking, a baseline bill and a place for someone to leave something behind. Do not switch on every optional Control Tower guardrail on day one, the extra checks cost money and make noise nobody reads.
Components: AWS Organizations with Control Tower, and a dedicated Migrations OU (The governance structure, with a low-friction landing zone for in-flight moves); IAM Identity Center with permission sets (How humans get into the new accounts); The keep-it-and-copy move, not the lift-the-account move (The actual mechanics of splitting); Transit Gateway or VPC peering plus centralized egress (Letting the new accounts talk to what is still in the old one); SCPs applied in report-then-enforce order (The guardrails)

### Three containers on ECS Fargate, not Kubernetes
Sounds like you if you would say: "We are a small team with about three services and someone wants to put Kubernetes under them."
The situation: We have a web app, a background worker and an admin tool. Someone on the team says we should run Kubernetes because that is what everyone uses.
The answer: Run the three containers on ECS Fargate behind one Application Load Balancer, with a managed Postgres database.
Cost: About 140 to 600 dollars a month. Roughly 90 to 140 for the containers, 18 plus usage for the load balancer, around 120 for a Multi-AZ database, 33 per zone for NAT. The bigger difference is time: about 2 to 5 engineer hours a month here versus 20 to 60 for a self run EKS setup.
How far it gets you: Good for about 0 to 15 services and roughly 2,000 to 5,000 requests a second, 50 to 200 GB of data, a few million people a month. Containers take 30 to 60 seconds to start, so a sudden traffic spike is served about 90 seconds late unless you keep spare capacity.
What breaks first: Pages get slow at the worst moment even though nothing looks busy. During a deploy, when old and new containers run at the same time, the database runs out of free connection slots and requests start failing. A single slow page can also hog those connections and drag down every other page.
Move on when: Go to EKS only when one of these is really true: you depend on vendor Helm charts or Kubernetes operators you cannot replace, you need GPUs which Fargate does not offer, your interruptible compute bill is over about 5,000 to 10,000 dollars a month, or you have a signed dated plan to run on another cloud or on your own hardware within 24 months.
Do not add yet: No service mesh, no Kafka, no separate database per service, no Argo CD, no extra Terraform abstraction layer, no multi account setup before you have a second team. Building an EKS plus Istio plus Argo plus Prometheus platform for three services takes 3 to 6 engineer months and then 20 to 60 hours a month forever, about 48,000 dollars a year of people time against 876 dollars a year of actual cluster fee.
Components: ECS on Fargate (Runs all three services as ECS services with rolling deploys and circuit-breaker rollback); Application Load Balancer (Single public entry point, path- and host-based routing to the three target groups); RDS PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ) (The single primary datastore for all three services); ECR + GitHub Actions (Build image, push, ecs update-service); CloudWatch Logs + Container Insights (Logs, metrics, alarms)

### One app you can deploy, not forty services
Sounds like you if you would say: "We have not nailed the product yet and I am about to split it into many services."
The situation: We are still figuring out what our product is and we change the data model every month. People keep saying microservices are how you scale.
The answer: Keep one app with clear modules inside it, one Postgres database, a queue and a worker in the same image, and feature flags.
Cost: About 200 to 800 dollars a month. One service, one database, one load balancer. The saving is not the bill, it is that you are not paying for 40 pipelines, 40 dashboards, 40 alarm sets, 40 on call runbooks and 40 schemas.
How far it gets you: Comfortable up to roughly 25 to 50 engineers and a few thousand requests a second. Past that, merge queues jam and a test suite over about 20 minutes starts to hurt.
What breaks first: Shipping gets painful before the app does. CI takes 40 minutes, so people merge in batches, a batched deploy breaks, and rolling back throws away four teams' work at once.
Move on when: Pull out a service when at least two of these are true for that one module: it needs very different scaling like 10x traffic or a GPU, it needs different uptime, it has a compliance boundary, one team owns it fully, and it has had no shared schema change for 3 months. Pull out one at a time, behind the interface you already have.
Do not add yet: No repo per service, no shared library published to a private registry, no API gateway between your own services, no tracing across services that do not exist yet. Splitting too early typically costs a 10 person team 4 to 8 engineering months plus a permanent tax: every feature that touches two services needs two deploys, two reviews and a version negotiation.
Components: One application, modules enforced in code (All domains in one repo and one process, with module boundaries enforced by import rules, not by the network); SQS + a worker process in the same image (Anything slow or retryable moves off the request path); RDS PostgreSQL, single database (One transactional store); Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or a flags table) (Decouple deploy from release, which is the actual benefit teams attribute to microservices)

### Get one region right before adding a second
Sounds like you if you would say: "Someone asked if we are multi region and we have never tested failover in the one region we have."
The situation: A board member or a big prospect asked if we are multi region. We have never actually tested a failover in the one region we already run in.
The answer: Run everything Multi-AZ in one region, use AWS Backup with a restore drill you actually run, and keep Route 53 health checks ready for later.
Cost: One region Multi-AZ costs your baseline plus about 1.6 to 2x on the database part only. Active in two regions is about 2 to 2.3x total infrastructure plus cross region data at around 0.02 dollars per GB. One published enterprise example priced full active active at about 2.16 million dollars a year and said no.
How far it gets you: One region with Multi-AZ already survives losing a datacentre. It covers everything except a whole region going down and hard data residency law. Region wide events are rare, so you are buying back a handful of hours over several years, and only if your failover really works.
What breaks first: With two live regions too early, customer data quietly gets wrong. Both regions take writes, replication falls behind, and the last write wins, so a customer's record is silently destroyed with no alarm. The other symptom is that region B has been broken for six weeks and nobody noticed because no traffic goes there.
Move on when: Go multi region when you have run at least two successful game day zone failures in one region, your last 90 days of uptime already meets your target and only region wide events eat the rest, or a signed contract or data residency law requires it, or one region cannot give you the capacity. Order: cross region backups, then pilot light, then warm standby, then active active.
Do not add yet: Do not build global write routing, cross region service discovery, or your own conflict resolver. A two region active active build for a mid size product usually takes 6 to 12 engineering months, doubles the infrastructure bill and halves deploy speed because everything ships twice. Sort workloads by how critical they are first, most of them only need backup and restore.
Components: Multi-AZ everything in one region (Survive an AZ failure, which is the failure that actually happens); AWS Backup + a scheduled restore drill (Proven recoverability, which is what the question behind 'multi-region' usually means); Route 53 health checks + failover records (pilot light, when you do need it) (The cheap second-region step that comes before active-active)

### Encryption at the load balancer, not a service mesh
Sounds like you if you would say: "We have a handful of services and want encrypted internal traffic and retries without running a mesh."
The situation: We have under twenty services and we want encrypted traffic between them, automatic retries, and a view of what calls what. Somebody said we need Istio.
The answer: Terminate TLS at the load balancer with ACM and security groups, find services with Cloud Map or ECS Service Connect, and put retries and timeouts in your HTTP client, with OpenTelemetry for tracing.
Cost: Almost nothing extra. A mesh instead adds a sidecar next to every pod, about 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB at 1,000 requests a second by Istio's own 1.24 figures, so 100 pods is about 20 vCPU and 6 GB of pure overhead, roughly 500 to 700 dollars a month of Fargate, plus istiod, plus 1 to 3 engineer months to adopt and forever upgrades.
How far it gets you: Fine to roughly 20 to 30 services and low thousands of requests a second. Past that, keeping retry and timeout rules consistent across many teams and languages by code review stops working, and that is the real reason to get a mesh.
What breaks first: With a mesh too early, upgrades bite. A small Istio version bump changes a default, the app container starts before its proxy is ready, and every outgoing call fails for the first 3 to 5 seconds of each pod's life. You get random errors that look like an app bug for a week. Also every hop adds 3 to 10ms, so a 5 hop request is 15 to 50ms slower than you planned.
Move on when: Get a mesh when you pass about 30 services in 3 or more languages, or a rule says every internal call must be encrypted in a way security groups cannot cover, or you need per request canary routing across many services, or you have a platform team that will own upgrades. Pick ambient mode when you do, Istio measures it at about 0.06 vCPU and 12 MB versus 0.20 vCPU and 60 MB for a sidecar.
Do not add yet: No sidecars, no traffic policy custom resources, no mesh wide authorization rules for a handful of services. Adopting Istio at 8 services usually costs 2 to 4 engineering months up front, turns every Kubernetes upgrade into a two system upgrade, and adds a kind of outage, proxy config, that your on call has no feel for.
Components: ALB / ACM with TLS termination, plus VPC security groups (Encryption in transit at the edge and network-level authorisation between services); AWS Cloud Map / ECS Service Connect (Service discovery and basic client-side load balancing); Retries, timeouts and circuit breaking in the HTTP client library (Resilience policy); OpenTelemetry SDK + AWS Distro (ADOT) -> X-Ray or CloudWatch (Distributed tracing)

### Normal database tables with an audit log
Sounds like you if you would say: "We want a proper audit trail without turning the whole system into events."
The situation: We need a history of who changed what. Now we are about to turn every single write in the system into an event with rebuilt views.
The answer: Keep normal tables in RDS Postgres, add an append only audit table filled by a trigger, and publish events with an outbox table to SNS or EventBridge.
Cost: Nothing extra beyond the database you already have. Event sourcing instead usually adds Kafka or Kinesis at about 300 to 1,500 dollars a month for a small cluster or a few shards, plus an event store and projection workers.
How far it gets you: Handles basically any startup write volume. Postgres on a db.m6g.large comfortably does thousands of writes a second with an audit trigger. You outgrow it when one Postgres primary cannot take the write rate, tens of thousands of writes a second, or when replaying history into new views is a real product need.
What breaks first: With event sourcing too early, changing anything gets painful. Six months in you need a different event shape, but old events are already saved and cannot change, so you write and maintain converters forever. And rebuilding a view takes hours, so a bug there means hours of stale data on screen with no way to speed it up.
Move on when: Go to event sourcing when the log itself is the requirement: double entry accounting, regulated trading or clinical records, anywhere a regulator asks you to reconstruct the exact state at a past moment, or where time travel queries are a user feature. Split reads from writes one area at a time, where the two loads really differ by ten times.
Do not add yet: No Kafka, no dedicated event store, no separate read database, no saga orchestrator. Teams that adopt this early usually lose 3 to 6 months building the plumbing, then live with a steady stream of timing bugs that are hard to reproduce and hard to explain to support.
Components: Normal mutable tables in RDS PostgreSQL (Current state, queried directly); Audit table populated by a trigger, or a temporal/history table (The 'who changed what when' that people actually wanted from event sourcing); Transactional outbox table + a poller publishing to SNS/EventBridge (Reliable domain events for the parts of the system that need them); Read replica for heavy reporting queries (The 'Q' of CQRS, when you actually need it)

### A nightly file dump you can query
Sounds like you if you would say: "Our only analytics need is weekly numbers for the founders."
The situation: The founders want some numbers once a week. Someone is trying to sell us a whole data platform for that.
The answer: Dump data nightly into S3 as partitioned Parquet files, query it with Athena using the Glue catalog, and point one BI tool at it.
Cost: About 20 to 150 dollars a month. Storage is 0.023 dollars per GB a month and Athena charges 5 dollars per TB scanned, and partitioned Parquet usually scans 1 to 5 percent of the raw data, so a daily dashboard costs cents. A small Redshift cluster is about 0.33 dollars an hour, roughly 240 a month even idle, and a Kafka plus Glue plus Lake Formation stack easily hits 1,500 to 3,000 a month.
How far it gets you: Comfortable up to a few hundred GB, single digit TB, and dozens of queries at once. Past that, or when analysts want instant slicing, you want a warehouse.
What breaks first: A report that was instant suddenly takes 90 seconds, because the job started writing lots of tiny files. Then someone runs a query over everything and you get a surprise four figure bill.
Move on when: Move to a warehouse like Redshift Serverless, Snowflake or BigQuery when Athena spend passes about 300 to 500 dollars a month, or more than about 10 analysts query at once, or you need dashboards under 5 seconds. Add streaming only when a real decision needs data fresher than your nightly batch.
Do not add yet: No fine grained Lake Formation permissions before more than one team reads the data. No Iceberg or Delta before you need row level updates or time travel. No Glue Studio pipelines, no dbt with 200 models, no Kafka. The classic waste is 4 to 9 engineering months and 1,500 to 3,000 dollars a month of standing infrastructure for a platform whose query log shows under 20 queries a month, all by the person who built it.
Components: S3 with Hive-style partitioning (The storage layer); Athena + Glue Data Catalog (SQL over the files, pay per query); RDS read replica + a scheduled export (Getting the data out of production without touching production); One BI tool pointed at Athena (QuickSight, Metabase) (The consumer — decided before the pipeline is built)

### Let AWS run your database
Sounds like you if you would say: "Running Postgres myself on a server looked cheaper than the managed one."
The situation: I compared managed Postgres with just running it on a server myself. The server looked about half the price, so I was going to run it myself.
The answer: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ, turn on Performance Insights, and let AWS Backup copy backups to another region.
Cost: RDS db.m6g.large Multi-AZ with 200 GB storage is about 300 to 400 dollars a month all in. Doing it yourself on two servers is about 150 to 200, so you save around 150 dollars a month. For that you take on backup scripts, failover tooling, patching and the one 3am incident a year.
How far it gets you: RDS goes from the smallest instance up to 64 vCPU and 512 GB. Most teams hit a write or connection ceiling on a single primary somewhere in the low tens of thousands of writes a second first. Aurora extends this to 15 read replicas and 128 TiB of storage.
What breaks first: You find out your backup was not a backup. The host gets retired or the disk degrades, the standby does not take over because one node was patched and the other was not, and the dump you restore turns out to be 19 hours old and missing part of the schema. Separately, you fall behind on patches because patching means downtime nobody wants to schedule.
Move on when: Run it yourself only when you need an extension or Postgres version RDS does not offer, or a tuning setting RDS locks is measurably costing you, or you are big enough to employ database engineers and the saving is tens of thousands a month. Move from RDS to Aurora when replica lag or storage growth is the real constraint.
Do not add yet: No Patroni, no do it yourself Postgres high availability, no read replicas before you have measured that reads are the problem, no sharding before one primary is actually maxed out. Teams that self manage to save about 150 dollars a month usually spend 2 to 4 engineering weeks setting it up and then carry an open ended on call burden for a saving smaller than one engineer day a month.
Components: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Multi-AZ (The primary database with automated failover); Performance Insights + Enhanced Monitoring (Finding the query that is killing you); RDS Proxy (only when needed) (Connection pooling for Lambda or many short-lived tasks); AWS Backup with cross-region copy (Recovery you have proven)

### Letting a service run your test and deploy steps
Sounds like you if you would say: "We are under 50 engineers and about to build our own deploy system."
The situation: Every time we ship, someone runs the same steps by hand. We want that automated, and a teammate wants to build our own system because our process is special.
The answer: Use GitHub Actions, and let it log in to AWS with a short lived role instead of stored keys.
Cost: Zero to about 150 dollars a month for most small teams. Runners cost 0.006 dollars a minute, with 2,000 free minutes a month on the Free plan and 3,000 on Pro or Team. 20,000 paid minutes is 120 dollars.
How far it gets you: Hundreds of builds a day. A team of 10 engineers usually runs 300 to 1,500 minutes a day, and this stays fine well past 100 engineers.
What breaks first: If you built your own, the person who wrote it leaves. A deploy fails on a Friday, the failure sits inside 400 lines of code nobody understands, so the team stops deploying. Releases pile up and the next incident is bigger. With the hosted service the first pain is slower builds and a rising bill, both of which you can see.
Move on when: When your build minutes cost around 2,000 to 3,000 dollars a month, or builds need hardware the service does not offer, or rules say build files cannot leave your network. Even then, run only the machines yourself, not the whole system.
Do not add yet: No Jenkins, no Spinnaker, no internal developer portal, no custom release tooling, no fancy rollout controller for three services. Building your own is normally 3 to 6 engineer months up front and 10 to 20 percent of one engineer forever, to replace a product that costs 0.006 dollars a minute.
Components: GitHub Actions (or GitLab CI / CodePipeline) (Build, test, push image, deploy); GitHub OIDC -> IAM role (Short-lived AWS credentials for the pipeline); ECR + ECS rolling deploy with circuit breaker (The deploy step itself); Self-hosted runners in a private subnet (only if needed) (Access to private VPC resources, or heavy builds)

### Letting someone else handle logins and passwords
Sounds like you if you would say: "We need users to sign up and log in, and we were about to write that ourselves."
The situation: People need accounts on our app. Someone said it is just a users table with a password column, so we were going to write it ourselves.
The answer: Use a ready made login service like Cognito, Auth0, Clerk or WorkOS, and keep your own code only for who is allowed to do what.
Cost: Cognito gives 10,000 monthly active users free, then 0.015 dollars per user, so 50,000 users is about 600 dollars a month. The cheaper Lite tier is 0.0055 per user for the first 90,000. Company logins cost 0.015 per user above 50 free users.
How far it gets you: Millions of monthly users. Logins will not be the thing that runs out.
What breaks first: With your own login code, password reset goes wrong first. Reset links turn out to be guessable, or reusable, or never expire, and you hear it from a stranger or a customer. Next, changing a password does not actually kick out the old session. The most costly one is a big customer deal stalling for three months because you cannot offer company sign in, which the ready made services turn on with a setting.
Move on when: Only when your identity model is truly unusual, or per user cost beats an engineer's salary at millions of users, or a regulator says passwords may never leave your systems. Even then use a trusted library and never write your own password hashing.
Do not add yet: No custom session store, no home made permission engine before you have more than three roles, no multi customer login layer before the second kind of customer exists, no self hosted Keycloak, which is running your own login system with extra steps. Writing your own takes 2 to 4 months and then a permanent job of tracking every new attack.
Components: Amazon Cognito user pool (or Auth0/Clerk/WorkOS) (Identity store, login, MFA, password reset, token issuance); API Gateway JWT authorizer or an ALB OIDC action (Verifying the token before it reaches your code); Application-side authorization with tenant scoping (What the user is allowed to do, which the IdP does not decide)

### Picking one cloud and staying there
Sounds like you if you would say: "I am worried about being stuck with one cloud provider."
The situation: Our board asked what happens if our cloud provider fails us, so we are thinking of running everything on two clouds at once.
The answer: Run on one cloud using plain containers, Postgres and object storage, and write an exit plan instead of running a second cloud.
Cost: Moving data between clouds costs about 0.05 to 0.09 dollars a gigabyte, so 10 terabytes a month is 500 to 900 dollars of pure waste. Teams doing this add 30 to 50 percent to every infrastructure project and give up six figures a year in volume discounts.
How far it gets you: This has nothing to do with size. One cloud is not the limit for almost anyone.
What breaks first: Your speed, quietly. Every idea now gets the question, and how does that work on the other cloud, so the team always picks the plain option and ends up running its own databases, queues and secret storage that either cloud would have handled. Then the second cloud goes stale because nothing real runs there, so it would not work on the day you needed it.
Move on when: When a signed contract demands it, when a regulator demands two providers, when something you need exists only on the other cloud, or after buying a company that is already there. Then put one workload there, not everything.
Do not add yet: No layer that hides the difference between clouds, no Kubernetes picked only for portability, since moving the scheduler is not moving your data, permissions or network, and no writing every record to both clouds.
Components: One primary cloud, chosen and committed to (Everything runs here); Containers + Postgres + S3-compatible object storage (The portability that is actually cheap to keep); A written exit plan instead of a running second cloud (The deliverable the board actually wants)

### Cutting the mystery network charge on your bill
Sounds like you if you would say: "There is a big line on my AWS bill and I have no idea what it is."
The situation: We followed the standard setup guide and now there is a four figure line on our AWS bill called EC2-Other that nobody can explain.
The answer: Run one NAT gateway and add VPC endpoints, which are private doors to S3, ECR, logs and secrets so that traffic never pays the NAT fee.
Cost: A NAT gateway is 0.045 dollars an hour, about 33 dollars a month, plus 0.045 dollars per gigabyte moved, in both directions. Three of them is about 99 dollars a month standing, and 5 terabytes of traffic adds about 324 dollars. Typical waste is 800 to 2,500 dollars a month, often running a full year before anyone reads the bill.
How far it gets you: One gateway carries up to 100 gigabits a second and about 55,000 open connections per destination. Capacity is rarely the problem, the bill is.
What breaks first: Not speed, connections. One outside service starts failing on and off when you are busy, even though overall traffic looks normal. The more common failure is money, a big bill line nobody owns.
Move on when: Add one gateway per zone once real customer traffic depends on it and losing a zone would mean an outage. Look at other options when the per gigabyte charge alone passes about 2,000 dollars a month.
Do not add yet: No Transit Gateway until you have more than about three networks to join, since it adds about 36 dollars a month per connection plus 0.02 dollars a gigabyte on top of NAT. No central exit network, no third party firewall box, and no NAT in every zone of your test environments.
Components: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (Keep the highest-volume AWS traffic off the NAT entirely); Interface VPC endpoints for ECR (api + dkr), CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, STS (The other chronic NAT consumers); One NAT gateway in one AZ (for dev/staging), three for production (Outbound internet for the traffic that genuinely leaves AWS); VPC Flow Logs into an Athena table (Finding out what is actually going through the NAT)

### Making a slow page fast without adding a cache
Sounds like you if you would say: "My pages feel slow and I am about to bolt a cache onto them."
The situation: One of our pages takes 800 milliseconds to load. Someone said put Redis in front of it.
The answer: Add the missing database indexes first, then CloudFront and normal browser caching headers, and only then one cache that expires on a timer.
Cost: Indexes cost nothing. A small managed cache is realistically 70 to 120 dollars a month, or about 12 dollars a month for a single tiny node, which loses its data if it restarts. CloudFront is 0.085 dollars a gigabyte for the first 10 terabytes. A cache added too early usually costs 70 to 120 dollars a month plus 2 to 4 weeks of work.
How far it gets you: A properly indexed Postgres on a mid size machine answers thousands of simple reads a second in single digit milliseconds. Most we need a cache problems are a missing index.
What breaks first: The cache restarts and every request misses at the same moment. The database was sized for the easy cached load, so it chokes and the whole site goes down. The other failure is a customer seeing old numbers now and then, which you cannot reproduce and take days to trace.
Move on when: When a query you have actually measured and indexed is still too slow, when the same heavy calculation repeats for many users, or when the database is above about 60 percent busy at peak with the queries already tidy.
Do not add yet: No Redis before you have looked at how the database runs your query. No stacking a local cache plus Redis plus a CDN, since each layer multiplies the ways old data sticks around. No cache warming jobs and no caching per user data before you have measured that it matters.
Components: Database indexes and query fixes (The actual fix in most cases); CloudFront in front of the ALB (Cache what is genuinely public and static or near-static); HTTP caching headers and ETags on API responses (Free caching in the client and the CDN); ElastiCache for Redis / Valkey — one cache, TTL-only (The cache you add last, for genuinely expensive computations)

### Keeping your infrastructure files boring and readable
Sounds like you if you would say: "Our infrastructure code is so layered that nobody can read a change any more."
The situation: Changing one server size means editing four files, and nobody can tell me what the change will actually create before we run it.
The answer: Write plain Terraform per environment, copy and paste between them on purpose, and make the plan output a required part of review.
Cost: No direct cost. The cost is time. A one line change often takes half a day to trace, and infrastructure work slips from minutes to days, which is 20 to 40 percent of an engineer forever with nothing on the AWS bill to show it.
How far it gets you: Works well up to about 3 to 5 environments and a few hundred resources in each file. It gets awkward past 5 environments or 20 near identical accounts.
What breaks first: Review stops meaning anything. Someone changes a default buried in a shared piece, and the preview for an unrelated service says it will replace a database. The preview is 900 lines of noise, so it gets approved, and production loses something nobody expected.
Move on when: Share a piece once the same combination shows up a third time and has stayed identical through at least one round of change. Add a DRY generator layer only at 10 or more accounts, when someone's actual job is the platform.
Do not add yet: No internal module library before three things use it, no custom Terraform provider, no policy framework beyond a few basic lint rules, and no full multi account landing zone for a single team product.
Components: Terraform (or CDK/Pulumi) — one state file per environment per blast-radius boundary (The whole infrastructure definition); Copy-paste between environments, deliberately (dev/staging/prod as three explicit directories); Public, well-maintained modules where they exist (VPC, EKS, ALB — the fiddly, standard pieces); Plan output in CI as a required review artifact (The safety mechanism)

===============================================================================
PART 4. THE QUESTIONS TO ASK BEFORE DESIGNING ANYTHING
===============================================================================


1. Who uses this, and from where on the map? Name the actual humans or systems, and the countries they sit in.
   Why it matters: Every latency number, every residency constraint, and the entire question of multi-region vs single-region falls out of this one answer, and it is cheap to answer on day one and ruinous to discover on month nine. A workload for 400 internal staff in one city and a workload for anonymous consumers across three continents share almost no design DNA, even when the feature list is identical. Physics does not negotiate: Mumbai to Virginia is roughly 190-200 ms round trip on a good day, so if the users are in India and the database is in us-east-1, you have already spent your entire latency budget before writing a line of code.
   It decides: Region choice and region count; whether CloudFront sits in front at all (it earns its keep for a globally spread audience mostly through TLS termination and TCP offload at the edge, not caching, which is why it beats serving directly from an ALB even for a fully dynamic API); whether you need Route 53 latency or geolocation routing; whether auth is regional or global; whether you can get away with one VPC.
   Worrying answers: "Everyone, globally" on a product with 50 named pilot customers — that is aspiration leaking into requirements, and it will buy you a multi-region design you cannot operate. "Just us for now" from a founder whose sales deck names three continents — the roadmap and the architecture are already diverging. "Mostly the US, plus a few in Europe" — probe the few: if any of them is a regulated European entity, GDPR has just entered the room and question 6 moves up the list. Silence about internal admin users is common and dangerous; the admin console is very often the surface with the worst latency and the widest blast radius.

2. How many users and how many requests today — actual numbers from a log, not an estimate — and honestly how many in twelve months?
   Why it matters: Almost all premature complexity traces to a number nobody measured. The gap between 50 requests per second and 5,000 is three architectural generations, and the gap between the two numbers a team gives you (today's real figure, and the one in the board deck) tells you how much of the design is being built for a fantasy. Ask for the number from an access log, a Stripe dashboard, or a CRM export. If the system does not exist yet, ask for the number of sales conversations in flight, which is a real number about a real pipeline.
   It decides: Compute shape and the entire stateless-tier decision: single ALB plus two Auto Scaling t3.medium/m7g.large instances carries a well-behaved JSON API to roughly the low thousands of requests per second before anything interesting happens, and a Lambda-per-request design becomes more expensive than always-on Fargate somewhere around 25-40 percent sustained utilisation of an equivalent container. It also determines whether the database is a single Multi-AZ RDS instance, an instance plus read replicas, or a sharded or Aurora Limitless design (which you almost certainly do not need).
   Worrying answers: "We need to handle a million users" with no current users — this is the single most expensive sentence in small-team architecture; it buys Kubernetes, a service mesh, Kafka and a six-month runway burn to serve 200 people. "We don't know" when the system is already live — the logs exist and nobody has looked, which tells you observability is absent and question 11 just got worse. A twelve-month number more than 100x today's without a named distribution channel is a fantasy; a number less than 3x is usually honest and should be believed. Also watch for users counted instead of requests: 10,000 registered users might be 3 requests per second or 3,000, depending entirely on question 3.

3. What shape is the traffic — flat, diurnal, or spiky — and is any spike predictable? Show me a week of requests per minute.
   Why it matters: Peak-to-average ratio is the number that decides whether you buy capacity or rent it. A flat workload at ratio 1.5:1 should be on Savings Plans or Reserved Instances and can be sized once. A workload that sits at 20 requests per second and hits 4,000 for ninety seconds when a marketing email goes out is a completely different animal, and the ninety seconds is where it will break. Predictability matters as much as amplitude: a predictable spike can be pre-warmed on a schedule, which is trivially cheap; an unpredictable one has to be absorbed by a queue, a cache, or shed deliberately. Scale-out is never instant — EC2 Auto Scaling realistically takes 2-5 minutes to place and health-check a new instance, and Lambda concurrency scales in bursts (1,000 immediately in most regions, then +1,000 per 10 seconds), so any spike that arrives faster than that must be absorbed, not scaled into.
   It decides: Whether writes go through an SQS queue and a worker fleet rather than straight to the database (the queue turns a 4,000/s spike into a 200/s sustained drain and is the single highest-leverage piece of small-team architecture); whether you use scheduled scaling ahead of a known event; whether Fargate or Lambda beats EC2 on cost; whether you need a provisioned-concurrency floor; and whether request-level load shedding with a 429 is part of the design rather than an afterthought.
   Worrying answers: "It's pretty steady" from someone who has only looked at a daily or monthly graph — minute-level resolution regularly reveals a 30x peak that hourly averaging erased entirely. "We'll just autoscale" — this is a statement of faith, not a design; it ignores the 2-5 minute lag and, far more often, ignores that the database does not autoscale with the web tier, so scaling out simply moves the failure into RDS. "We send a push notification to all users at once" delivered casually — that is a self-inflicted thundering herd and it needs jitter at the source before it needs any infrastructure at all.

4. What does one hour of this being down cost, in money? Not in adjectives — in rupees or dollars.
   Why it matters: This is the question that converts an argument about architecture into an arithmetic problem. Multi-AZ RDS roughly doubles the database bill; a warm standby in a second region roughly doubles everything. Those are justifiable if an hour of downtime costs 400,000 rupees and unjustifiable if it costs 4,000. Without this number, availability decisions are made by whoever is most anxious in the room, which is how small teams end up with active-active multi-region designs protecting a workload whose users would not notice a two-hour outage on a Sunday. The number also has a shape: downtime at 3am on a Tuesday and downtime during the Friday billing run are not the same event, and the architecture should protect the expensive window.
   It decides: The target availability tier, and therefore: single-AZ vs Multi-AZ RDS; one Availability Zone vs three; whether you keep a pilot-light or warm standby in a second region or simply restore from backup; whether deployments are rolling or blue/green; whether you buy an AWS Business Support plan (roughly the greater of 100 dollars a month or 10 percent of spend, and worth it the first time you need a 1-hour-response case on a production outage).
   Worrying answers: "We haven't thought about it" is the real finding, and it should stop the conversation. It means nobody has asked the business what this system is worth, which means every subsequent availability decision will be a guess wearing a number. Do not move on: make them estimate on the spot, badly, out loud — revenue per hour, staff idled, contractual penalty, churned customers. A bad number beats no number because it can be argued with. "It can never go down" is the other bad answer and it means the same thing: no one has priced it. Push back with the real cost of the next nine and watch the requirement soften. Also treat "our SLA says 99.9%" as unverified until you see whether anything is actually owed on breach — an SLA with no penalty is marketing, not a constraint.

5. What does losing one hour of data cost? And is there any data where losing five minutes is unacceptable?
   Why it matters: RTO and RPO are different questions and teams reliably conflate them. A system can be down for four hours with no lasting harm and still be destroyed by losing four minutes of financial transactions. RPO is usually not uniform across the data: the ledger, the audit trail and the uploaded documents have a different tolerance from the session cache and the derived analytics table. Sorting data by RPO before designing storage is what stops you paying for the strictest tier across everything.
   It decides: Backup and replication design: whether RDS automated backups (daily snapshot plus transaction logs, giving roughly 5-minute point-in-time recovery within the retention window, up to 35 days) are sufficient, or whether you need cross-region automated backup replication, an Aurora global database with sub-second typical replica lag, or synchronous write confirmation to a second store. It also determines S3 versioning and Object Lock, DynamoDB point-in-time recovery, and whether deletes in the application are soft.
   Worrying answers: "We have backups" — a backup nobody has restored is not a backup. Ask when the last restore test ran and how long it took; if the honest answer is never, the real RPO is unknown and the real RTO is unbounded. "Everything is in the database, it's fine" — ask about the S3 bucket of user uploads, which very often has no versioning and no lifecycle policy and is the thing that actually cannot be reconstructed. "Zero data loss" for a workload with a 500-rupee-per-hour downtime cost is an unpriced demand; synchronous cross-region durability costs latency on every single write, and the team should be made to feel that cost before agreeing to it.

6. Is any of this data regulated, and under which specific regime? Personal data, health data, cardholder data, financial records — and whose law applies?
   Why it matters: Regulation is a constraint, not a feature, which means it cannot be retrofitted cheaply and it silently invalidates otherwise good designs. India's DPDP Act, GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS each impose different and sometimes contradictory obligations — data residency, breach notification windows, the right to erasure, retention minimums that directly conflict with erasure, and audit trails that must themselves be tamper-evident. The right to erasure is the one that most often breaks an architecture built without it: it means personal data cannot live in an append-only event log, an unversioned analytics warehouse and four denormalised caches unless you have a way to reach all of them.
   It decides: Region selection becomes a hard constraint rather than a latency optimisation; encryption at rest and in transit stops being optional; KMS customer-managed keys vs AWS-managed keys; whether logs can contain request bodies at all; VPC endpoints instead of NAT for service traffic; how tenancy is enforced (row-level security forced at the database, not filtering in application code); data retention lifecycle rules; and whether a third-party subprocessor can be used for anything.
   Worrying answers: "It's just email addresses and names" — that is personal data under both GDPR and DPDP and the obligations attach immediately. "We'll get compliant later" — later means re-architecting storage, rewriting the logging layer and re-signing every customer contract. "Our customers haven't asked" — enterprise procurement will ask, in a security questionnaire, at the exact moment a deal is closing. And be alert to the inverse failure: a team asserting HIPAA or PCI scope that they are not actually in, which buys enormous cost for nothing. Make them name the specific regime and the specific data element that triggers it.

7. Is there a hard latency requirement, and for which operation specifically? Name the endpoint and the percentile.
   Why it matters: "It must be fast" is not a requirement. "The search endpoint must return in under 300 ms at p99 for users in India" is a requirement, and it is testable. Percentile matters more than the number: a p50 target is nearly free, a p99 target constrains your garbage collector, your connection pool and your cold starts, and a p99.9 target constrains your retry policy and your dependency graph. Almost always only one or two operations have a genuine latency requirement — the checkout, the autocomplete, the login — and everything else can be slow without anyone caring. Finding the one or two is what lets you spend effort precisely.
   It decides: Whether a cache tier exists at all and where (ElastiCache/Valkey in front of the database only beats a well-indexed query when the working set is hot and the query is genuinely expensive — a Postgres primary-key lookup on a warm buffer cache is already sub-millisecond, so a cache in front of it adds a network hop and a cache-invalidation bug for no gain); whether Lambda is disqualified by cold starts on that path (typically 200 ms to well over 1 s for a JVM or heavy Python function, which SnapStart or provisioned concurrency mitigates at a cost); whether the database must be in the same AZ as the compute; whether synchronous calls become asynchronous.
   Worrying answers: "As fast as possible" — no budget, so no design. "Under 100 ms" for users on the other side of the planet — physically impossible without edge compute, and the person saying it has not done the round-trip arithmetic. "We measure average response time" — averages hide exactly the tail that users experience and that pages the on-call; ask for p99 and if the tooling cannot produce it, that is a finding about observability, not latency. Be suspicious of a latency requirement attached to a batch or reporting endpoint; it is usually a UI problem that should be solved with an async job and a progress indicator rather than with infrastructure.

8. What is the read-to-write ratio, and is a read allowed to be a few seconds stale?
   Why it matters: This is the question that decides whether scaling is easy or hard. A 100:1 read-heavy workload is a solved problem — cache it, replicate it, put it behind a CDN, and it scales almost indefinitely on commodity parts. A write-heavy or write-contended workload cannot be scaled by adding replicas at all, because every replica makes the write path more expensive, and it pushes you towards partitioning, queueing or a different data store entirely. The staleness half of the question is what unlocks the cheap solutions: if a read may be 5 seconds old, read replicas and caches are available to you; if every read must observe the immediately preceding write, they are not, and a replica will produce bugs that surface once a month and take a week to diagnose.
   It decides: Whether you add RDS read replicas (and whether the application has a routing layer capable of using them, which most do not until someone builds it); whether CloudFront or ElastiCache carries the read load; whether writes need a queue; whether DynamoDB's single-digit-millisecond reads and predictable partition behaviour beat relational, and whether you can live with eventually consistent reads at half the cost of strongly consistent ones.
   Worrying answers: "Roughly even" — usually wrong, and usually means nobody has instrumented it; real CRUD applications are frequently 20:1 or 50:1 read-heavy and the team is leaving free scaling on the table. "Everything must be immediately consistent" asserted without a case — ask for the specific operation where a 2-second-stale read causes a real problem. Often it is exactly one flow (read-after-write on the user's own profile, or a balance check before a payment) and that one flow can be pinned to the primary while everything else reads from replicas. "We'll just scale the database" — vertical scaling ends, and it ends abruptly; note that a db.t3.medium (4 GiB) allows only about 450 Postgres connections under the default LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392},5000) formula, and an unpooled application will exhaust that long before CPU becomes the limit.

9. How big does the data get, how fast does it grow, and what fraction of it is ever read after thirty days?
   Why it matters: Data volume determines storage cost, backup duration, restore duration and — the one people forget — the feasibility of schema migrations. A table with 50 million rows can be altered in a maintenance window; the same alter on 5 billion rows is a project. Growth rate matters more than current size, because it tells you when you hit the wall, and the shape of access over age tells you whether the wall is avoidable: most operational data is written once, read hard for a week and then never touched again, which means the expensive hot store only ever needs to hold a small slice of it.
   It decides: Storage class and tiering (S3 Intelligent-Tiering vs explicit lifecycle rules to Standard-IA and Glacier); whether you partition tables by time and detach old partitions; whether cold data moves to S3 and is queried with Athena rather than living in RDS storage that you pay for at roughly ten times the price; the provisioned IOPS decision (gp3 gives a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s baseline free of provisioning, which covers far more workloads than people assume, and io2 is usually a symptom of a missing index rather than a genuine IO requirement); and the realistic restore time, because restoring a 4 TB snapshot is not a 5-minute operation.
   Worrying answers: "It's not much" with no figure — get GB and GB per month. "We keep everything forever" — that is a cost curve with no ceiling and, if question 6 turned up a regulated regime, it may also be a compliance violation, since retention minimums are not retention permissions. "We'll archive it later" — later never arrives, and the lifecycle rule costs ten minutes to write today. Watch for logs and uploaded files being excluded from the estimate; they are routinely larger than the application database and growing faster.

10. Who gets woken at 3am when this breaks, and what do they actually know?
   Why it matters: An architecture is not a diagram, it is a thing that has to be operated by a specific tired human at a specific bad hour. A design that exceeds the operational capability of the people who will hold the pager is a design that will fail in production regardless of its technical merit. This is the single most common reason elegant architectures collapse at small companies: a five-person team with no Kubernetes experience inherits an EKS cluster from a contractor, and the first time a node group fails to roll, nobody can diagnose it. The honest version of this question is less about seniority than about specifics: has this person ever restored a database, read a CloudWatch Logs Insights query, or interpreted a 5xx spike on an ALB target group?
   It decides: The managed-versus-self-managed line across the whole stack, which is the biggest single cost-and-risk lever available: RDS over self-managed Postgres on EC2, Fargate or ECS over EKS, SQS over self-hosted RabbitMQ, ALB over nginx you maintain. It also determines how much of the budget goes to observability rather than compute, whether runbooks are a deliverable in the same sprint as the feature, and whether the design can contain any component that requires deep expertise to recover.
   Worrying answers: "We'll figure it out" — there is no on-call, which means the real RTO is "whenever someone notices," which contradicts whatever was answered at question 4. Go back and reconcile the two. "The developer who built it" — a single point of failure that takes holidays and resigns; ask what happens in the week after they leave. "We have alerts" — ask what fired last month and what was done about it; if the answer is that alerts fire constantly and are ignored, there is no monitoring, only noise, and adding more will not help. And if nobody on the team has ever performed a restore, the backup strategy is unproven and question 5's answer is fiction.

11. What is the actual monthly infrastructure budget — the number someone has already agreed to pay — and what is the ceiling before it needs a new approval?
   Why it matters: Budget is a design constraint of exactly the same kind as latency, and treating it as a footnote is how teams produce architectures that get cancelled in month three. The number must be the approved one, not the aspirational one, and it must include the things people forget: NAT Gateway (roughly 32-45 dollars a month per gateway before data-processing charges, and three gateways for three-AZ high availability is over 100 dollars before a single byte moves), cross-AZ data transfer, CloudWatch Logs ingestion (which regularly becomes a top-three line item on a chatty application), and support plan. Knowing the ceiling matters as much as knowing the number, because it tells you where the design must degrade gracefully rather than fail an approval.
   It decides: Nearly everything about the first version: single NAT gateway with the accepted AZ risk versus one per AZ; whether non-production environments run at all outside business hours; Graviton instance families as the default (typically 20 percent better price-performance for the same workload, and essentially free to adopt for interpreted languages); Fargate Spot for workers; log retention set to 14 or 30 days rather than never expiring; and whether Savings Plans are bought at all, which requires question 3's answer about how flat the load is.
   Worrying answers: "Cost is not a concern" — it becomes one, abruptly, usually at the first finance review, and the architecture will then be cut under pressure rather than designed to a number. "As cheap as possible" paired with a 99.99 percent availability answer at question 4 — those two are incompatible and the contradiction must be surfaced now rather than discovered later. "We have credits" — credits expire, and an architecture calibrated to free capacity becomes unaffordable on the day it converts to a real bill; ask what the post-credit run rate is. No AWS Budgets alarm configured is itself the finding: without one, the first signal of a cost problem is an invoice.

12. How fast must the first version be in front of real users, and what specifically must it do on that date?
   Why it matters: Time is the constraint that determines how much architecture you are permitted to have. A six-week deadline forbids anything the team has to learn first; a six-month runway permits one, at most one, significant new technology. This question also separates the deadline from the scope: a date that cannot move with a scope that cannot move is not a plan, and forcing that conversation early is more valuable than any technical decision you will make. The right posture is to ask what must be true on launch day for the launch to count, and to design exactly that, plus the seams that let the rest arrive later.
   It decides: How much is managed versus built; whether infrastructure is CDK/CloudFormation from day one (it should be — the cost is a few days and the alternative is an environment nobody can reproduce) versus hand-built; whether the first version is a monolith behind one ALB with one database, which for almost every small team it should be; and which parts get a deliberate seam — an interface, a queue boundary, a separate schema — so they can be pulled out later without a rewrite.
   Worrying answers: "Yesterday" — means scope has not been negotiated and quality will be the silent variable that absorbs the pressure. "No fixed date" — surprisingly dangerous, because a project with no date accretes architecture indefinitely and ships nothing; ask what event or customer the launch is tied to. "Three months, and we're also going to move to microservices" — the deadline and the migration are competing for the same weeks and one of them is going to lose; say so now. And any answer that assumes no time for testing, deployment pipelines or monitoring is really an answer about what will be missing on launch day.

13. How many engineers will build and own this, and what do they already know well enough to debug under pressure?
   Why it matters: Team size sets the maximum number of moving parts the system may have, and existing skill sets the shortest path to a working system. A three-person team can genuinely operate one application, one database, one queue and one cache. It cannot operate eleven services, a service mesh and a streaming platform, no matter how correct that design is in the abstract — the arithmetic of who is awake and who has context does not work. Existing knowledge is worth more than theoretical fit: a team fluent in Postgres will build a better system on RDS Postgres than on a document store that is a marginally better shape for the data, because they will index it correctly, read the query plans, and know what a lock wait looks like.
   It decides: The number of deployable units (the honest default for a team under about eight engineers is one); the language and runtime; whether to adopt Kubernetes at all (below roughly 15-20 engineers and a handful of services, ECS on Fargate delivers most of the benefit with a fraction of the operational surface); whether infrastructure-as-code is CDK in the team's own language or Terraform; and how much of the design budget must be spent on documentation and runbooks because the knowledge is concentrated in one head.
   Worrying answers: "We'll hire" — design for the team you have, because hiring takes months and the new people will inherit whatever you built before they arrived. "Everyone is full-stack" — often means nobody owns the database, which is where the incidents will come from. "We want to use this project to learn X" — a legitimate desire and a terrible reason to put X on the critical path of a production system with a deadline; find a lower-stakes place to learn it. Also note when the answer names a contractor or agency: the person building it and the person who will operate it are different people, and question 10 is the one that matters, not this one.

14. If this fails commercially in twelve months, what happens to it — and if it succeeds beyond plan, what is the first thing that breaks?
   Why it matters: Both branches inform the design and both are routinely skipped. The failure branch asks how much unamortised commitment you are willing to make: three-year Reserved Instances, a proprietary managed service with no export path, a data model that only one vendor can read. The success branch is a forcing function for honesty — asking the team to name the first component that breaks at 10x is the fastest way to find out whether they understand their own system. If nobody can name it, nobody has thought about capacity, and the real answer is that it will be the database, because it almost always is.
   It decides: Commitment depth (on-demand and Savings Plans with a one-year term rather than three-year RIs when the future is uncertain); portability decisions (Postgres over a proprietary dialect, containers over a vendor-specific runtime, S3-compatible access patterns) — noting that portability has a real cost and is only worth buying where the exit risk is real; data export tooling built in from the start; and which single scaling seam gets designed now (usually: the write path can be moved behind a queue, or the read path can be moved to replicas) even though it is not built now.
   Worrying answers: "It won't fail" — everyone says this, and the architectures that survive are the ones built by people who nevertheless answered the question. "We'd just shut it down" without knowing what the contractual data-return obligations are, especially if question 6 found a regulated regime — customers may have a legal right to their data in a usable form, and that is a feature, built in advance. On the success side, "we'd add more servers" is the answer of someone who has not identified the stateful bottleneck; press until they name the component and the number at which it goes, and if they cannot, that measurement is the first piece of work.

15. Now say it back: given all of the above, what is the smallest system that satisfies every stated constraint — and what did we deliberately leave out, and what would adding it have cost?
   Why it matters: This is the step that converts fourteen answers into a design, and it is the step that prevents premature complexity, which is the most expensive mistake small teams make. The deliverable is two lists of equal weight: what is being built, and what is explicitly not being built yet, each exclusion paired with the trigger that would change the decision. An exclusion without a trigger is procrastination; an exclusion with a trigger is architecture. Writing this down also makes the next architect's job possible, because they inherit the reasoning and not just the result.
   It decides: The actual build list, and — equally — the documented not-yet list with its triggers. Typical entries for a small team: no Kubernetes until there are more than about ten independently deployed services or a dedicated platform person (EKS is roughly 73 dollars a month for the control plane before a single node, and the real cost is the weeks of learning and the 3am unknowns); no microservices until team ownership boundaries genuinely conflict inside one repository (the distributed monolith costs you network failures between things that used to be function calls, and distributed transactions you did not have); no multi-region until question 4 produced a downtime cost that justifies roughly doubling the bill and permanently doubling the operational surface; no Kafka until SQS or Kinesis demonstrably cannot carry the ordering or replay requirement (MSK starts in the hundreds of dollars a month and requires someone who understands partitions, consumer groups and rebalancing at 3am); no service mesh below roughly 20 services; no separate caching tier until a specific measured query proves it is needed; no custom autoscaling logic until target-tracking has been observed to fail.
   Worrying answers: A design that contains a component nobody can trace back to a specific answer above is a design containing someone's resume. A not-yet list that is empty means the exercise was not done. And an answer that claims all fifteen constraints are satisfiable simultaneously deserves one more pass: usually budget and availability, or deadline and scope, are in genuine conflict, and the architect's job at this point is to name the conflict precisely and hand the trade-off back to whoever owns the money — not to quietly resolve it with optimism.
